body:
> Any use case in mind?

Sometimes I wish to attach a temporary piece of context information to a net_buf when passing them between threads via FIFO's (add the context before `net_buf_put` remove after `net_buf_get`).
Context information can be added in 3 places:
1. In the user_data parameter
2. Before the main data (after reserving headroom)
3. After the main data

I have already increased the user_data size and do not wish to increase it further to accommodate occasional requirements.
I already have a defined use for the headroom and don't want to add a secondary use.
Sometimes it just seems cleaner to append temporary information than to prepend it.

I couldn't see a reason why we shouldn't have the option to remove data from the end as well as the front.

body:
I think this is what's happening: according to rfc7668, 6lowpan over BLE does not need solicited node frames, and neighbor discovery [happens with NS messages](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7668#section-3.2.3) with Address Registration Option (described in [rfc6775](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6775#page-15)), which supposedly keeps the neighbor cache hot on the border router:

>    Registration:
      The process during which a LoWPAN node sends a Neighbor
      Solicitation message with an Address Registration Option to a
      router creating a Neighbor Cache Entry (NCE) for the LoWPAN node
      with a specific timeout.  Thus, for 6LoWPAN routers, the Neighbor
      Cache doesn't behave like a cache.  Instead, it behaves as a
      registry of all the host addresses that are attached to the
      router.

Now the problem is that there's no implementation for this in the zephyr ipv6 stack as far as I can tell, and it seems like ARO is not supported in Linux either (that would have to be defined [here as option 33](https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/latest/source/include/net/ndisc.h#L42)).

So since the node does not send NS ARO messages, Linux tries to do normal host initiated neighbor discovery, which fails because the node stack is discarding those frames.

rfc7668 also states that link local addresses do not have to be registered

> A Bluetooth LE 6LN MUST NOT register its link-local address.

so I don't quite get the full story of how link-local address are supposed to be resolved.

Either way, this does not work with the current code base without address registration plus solicited node filtering, and I think that even if we had address registration, it would not work without explicit handling in Linux.

@jukkar: would it make sense to remove NET_L2_MULTICAST_SKIP_JOIN_SOLICIT_NODE from the 6lowpan bluetooth stack as a workaround until rfc6775 is fully implemented? I'll update the PR with that in the meantime, just in case someone else wants to test it.

body:
Very interesting PR! this is something that was clearly missing...

 It would be interesting  to split the rpmsg-service.c into 2 separate files
- rpmsg-service.c:
  - rpmsg_init_vdev
  - services related to the rpmsg endpoint 
  - IPM callback and process
- rpmsg_backend.c ( or another name):
  - metal initialization 
  - vrings initialization
  - IPM initilaization
  
The reason of this suggestion is that there are 2 different topologies  supported in Zephyr.
- Zephyr <-> Zephyr
  This is the topology you implement. 
- Linux <-> Zephyr 
  The zephyr is running on a co-processor and Linux on an application processor. The vrings for the  inter-processor communication are defined  in a shared table named resource table, and initialized by the Linux.
  A sample is available here:
  https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/master/samples/subsys/ipc/openamp_rsc_table/src/main_remote.c
 
Splitting code in 2 files would allow to extend your dev in a next step to support the second topology and potentially new ones.

Hi @JordanYates, thank you for the present PR.

As commented in issue #31073 the use of this PR will generate problems when the flash layout is different from application + storage. The storage would always need to be removed from the application.

author: Laczen

body:
> As commented in issue #31073 the use of this PR will generate problems when the flash layout is different from application + storage. The storage would always need to be removed from the application.

The conditions that 'could' cause a problem are the following:
1. The board uses the `.bin` file for flashing
2. Multiple `linker-region` properties are defined
3. Variables are instantiated in the second (or later) `linker-region` partitions.

Under these conditions, the `.bin` will generate padding bytes through the first partitions. This will overwrite any data in these partitions when flashed, which may or may not be a problem.

My position is that this is a limitation of the `.bin` data format. Because this functionality is adding the ability to modify the linker, it will always be possible to break things if the user doesn't know what they are doing. IMO 'user beware'.

> Next the absolute addressing is only valid if only one variable is declared in the section, for multiple variables in a section this is not the case.

This is only tangentially related to this PR, which adds the memory region functionality but says nothing about how the sections are defined. There are multiple ways of using this:
* The single variable could be a struct
* The variables could all be of the same type, allowing iteration
* As many linker sections could be defined within the memory region as you have variables

> To allow for variables to be instantiated in a partition at a fixed address a approach of defines could be used that instantiate the variable at a certain location and create a pointer to it without adding sections to the linker.

Please provide a minimal snippet of C code which instantiates a `uint32_t` at some fixed memory address at compile time.
As far as I am aware this is impossible without the use of memory regions.

body:
> A limitation that I spot in the current implementation is that all the flash area beyond the storage_partition (or, rather, the first partition with the linker-region property) cannot be used by the Zephyr for the application image. This is problematic for all the boards that define the storage partition right after the boot partition. There has to be found a way to by pass this limitation (alternatively all the boards that not define storage_partition at the end will need to re-adjust their existing flash layout)

Without changes to this PR, the resolution is simply to not put `linker-region` on those storage partitions that exist at the start of ROM. #27471 is not a problem for those boards currently as they must be manually setting `CONFIG_FLASH_LOAD_OFFSET` to work. Therefore it is already impossible for the partition to be overrun.

The special cases/behavior are starting to pile up however, and the solution no longer seems as clean as it did originally.
Having considered this problem in the light of your PR, I believe the core problem is the implicit behavior of the FLASH region when building standalone applications. Because the user is not explicitly saying where the code should live, we are left to make assumptions (currently "use it all!"), which will always be incorrect in odd cases. IMO the only watertight solution is to force the user to make this information explicit in some way. Once the FLASH region is using a defined memory space, my desired functionality can be implemented entirely by the linker snippet system.

Your `single-image` partition is one method of doing this. An alternative that wouldn't require touching existing board files would be to define FLASH as the total space occupied by `boot_partition`,`slot0_partition`,`slot1_partition` and `scratch_partition`, with the caveat that they couldn't have other partitions inserted between them.

body:
> > A limitation that I spot in the current implementation is that all the flash area beyond the storage_partition (or, rather, the first partition with the linker-region property) cannot be used by the Zephyr for the application image. This is problematic for all the boards that define the storage partition right after the boot partition. There has to be found a way to by pass this limitation (alternatively all the boards that not define storage_partition at the end will need to re-adjust their existing flash layout)
> 
> Without changes to this PR, the resolution is simply to not put `linker-region` on those storage partitions that exist at the start of ROM.

I believe, this is not ideal, it breaks uniformity across storage partition definitions in the various boards. I would not recommend this way forward; we should be trying to introduce common rules and conventions across definitions.

> #27471 is not a problem for those boards currently as they must be manually setting `CONFIG_FLASH_LOAD_OFFSET` to work. Therefore it is already impossible for the partition to be overrun.

Unfortunately, this does not always hold - I am sure many they are not (so we're just lucky the samples and tests they run fit in the area preceding the storage partition, or the storage partition is not used in in-tree samples).

> 
> The special cases/behavior are starting to pile up however, and the solution no longer seems as clean as it did originally.
> Having considered this problem in the light of your PR, I believe the core problem is the implicit behavior of the FLASH region when building standalone applications. Because the user is not explicitly saying where the code should live, we are left to make assumptions (currently "use it all!"), which will always be incorrect in odd cases.

>  IMO the only watertight solution is to force the user to make this information explicit in some way. Once the FLASH region is using a defined memory space, my desired functionality can be implemented entirely by the linker snippet system.

Agreed. And that's why I said initially that #31077 is rather a complement for #29794, not an alternative. We need to make it explicit which area can be used by the image code in **all** cases - not only when we build with boot loader.
 
> Your `single-image` partition is one method of doing this.

The implementation #29794, although it does do the job, as you point out, it is not accepted by @galak @mbolivar-nordic, so we have to look for an alternative.

> An alternative that wouldn't require touching existing board files would be to define FLASH as the total space occupied by `boot_partition`,`slot0_partition`,`slot1_partition` and `scratch_partition`, with the caveat that they couldn't have other partitions inserted between them.

So you suggest to "do some math" at Kconfig and/or linker stage :) It could theoretically be an alternative. I don't get why this would be a better solution, though. 

 To clarify, my "problem" here is that **the logic to decide where to place and how to size the code partition (and other partitions) is split in 3 Zephyr main "components"**:
- DeviceTree: where partitions are initially described, in the boards's dts files,
- Kconfig: where chosen symbols become enabled, based on Kconfig input **not** available to DT (IS BOOTLOADER, IS chain-loadable image, etc.) and other Kconfig symbols are initialized (e.g. FLASH_LOAD_OFFSET/SIZE, ROM_START_OFFSET, etc.)
- Linker script (where logic is used to further manipulate regions an entries, based, again on DT and/or Kconfig input). Your #31077 is actually injecting additional logic at the linker.)

IMHO this is far from ideal. The solution is hard to follow and developers have a hard time to learn what is going on.

My attempt in #29794 was to move as much as we can at the DeviceTree stage, basically, "doing all the math we need" at DeviceTree partition layout descriptions, and then let Kconfig select the right layouts/partitions and initialize the proper symbols, so the Linker would not have to do anything (just accept the incoming configuration without further "internal" logic to derive region boundaries)

If we keep doing "partitioning" calculations at Kconfig/Linker stage, I would argue: why do we, then, need to define partitions in DeviceTree, at all? At Kconfig stage we already know the flash size and start address, so we could even do all the partition layout calculationss there, and remove all stuff from DeviceTree.
author: ioannisg

body:
> It could theoretically be an alternative. I don't get why this would be a better solution, though.

It's not a better long term solution, but I think it would be a less invasive short term one. It doesn't change the current split of information across across devicetree/kconfig/linker, so it doesn't solve your problem, but it does make the error condition in #27471 impossible. Potentially that makes it a more acceptable solution given the `dev-review` comments around post-LTS.

The behavior change would be:
* For applications that don't specify `FLASH_LOAD_OFFSET`, the linker script finds the lowest address from the listed partitions to use
* For applications that don't specify `FLASH_LOAD_SIZE`, the linker script finds the highest address from the listed partitions and subtracts the value from the first step.

The main advantage is that user `.dts` files would not need to change in most cases.

> If we keep doing "partitioning" calculations at Kconfig/Linker stage, I would argue: why do we, then, need to define partitions in DeviceTree, at all? At Kconfig stage we already know the flash size and start address, so we could even do all the partition layout calculationss there, and remove all stuff from DeviceTree.

I think the primary motivating reason is the `flash_map` API. When the partitions are in devicetree, you can iterate over the compatible using the C macros to instantiate each partition as a `flash_area`. This functionality is lost if partitions are defined in Kconfig.

body:
> I meant if you generated for every partition regardless of `linker-region` being set. I'm trying to see if we can remove the property, have the generation always occur, and its just based on use/application that a given region ends up coming into play with the linker.

So this works, even with overlapping memory regions, as long as you don't have multiple variables attempting to be placed at the same address. For example:
```
    FLASH                 (rx) : ORIGIN = ROM_ADDR, LENGTH = ROM_SIZE
    BOOTLOADER            (rx) : ORIGIN = 0K, LENGTH = 10K
    IMAGE_0               (rx) : ORIGIN = 10K, LENGTH = 100K
    IMAGE_1               (rx) : ORIGIN = 110K, LENGTH = 100K
    IMAGE_SWAP            (rx) : ORIGIN = 210K, LENGTH = 10K
```
Trying to place a variable in BOOTLOADER results in an error (overlaps with the application in FLASH)
While placing the variable in IMAGE_SWAP works, even though it overlaps the FLASH region (although not the data in FLASH).
```
[2/6] Linking C executable zephyr\zephyr_prebuilt.elf
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
           FLASH:       81148 B         1 MB      7.74%
      BOOTLOADER:          0 GB        10 KB      0.00%
         IMAGE_0:          0 GB       100 KB      0.00%
         IMAGE_1:          0 GB       100 KB      0.00%
      IMAGE_SWAP:           4 B        10 KB      0.04%
            SRAM:       16016 B       256 KB      6.11%
        IDT_LIST:         104 B         2 KB      5.08%
[6/6] Linking C executable zephyr\zephyr.elf
```
This would not be a solution to the problem without further changes however. The storage partition for example never has any variables in it, so there would still be no errors as FLASH encroaches into it. The linker output is also rather misleading as it implies that there is more flash available than there actually is. The region that the application is put into needs to accurately reflect the space available to it.
author: JordanYates

body:
If we are willing to live with the misleading linker output, we could:

1. Generate linker regions for all partitions under `zephyr,flash`
2. Add an overlapping partition for standalone code as in #29794
3. Add a new Kconfig symbol `CODE_PARTITION`, which would default to 'standalone', with alternate defaults when `CONFIG_MCUBOOT` or other symbols
4. Remove the `zephyr,code-partition` chosen node, `DT_USE_CODE_PARTITION`, `FLASH_LOAD_OFFSET`, `FLASH_LOAD_SIZE`, etc
5. Add an alias to map FLASH to the region we actually want in the linker file `REGION_ALIAS(FLASH CONFIG_CODE_PARTITION);`

This approach has much to recommend it IMO. Flash sizes for standalone applications become explicit. A significant chunk of the devicetree Kconfig interaction is reduced to a single symbol with minimal meaning (what partition does the application go into).

body:
> > what if we would generate linker sections only for partitions under the selected code-partition
> 
> I'm not sure what you mean here, it is memory regions we need to generate, not sections.
Semantics, read as memory regions.
> Additionally, `code-partition` points at a partition, not a collection of partitions. I am also proposing to do away with that chosen node altogether.

If the partition it points to has subpartitions it can also point to a collection of partitions.

> 
> > Defining a (sub)partition with label "image" could identify where the image should go. So the REGION_ALIAS() could map FLASH to "image".
> 
> This would break the ability for the same application to compile as standalone or chain-loaded. The purpose of the Kconfig symbol is to allow `CONFIG_MCUBOOT` to continue 'just working'.

The proposal would not break this ability. When there are no subpartitions everything would remain as is and `CONFIG_MCUBOOT` would continue to just work. However it would be possible to use an overlay with a more detailed split up and remove the usage of `CONFIG_MCUBOOT` (and avoid having to change Kconfig.zephyr for other bootloaders). Depending on whether a subpartition with the label "image" is defined the REGION_ALIAS() could either point to the complete partition or the subpartition with label "image".

A fit for all applications could be defined in one dts-file:
\flash0\image
\flash0\image\bootloader
\flash0\image\bootloader\image
\flash0\image\image0
\flash0\image\image0\image
\flash0\image\image0\image\image-hdr
\flash0\image\image0\image\image
...
\flash0\storage

compiling for `code-partition = &flash0` would generate memory regions image and storage and maps FLASH to image,
compiling for `code-partition = &bootloader` would generate memory region /image/bootloader and map FLASH to image/bootloader/image,
compiling for `code-partition = &image0` would generate memory regions /image/image0/image and map FLASH to image/image0/image.
compiling for `code-partition = &image0/image` would generate ... and map FLASH to image/image0/image/image.

The partitioning could probably be simplified if the is some rule like: "if there is no subpartition labeled "image" then map the flash to the complete partition".

body:
>  it seems like we can drop the error-prone documented requirement and just let CI handle the job

even if CI check for this, then it should still be documented that we have such a requirement.

> If the name defaults to the final path component of the module repository when not set, and we have a check that the name always matches the west project name, 

Even in the case that the path name matches the project name in `west`, then I still think the module should have the name field.

Due to module glue code is being located external to the module, then it is important that the name is explicit given in the module.
Remember:
1. `west` is optional
2. a module could be relocated, like: 
   ```
   - name: a-project               -->    - name: projectA
     path: some/path/a-project     -->      path: some/path/projectA
   ```
   Such a change would still honor the `west` project name/path rule, but this move would break the build system integration, when `a-project/zephyr/module.yml` has `cmake-ext: True` or `kconfig-ext: True`.

   The glue code in Zephyr would suddenly not be found, as that code is under `modules/a-project`.

Because of 2. I think `name` field should be a requirement whenever `cmake-ext` or `kconfig-ext` is used, to ensure the code is still found, even if code is relocated.

So I think we should have both.
- If `cmake-ext` or `kconfig-ext` is used, the `name` key is required.
- If `basename(module path) != west project name`, the `name` key is required (regardless if the module has glue code in Zephyr or not). CI check. 

Those are two different rules, one rule to increase robustness of the build system, the other rule for out own sanity.

body:
> @dleach02 I had to add back the insecure random number generator, sys_rand_get(), in order to pass CI tests.

This is a bit deeper of a problem than just this change. At one point, we had an insecure source of entropy available, but this is a pretty bad idea if it makes it into an actual device. (e.g. [Netscape](http://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~daw/papers/ddj-netscape.html)).

@dleach02 How do we solve this for other users of the crypto random sources? Do we need to come up with a more general solution here? It is probably ok to have insecure random numbers on CI targets, but we really need to make sure that never makes it onto an actual device.

I don't think the solution is to put the weakness into this auth code. The auth code needs strong random numbers, and so should be asking for them. We just need to figure out how to test this in CI.

body:
> What's the difference between wifi esp and wifi esp32? are the drivers incompatible or?

@tbursztyka This is a interesting question and I should have added some explanation before.
All existing `drivers/wifi/` are offloaded external wifi peripherals connected over UART or SPI, including the `drivers/wifi/esp`.
It all works linked to the WIFI_MGMT API.

This PR adds support for soc ESP32 WiFi (non-offloaded).  
1) It is not compatible with the current `wifi/esp` implementation.
2) It can't be attached to WIFI_MGMT api yet because it needs a new wifi subsys for soc wifi devices. Please, read #29394 regarding this.
3) As you see, the wifi sample code uses raw esp-idf wifi calls.

I am open to any suggestion regarding the placement of this wifi driver.

> 
> Initially raised by @cvinayak here: #32360

Reading the Bluetooth Specification v5.2 Vol 1, Section 8, most commonly used term is "Direction Finding" and the methods being the Angle of Arrival (AoA) and Angle of Departure (AoD), and the transmitter (TX) and Receiver (RX) roles. There is no mention of `DF` in the Acronyms and Abbreviations. (I am against `DF` in the samples folder, which is the first match to `DFS` Dynamic Frequency Selection in the specification document).
 
Earlier proposed `direction_beacon` does not clearly relate to specification terminology.

Hence, my choices, going by the Direction Finding using Bluetooth Low Energy section in the specification document are:
`direction_finding_aoa_tx` or `direction_aoa_tx`
`direction_finding_aoa_rx` or `direction_aoa_rx`
`direction_finding_aod_tx` or `direction_aod_tx`
`direction_finding_aod_rx` or `direction_aod_rx`

For the connected roles, we can suffix `peripheral` or `central`.

Mentioned section does  not distinguish two methods the direction finding is realized according to protocol that are: connectionless (periodic advertising), connect. What more AoA and AoD terms are connected with transmitter and receiver roles in both possible realization ways. 
So it is possible to have e.g. `direction_finding_aoa_aod_tx` and `direction_finding_aoa_aod_rx`.

device responds successfully").

I would like to have sample name that informs end user about feature it uses, realization mode (connectionless, connection) and role transmission, reception. So I suggest to use `direction_finding_connectionless_rx` for current `df_per_adv_beacon`. All parts of the new name have references in BT specification. For direction finding realized by connection I'll suggest to use `direction_finding_connection_rx`, `direction_finding_conection_tx`.

body: @andyross following approach is used: logging operates with a circular packet buffer (contrary to list of fragmented messages allocated from memslab). When logging is processing it passes the pointer to the message from the packet buffer to each backend. Call to the backend is synchronous so logging expects that when it returns message is no longer used by the backend. Backend has two option: block the logging thread and process the message or copy the message to its own memory and return.

Except for the following:
- No CMake code in Zephyr or Zephyr modules uses `HEX_FILES_TO_MERGE` (or in NCS for that matter)
- The `HEX_FILES_TO_MERGE` uses a fixed name name `merged.hex` which is actually not so nice. Such output names should ideally be user configurable.
- The runners will not flash the `merged.hex` per default, even when using `HEX_FILES_TO_MERGE`.

Therefore I think that doing this in Zephyr, as currently proposed in this PR is only a partial solution.

In NCS, the actual hex to flash is handled by modifying the runners yaml properties, like this:
https://github.com/nrfconnect/sdk-nrf/blob/20e438ad68ff982985ec7334dcdd098586c580d5/cmake/partition_manager.cmake#L541-L550
```
get_target_property(runners_content runners_yaml_props_target yaml_contents)

string(REGEX REPLACE "hex_file:[^\n]*"
  "hex_file: ${merged_hex_to_flash}" new  ${runners_content})

set_property(
  TARGET         runners_yaml_props_target
  PROPERTY       yaml_contents
  ${new}
  )
```

so therefore, this is not something that happens in a vanilla Zephyr today.

What i'm asking, is that if we want to base this on `HEX_FILES_TO_MERGE` as you state in the commit message, I would like to see a proper integration of `HEX_FILES_TO_MERGE` and the flashing of that hex-file by the runner.
This will also be beneficial for this use-case:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/32490#pullrequestreview-596230831

where it was discussed offline that a more generic solution should be used, but a nRF53 specific solution was acceptable short term.

> > * Being able to create a list of hex files to use for the runner.
> 
> That is the logical effect of HEX_FILES_TO_MERGE.

No, this still doesn't provide a list of files to the runner itself.
It provides a single merged file to the runner, a file which then has to be split by the runner.

What I'm asking, as the possibility to provide a list of files to flash and / or list of runners to use (each domain to flash could require dedicated arguments, just like the nRF53, that requires different `--coprocessor` arguments.)

The principle of splitting merged hex files is not scalable among multiple socs / runners.
As example, this fix won't work if flashing using the JLink runner.

That was not intended as a statement of policy; it was an insufficiently clear statement of fact: the term `blocklist` appears in Zephyr mainline only in the west guide documentation and when paired with "passlist".  It has not yet been used in Zephyr RTOS code.

> You're saying "Zephyr" but I disagree with whoever in the community ruled this out, and the fact that west is already using these terms de facto means they're going to be used by Zephyr users. So I stand firm on keeping them.

That's fine.  My position was we had three perfectly adequate names, where the positive and negative verbs are natural antonyms:  "allow/deny", "pass/block", and "accept/reject".  

I don't find "allow/block" to be a natural pairing.  I also am tired of all the bikeshed discussions, and figured that since for this case we actually had a documented set of recommended names it was reasonable to propose sticking with them rather than introducing yet another arguably gratuitous variation.

body:
> @alxelax, IIRC this delayed storage was introduced to avoid to frequent storage that could reduce flash life. Does the change allow to leave it in a state where it will always do immediate storage ? If so would it not be better to have a routine that changes to immediate storage, do the flush, and set it back to delayed storage ?

Yes. The reason to have a timeout-based approach is to avoid frequent storage and to have a more or less determined device lifetime.
However, I'd prefer to keep the decision-making logic outside the settings subsystem and keep it as a configurable service.

The main idea to add this functionality to allow emergency termination of mesh stack activity with the ability to restore the device in the network later. 

Simple use case: 
The battery-powered device is out of power. It stores all data (including ongoing replay protection cache) asap. Then human changes batteries and the device is back to the network.  

If the setting subsystem logic is responsible for latching the timeout-based approach back then there is no guarantee that one more frame sneaked into RPC after latching the timeouts back. In this case, the setting subsystem will require monitoring stack data\events and understand the importance of data to make decisions correctly. Otherwise, the incoming traffic after power-up will be rejected due to lost RPC entries. It is a kind of tradeoff between a device's life cycle and security vulnerabilities.  
I'd prefer to provide decision-making to the upper layer with global mode (smth like power-down). Furthermore, the setting subsystem is not the public Bluetooth Mesh API and not documented well. It is the second reason to implement logic responsible for switching forth and back the timeout-based approach on the upper layer with a good description of purposes and recommendations.

body:
> This is quite a limitation.

True. As far as I can tell, there's no pattern for running multiple build targets in the same test in twister. Ultimately, I'd like to add a build target reference as an optional parameter in the `bsim_tests` list entries, but as I couldn't find an existing pattern for this, and as I didn't need it to convert the existing tests, I decided to wait and gather some feedback first. 

> Everything is wrapped in a very pre-caned solution which complicates that kind of easy hacking, which is one of the big benefits of the simulator.

This is also true, but I'm not convinced that this is necessarily a bad thing. In the three years since support for BabbleSim was added, there are only 4 tests added for it, 2 of them yours. This is far less than what BabbleSim deserves in my opinion, given how incredibly powerful it is. To me, this means that developers either haven't discovered it, or have been too intimidated or confused by the hoops they have to jump through to use it. I hope that adding support for this in twister can help with both these issues, and increase the overall usage of BabbleSim in the development process - both for the Zephyr Bluetooth stack and for the applications built on top of it.

For hacking and connecting debuggers, perhaps we could add  a `skip` parameter to the `bsim_tests` entries, and print the skipped command instead of launching it? This way, users could easily launch that process on their own in parallel, similar to the skip behavior I added for the mesh tests. There are also twister parameters for running valgrind and gcov, which could be supported here.

> Trying to add a test that uses anything not supported in twister is much more difficult (and these tests now depend on twister, which they did not before).

As this patch doesn't remove the shell scripts, I don't believe it damages the existing workflow for adding tests at all. The framework scripts are still there, and it still runs in CI. 

> Would it be a possibility to maybe have something like a "external shell script" harness, which just calls whatever shell script, and checks the return value?

Yes, but this wouldn't really help get rid of the hurdle of the shell scripts in bsim_bt. I'm all for extending twister though.

>As far as I can tell, there's no pattern for running multiple build targets in the same test in twister

That is one of the main issues here. The other being running an arbitrary set of things for different tests.

> This way, users could easily launch that process on their own in parallel, similar to the skip behavior I added for the mesh tests. 

Partially. We also need to make twister not timeout the rest.
Twister is mostly just meant to run tests in batch, where those tests follow a "build an image", "run that image" pattern. If you want to repeat that by hand, it is trivial: You build it by hand and run it by hand however you please.

>To me, this means that developers either haven't discovered it, or have been too intimidated or confused

We would need to ask the people who has used it (or not) why they have or not used it and why they have or not added more tests in the main public repo. (I'd be happy to hear from you in a private chat). I have my doubts that this direction would really help make the potential babblesim users more comfy (it would make it easier to run the tests without knowing what you are doing, and add a test that is very close to the tests that are there, but going beyond that is another thing).

Anyhow, how this PR attacks it, we are moving a lot of knowledge up to twister, about things that are not known. For ex, what parameters one needs to use depend on what one is running. Say, for mesh, I could imagine you would like to have devices at different distances/attenuations where not all are in range of each other, and where they come in an out of range. In some cases you may want to use one channel or modem model, in other cases different ones. Exposing all that to twister at a parameter level would be impractical to be mild.

>but this wouldn't really help get rid of the hurdle of the shell scripts 

Shell scripts are quite handy for running a bunch of seemingly arbitrary shell commands repeatedly :p

IIRC...
We used to have no default memory domain. When a memory domain is deleted, the arch code needs to clean up for all associated threads (e.g. reset MMU settings). Now we have a default memory domain. Those threads are simply moved to the default domain. This calls the same functions for moving between domains.

> Are we 100% sure we're reading that rule correctly? ANSI put the struct tag into a separate namespace from symbols way back in the 80's precisely to prevent collisions like this and permit code like exactly the stuff this patch is changing. Why would MISRA care?

I think the interpretation  is correct, the rule says that a tag name has to be a unique identifier. According with the C standard an identifier can be an object, a function, a tag, a member of a struct, union, typedef name, ....

My understanding is that the main problem that the rule address is the re-use of a tag for different types, but *probably* based on observation or some kind of statistical analysis they identified that reusing a tag name lead developers to make mistakes and recommended to not do this.

body:
> 
> 
> > @galak also notice, `kconfig.py` already does various checking of the Kconfig tree today:
> 
> Those checks don't seem to be zephyr specific, which is my concern about adding this check directly to scripts/kconfig/kconfig.py

Those checks are exactly Zephyr specific.
They are needed because Zephyr samples / tests uses handwritten Kconfig files in the form of `prj.conf`.
Because of this, in kconfig.cmake, we do this:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/c1f7b9f45a78d7e082a131474cf5c4592a1aaba8/cmake/kconfig.cmake#L239-L240

when we generate the first `.config` file.
In that case we want to carry out the previous 3 checks I linked.

Once we have the `.config` in place, even promptless symbols gets values assigned.

As example, kconfiglib itself allows value assignment to promptless symbols, but in Zephyr we don't want values assigned to promptless symbols in `prj.conf` and other Kconfig fragments. That's why we have those checks in kconfig.py, which is a Zephyr specific python script.

Waiting for unprovisioned beacon...

But after changing the configs above to stop blasting out log messages and to possibly support 16 nodes, this sample is still *far* from providing a satisfactory out-of-box experience.  Back in spring 2019 I had a Zephyr mesh sample in C++ that I managed to make work, and it was *far* more responsive.  After several attempts at wiping out state and starting over, I still can't get a reliable 3-node mesh running where button presses are visible across the mesh in less than one second.

body: Part of the confusion is because of the logic in `button_pressed()`, which ignores the actual local state of the LED in favor of only tracking the state of local button presses: if the local button pressed state is off, and the local LED state is on, pressing the button will transit an ON request rather than an OFF request, resulting in the press having no effect.  This is not what people will expect.

body:
> @Thalley Sample looks ok, but have you considered what happens when the central disconnects in the middle of the main loop. Wouldn't it get stuck between the k_sem_waits?

That's a good question @joerchan . If it disconnects after `err = k_sem_take(&sem_conn, K_FOREVER);` then it would still wait for the PA sync and then `bt_le_per_adv_sync_transfer` would fail  as the connection pointer would be invalid, it would return, if it doesn't create a new connection before that (the `disconnected` callback starts the scan again which will attempt to connect again). It is actually worse if we lose the PA sync, as that isn't handled very well. 

It isn't trivial to ensure both features (conn and pa_sync) are in the right state all the time in a single thread. I had considered creating a separate thread handling the PA sync, such that we could have 2 while loops running, each ensuring that their respective feature is handled. 

Do you have any ideas of handling this?

body:
Thanks @lgirdwood for a detailed explanation. The problem here is more specific. When we send audio data to the I2S driver we place it in a large buffer and pass to the driver using one system call. So far the I2S API assumed that the data are always packed in an optimum way. E.g. an 8-bit sample will require one byte of storage, that is to send 16 8-bit samples we will need a buffer of size 16. However, the LPC driver in this PR is not able to cope with such data. Its DMA engine can do 32-bit transfers only. It can transfer one 32-bit sample or two 16-bit samples at minimum.

We were wondering how such hardware limitations are dealt with in case of SOF. Does the application need to query the data layout supported by the driver? You only support one specific data layout?

ALSA library has [snd_pcm_format_physical_width()](https://www.alsa-project.org/alsa-doc/alsa-lib/group___p_c_m___helpers.html#gaa3e0ff7560342e5af2b5c7bd2d63a307) function which lets the application figure out the `sizeof` a single data sample.

body:
API meeting 2021.03.30

- Proposal to add a hidden `CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL` option that indicates that at least one experimental feature has enabled. All experimental features would then `select EXPERIMENTAL` (they would not depend on it)
- The script can then find all options `select`ing `EXPERIMENTAL` and warn as with this PR
- Review all options that are currently marked as `EXPERIMENTAL` in their title
- With this mechanism, we could add an additional `CONFIG_UNSAFE`  that is selected and warned. This could replace many custom warnings that are today spread among the mulitple `CMakeLists.txt`.
- Let's make this extensible so it serves as a generic Kconfig warning mechanism
- Rationale for the removal of `depend on EXPERIMENTAL` from the Linux kernel: https://lwn.net/Articles/520867/

body:
@marc-hb 

> > It is meant to be used with other plugins such as breathe in order to improve the user experience.
> 
> I'm afraid I don't see yet what is the "user experience" benefit of making doxygen dependent on sphinx. Most people use some higher level target and shouldn't notice any difference. For others who use lower level targets (for troubleshooting or performance reasons), this will make it more complicated or even impossible to run doxygen directly, adding a layer of indirection in an area (the build) that already has too many layers of indirection.

It's not the first plugin to do this. Others such as [exhale](https://exhale.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) do this. Even `breathe` seems to support that (doesn't seem really well designed though), see https://github.com/michaeljones/breathe/blob/master/breathe/process.py. Regarding debug, Doxygen logs can be obtained from the Sphinx output if the silent option is not disabled (and `QUIET=NO` in the Doxyfile, not true as of today).

> 
> Considering this PR increases the number of lines there should be some obvious benefits. I've done some testing and it makes no performance difference for incremental builds.

I started this extension in order to simplify the Doxygen build, which now depends on a combination of CMake and an external script. It turned out that the external script is not strictly needed (more details below), so it is true that we could keep using CMake for the Doxygen part. The main benefit right now is that we do not need to keep Doxygen input file list duplicate in both Doxyfile and CMakeLists.txt. The extension takes care of parsing that to then keep track of Doxygen changes.
> 
> Speaking of number of lines there was BTW a never implemented suggestion to greatly simplify the timestamp script and maybe even replace it with single recursive copy python call: https://sourceforge.net/p/doxygen/mailman/message/36582383/

The modification time script becomes mostly redundant once input dependency tracking is introduced. With that feature in place, Doxygen is only run when any of the input file is changed. There is an edge case that the script could solve: what if I edit .c/.h, but I don't change any docstring? In theory the generated XML files should be the same, so I could skip updating the XML files given to Sphinx. We can add this case to the extension, I wonder though if it is worth it.

> 
> > Doxyfile can be optionally preprocessed so that variables can be inserted
> 
> CMake can pre-process anything, that's routine and does not require a sphinx plugin.

That's true. I added this facility to make transition easier (it's really 5 LOC + extension options).

> 
> > The script to modify timestamps is not used anymore. It was redundant since Doxygen is only run if any of its input files changes and
> 
> Doxygen runs really fast and running it never had any _direct_ performance impact, only an indirect one on breathe.
> 

Detailed above.

> > in case there are no doc string changes, Doxygen still changes rendered timestamps in all XML files...
> 
> I'm very confused by this:
> 
> * The previous line just stated that Doxygen is not run anymore when there no changes

And that's true because there is input dependency tracking.

> * The second line seems to miss the entire purpose of the timestamp script described in its --help and in fact the new script seems to re-implements more or less the same thing. For the record this script made incremental, non-doxygen builds orders of magnitude faster, see #13159 and also #13442

At the time #13159 was introduced CMake did not track Doxygen input file changes. This is not true anymore in both current CMake nor the `doxyrunner` extension. 

Maybe I'm missing something here, but on my tests I see the expected behavior without caring about modification times at all. Do we want to keep accounting for the edge case mentioned above?  edit: last changes add support for this feature.

body:
@marc-hb @mbolivar @tejlmand I think the point here to be discussed is whether we want to move some of the functionality that is currently being offered by CMake into Sphinx plugins. I certainly see some advantages:

- A single programming language, everything is written in Python
- A single framework, Sphinx takes care of everything. In the future we could go as far as removing the CMake file altogether
- CMake is currently being used as a scripting language in `doc/CMakeLists.txt`. The single exception to that is the `DEPENDS ${DOXY_SOURCES}` statement in Doxygen custom command. That makes use of CMake's ability to track changes to dependencies, and has been rewritten in Python here

In general using CMake as a scripting language is not something I believe we should do, because it's more verbose and hard to follow, and you anyways always need to delegate to Python sooner or later as tasks become more complex, so it ends up becoming a combination of languages that you need to integrate with each other. So for that reason only I think it's worth considering a transition to `sphinx-build` as our main entry point for the documentation build instead of CMake. But I do agree that "losing" the ability to track file changes in dependencies is a downside.

body:
> Sorry I don't have the time to review everything right now, maybe in a few days (=too late?) So I'll just share my "core" principles that seem relevant here:
> 
> * As fewer layers of indirections as possible. So, if this PR adds one layer of indirection to run doxygen: bad. If this merely replaces the CMake indirection with a sphinx indirection: OK but see below.

To be precise it replaces one level of indirection (CMake) with a Sphinx extension. After these changes CMake becomes purely a scripting facility in regard to Sphinx, which means we could potentially remove it in the future.

> * Layers of indirections should be as transparent and "optional" as possible. "Optional" for the lack of a better word: I mean the ability to quickly "peel" the layer of indirection and copy/paste the lower-level command directly for investing its failures. For instance `CMake's VERBOSE=1` achieves this, it prints commands that can be most of the time re-run by merely copying them to the command line. So this PR should preserve the ability to just copy/paste the doxygen invocation on the command line to re-run doxgen alone and debug doxygen failures directly and quickly.

`doxygen` target is still offered, so the extension is optional for the standalone build. The extension is actually quite transparent, it offers the option to "print" the Doxygen logs (setting `doxyrunner_silent = False`) and fails if Doxygen returns non-zero.

> * I agree CMake is a terrible scripting language, Python all the way, except for... tracking dependencies of course! That's why CMake sits at the top-level. I mean it's better to have CMake invoke a sequence of smaller Python scripts that can be run independently compared to running one giant and opaque Python script that does everything in one go. Modularity and incremental builds for the win and I doubt sphinx can do that.
> 

I think Sphinx extensions comply with the modularity principle. They integrate well with the Sphinx runner and offer access to all the Sphinx facilities. In fact, I think complexity is reduced since we remove a non-trivial dependency (CMake) or duplicate Doxygen input file list.

> I quickly wrote the following Python function below that can implement the "restore timestamps" simplification suggested in https://sourceforge.net/p/doxygen/mailman/message/36582383/ and in #13639 and it seems to work. Maybe it could help simplify this PR too?

I think current `sync_doxygen` function solves the timestamp problem with ~30LOC, and anyway, it's an edge case as mentioned previously.

> The idea is to replace the "two ways" synchronization with this simpler, one-way build:
> 
> ```
> C sources ---doxygen()--->  dumb doxygen output  ---recursive_copy_if_changed()---> smart doxygen output
> ```
> 

This is already achieved with the current implementation.

> ```python
> def rec_copy_if_changed(src, dst):
> 
>    def unchanged_files(srcdirstr, all_files):
>        # closure on dst and src
>        srcdir = Path(srcdirstr)
>        reldir = srcdir.relative_to(src)
>        dstdir = dst / reldir
> 
>        unchanged = []
>        for f in all_files:
>            srcf = srcdir / Path(f)
>            if srcf.is_symlink() or not srcf.is_file():
>                continue
> 
>            dstf = dstdir / Path(f)
>            if not dstf.exists():
>                continue
> 
>            if filecmp.cmp(srcf, dstf):
>                unchanged.append(f)
> 
>        return unchanged
> 
>    shutil.copytree(src, dst, ignore=unchanged_files, dirs_exist_ok=True)
> ```
> 
> `dirsync` can probably do the same however it's yet another Python dependency, as @carlescufi said not worth it to save just a few lines.

body: @mbolivar-nordic The biggest uncertainty is the size of the hash table generated by gperf. It is partially related to how many kernel objects in the build. However, gperf tends to insert empty elements in the hash table and this contributes to the issue at hand. It is impossible to know how many empty ones will get inserted. When the address of one kobj moves, the new hash table may be vastly different. One might simply reserves too much space (and thus wasting a bunch), or reserves too little so they are constantly chasing a moving goal post. Here is another solution (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/33687) where the reservation of space is done automatically during build time. It's not perfect, but does keep using the hash table.

body:
> Thanks @lgirdwood for a detailed explanation. The problem here is more specific. When we send audio data to the I2S driver we place it in a large buffer and pass to the driver using one system call. 

I would just pass the pointer and bytes in this call (we do). The DMA and I2S are configured with other calls first as this allows for continuous playback..

>So far the I2S API assumed that the data are always packed in an optimum way. E.g. an 8-bit sample will require one byte of storage, that is to send 16 8-bit samples we will need a buffer of size 16. However, the LPC driver in this PR is not able to cope with such data. Its DMA engine can do 32-bit transfers only. It can transfer one 32-bit sample or two 16-bit samples at minimum.
> 
> We were wondering how such hardware limitations are dealt with in case of SOF. Does the application need to query the data layout supported by the driver? You only support one specific data layout?

The HW link formats are defined in the pipeline topology and programmed by the DAI drivers when streams are in use. This can also mean the pipeline will react to use case input format from a media player and align this format with the I2S configuration (i.e. via SRC or format conversion).

Generally, if an application tries to open a PCM device where the HW format is incompatible with the HW AND no conversion is possible we will fail. 

> 
> ALSA library has [snd_pcm_format_physical_width()](https://www.alsa-project.org/alsa-doc/alsa-lib/group___p_c_m___helpers.html#gaa3e0ff7560342e5af2b5c7bd2d63a307) function which lets the application figure out the `sizeof` a single data sample.

We have something similar to ALSA (disclaimer: I'm also an ALSA developer) in that we ```frame_size``` parameter for the audio PCM data that corresponds to the number of channels * sample size (frame_format) e.g.
```c
/* stream PCM frame format */
enum sof_ipc_frame {
	SOF_IPC_FRAME_S16_LE = 0,
	SOF_IPC_FRAME_S24_4LE,
	SOF_IPC_FRAME_S32_LE,
	SOF_IPC_FRAME_FLOAT,
	/* other formats here */
};
```
i.e. Stereo S24_4LE is 2 * 4 bytes = 8 bytes frame size.  Please note we dont have 8bit formats, this would sound terrible. 16 bit stereo is pretty much the default supported by all codec HW.

This is all that is needed for copying data from memory to memory (i.e. host to DSP). To copy data to peripherals over TDM, PCM or I2S protocols you also need to include a HW frame_size which may be larger that the PCM data frame size (i.e. we have I2S running with 64BCLKs per FRAME for stereo 16bit PCM will mean the link will have 16 unused BCLKs for L and R - HW frame_size is 64 and PCM frame_size is 32..

body:
I believe it would be better to make it look similar to
- `dts/bindings/gpio/silabs,gecko-gpio.yaml`
- `dts/bindings/gpio/silabs,gecko-gpio-port.yaml`

The SiLabs GPIO module is a SoC internal one, but we could take a similar approach and split the device in one node with `compatible = "cypress,cy8c95xx"` and several nodes with `"compatible = "cypress,cy8c95xx-port"`. The reason for splitting is the architecture of the cy8c95xx. All the device registers are accessible via a single I2C address, this will be represented by `compatible = "cypress,cy8c95xx"` node. And the device can have up to 8 ports, they will be represented by "compatible = "cypress,cy8c95xx-port"`.

In all cases the `reg` property should have only address cell, no size cell, i.e. for `compatible = "cypress,cy8c95xx"` it should be `reg = <0x20>` representing the address on the I2C bus. For `"compatible = "cypress,cy8c95xx-port"` the reg property could represent the port number, i.e. be defined as a `reg = <n>` where n is a number between 0 and 7.

@galak, could you double check that the above approach is the right one.

> Putting a -1 on this for now as I don't think a common folder is necessarily the right thing.
> 
> These scripts have different requirements on their test environments and I think it's good that they are allowed to differ.

The idea is to have a folder for the common cases, that does not force people to use it (e.g. `dts` has its own set of tests). I think pytest is flexible enough to accommodate different needs, e.g. we can have tags, multiple conftest.py for fixtures/specifics that only apply to tests on a subfolder, etc.

What I'd like is to have a place to add my `test_x.py` unit-test suite and see that CI exercises it without more effort. Stuff like `scripts/west_commands/run_tests.py` or a custom `README.md` for twister tests makes things unnecessarily complex and more difficult to maintain. If we talk about system-level testing, then I understand that requirements may be more diverse and it may justify a completely separate CI/test suite.

Changes implementation of `hci_df_set_cl_cte_rx_enable` to hide an issue with Bluetooth Core Spec. Vol 4,Part E, sec 7.8.82. There is no right way to set receive of AoD CTE for devices with single antenna. The spec requires minimum antenna switch pattern to have at least two antennas. 

 To hide that from end user, the function verifies cte_type. If there is an AoA type enabled, slot_durations, num_ant_ids and ant_ids must contain valid values. 

Besides that cte_type is stored in `struct bt_le_per_adv_sync`. `hci_le_df_connectionless_iq_report` uses it to drop IQ sample reports that has type not set in cte_type.

Just before that loop the `ate_size`, which is used to figure address of the last ate in sector, is aligned to *the current* write sector; if you assume that for example write alignment doubled, this means that it will start read at the second ate from the end of sector and that may contain old size ate followed by "not-closed" old size ate, but will be detected as one closing ate as a whole;  such situation may lead to detecting all sectors as closed.

body:
> 
> 
> @de-nordic, i didn't consider an ate size change (this would only happen when changing from <=4 byte alignment to 8 or vice versa). Then none of the ate's would be valid (crc8 is in the wrong place).

I think it might be detected as ok. The `nvs_ate_crc8_check` is calculating crc on ate entry taking the size of `nvs_ate` structure minus the size of crc:
`crc8 = crc8_ccitt(0xff, entry, offsetof(struct nvs_ate, crc8))`
the update of crc is done with `nvs_ate_crc8_update` that does:
```
crc8 = crc8_ccitt(0xff, entry, offsetof(struct nvs_ate, crc8));
entry->crc8 = crc8;
```
So it operates within `nvs_ate` structure that is then directly written/read at the write_block alignment.
This means that the write block is N times greater then the size of `nvs_ate`  the `nvs_ate` at the beginning of the block, if there is one, will be checked and detected to  be ok.

If the crc would be put in `write_block - sizeof(crc)` byte of the ate write_block then indeed the change in the crc calculation could fail in case when write_block changes.

It may be possible to add a generic wrapper to every api call to avoid adding enter/exit macros inside a function (which becomes problematic for maintenance with functions with multiple return locations). body:
> is it possible to use something like "platform_allow" in sample.yaml, but select the whole STM32 family instead of a board name like nucleo_xxx?
Or how to restrict buildkite in a proper way?

You can use 'filter' field, for instance:
```
tests:
  sample.drivers.flash.shell:
    tags: flash shell
    filter: CONFIG_FLASH_HAS_DRIVER_ENABLED
```
You can also base the filter on dts, which could be even more fine-grained:
```
    filter: dt_compat_enabled("st,stm32-window-watchdog")
```
You can also use operators: `not`, `and`, `or`, ...

body:
@de-nordic, I can understand that from your perpective (mcuboot, mcumgr, DFU) this PR gets -1. But maybe your perspective needs some adaptation :-).
The goal of this PR is to provide a simple method for ZEPHYR applications to use partitions. These applications are nvs, fcb, simplefs, ... They all don't need a flashmap description of all partitions that are available, they just need (secured) access to the partition so that there actions are limited to the partition itself.
This PR would reduce the size of applications by:
a. eliminating unused info
b. providing a simple routine for retrieving the erase block size that just requires 1 extra uint32, while removing the code for searching the blocksize and removing the need for CONFIG_FLASH_PAGE. This can just be defined as a partition property in the dts.

body:
@yashi, Thanks for looking further into this. The situation reminds me my experience with hacking POSIX and/or libc subsystems, when seemingly simple changes leed to cascade of issues and follow-up changes. So, you're not alone ;-).

I looked into the situation myself. mps2_an385 supports 8 MPU regions, and one after another protection features enabled, that trickles into 3 "free" partition slots available for application code. Having additional libc partition indeed gets this down to 2 free partition slots, which causes the mem_protect/userspace test to fail.

I was able to get it pass with `CONFIG_TEST_HW_STACK_PROTECTION=n`. So, we could potentially make another test config for mps2_an385 with that option and exclude it from normal tests. I don't think that would scale, because 8 MPU regions is standard for Cortex-M0/Cortex-M3 devices, so the same problem would happen to many other (real) devices, the only special thing about mps2_an385 is that it's emulated via qemu, and we run this emulation during CI. Try to filter all affected devices would be too adhoc and cumbersome, and I guess we'd really like to run the rest with stack protection anyway.

So, I'd suggest to do partition plucking on where we add it now - on minimal libc size. It shouldn't be too bread-crumb configuration either, so instead of e.g. CONFIG_MINIMAL_LIBC_RAND, I'd suggest to add something like CONFIG_MINIMAL_LIBC_GLOBALS with a description like "Support C library functions which implicitly access global/static data, e.g. rand(). Such data must be put into a memory partition, and disabling this option may save an entry for application defining many custom partitions. ..."

Then disable this option for the affected test(s).

body:
To really introduce the replay protection as required by bt-mesh there might be an alternative.

At the moment it is not compliant as it is possible to replay messages that are within the rpl storage period. To add some storage method for a planned shutdown does not really help. 

If the saving method would be changed to a non period based approach but instead value based it is possible to provide full replay protection: instead of storing the current SEQ we store the current SEQ with some added (configurable) value. Each time the current SEQ reaches this stored value, the value is recalculated and stored. Upon restart this stored value is reloaded. The configurable delta can be used to limit the storage requirements.

There is a downside: after power on it might require multiple messages before the stored SEQ is reached. But this would just be a nuisance that can easily be handled.

body:
> there is no security issue, both messages are no longer valid. The unlock message will not be accepted. It is bullet proof, the sender will need to increase it's "counter" until it has reached the stored value.

If we don't store the sequence number of the incoming message in flash, it will be lost after a power cycle, and we will have no way to tell whether it's valid. If this happens, anyone can replay those messages from when we power cycle until the actual source of the unlock message sends another message with a higher sequence number. It won't matter that we received more messages from that node after the unlock message if we didn't store them.

body:
> > there is no security issue, both messages are no longer valid. The unlock message will not be accepted. It is bullet proof, the sender will need to increase it's "counter" until it has reached the stored value.
> 
> If we don't store the sequence number of the incoming message in flash, it will be lost after a power cycle, and we will have no way to tell whether it's valid. If this happens, anyone can replay those messages from when we power cycle until the actual source of the unlock message sends another message with a higher sequence number. It won't matter that we received more messages from that node after the unlock message if we didn't store them.

It is always possible to replay messages, the important thing is that they are not considered valid. As the restore after a power down would set the sequence number to a higher value they would not be considered valid so replaying them has no influence. The only thing is that valid messages would be ignored as long as the sequence number is not reached, but there is AFAIK there is nothing that says messages have to be accepted (they could get lost anyhow).

Maybe it was not completely clear that the sequence number would be stored, it would. Just the restore from flash would set a higher sequence number. So suppose the sequence number would start unintialized. The first received message would set the sequence number at 233 and the 'saving interval' would be set at an increase of 5 messages. The first store would be 238 and as long as the sequence number does not reach 238 nothing is stored. After some messages the sequence number hits 238 (or whatever is higher) then the new value stored is 243 (or the higher number +5). when a power down is done and the values are restored the new sequence number for accepted messages would become 243 (or the higher number + 5).

And to be complete, when a message with sequence 243 or higher is received, the number 248 (or the higher value + 5) is stored.

body:
>     1. Why do we need `zephyr,reserved`?

To quickly access the node using `DT_CHOSEN` but I can probably remove that.

>     2. Why do we need linker sections for this?

Given that you could have this done using memory regions "far" from the used kernel space and accessing the memory using direct pointers in memory having sections is handy for several reasons:
- If your reserved memory is overlapping with some other section you get an error at compile time
- Having sections allows you to put variables in that section using `__in_section()`
- Allows the code to create linker symbols and a set of helpers to easily manage the reserved region

>     3. How does this play with the existing uses of reserved memory in devicetree already in tree today?

The `reserved-memory` node today in Zephyr is not currently doing anything, it's just creating nodes to be used by some other code in an arbitrary way. It is also slightly misused because the sub-nodes are not defining reserved memory regions as but are mostly used to partition the space. We can make the approach in this PR co-exist with the current use by introducing a property in the nodes (for example something like `create-section;`) and create regions/sections/linker symbols only for the regions for which this property is defined, basically the equivalent of `linker-region;` property for #31077.

body:
I certainly agree with @ioannisg that devicetree is the place to be doing this sort of configuration. I am a little concerned that while this definitely solves a real problem, it either only solves a part of it, or it conflicts with other mechanisms we have for partitioning the address space.

Based on my (minimal) understanding of how the Linux memory allocation works, `reserved-memory` is intended to describe RAM reservation only. If this is how it should be used under Zephyr, it should be documented as such. If is is also intended to be used for FLASH reservation, then this conflicts with the use of `fixed-partitions`. Would we need to add the settings partitions to both in order for the region to both show in the linker and appear under `flash_map.h`?

Right now this is creating a second instance of #27471, except this time in RAM instead of FLASH. `linker.ld` is still generating the `SRAM` region naively from `zephyr,sram`, regardless of `reserved-memory`. If the reserved regions are for placeholding rather than compile time variables, the linker will happily allocate application RAM into our reserved memory regions without warnings.

Ideally the solution would also allow us to remove the `DT_REGION_FROM_NODE_STATUS_OKAY` macros from `linker.ld`. Most of them are specifying RAM devicetree nodes, it seems silly to be generating RAM memory regions via two different mechanisms.

I feel that a complete solution to these problems requires one partitioning method for FLASH (application location/size, settings partition, etc) one for RAM (application location/size, displaybuffer mem, etc). This would imply that `reserved-memory` should also be used for specifying application RAM.

In short, I'm not convinced that the Linux `reserved-memory` concept is sufficient for the problems that we need to solve for embedded systems. I would be leaning towards a RAM version of `fixed-partitions` which can be placed under any RAM devicetree node.

One of the Zephyr Development Summit Mini-Conference's is intending to address precisely this problem and others, so I would suggest that we hold off on merging this pending the outcomes of that discussion (June 10th).

body:
> Based on my (minimal) understanding of how the Linux memory allocation works, `reserved-memory` is intended to describe RAM reservation only. If this is how it should be used under Zephyr, it should be documented as such. If is is also intended to be used for FLASH reservation, then this conflicts with the use of `fixed-partitions`. Would we need to add the settings partitions to both in order for the region to both show in the linker and appear under `flash_map.h`?

No. This commit is not intended to tackle FLASH reservation or mappings. The only allowed use for the `reserved-memory` mechanism is for RAM reservation. I can make that explicit but this commit wants to follow the usual (aka Linux) intended use for the `reserved-memory` node, that is RAM reservation and partitioning. FLASH is out of this picture.

> Right now this is creating a second instance of #27471, except this time in RAM instead of FLASH. `linker.ld` is still generating the `SRAM` region naively from `zephyr,sram`, regardless of `reserved-memory`. If the reserved regions are for placeholding rather than compile time variables, the linker will happily allocate application RAM into our reserved memory regions without warnings.

This is correct. As I mentioned before one possible solution is to create compile time variables in the sections to get at least a compile time error. On this point I didn't have any better idea and I'm open to any suggestion. Without MMU is hard to actually "reserve" memory and exclude that from normal usage.

> Ideally the solution would also allow us to remove the `DT_REGION_FROM_NODE_STATUS_OKAY` macros from `linker.ld`. Most of them are specifying RAM devicetree nodes, it seems silly to be generating RAM memory regions via two different mechanisms.

This PR is mostly an extension to that, trying to gather the data directly from DT and adding the sections for a very precise goal, `DT_REGION_FROM_NODE_STATUS_OKAY` is a more general partitioning tool. Actually for what I'm trying to do in this PR memory regions are not even needed at all, I could create only sections instead if we want to reduce the overlap.

> I feel that a complete solution to these problems requires one partitioning method for FLASH (application location/size, settings partition, etc) one for RAM (application location/size, displaybuffer mem, etc). This would imply that `reserved-memory` should also be used for specifying application RAM.

Again, I'm not sure why FLASH is being brought on the table. The `reserved-memory` node is used to create reserved portion of memory for DMA, direct access, shared memory, CMA, etc... I'm not sure what are the requirements for FLASH partitioning, but the tool introduced in this PR is not dealing with that.

> In short, I'm not convinced that the Linux `reserved-memory` concept is sufficient for the problems that we need to solve for embedded systems. I would be leaning towards a RAM version of `fixed-partitions` which can be placed under any RAM devicetree node.

What's the difference? Only the davicetree location? Because on the contrary I think that we should follow what has been already implemented on Linux, with a specialized `reserved-memory` node listing all the reserved regions.

> One of the Zephyr Development Summit Mini-Conference's is intending to address precisely this problem and others, so I would suggest that we hold off on merging this pending the outcomes of that discussion (June 10th).

Yup, I won't miss that.

body:
> I included the FLASH comments because @ioannisg mentioned flash partitioning and I wasn't clear on the Linux binding. It does have some relevance in that we need to partition both FLASH and RAM somehow, and the closer the two solutions are to each other the more we can share in the implementation.

Thanks for your feedback @JordanYates. My apologies for mentioning FLASH here, too; I understand it was confusing, as it leads to thinking about physical memory partitioning. So, let's focus on RAM.

I believe that the intention of this RFC PR is **not** to solve the problem of physically partition memory areas; a problem that concerns primarily, multi-image, multi-core applications with a common (e.g. global) memory resource. To my understanding, this PR aims at addressing a simpler problem: in a single-core single Zephyr images, we would like to have more control on some areas of the image memory that will be used by certain components of our application. By control, I am referring to:
- being able to reserve parts in the image RAM and place these areas there
- generate and expose linker symbols that reference the boundaries of the areas
- allocate certain variables/buffers there
- configure (attribute) these areas in a custom way, based on the application needs

Since all this is done inside a Zephyr image, I believe this problem is orthogonal to the partitioning-problem, which concerns mainly multi-image applications.

In brief, we would like to add some more user-control on how the build system (linker) is generating and populating sections. 

Note that this is already the case for some existing features (e.g `config NOCACHE_MEMORY`), where we instruct the linker to reserve some sections for defining non-cachable  buffers.

Historically, we have been defining several sections in our linker for the various kernel and application needs (user memory, read-only stuff, heap, execute-from-ram etc.), but now we would like to put a bit more control over the properties of some of these sections.

Assuming that all the information about the "control" we want to apply, is available at build time, I believe that DeviceTree is the right place to describe our needs, and the reserved-memory seems to be a convenient concept to use (open to alternative suggestions here).

My point is that we should not hold this back, until we have a holistic approach that addresses, also, the multi-image fixed partitioning problem, as I do not anticipate much overlap. I'd suggest we de-couple the two problems from each other.

As the focus is on creating sections from DT information, would you be more comfortable with this proposal, if we do not include the framework for defining regions? I understand that it is not ideal to generate _regions_ by two different mechanisms.

author: JordanYates

body:
> I'm not sure I follow you here, sorry. As in the example reserved regions should be located far from the image sections, possibly at the end, otherwise as stated before you would get a linker error. If we get no linker error we can be pretty sure that no Zephyr variable is going to be allocated there (pretty much everything in Zephyr is inside some section).

I am trying to explore the combination of two concerns. Firstly you state that sometimes you have no control over where these special memory sections should be placed. The second is that the location that you place the first `reserved-memory` section at is now essentially the end of application RAM, baring other dedicated `reserved-memory` sections after the first.

Using your example:
* SRAM0 starts at 0x40000000, 128MB (Ending 0x48000000)
* reserved starts at 0x42000000, 32KB (Ending 0x42008000)

How do variables get placed in the memory region <0x42008000 - 0x48000000> now?
Using less than 32MB of RAM is fine, as that fits before 0x42000000.
Using more than 32MB of RAM will never compile, because it overlaps with `reserved`.

Therefore by adding this `reserved-memory` section, you only have automatic access to 32MB of RAM instead of 128MB.
For your example you can just move the address, but what about for those regions which must be at defined addresses?

Note that I don't think there is necessarily a solution to this problem, I just think it has been ignored. In this particular example, the 'best' thing to do would be to shift all of your application ram to start at 0x42008000, at least then you get ~95MB of RAM instead. This was another benefit of the partition approach, for this example you could just switch `zephyr,sram` to `sram_end` (from your previous comment).

This is my reasoning as to why the Linux approach may not be the best for us. With dynamic memory allocation you just allocate around `reserved-memory`, whereas we are doing all of our memory assignment at link-time.

body:
> In that case it feels like this PR (or a precursor) should be addressing/fixing the existing in-tree usage of reserved-memory.

This is what I tried to do adding the `linker-section` property. The sections are created only if this property is present, otherwise nothing is done, and the existing in-tree usage of reserved-memory are still valid.

> Using your example:
> 
>     * SRAM0 starts at 0x40000000, 128MB (Ending 0x48000000)
>     * reserved starts at 0x42000000, 32KB (Ending 0x42008000)
> 
> How do variables get placed in the memory region <0x42008000 - 0x48000000> now?

We have two cases:
1. Nothing is placed in that memory region and we are fine (and we know that at compile time already)
2. Something is going to be placed there and we get an error at compile time so we can fix it, possibly moving around the reserved section

I think this is acceptable TBH.

> Using less than 32MB of RAM is fine, as that fits before 0x42000000.

Yup.

> Using more than 32MB of RAM will never compile, because it overlaps with `reserved`.

Correct. And why this is a problem? I think this is a perfectly reasonable behavior. I know that this is not the same as on Linux where we can work around the region, but I think this is the best we can do with what we have right now.
 
> Therefore by adding this `reserved-memory` section, you only have automatic access to 32MB of RAM instead of 128MB.

Ok I think this point needs a bit of discussion because I think that even without the `reserved-memory` section you are only using the 32MB. All the sections (stack, bss, heap, etc...) are mapped in different sections that are allocated before `_image_ram_end` / `z_mapped_end` symbols, that means that the space between `_image_ram_end` and `__kernel_ram_end` is available for reserved sections.

Let's make an example, `samples/synchronization` for `qemu_cortex_a53_smp`. With no reserved memory regions defined, the end of the map file shows:
```
0x0000000040060a78                __data_ram_end = .
0x0000000040061000                . = ALIGN (_region_min_align)
0x0000000040061000                _image_ram_end = .
0x0000000040061000                _end = .
0x0000000040061000                z_mapped_end = .
0x0000000048000000                __kernel_ram_end = 0x48000000
0x0000000007ff7000                __kernel_ram_size = (__kernel_ram_end - __kernel_ram_start)
```
My question is: can we say that all the variables (in data, bss, heap, stack, ...) are allocated somewhere before the `_end` symbol so that we can safely use the space between `_end` and `__kernel_ram_end` to host the sections for the reserved memory regions?

If we agree on this point (and please, correct me if I'm wrong) then the presence of the `reserved-memory` sections is not reducing at all the available memory, we are just using some space that it wouldn't be used anyway.

> For your example you can just move the address, but what about for those regions which must be at defined addresses?

Yes, agree that we have a problem when the regions at a defined address overlap with the used portion of the memory, but there is no easy solution to that. In that case the user should find a way to change the address.

> Note that I don't think there is necessarily a solution to this problem, I just think it has been ignored. In this particular example, the 'best' thing to do would be to shift all of your application ram to start at 0x42008000, at least then you get ~95MB of RAM instead. This was another benefit of the partition approach, for this example you could just switch `zephyr,sram` to `sram_end` (from your previous comment).

I don't think that you can always move the RAM location as you please (I'm thinking for example when using Zephyr as EL3 payload with TF-A), but if we agree on the point above I think that this is not even needed given that we are not going to use the full 95MB anyway.

> This is my reasoning as to why the Linux approach may not be the best for us. With dynamic memory allocation you just allocate around `reserved-memory`, whereas we are doing all of our memory assignment at link-time.

Totally agree, I'm just trying to come up with a poor man's implementation of that :smiley:
