body:
> Technically true, but the meaning of reserved-memory has changed from: "A way to define a memory range in devicetree for any purpose" to "A way to define a memory range in devicetree, and if you add this special flag, and the range is in RAM, you will get a linker section". It's not the end of the world, but it doesn't feel great.

That's probably accurate, but I do not see why this is a problem: we're shaping reserved-memory to a more flexible definition, where it can accommodate the needs of different use-cases. The reserved-memory concept is not widely used in Zephyr today (as you mentioned there are ca 15 uses of it, and at least 2 uses on defining flash regions are missuses and needs to be corrected), so it will definitely not result in any considerable "noise" in the Project. The solution ensures backwards-compatibility with respect to the existing usage of reserved-memory, anyways.

> but that is starting to look a lot like a RAM fixed-partitions 😄.

Well, might be. But I do not think the intention is to partition an image RAM into fixed-partitions. The main intention is to reserve some RAM inside the image for exclusive use and/or attribution.

True, we do, currently, use the reserved-memory to define allocated RAM in multi-image builds, so that is not new in this RFC, though. Reserved-memory has been promoted as a better way to describe how to allocate RAM in multi-image builds, instead of using fixed-partitions: I recall the community argued that fixed-partitions were suitable to describe actual flash partitions, but  did not favor extending fixed-partitions usage on RAM.

body:
Clarification on how it works (perhaps I should make this clear in API). The key pair can be either dynamic or static.

To use dynamic key:
1. Set `pub_key_set` to `BT_MESH_PUB_KEY_OOB`;https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/include/bluetooth/mesh/main.h#L115
2. Call `bt_mesh_prov_local_pub_key_cb_register` to retrieve generated public key before provisioning starts to send it OOB;https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/include/bluetooth/mesh/main.h#L304

Dynamic pair re-generated on every provisioning attempt (as without OOB Public Key). The user callback will be called every time when a new public key is generated. Perhaps, this won't happen, if the key pair is re-generated implicitly by BLE stack before the provisioning happens.

To use static key pair:
1. Set `pub_key_set` to `BT_MESH_PUB_KEY_OOB`;https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/include/bluetooth/mesh/main.h#L115
2. Initialise `public_key` and `private_key` pointers before provisioning is started;https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/include/bluetooth/mesh/main.h#L117-L120

In case of static key pair, DH key generated directly in provisionee module instead of using controller: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/subsys/bluetooth/mesh/prov_device.c#L149-L150
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/subsys/bluetooth/mesh/prov_device.c#L346-L348
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/fa57145f180e1249948b273c7e2dc006ce53f21e/subsys/bluetooth/mesh/prov_device.c#L312-L338

body:
> So, let me be explicitly -1 on it, and suggest to make a bisect to find what broke the correct behavior and look into fixing it.

The problem I faced (no DHCP server) was introduced by this change specifically:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/commit/d44b4252b7fbfe8e02c807d2a6b3baf66876d8e2 (which came as a part of a larger rework https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/30995). The exact problem is that GW address is cleared on an interface on DHCP startup, so it's no longer possible to send packets to the outside network (we can discuss whether it's correct or not).

But, even with a DHCP server around (I've tested this scenario as well), I'm still not convinced if setting a static address first is a right approach. In my case, the sample established TCP connection, downloaded some data, and then after DHCP kicked in (it starts after a random backoff now), my device got assigned a new IP address, which became a problem. No more packets from the previously established connection could reach the device, so the open socket just kept hanging on the `recv()` call waiting for data that'd never come. 

I'm not sure what Linux does in this case, but maybe a correct way would be to invalidate the socket if the IP address it was bound to was removed from the system? Another point is whether the statically configured IP address should be removed in that case, probably not.

So you are totally right that we don't need this feature in most drivers, but supporting multiple compatibles in one driver is already possible.

It looks like this:

```c
#define DT_DRV_COMPAT vnd_foo
#define DEFINE_FOO(inst) ...
DT_INST_FOREACH_STATUS_OKAY(DEFINE_FOO)
#undef DT_DRV_COMPAT
#define DT_DRV_COMPAT vnd_bar
#define DEFINE_BAR(inst) ...
DT_INST_FOREACH_STATUS_OKAY(DEFINE_BAR)
```

As long as the resulting device structures can be supported by the same callbacks, it works fine. That should be the case here since it's really just about different delays and color mappings, and you are changing the bindings and driver code to be generic about that.

body:
> The removal of the old API should follow the stable API process, right @carlescufi ?

For every stable API (and Bluetooth is one of them) there are two ways to modifying it:

- Deprecate the old one, introduce a new one. Maintain the deprecated one for 2 releases, then remove it
- Follow the [Stable API change procedure](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/reference/api/api_lifecycle.html#introducing-incompatible-changes) to avoid going through deprecation

So it's one or the other, but it needs to be one of those.

body:
@rlubos :

> The problem I faced (no DHCP server) was introduced by this change specifically:
d44b425 (which came as a part of a larger rework #30995). The exact problem is that GW address is cleared on an interface on DHCP startup,

Thanks for bisecting and finding the culprit commit. So, apparently clearing should happen not on "DHCP startup", but only when a valid IP address (and other config) was received/confirmed over DHCP.

> But, even with a DHCP server around (I've tested this scenario as well), I'm still not convinced if setting a static address first is a right approach.

I'm not sure the word "right" is the right one to use here. It should be *possible* to have both static IP config and DHCP enabled, and it should work as described above (and as Linux solutions work) - static IP config should be used until DHCP config is fully received and confirmed, and switchover should happen in as atomic way as realistically possible. What we have now is effectively a race condition between static config and DHCP, when just enabling DHCP leads to conflict with static config, even if DHCP won't really be used (i.e. when there's no DHCP server around, and DHCP requests sent from a Zephyr device won't be responded to). 

> In my case, the sample established TCP connection, downloaded some data, and then after DHCP kicked in (it starts after a random backoff now), my device got assigned a new IP address, which became a problem. 

And in my case (I usually run with direct device-host connection, i.e. without DHCP), the app downloaded some data, then DHCP kicked in and overthrown the proper config, and everything hanged. And the only solution is to disable DHCP in the config. That's why I say we have been having a regression for some time now, and why I say this patch just masks the issue instead of properly resolving it. (Again, this sample specifically had this configuration to ensure that static IP + DHCP works in an expected way - failing us to have a proper unit test for that.)

> No more packets from the previously established connection could reach the device, so the open socket just kept hanging on the recv() call waiting for data that'd never come.

That's orthogonal issue. It's quite well-known that one can't write real-world robust applications without timeouts for I/O (in particular, networking) operations. This sample was intended to be a simple one, and was written before we had timeout support for recv/send. We now have it (TODO: check that we actually have support for both by now), so if you'd like to add timeout for recv() here, I'm +1.

Note that IP may change under app's feet at any time. For example, DHCP has lease time, when it ends, a device should query again and may get a different IP address, and lease time may be 5min or so. That's again why I say that this patch just masks the issue, and that instead we should value this sample's config as something which exposes the issue and allows us to manage it (hopefully even improve over time).

Finally, we have had https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/7630 for quite some time, raising attention to these issues. That's why I'm keen to at least preserve/recover previous state of affairs, and not mask/deteriorate it.

> I'm not sure what Linux does in this case, but maybe a correct way would be to invalidate the socket if the IP address it was bound to was removed from the system?

These ideas is what's #7630 dedicated to. But those are outside BSD Sockets API, and the baseline is that interface vs sockets layers are separate in the network stack, and each works independently, and there's a generic timeout mechanism available for apps to catch *any* connectivity issues on the socket level - timeout.

> Another point is whether the statically configured IP address should be removed in that case, probably not.

I see no ambiguity here (taking Linux experience as the baseline) - if DHCP is enabled on/for interface, it overrides interface's IP address - once the address is successfully received. From Linux PoV, if I'd like to have both static and DHCP address on the same interface, I'd need to create a virtual sub-interface (e.g. eth0.1), and have static IP on eth0 and run DHCP on eth0.1. (Other trickier option may be to settle that DHCP overrides if's *first* IP address, so way to have both DHCP and static is to configure the latter as 2nd).

@jukkar 

> Having both static and dynamic (DHCP) address set to the interface can lead to these weird connectivity issues.

The talk is more about co-existence of static and DHCP configuration on the interface, where static is the default/fallback, and DHCP overrides it, once successfully received - without race conditions.

> Most likely the addresses are allocated from different subnets and we are not able to use the static addresses after the DHCP has managed to allocate an address. Then we are left with system that might not be able to communicate anywhere without first closing the sockets.

That's realistic situation anyway (any network connection may break/stall for many reasons, including those beyond IP addresses being changed behind app's back), so an app should be ready to deal with those (standard generic means for that is having timeouts on I/O operations, and when those fail, retry the entire connection attempt).

body:
> Maybe it is possible to move the "positive" definitions (setting it as a linker region, ...) into the usage by the driver (if required). And to leave the negative definition only in the reserved-memory: reducing/splitting the SRAM section. There also exists the possibility to add a "positive" definition using region@...

I'm not sure I fully understood your proposal but that looks like similar to what @JordanYates is proposing. So basically there are two proposals on the table right now.

1. My idea is leveraging this PR. This solution doesn't touch SRAM but each `reserved-memory` node is creating an overlapping region to SRAM containing a section. Since you won't get any error if two sections are overlapping when one is empty we have to be sure that the reserved-memory region contains a "filling" variable so that you get a linker error if you are stepping over something else in SRAM, in that case you simply relocate your reserved-memory region to a different address. This proposal has the problem that you can access the reserved-memory region only by direct memory pointers (because of the "filling" variable) but that is usually not a problem. On the other hand it's an easy solution, you don't touch your SRAM and as long as your reserved memory nodes are not stepping over something important, you can organize your memory regions pretty easily.

2. @JordanYates proposal is more convoluted but what he is proposing is basically using for the reserved-memory node a non-overlapping memory region. This means indeed that when you add a new reserved-memory node, you have to shuffle and reorganize your memory map (for example splitting the SRAM if the reserved-memory region is in the middle) manually to accommodate things. For example with 2 reserved memory nodes you will have two regions for those and your SRAM split in 3 parts and you also have to think which one is the biggest / more suitable to host your .bss / .data / etc...

Do you have a different proposal?

> > You squashed your work in a commit that has just been merged in main instead of rebasing on the top of the main branch (your commit is then also containing the work from this commit )!

It seems OK now, looking forward to your comments. My guess is that there will be some discussion, so a few words to explain the state of the suggested commit.

- it preserves backward compatibility with the original API, the sample/boards/bbc_microbit/display works - almost - unchanged.
- what is changed is that the new driver uses a NRF hardware timer. It can be chosen in order to resolve conflicts, but so the project file must activate the chosen timer. I don't understand Kconfig enough to make this more automatic, maybe somebody has a suggestion.

- Before opting for pixel based refresh (which means 2500 interrupts per second), I tried line based multiplexing. As expected, the line based multiplexing has a problem with the parallel current in case of several LEDs in the same line active. To make it short, as the current drain rises there is a voltage drop and this results in lower luminosity.  It turns out that with a very small ISR, the system load resulting from the refresh is something like 0.4%. It also turns out that it is much easier to write modular code that works for both matrices (9x3 for V1 and 5x5 for V2). A single table encoding the two pins connecting each LED and representing the topology is sufficient.

There are a few improvements possible, at least for micro:bit v2: For instance, either cathode or anode could be substituted by a PWM output. As a result, one might without additional cost change the brightness. Also, if someone should find the brightness too low, it is possible to change from standard drive to high drive. Inspite of pixel oriented refresh, with high drive the display is blindingly bright.

- The final topic concerns the API. The original API has a completely useless argument to all functions, the driver object. It is clearly preferable to have it statically allocated, but then why pass it around. So right now, I put two header files, one for compatibility, the other without these arguments. Otherwise, I think that the API does what is expected of it.

Thank you for your opinion.

body:
During the dev-review meeting there was a concern by @d3zd3z regarding the definition of a fixed erase block in a partition.

First of all: as the flash device is known in the flash partition there is no limit what so ever to define a `get_sectors` routine.

More important, why making a fixed setting (configurable in devicetree):
a. Most applications use a fixed erase-block-size,
b. WITHIN a partition support of varying block sizes would be highly questionable, this is certainly not supported by any system I have seen.
c. It would allow easy definition of a block-size for use in block-devices.
d. It would allow very easy definition of the number of sectors used by nvs/fcb: size/erase-block-size, no need to do whatever code to step over sectors.
e. By defining it at the partition level there is no need to define it again inside a subsystem (e.g. sector-size and sector-number in nvs). 
f. As the value is valid as long as it is a multiple of the page-size, it is possible to change the value so that it best matches the requirements.

> All extensions, that are currently not required, should be moved to separate PR; this is extension to structure that takes memory space and has not been proven, in code change, to be needed so far.
> Inclusion of `erase_block` and `read_only` should be in separate PR, and discussed there; discussion on them distracts from the main purpose of the PR: is this the valid and ready replacement for the current functionality of flash map API.

@de-nordic, thanks for the comment. This PR proposes a new api to work with partitions, it is not meant ONLY as a direct replacement of what we have now. At the moment we do NOT have a good way to work with partitions (as illustrated by the comment of @jfischer-no during the dev-review meeting). The PR aims at providing a API to work with partitions. It does however still takes into consideration that it is also to be used by the flash_map API so that a transition from flash_area to flash_partition is not impossible.

As this is a PR it is open for improvements and I am always open to discussions about why a certain solution/addition was chosen.

Regarding the addition of read-only: it has been possible for a long time to make a partition read-only, it was however neglected by the flash_area API -> this is a correction, that should be in the initial PR.

Regarding the addition of a erase-block-size: this does not increase the size at all, it reduces the size as there no longer is a requirement to find out the sector size using the `get_sectors` routine. Suppose in the present solution we need to get the sector-size and there is a `get_sectors` routine, everytime we need the `get_sectors` routine there will be a pointer to this routine inside the code. The size of this one pointer is what is taken up by the `erase-block-size` in the proposed solution, the `get_sectors` routine is removed from flash and this is what is saved.

The question is "are heterogeneous sectors needed inside a partition ?", my proposal answer is "No" and use that as a means to reduce code. If the answer is, "Yes, we need that because then I can ...", a revision of the API would be needed (I do not consider "this is how we have it at the moment" a valid "Yes").

If this is just a question about naming, would it not be better to specify a "default-erase-block-size" instead of specifying "erase-block-size", no problem.

Regarding other discussion topics: "should the `flash_partition_check` be inside the API ?" My answer would be "No", this is not a property of a partition but of an image inside a partition. So IMO `flash_partition_check` should be removed.

Depends of designation: if it is for streamed, sequential, data, or image of an application or data that is read only then
no, because "sectors"/"pages" are erased as data crosses from one to another; the `erase_block` is then useless;

In case of file systems: yes;  you can not reliably write efficient file system when your sectors change in size and if system does not use direct flash/mtd/magnetic device sector size, it will affect wear and/or speed.
Btw. the problem of non-uniform "sectors"/"pages" is nearly completely relevant to internal flash of SoC.

The FAT file system is an example of the problem: we define sector, for compatibility, to be 512 bytes, but on nrf flash it is written to 4096 byte pages, this means that each time one of sectors is to be written, there is possibility that the entire page needs to be erased and rewritten. Addition of the "erase_block" in API that should only limit flash access by offset and size is another level this can be broken or misconfigured.

I guess that the `erase_block`  would collect several pages as one bigger chunk: not useful for image/stream writes; bad for file systems.

The `flash_pages_info`, the flash_area_get_sectors` may need fix instead.

None. The flash partitioning, as the any other partition scheme, like MBR, GPT, Amiga RDB, BSD label, and so on, should never dictate sector size (effectively erase block), it may dictate partition start alignment, but not sector size - this is always taken from the hardware for software to decide what to do with the info.

This may be moved to separate unit or as library function. The removal of functions that are considered non needed is separate issue.

body:
Regarding handling flash devices where the erase blocks vary in size. So far, everything I can find that uses MCUboot on these types of devices, always limits it to a set of sectors that have the same erase size. Although MCUboot has a bunch of code to try and support partitions that don't have constant sector sizes, I'm not sure how well this actually gets tested. The only configuration I see as needing to be supported is when the upgrade slot is an external device, in which case it can have a different erase size than the main device.

I would suggest we try to propose simplifying the use of variable erase block sizes within MCUboot, and if we can successfully do that, then having this new API just return a simple erase block size.

This could still be supported on devices with varying block sizes, as long each individual partition does not cross a boundary between sizes.  For example an ST device has 4 16K blocks, a 64K block, and 3 128K blocks. Typically, MCUboot resides in a 64k block, and the 3 128k blocks are used for images. The 16k blocks are used for persistent storage.

If anyone is aware of an MCUboot configuration where it tries to store code images in a partition where the block differs, please let us know.

author: Laczen

body:
> b. Should the flash partition API always use the erase block size retrieved from a flash page API or should it be possible to specify a block size in the partition configuration (by no means limiting the usage to only this block size) ?

It makes me uncomfortable when the flash API doesn't convey information about the true characteristics of the underlying flash device. Sometimes, this gets implemented writes that silently read/erase/write with the idea that they will help out application code that isn't expecting flash devices to be complicated. This can result in devastating data loss if power is lost between the erase and the data being rewritten. The loss situations of lying about erase blocks seems less significant, but there are still possible scenarios.

The conclusion I draw from this, is that if we do decide to drop the variable sector size mapping part of the API, then we are also asserting that partitions can never contains blocks of different sizes. For example, in the ST 4*16+64+3*128 device, there could be one or more partitions covering the 4 16K blocks, a partition covering the 64Kb block, and 1 or more covering the 3 128Kb blocks. But, a partition that includes say the 4 16K blocks and the 64K block (stating that there are just 2 64K blocks) should not be allowed.

As far as I can tell, all of our use of the ST device is this way, and I'm trying to investigate to see if there are any other configurations that people use. Given that MCUboot doesn't really test these varying-block-size partitions, I don't have high expectations that the code works, either.

body:
@de-nordic, @nvlsianpu, @d3zd3z, I have been thinking about the variable block size problem, here is what I have come up with:

a. An optional parameter block-size can be specified for a partition.
b. When this block-size is specified `flash_partition_get_ebs()` returns this optional parameter.
c. When the block-size is not specified and FLASH_PAGE_LAYOUT is enabled `flash_partition_get_ebs()` returns the constant block size (if it is constant), if it is not constant it returns an error-code (`-EINVAL`).
d. A function `flash_partition_get_block_of(fs, off, &block)` that returns the block-offset (in the partition) and the block-size of the address `off` is pointing to. This function will be different based on the FLASH_PAGE_LAYOUT property.
e. When FLASH_PAGE_LAYOUT is not enabled and the optional parameter is not specified the partition is considered as one erasable block (so `..._get_ebs()` returns the partition size).

This way:
a. Variable block sizes are supported, and construction of "sectors" is also supported,
b. There is a way to detect a non-constant block size for a user that needs it,
c. There is a way to "short-circuit" the flash page layout when it is known that the device has a constant blocksize,
d. By default nothing changes if FLASH_PAGE_LAYOUT is selected.

@de-nordic, Your reaction is rude and impolite.

From the start I have stated that this PR was NOT a replacement or a quick adaptation of flash_area. It is a proposal API to work with partitions.

The proposal allows the writing and reading and erasing of blocks in a partition and also provides some other functions that can be handy when working with partitions on flash.

It also guarantees that when using this API there will be no accidental overwrites of data stored in read-only partitions.

It also adds a **optional** property that allows a partition to specify a erase-block-size that is larger than(or equal to) the erase-block-size that is dictated by the hardware erase block size. This is usefull for users that could take advantage of it and allows significant reduction in image size. Yes this can be wrongly defined, but so can a hardware pin in the dts, when someone modifies a dts it is expected that there is basic knowledge on hardware limitations. **There is no intention (and there never was) to limit erases to this specified block size.** 

As examples where this optional property can be used:
a. To define a sectorsize (and thereby sectorcount) in nvs and fcb,
b. To define a blocksize (if possible) on a partition that has different hardware erase-block-sizes internally, but is used by a system that expects constant block sizes,
c. To define a erase-block-size for a block device that would store multiple blocks on one erase-block and where the hardware page size is no good fit. As an example of this a UBI like logical block to physical block translator that would store 512 byte blocks on a 1024 byte page size system.
d....

@nvlsianpu, thank you for trying to negotiate, but I can't see any good reason to remove both read-only and the optional erase-block-size from the API.

@de-nordic, remove yourself as a reviewer.

According to the specification MshPRFv1.0.1 5.4.2.5 Distribution of provisioning data:

``` sh
Upon receiving the Provisioning Data PDU from the Provisioner, the device shall decrypt and authenticate the provisioning data, 
Upon successful authentication of the provisioning data, the device shall set the network key (identified by the Key Index), set 
the IV index, set the IV Update procedure state based on the IV Update Flag, set the Key Refresh Phase based on the Key Refresh
 Flag, and assign unicast addresses to all device elements starting from primary element using consecutive range of addresses 
starting from provided unicast address value. Upon successful completion of the address assigning procedure, the device shall 
respond with a Provisioning Complete PDU to confirm that it has been provisioned. If the address assigning cannot be 
successfully completed, the device shall assume that provisioning failed and respond with Provisioning Failed PDU with the Error 
Code parameter set to Cannot Assign Addresses.
```
Therefore I agree with trond's suggestion(https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/36721#issuecomment-878286532) that this PR will be closed (although I don't really want to).

body: @ppryga Maybe someone can confirm this, but as far as I understand it, when device we request read from returns `BT_ATT_ERR_NOT_SUPPORTED` we handle this response as normal, but we also try again reading using `gatt_read_mult`. We expect `BT_ATT_ERR_NOT_SUPPORTED` from devices that support CORE spec <5.2, so not supporting `EATT`. So we test if maybe they support `gatt_read_mult`. This PR doesn't get rid of this fallback method; this PR gives tool to request `gatt_read_mult` straight away, when we know the second device doesn't support `EATT` or maybe we know that characteristic lengths are the same and we want to use more efficient method.
author: KKopyscinski

body:
@KKopyscinski I'm not author of the code but... For me, it looks like the fallback implementation that was provided to give possibility to read multiple varying length characteristics without change in API (that is fixed by this PR).
Consider situation described in my last comment: one tries to read #N variable length characteristics. 
In case the other site does not support `EATT` but supports reading of multiple characteristics then he will get response based on `ATT_READ_MULTIPLE_RSP`. This line will be used to call user callback function: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/2759fc79147467e727c80dbbe3e2fb896361c7fd/subsys/bluetooth/host/gatt.c#L3941
In case of `ATT_READ_MULTIPLE_VARIABLE_RSP` there may be a number of call to user callback function:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/2759fc79147467e727c80dbbe3e2fb896361c7fd/subsys/bluetooth/host/gatt.c#L3991-L4008

After merge of your PR, the user may expect to receive callback related with `ATT_READ_MULTIPLE_VARIABLE_RSP` only, due to setting `params->multiple.variable == true`. 

Also content of PDU in calls of user callbacks will be different:
- for `ATT_READ_MULTIPLE_RSP` it will be tuple of values
- for `ATT_READ_MULTIPLE_VARIABLE_RSP` it will be tuple of pairs length, value.

I'm not sure it the implicit fallback solution is a right decision unless clearly stated in the API description.
Also If I were the end user, I would like to have a possibility to disable the fallback.

body:
@Thalley GATT does not expose different callback for different sub-procedures for `bt_gatt_read`. 

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/2759fc79147467e727c80dbbe3e2fb896361c7fd/include/bluetooth/gatt.h#L1348-L1362

Handling of responses for `bt_gatt_read` depends on sub-procedure called. In case of this PR `gatt_read_mult_rsp` and `gatt_read_mult_vl_rsp` are responsible for delivery of results of `bt_gatt_read` call to end user.

`gatt_read_mult_rsp` provides complete PDU received from peer device: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/2759fc79147467e727c80dbbe3e2fb896361c7fd/subsys/bluetooth/host/gatt.c#L3941

`gatt_read_mult_vl_rsp` provides response on a per-characterictic basis (loop that iterates over length, value tuples):
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/2759fc79147467e727c80dbbe3e2fb896361c7fd/subsys/bluetooth/host/gatt.c#L3991-L4008

So handling of responses if different depending on sub-procedures.
If read-multiple-variable-length-characteristics is expected and user receives complete PDU filled with multiple characteristics values, the PDU will be interpreted wrongly as **single characteristic value**.

@KKopyscinski 
In my humble opinion, fallback call to `gatt_read_mult` may lead to errors in application level. Thus it should be removed.

There is a major issue with the current implementation of this driver. The peripheral has a limitation that is also documented in the hal API that is used to set/change the PWM period:
[SCTIMER_SetupPwm](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/hal_nxp/blob/6d34c83c485865c25f90456d00e054947ca54978/mcux/drivers/imxrt6xx/fsl_sctimer.c#L240)

In short: the PWM period is not (really) reconfigurable (hal API/implementation limitation) and shared between all channels (peripheral limitation), only the pulse width is changeble per channel. Changing it for one channel changes the period for all. The driver does not prevent that, but it should.

I have tested it with the lpcxresso55s28 board (should be the same IP core) and the blinky_pwm example that fails because the limitation (driver errors out after changing period for more than numer of available channels.)

To make the driver usable for now with the limitation and minimal changes, the period could be fixed after first configuration.

body:
Before doing any more changes, I'd like to have a clear roadmap on where we want to go, otherwise every PR will take ages to merge and as a result we'll keep having a device PM subsys that is far from solving the PM problem. I think that if the goal is clear, and the current PM subsys status is well understood/recognized, things will be easier. I have the feeling that device PM in particular is _sold_ as ready when it is clearly not, and, as far as I know, I'm not the first person to mention that.

Let's take a couple of examples to illustrate my argument:

- The `ctrl_command` argument was, in theory, added to support arbitrary commands. The reality, however, is that it has only been used to set/get the device state (with a command name `PM_DEVICE_STATE_GET/SET`, same prefix as actual device states). I think everybody agrees that keeping local states is, in general, a bad idea. Removing the "get", we're left with a single command to set the state. So in reality, the callback is de-facto being used with an _action_, that is, we combine a "set" command with a "state" argument. An example to make it clear: `"set + active" == "resume"`. The `void *context` was replaced in the last release in favor of a `uint32_t *state` and now with `enum pm_device_state *state`, meaning a generic command can hardly be implemented now. So the reason to keep `ctrl_command` doesn't hold anymore. What this PR does in the end is to continue the same design pattern (use states as actions), just removing a redundancy (the ctrl_command), so I don't see what is wrong with this approach as an intermediate step to a proper solution as suggested in #36125.
- The runtime API is another example of something that has existed, but nobody (except a single driver) uses it. It lacks proper documentation and usage guidelines, it doesn't handle device dependencies, etc. Let's talk about a problem I have already mentioned with this API. It basically puts devices into `ACTIVE` or `SUSPEND` states. But what about `LOW_POWER`? Let's see: according to the specs, `LOW_POWER` should be used when context is not lost. In many devices this holds for low power states, so a driver for such device will pick `LOW_POWER`. But then, how can runtime PM be implemented? What happened in reality: most drivers handle all the "low power states" the same way, which is wrong and leads to inconsistent behavior (it's incompatible to implement low power/suspend/off the same way). This is a common pattern in the PM subsystem: there are many APIs that have been created without really analyzing if they can solve a real problem.

My feeling is that the PM subsystem was designed in a rush, with a quick implementation that likely solved immediate problems, but it is now showing its limitations and requires some fundamental changes. We're not talking about some fixes, API extensions, etc. but a refactor/re-write in some areas. This is difficult, painful and likely means a period of some instability, but it is sometimes necessary to make progress. And let's be honest: we'll not either get it 100% right this time.

body:
Hi @bdkrae.

Thanks for adding support to the mcux driver.

I'll make the change for the boot priority.

The other changes you requested are specific to handling SoCs where the MDIO registers are shared with Ethernet driver. This isn't always necessarily true and may not be going forward. Conceptually the MDIO is just a bus. Ethernet is a peripheral. They are different things and need different drivers. We'd be making API and design decisions to accomodate architectural decisions made by specific SoC designers to comingle the two into the same register speace. I don't think that is the way to go. It doesn't scale to every sitaution. Also a PHY can use I2C, or SPI, or SMI for communication. This was the reason I created the PR in the first place -- to break the forced coupling of PHY to MDIO. We can't assume that MDIO driver will always be needed or present when Ethernet is.

I think the better approach to accomplish what you want is to have your mcux ethernet driver invoke functions in your mcux MDIO driver directly; for example to complete the MDIO part of an interrupt task. Similarly both MDIO and Ethernet drivers can call the same shared function to initialize the peripheral clocks and registers that is aware of double initalizations. 

It is important to ensure that either driver compiles and works without the other, or at least the Ethernet works without the MDIO driver. So some macro checks or weak functions may be necessary. We want to support cases where the user needs the SoC's ethernet driver but the PHY doesn't use MDIO.

> I am considering whether an approach where `gatt_read_mult` is handled the same way as `gatt_read` and `gatt_read_mult_vl`, i.e. the callback is called for each entry. The callback handling of `gatt_read_mult` and `gatt_read_mult_vl` has seemingly been implemented by two different people 4 years apart, which probably explains why they were not implemented in the same way.
> 
> The documentation of `bt_gatt_read_params` nor `bt_gatt_read_func_t` really describes the intended behaviour or either multiple reads. Maybe @Vudentz or @sjanc can weigh in here.

iirc the problem is that for the non-VL procedure we don't know the actual length of each attribute/handle to break them down, so past qualification test this API is pretty useless, also since the client can't really know in advanced if the server would comply with the length it basically unreliable even if we were to add an API for user to enter the expected length, it is just a guess the server could in turn return a different length which would cause unexpected results.

Because of the above I would argue that there is just 2 procedures in GATT that can be used, Read or Read Multiple Variable Length, if the later is not supported the former should be used instead for each handle.

Also if we were to make changes to the API perhaps it would have been better to split them into bt_gatt_read and bt_gatt_read_multiple and either remove the old Read Multiple procedure entirely or make it clear that is unreliable by design and so client has to take action to parse the entire response which would most likely limited to be used for qualification purpose.

body:
> iirc the problem is that for the non-VL procedure we don't know the actual length of each attribute/handle to break them down, so past qualification test this API is pretty useless, also since the client can't really know in advanced if the server would comply with the length it basically unreliable even if we were to add an API for user to enter the expected length, it is just a guess the server could in turn return a different length which would cause unexpected results.

For most GATT services the characteristics are fixed-lengths and the client will absolutely know this. For those (which is by far a majority of characteristics), it absolutely makes sense to use the read multiple fixed-length request for performance reasons. 

> Also if we were to make changes to the API perhaps it would have been better to split them into bt_gatt_read and bt_gatt_read_multiple and either remove the old Read Multiple procedure entirely or make it clear that is unreliable by design and so client has to take action to parse the entire response which would most likely limited to be used for qualification purpose.

Given the above, where the upper layers (i.e. the specific GATT profiles) determines whether on not it makes sense to use variable or fixed length reads, I think this could make sense. 

So basically 

- if the client knows that 2 or more characteristics are fixed length, it could (should?) use read multiple fixed length
- if the client doesn't know, or knows that 2 or more characteristics are variable length, it could use the read multiple variable length
- else simply read a single characteristic at a time

The current GATT API doesn't support the above choices for the client. The current API is simpler but with more potential overhead, and it begs the question whether or not it really makes sense to modify the API, as @Vudentz also mentioned, to accommodate the additional performance potentially gained by using fixed length reads at all.

No unfortunately the client doesn't know it, not without proper caching support which we don't have, also if you are reading a known characteristic UUID you should use Read by Type procedure, not Read Multiple, since the later is prone to handles changes while the former you just give the range where the could be so there is no chance for the server to respond with an unexpected result.

> > Also if we were to make changes to the API perhaps it would have been better to split them into bt_gatt_read and bt_gatt_read_multiple and either remove the old Read Multiple procedure entirely or make it clear that is unreliable by design and so client has to take action to parse the entire response which would most likely limited to be used for qualification purpose.
> 
> Given the above, where the upper layers (i.e. the specific GATT profiles) determines whether on not it makes sense to use variable or fixed length reads, I think this could make sense.
> 
> So basically
> 
> * if the client knows that 2 or more characteristics are fixed length, it could (should?) use read multiple fixed length

I recommended to never use the fixed length given it is unreadable since we cannot determined if the server would return the expected length, for attributes of the same type Read By Type shall be used.

> * if the client doesn't know, or knows that 2 or more characteristics are variable length, it could use the read multiple variable length
> * else simply read a single characteristic at a time
> 
> The current GATT API doesn't support the above choices for the client. The current API is simpler but with more potential overhead, and it begs the question whether or not it really makes sense to modify the API, as @Vudentz also mentioned, to accommodate the additional performance potentially gained by using fixed length reads at all.

What I was trying to suggest is something along these lines:

bt_gatt_read:
 - Read procedure
 - Read by Type procedure

bt_gatt_read_multiple
  - Read Multiple VL procedure
  - Fallback to bt_gatt_read to read handles one by one if Read Multiple VL is not supported.

The result callback can probably remain the same for both API since these procedures allow the verify proper responses, this should cover what we currently have without bloating the API with a procedure we can't verify the response has been properly formatted.

body:
> @tejlmand Thank you so much! the PARENT_SCOPE solved the issue. 

Great to hear.

> Any how I think that this feature is nice and it works the same way for other params like dts_root.

The difference here is that the additional roots are for the build system, so that it allows board, dts, etc. out of tree.
All the roots contains files that integrates closely to the build system itself, like Kconfig or CMake files.

The syscall is a include folder, which is of course important for the source files being compiled, but not an integrated part of the build infrastructure as such.

So it would not really be a `root` per se.

CMake already offers functionality for include folders, so we should be careful not to re-invent our own mechanism here.
Note: the root description above is not covered as a CMake feature, and thus makes sense as part of module description.

> At least documentation should be added. What do you think?

I think that sounds like a good thing.
This could possibly be done in a generic way, so that it covers specifying Zephyr CMake variable from a Zephyr module in general.

And then we keep the CMake part inside the CMake code where it really belongs.

Hi @gmarull ,

Cypress require by pin configurations, see below:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/374aab1ea383f4eb86f3a3089123133913f666de/dts/arm/cypress/psoc6-pinctrl.dtsi#L11-L16

I'm not complete sure if with states we can represent this SoC. However, if we can continue to define by pin + by group, it can be advantageous.

This is the autogenerated devicetree documentation:

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/374aab1ea383f4eb86f3a3089123133913f666de/dts/arm/cypress/pinctrl_cypress_psoc6.h#L73-L83

Since properties are defined direct on pins, that allows create a common API between gpio and pinctrl .

It can work if the properties defined at states are propagate to all pins that are defined inside that state. This way we can have both definitions and maybe share a common API between gpio and pinctrl.

This will allow less rework on Cypress/Atmel boards because it will be necessary only create the pin groups.

body:
I've heard that the main concern against this PR is that it tries to introduce multi-image building, which should better be handled at the build system level. However, I will try to explain the purpose of this PR from my perspective.  
The main goal of this PR is to add tools allowing for performing more complex test scenarios in Twister. The current workflow is quite limited. It 

1. builds
2. flashes
3. check results

 of a single image being flashed on a board and doesn't allow for any interaction with the board during the test. MCUboot tests require more steps within a single test. Three independent images are built and signed, each image is flashed consecutively on the same board, and then the board is reset. The output is verified after each step. This kind of test is currently not supported.
In my solution, I am using the already existing build system. Each image is built independently with its own arg, there is only a wrapper in Twister, that allows to switch between each build catalog and allows to have the workflow executed under a single test scenario. 
IMO ability to perform more complex testing scenarios should be the part of the test runner, i.e. Twister. Like in MCUBoot tests, where a reset of a board is required and the behavior of the firmware is tested. My PR proposes tools for easy implementation of such tests with the introduction of test stages that a user can define in a testcase.yaml.  The stages library can be expanded to allow for more interactions during a test.  In particular, the plan is to allow scenarios like:

1. build an image
2. flash it
3. verify the output
4. reset the board
5. verify the output

The point of the PR is to automatize steps that a user would have to perform manually during a more complex scenario testing.  IMO having such orchestration under the build system instead of the test runner would obfuscate the workflow of such tests and would be harder for developers to implement. My idea was to provide a simple way of adding configurable test stages on a testcase.yaml level which are then interpreted and executed by twister.  
@nashif @galak @mbolivar-nordic @carlescufi what are your thoughts on this topic? Who else should also be asked?
author: PerMac

body:
To add to @PerMac's arguments, I think this approach would allow us to replace the BabbleSim test shell scripts with a standardized Twister approach. This would make it much easier to add tests based on BabbleSim (especially for external repos, which cannot hook into the current BabbleSim test system at all), and we wouldn't have to run it as a separate stage in CI. 

I made #33388 to make this happen a few months ago, but abandoned it in anticipation of this PR, which resolves most of the issues I encountered. Neither the build system, buildkite or the github actions provide sufficient functionality to implement this at the moment.

Add a patch that fixes an SMP regression on APL.  One part is straightforward: I accidentally removed code that unmasked the IDC interrupt on the target core.  That's benign on 2.5 where the startup-on-IDC behavior is handled by a state machine outside the interrupt controller, but on earlier hardware that's a software handler in ROM!

The other bit is sort of voodoo: the new scheme sets up the RPO memory mapping "TLB" registers, which is required on 2.5 where we handle the hardware handoff ourselves.  But trying to re-write them to the same values already set by the ROM is causing hangs.  We never used to do this, and it's needless since the ROM already does it, so remove.  But I don't know why that shouldn't work.  Maybe the cache controller (which has active lines for the region) is messing things up?

body:
OK, indeed @lyakh found the magic.  That irq_enable() was also setting the Xtensa INTENABLE SR, not just the second level interrupt controller.  So the interrupt would be able to reach the core but would still be masked by the CPU itself.  Under Zephyr-internal code, that was hidden by the fact that the timer driver initialization on the second core (which shares the same L2 interrupt) was then enabling it before any user code ran.

But on SOF, secondary core initialization happens later, and the IPC task run immediately after core start needs to be able to run synchronously **on that core**, and can't wait for a timer setup.  Instead it was being picked up on core 0 and failing.  (Which is sort of a SOF bug, actually -- if the task has to run on a specific core for correctness it should be pinned to run only on that core, can fix later.)

body:
Some pros/cons on storing or not a reference of `struct pinctrl_config` in `struct device`.

## Option 1: No references in `struct device`

This is the current approach in this PR.

Pros:
- Drivers that do not require pinmux do not waste extra ROM space. This is a relevant point on systems where `num(non-SoC device drivers) >> num(SoC device drivers)`

Cons:
- More driver boilerplate. Drivers need to store themselves a reference to `struct pinctrl_config`. See `.pinctrl_config = PINCTRL_DT_CONFIG_GET(UARTE(idx)),` in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/37572/files#diff-ad7eb7605ae0d455f16d9a4183fcbaca5249e8e6f8cc7338c5dea4f1d48bd453R1906
- Pins remap at runtime require an extern declaration to `struct pinctrl_config`. See `PINCTRL_DT_CONFIG_DECLARE(DT_NODELABEL(uart1));` in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/37572/commits/bd3f0b2326d1a688af7c81c2858f727400d3a837#diff-39e938c0575d0168b69e290223f5030982743802760c68e5846c58aee04bcfb7R12
- It is a bit more difficult to do pinmux operations from outside the driver, since there is no mapping between `struct device` <> `struct pinctrl_config`. For example, the `init` state would require a bit more work (e.g. store configs in a special linker section that can be iterated at early stages, and let driver take care of setting `init` back if it gets de-initialized).

## Option 2: Reference of `struct pinctrl_config` in `struct device`

PoC available here (was initial version of this PR): https://github.com/teslabs/zephyr/tree/rfc/pinmux-device-storage

Pros:
- Less driver boilerplate. We can go as far as zero driver boilerplate. This is actually the Linux approach. A device that only uses a single state (i.e. `default`) does not need to do anything regarding pin control (not even during initialization).
- No need to declare `struct pinctrl_config` in runtime case. See `PINCTRL_DT_CONFIG_DECLARE(DT_NODELABEL(uart1));` in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/37572/commits/bd3f0b2326d1a688af7c81c2858f727400d3a837#diff-39e938c0575d0168b69e290223f5030982743802760c68e5846c58aee04bcfb7R12
- Easier to implement things like the `init` state, a state applied at early stages (before device driver initialization) or after de-init. It could be easily done from outside the driver.

Cons:
- Drivers that do not require pinmux (i.e. all non-SoC device drivers) will waste an extra pointer in `struct device`.

body:
> Common overlays for different applications still need to be copy-pasted into each application.

Yes, such feature is outside the scope of this PR.
And regarding such feature as sharing Kconfig fragments between applications we should be careful.

Today a user can go into a sample, like `samples/net/sockets/echo_server`, and find all needed configs that will work with that sample.

If multiple samples start sharing Kconfig fragments, such as: `overlay-802154.conf` from another folder, lets say `config/common/`, then as a user I need to consider: `Is this Kconfig fragment compatible with sampleA that i'm building ?`

It makes it harder for a user to create a custom app based on an existing sample.
Today a user may simply do:
```
$ cp sample/<name> <my_repo>/app
# Adjust and extend sample to personal needs
```
but if we start placing Kconfig fragments in multiple places, users need to:
```
$ cp sample/<name> <my_repo>/app
# Find additional Kconfig fragments from folder A, B, and C
$ cp <extra-configs-dir-A>/fragment.conf <my_repo>/app
# or adjust `prj.conf` with content of said fragment.conf.

# and finally adjust and extend sample to personal needs
```

I'm not against common locations for simple settings, but we need to be careful.
Zephyr is already rather complex, and start placing additional configs at multiple locations might make it harder for users.

So we need to be very careful in such regards, and thus it is not part of this PR.

body:
> Some pros/cons on storing or not a reference of `struct pinctrl_config` in `struct device`.
> ## Option 1: No references in `struct device`
> 
> This is the current approach in this PR.
> 
> Pros:
> 
>     * Drivers that do not require pinmux do not waste extra ROM space. This is a relevant point on systems where `num(non-SoC device drivers) >> num(SoC device drivers)`
> 
> 
> Cons:
> 
>     * More driver boilerplate. Drivers need to store themselves a reference to `struct pinctrl_config`. See `.pinctrl_config = PINCTRL_DT_CONFIG_GET(UARTE(idx)),` in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/37572/files#diff-ad7eb7605ae0d455f16d9a4183fcbaca5249e8e6f8cc7338c5dea4f1d48bd453R1906
> 
>     * Pins remap at runtime require an extern declaration to `struct pinctrl_config`. See `PINCTRL_DT_CONFIG_DECLARE(DT_NODELABEL(uart1));` in [bd3f0b2#diff-39e938c0575d0168b69e290223f5030982743802760c68e5846c58aee04bcfb7R12](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/commit/bd3f0b2326d1a688af7c81c2858f727400d3a837#diff-39e938c0575d0168b69e290223f5030982743802760c68e5846c58aee04bcfb7R12)
> 
>     * It is a bit more difficult to do pinmux operations from outside the driver, since there is no mapping between `struct device` <> `struct pinctrl_config`. For example, the `init` state would require a bit more work (e.g. store configs in a special linker section that can be iterated at early stages, and let driver take care of setting `init` back if it gets de-initialized).
> 
> 
> ## Option 2: Reference of `struct pinctrl_config` in `struct device`
> 
> PoC available here (was initial version of this PR): https://github.com/teslabs/zephyr/tree/rfc/pinmux-device-storage
> 
> Pros:
> 
>     * Less driver boilerplate. We can go as far as zero driver boilerplate. This is actually the Linux approach. A device that only uses a single state (i.e. `default`) does not need to do anything regarding pin control (not even during initialization).
> 
>     * No need to declare `struct pinctrl_config` in runtime case. See `PINCTRL_DT_CONFIG_DECLARE(DT_NODELABEL(uart1));` in [bd3f0b2#diff-39e938c0575d0168b69e290223f5030982743802760c68e5846c58aee04bcfb7R12](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/commit/bd3f0b2326d1a688af7c81c2858f727400d3a837#diff-39e938c0575d0168b69e290223f5030982743802760c68e5846c58aee04bcfb7R12)
> 
>     * Easier to implement things like the `init` state, a state applied at early stages (before device driver initialization) or after de-init. It could be easily done from outside the driver.
> 
> 
> Cons:
> 
>     * Drivers that do not require pinmux (i.e. all non-SoC device drivers) will waste an extra pointer in `struct device`.

My preference is for Option #1.  We should avoid adding extra space.

We can address the extern issue the same way we do for `struct device` and add something to `scripts/dts/gen_defines.py` similar to what was done in commit 98b6e4f834d0be4fadabcfeb648b6128b9706217

> This adds very complex logic and very complex syntax to Twister, I keep hearing that twister is way too complex already with its own options.

Complexity itself is not necessarily a problem for software. The problems start when the code and functionality are hard to understand. To be honest it took me a while trying to find a way how to add new functionality within the existing workflow, mainly due to low modularity where one function does all the things. I tried to use good coding practices when writing stageslib.py, where most new functionality comes. I didn't want to modify the twisterlib.py code too much and tried to follow the existing structure only modifying crucial parts, like extracting a function to lock a single device.  Nevertheless, I am open to suggestions on what to improve in my code.

I fully agree that we want the build to be easily reproducible without twister. That's why I follow exactly the same workflow as it was used in twister for building, only the build directory is changed between builds in the background. But I think I might figure out a way to make it even cleaner and easier to reproduce.

I understand that "multi-image" shouldn't be interwind with Twister. Luckily, in MCUboot tests, there are 3 consecutive builds that don't have to relate to each other. **Would you @nashif  then agree to some temporary middle-ground solution? I can try to make the building stage working in a way, that there will be 3 consecutive calls for "west build" with clearly defined arguments, and anyone would be able to rerun it independently from twister by just calling "west build" commands that will also be printed out in the verbose output? Later on, when the multi-image builder will exist in Zephyr, we would just replace the paths from where the images are flashed?  I can also update the configuration, so it can be tested on reel_board.**

If so, could you please check other parts of my proposed solution? In most cases, Twister is just used as a wrapper, invoking other scripts, like `west sign` but within a single workflow, so a scenario could be run without interferences. 

I would like to know where are we standing now.  I've heard that these kinds of bootloader tests can be worth having in Zephyr. I am open to all suggestions related to the code/workflow and how it can be improved. However, if my argumentation for the overall idea of more complex test scenarios doesn't work for you I will have to start working on another solution for it.

The other main reason why 2.4 GHz and Sub-1 GHz should not be in the same file is that they can both be be active at the same time in a multi-phy scenario. If driver initialization were initiated from device tree, then it would make sense for each radio to have their own init macros at the bottom of separate files.

(rebase, turned I'd somehow put this on a two-week-stale tree, oops)

> What about using some sub-system or OS service for that?

Yeah, this is sort of a hole we have right now.  There are like nine different ways we use the linker to calculate bounds for heap-like memory in different contexts, and in general only on a handful of platforms.  It would be really nice to have a framework for this, even if it's a little out of scope here.

But I guess I'll note that the specific hardware being targetted by this work (the intel_adsp family of DSPs) is so complicated that I doubt a generic framework is every going to help (Four different memory types!  One of which has translation capability and bank-level power control, one is an outrageously slow window into system dram, one is low power, even one that is CPU-local.  And all of those can be selectively accessed via the L1 cache or via a bypass mapping!).   So there's a limit to how much something like that can help.

body:
> @tejlmand, would you please elaborate me about the line

Sure, the `project()` will setup needed project settings, such as the `PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR` and `PROJECT_BINARY_DIR`, which we are using in the project.

Now, originally, the `project()` function was located in the `${ZEPHYR_BASE}/CMakeLists.txt` but moved with this commit:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/commit/bb6a6e8fcca039f95d5aa0113b258e285c7504f8 for reasons unknown to me.

Note, that commit also overwrites the `PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR` and `PROJECT_BINARY_DIR` created by the `project()`.
And because we call `enable_language()` explicitly, then I assume this is the reason that things appear to work correctly in a basic case.
But I could fear that subtle errors could start to appear at unexpected locations if we remove the `project()` and only rely on those two variables being set manually, plus the `enable_language()` call.

The `project()` command also sets the `CMAKE_PROJECT_NAME`, `PROJECT_NAME`, `PROJECT_VERSION` and specifically `Zephyr-Kernel_VERSION`  variables which may be used by Zephyr modules if they so like.
For example the `Zephyr-Kernel_VERSION` can be used by a module to ensure it is only used with a known / compatible Zephyr version.
I don't know if any Zephyr modules are using this information, but the possibility is there.

body:
> Is this a breaking change for samples

No.
For example you can still have:
```
<app>
  |--- prj.conf
  |--- boards/
          |--- nrf52840dk_nrf52840.conf
```
in which case the `nrf52840dk_nrf52840.conf` will be merged with the `prj.conf` when building for the `nrf52840dk_nrf52850` board, just like today.

But if the `boards/nrf52840dk_nrf52840` is a folder, then it will be treated as the `APPLICATION_CONFIG_DIR` and config files will be picked up from there instead, for example.
```
<app2>
  |--- prj.conf                      # <--- Default prj.conf used, used for any other board.
  |--- boards/
          |--- nrf51dk_nrf51422.conf # <--- Board fragment used together with `prj.conf`, just like today.
          |--- nrf52840dk_nrf52840/
                  |--- prj.conf      # <--- prj.conf used for `nrf52840dk_nrf52850` board.
```

This also means that a downstream user can decide to only have:
```
<userapp>
  |--- boards/
          |--- boardA/
          |       |--- prj.conf
          |
          |--- boardB/
                  |--- prj.conf
```
and that way indicate that this application can only be used with `boardA` or `boardB` because there is no common `prj.conf`.

Such a construct could also be usefull in Zephyr, for example in the IPC samples where there are constructs like this:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/ef0d955758e549f39d97b07089dedc4bdd05bc0e/samples/subsys/ipc/ipm_mcux/CMakeLists.txt#L9-L15
So that only supported boards will have a `boards/<supported-board>/prj.conf`.

Note, the IPC case still need a solution for the remote board to cleanup the CMakeLists.txt file, which is outside the scope of this PR. But this PR takes us one step closer in handling this kind of cases.

All samples works the same as always per default with a `prj.conf` located directly under `<sample>/prj.conf`.

Only samples that want to use the new scheme can do so by creating a specific `prj.conf` for a given board under `boards/<board>/prj.conf` for that particular board.
That doesn't break how existing samples works.
Today the `boards/` in a sample only contains files, such as `boards/nrf52840dk_nrf52840.conf` or `boards/nrf52840dk_nrf52840.overlay` not folders.

If you are concerned for samples that might have a `boards/<board>/` folder already, then no Zephyr sample has that (already checked).

And we can't consider a downstream project that might have decided to create such a folder under boards a breaking change.
If we did so, then we could never introduce a new folder, cause somewhere downstream someone could already have been using such folder for custom purposes.

author: yperess

body:
So... thinking about this designwise. You don't want to be using a waitq here, it's not providing any benefit.  The waitq mechanism is designed to be a priority-sorted container of threads (backed by either a dlist or a rbtree).  But the sorting isn't helping, because the design of the API is to enumerate over the whole queue every time anyway.

Instead: use a simple dlist to store the threads in a list (you can union that node storage into the existing queue node).  The resulting code will be smaller and faster.  And because dlists have a FOR_EACH_SAFE iterator, you won't need the temporary list to store the unpended threads, you can just pull them off the list as you find them.  And so that word goes away too.

The only gotcha is that right now the scheduler internals don't provide an API to "atomically pend, but not on a waitq".  You'd need to handle this manually the way k_sleep() does (unready the thread, then suspend, and handle timeouts carefully).  Or we could augment the scheduler API to have a lower level pend(), or to take a null waitq, etc...

body:
> I have several concerns/questions about the overall approach.
> 
> Why should we introduce a new scheme for power domains when we already have the `regulator-fixed`/`regulator-sync` devices, and the corresponding DT properties in `power.yaml`?

Because they a power domain is not necessarily a regulator. Basically the idea is:
```
 - Power Domain - Electronic circuit that is supplied its input power by the
                   output power of a regulator, switch or by another power
                   domain.
                   The supply regulator may be behind a switch(s). i.e.
                   Regulator -+-> Switch-1 -+-> Switch-2 --> [Consumer A]
                              |             |
                              |             +-> [Consumer B], [Consumer C]
                              |
                              +-> [Consumer D], [Consumer E]
                   That is one regulator and three power domains:
                   Domain 1: Switch-1, Consumers D & E.
                   Domain 2: Switch-2, Consumers B & C.
                   Domain 3: Consumer A.
                   and this represents a "supplies" relationship:
                   Domain-1 --> Domain-2 --> Domain-3.
                   A power domain may have regulators that are supplied power
                   by other regulators. i.e.
                   Regulator-1 -+-> Regulator-2 -+-> [Consumer A]
                                |
                                +-> [Consumer B]
                   This gives us two regulators and two power domains:
                   Domain 1: Regulator-2, Consumer B.
                   Domain 2: Consumer A.
                   and a "supplies" relationship:
                   Domain-1 --> Domain-2
```

> 
> This PR doesn't add support for even the simplest of setups that would need to use this API, i.e. a GPIO regulator with a device on it.

Can you elaborate more ?If you declare a domain that controls the GPIO regulator and the device uses this domain the workflow is correct isn't ?

> 
> There is no support for notifying other devices on a power domain that they have suddenly powered on. There are plenty of devices that boot up in silly modes that draw milliamps, which is not compatible with low power operation.

That is a good point, I can review it.

> 
> Because there is no functionality beyond calling `pm_device_get` on any `power-domain` phandle attached to a device, any iteration code to do the above would need to be duplicated in all devices implementing `power-domain`.

Are you talking about the notification for devices using the same power domain or is it something else ?

> 
> Personally I think that power domain support needs to be a new API (`pm_device_power_get` or similar), that has explicit behavior in terms of turning on nested domains and notifying supported devices that they have had power applied/removed.

I particularly don't see a good reason to have a new API, couldn't just the subsystem ensure that when a  power domain change status your dependents are notified ? And by notified it can be as simple as call `dev->pm_control` with the right action.

body:
>> The inability to register new event subscribers at runtime is not great.

> I see your point, but as you already mentioned option to dynamically add modules is generally unsupported yet in Zephyr. In my opinion first this option should be included in Zephyr and then it should be implemented also in Event Manager.

Dynamic modules is one thing, but modules themselves can't explicitly state "I now care about these events" and "I no longer care about these events" via the API. It needs to be done via some global boolean flag in your callback (while making sure everything is thread-safe).

> Its aim is to enable easy and safe communication between modules.

Right, but there are BIG caveats in terms of how much this subsys is helping you do that. All that this really gives you over a standard `sys_slist_t` of callbacks is that you can (only) register for callbacks at compile time, iteration over the callbacks happens on the system workqueue, and some fancyness around mapping an event type to a list of callbacks. There is no deeper level of integration.

> If you have a module with an external sensor and you sample it every 2s you would probably store latest result in some variable

Coming back to the accelerometer example, this would require (768 * (N+1)) bytes of `CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE`, where N is the number of modules interested in accelerometer data. This gets large fast, when conceptually you only really need 768 bytes.

I know that I am being pretty critical without offering any solutions. I am contrasting this with an internal subsys we have that performs a similar function without the limitations above. I need to have a conversation with my management around whether we want to at least propose our solution as an alternative.

It can be done locally in the listener by simply checking if given event is enabled for me. I guess it could be moved to internals of event manager, use some bit mask and CLZ to quickly iterate over enabled listeners. It is only the optimization. 

Regarding collecting sensor samples to a database which could be shared between the modules, i don't think it is the scope of event manager. Event manager just distributes event to loosely coupled modules. One of those modules can be a database that collects the samples.

Regarding use of heap, there are discussions to add an option to use dedicated buffer space instead of heap (e.g. mpsc_pbuf could be used which serves the event manager case - multiple producers, single consumer).

Consequently, they may have an intermediate low-power state between "off" and "active" that takes less time to wake up than from a cold boot.

And that is fine, they can have internal states based on system power states. But from the kernel perspective, the device is not active. The problem in having a third stage is, how is supposed to be used ? when kernel should set a device to OFF ?  If a another device is explicitly doing `pm_device_state_set(dev, PM_DEVICE_STATE_OFF)`, it is doing it wrong, this API is not intended to  be used for runtime device power management. body:
> Not sure how I feel about making atomic_t a variable-sized type. Seems like it would be safer and more portable[1] (but obviously a lot more boilerplate) to have two types and two sets of functions?

Very good point and I considered that as well.

Technically, we could use [C11 generics](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/generic) to alleviate some of that pain. For perspective, the Linux kernel has `atomic_t`, `atomic_long_t`, and `atomic64_t`.

> Also: a wart you might want to fix while you're in here is that atomic_t has always been a typedef and not an opaque struct. There have been **many** situations noticed over the years where code was incorrectly modifying them in an unsynchronized way (which then begets discussion in review about whether or not the locking environment makes that safe or not, etc...).

I kind of want to just use `<stdatomic.h>` to be honest, but that's an even bigger change. I can't recall if C++ and C are finally copasetic in terms of `<stdatomic.h>` and `<atomic>` either, but that might weigh in to consideration.

Is adoption of `<stdatomic.h>` something that we could aim for, for the v3.0.0 Milestone?

The features that would be tricky but important to keep by adopting `<stdatomic.h>` are arch-specific implementations - `<stdatomic.h>` would push all of that responsibility back to the compiler (although that is kind of an attractive option!).

> [1] Consider the case of a 64 bit app that works fine being built on a 32 bit platform and then failing due to synchronization overflows or signedness bugs that were invisible on the larger word.

Definitely. Originally I was using `CONFIG_64BIT`, but now I've opted to use `sizeof(void *) == sizeof(uint64_t)` instead and it seems to have eliminated a number of test failures.

I also think that the current implementation would prevent 32-bit builds from using 64-bit atomics, even if the HW had the capability (but that also is not supported in the current implementation).

author: ceolin

body:
> The workflow is what I have in mind for domains, the part that I am missing is, what conditions / information you are using to decide to set a device to LOW_POWER or OFF. If this is generic enough and a common case I want to cover in the subsystem, if not, I want, at least, not interfere and let others do what you are doing.

After the domain is powered up, all supported devices are unconditionally set to `LOW_POWER`.
Just before the domain is powered down, all supported devices are unconditionally set to `OFF`.
Runtime PM handles any intermediate transitions between `LOW_POWER` and `ACTIVE`.

Currently individual devices set their own initial power state to `LOW_POWER` or `OFF` at boot depending on whether they are attached to a power domain in DT.

If you call `device_rel_power_domain` before `pm_device_put`, you'll end up in a bad state, but that's why you power it off after you are done with it, not before :).

body:
> > For platforms / drivers where there is not a 64-bit register (or a pair of lo / hi 32-bit registers), the approach I would like to take is to increment a 32-bit value when we have detected that the 32-bit counter has overflowed.
> 
> The kernel already keeps track of the uptime ticks as 64-bit integer, so `k_uptime_ticks` effectively achieves the same thing as what is described here.

Interesting. On platforms without a 64-bit counter (and in particular when a 32-bit overflow interrupt is not really available), it might make sense to simply perform some arithmetic on the 64-bit tick counter to get the "top half". E.g. 

```
// unshifted
top_half = ((k_uptime_ticks() * CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC) / SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC) & ~((uint64_t)UINT32_T_MAX);
```

> My concern is:
> 
> 1. Given that there are not that many hardware timers out there (especially for MCUs) that support 64-bit count register, does it make sense to define `sys_clock_cycle_get_64`?

I think it does make sense, for consistency. 

> 2. Should a timer hardware driver be responsible for emulating `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` when the hardware itself does not provide a 64-bit count register? IMO, the driver should just return something like `ENOTSUP` and the kernel should be responsible for such emulations/abstractions.

That's one option. Given that most 64-bit hardware timers will not overflow for thousands of years, a negative return value from `k_cycle_get()` could mean a failure (e.g. `-ENOTSUP`). Of course, returning an integer representative of the cycle count would also work. If it's semi-trivial to do that, then there might not be much of a down side.

> 3. Is `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` really all that useful when we have `k_uptime_ticks` that returns 64-bit uptime tick count?

If the hardware is there and it's supported, it really does make sense to take advantage of the numerical accuracy, because ticks are often not as accurate.

I would like to take a step back and understand why I created #38251.
 The source of confusion on my part was that I thought `DTC_OVERLAY_FILE` is analogue to `OVERLAY_CONFIG`, but it's actually analogue to `CONF_FILE`. I was not aware of that back then, but it's clear now that there is no counterpart for `OVERLAY_CONFIG` for device tree. This is something @tejlmand agreed being confusing in general.

> Honestly, I agree with you, having `OVERLAY` in those two names `OVERLAY_CONFIG` and `DTC_OVERLAY_FILE` that have very different behavior can be very confusing.
_Originally posted by @tejlmand in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/38251#issuecomment-932196029_

IMO, anything we do in the docs now won't solve the main problem -> that `DTC_OVERLAY_FILE`  variable can, in some cases, displace another file automatically -- which contradicts OVERLAY in its name. This can not happen with `OVERLAY_CONFIG`. Having same syntax but different semantics will keep confusing new users because when you're new and trying to learn new concepts you are using analogies everywhere, it's just the way people learn new stuff.

@tejlmand changes should help, as having `Otherwise` keyword will better document underlying CMake if-elseif syntax for setting `DTC_OVERLAY_FILE` variable.

> Regarding collecting sensor samples to a database which could be shared between the modules, i don't think it is the scope of event manager. Event manager just distributes event to loosely coupled modules. One of those modules can be a database that collects the samples.

While in a less constrained environment that would definitely make sense, many micro's and applications aren't going to have that much spare RAM to throw around.

My point is that to ensure sane operation of this subsystem, you are practically forced to increase the heap size by the sum of the sizes of all the individual events. Therefore, you are already adding enough memory to your application to implement this functionality for free (minus some synchronization primitives).
