body:
> I have seen a number of drivers that return 0 for `elapsed()`. But really why differentiate "ticks" and "cycles" if they are the same? From what I understand, they are different concepts, hence
> 
> ```
> CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC
> CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC
> ```
> 
> > It does seem that the value returned by `sys_clock_cycle_get` can be independent of the timer "ticks," although almost all system timer drivers we currently have seem to return the timer tick value.
> 
> Perhaps it's a good time to unify that concept.

We currently have many drivers that define something called `CYCLES_PER_TICK`, which directly correlates "ticks" to "cycles"; but, according to the documentation, that does not necessarily have to be the case (e.g. "cycle" counter/timer can be a completely separate counter/timer instance from the "tick" counter/timer, that is running in a separate clock domain).

IMO, in that case, there should be two separate drivers: low frequency timer driver for "ticks" (i.e. for tickless kernel/wakeup) and high frequency timer driver for things like nanosleep.

Ideally, the whole thing should be refactored to use some form of generalised timer driver interface that can be mapped to each timer class via the `chosen` nodes in the devicetree, as we do with the rest of the drivers; but, that is something for another day.

Perhaps, someone who architected this can give us a better insight as to why it was done this way and if there is any reason not to do what I suggested above; though, my guess is that it was likely done this way because this "system timer driver" scheme predates the introduction of devicetree.

body:
> > > 1. Is `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` really all that useful when we have `k_uptime_ticks` that returns 64-bit uptime tick count?
> > 
> > 
> > If the hardware is there and it's supported, it really does make sense to take advantage of the numerical accuracy, because ticks are often not as accurate.
> 
> The "ticks" returned by `k_uptime_ticks` are the system timer ticks.
> 
> https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/339a6bdafbe558e3ad0ea57336e2ead62e2237ac/kernel/timeout.c#L288-L291
> 
> 
> https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/339a6bdafbe558e3ad0ea57336e2ead62e2237ac/kernel/timeout.c#L269-L277
> 
> Unless you have a buggy system timer driver that returns incorrect value from `sys_clock_elapsed`, the value of `k_uptime_ticks` and the proposed `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` here should be the same (in theory).

I have seen a number of drivers that `return 0` for `elapsed()`, and anecdotally, I've usually seen ticks as some multiple of `HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC`.

But why differentiate "ticks" and "cycles" if they are the same? FWIU, they are different concepts, hence the separate config variables.

```
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_EXISTS
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC
```

> It does seem that the value returned by `sys_clock_cycle_get` can be independent of the timer "ticks," although almost all system timer drivers we currently have seem to return the timer tick value.

Perhaps it's a good time to unify those concepts.

Also, if cycles and ticks are synonymous, then we are already emulating a 64-bit counter on ***every*** system whether or not it has a 64-bit hardware counter. In that case, the current situation is somewhat at odds with @andyross' earlier change request (to not emulate a 64-bit counter).

A possible improvement would be to refactor drivers to centralize emulation of the upper 32-bits of the counter in e.g. `drivers/timer/sys_tick.c`, where there is simply a callback to increment a value when the timer driver detects 32-bit overflow.

```cpp
static uint32_t top_half;
void z_timer_cycle_32_has_overflowed(void)
{
    ++top_half;
}

uint64_t sys_clock_cycle_get_64(void)
{
    uint64_t ret = sys_clock_cycle_get_32();
    ret |= (uint64_t) top_half << 32;
    return ret;
}
```

```cpp
// int64_t for compatibility reasons
static inline int64_t k_uptime_ticks(void)
{
    return (int64_t)k_cycle_get_64();
}
```

Cycles and ticks are conceptually different counters running at different rates and potentially skewed relative to each other (i.e. on the default nRF5 configuration, you will see the two clocks drift because one is a crystal and the other a counted software loop on a CPU clocked by the unsynchronized internal oscillator).

```

So that was a purely technical part of pretty much no interest because of its simplicity.

Now here comes a bit more interesting part. Why that callback is needed in the end one may ask? What could be easier than reading back memory contents and calling it a day? The answer is - nothing. But it might be really painfully slow and take as long as it took to load the binary initially. And image of a few MiB's might easily take a handful of minutes to load. Have yet another coffee for verification step might be too much of caffeine at once. Is there a better way?

Surely there is. Instead of piping the binary over slow JTAG we may ask our X GHz target processor to do some CRC calculation in its DDR5 and then compare of the same checksum calculated on host. Looks nice!

But the problem is we need a tiny service application on target to do that. And quite probably such an applet was not a part of the image we need to verify. And those are arch-specific and could be found in `contrib/loaders/checksum`. But it's not only that. We also need to take care and act so as if there was nothing executed on the target CPU in between binary load and its subsequent execution. I.e. we need to save and then restore registers potentially polluted by the CRC calculation applet, IRQ mask etc. Moreover set a breakpoint or a watchpoint to catch the applet termination.

That said convenience here comes for a price of machine-specific OpenOCD updates, which are unfortunately missing for ARC as of today and I guess we won't get it implemented now...

Fortunately for poor folks like us there's a handy fallback to an olde good and simple full image read-back, see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/openocd/blob/zephyr-20210630/src/target/target.c#L2529:
```c
int target_checksum_memory(struct target *target, target_addr_t address, uint32_t size, uint32_t *crc)
{
...
	retval = target->type->checksum_memory(target, address, size, &checksum);
	if (retval != ERROR_OK) {
...
		target_read_buffer(target, address, size, buffer);
...
		image_calculate_checksum(buffer, size, &checksum);
...
		free(buffer);
	}
```

And so with as simple change as:
```
diff --git a/src/target/arc.c b/src/target/arc.c
index 02eedc5d3..1c4e27fce 100644
--- a/src/target/arc.c
+++ b/src/target/arc.c
@@ -2475,6 +2475,13 @@ int arc_cache_flush(struct target *target)
        return ERROR_OK;
 }

+static int arc_checksum_memory(struct target *target,
+               target_addr_t address, uint32_t count,
+               uint32_t *checksum)
+{
+       return ERROR_FAIL;
+}
+
 /* ARC v2 target */
 struct target_type arcv2_target = {
        .name = "arcv2",
@@ -2501,7 +2508,7 @@ struct target_type arcv2_target = {

        .read_memory = arc_mem_read,
        .write_memory = arc_mem_write,
-       .checksum_memory = NULL,
+       .checksum_memory = arc_checksum_memory,
        .blank_check_memory = NULL,

        .add_breakpoint = arc_add_breakpoint,
**
```

we may do much better:
```
openocd -s .../git/openocd/tcl '-c set _ZEPHYR_BOARD_SERIAL 251642000147' -f boards/arc/hsdk/support/openocd.cfg -c init -c targets -c 'reset halt' -c 'load_image build/zephyr/zephyr.elf' -c 'verify_image build/zephyr/zephyr.elf' -c shutdown

BTW see how blazing fast it is still for real Zephyr image - 0.1s!

Let us do that change at least in Zephyr's OpenOCD fork and than that PR will be good to go!

I disagree with this analysis.

If you want to draw an analogy, BOARD.dts is analogous to CONF_FILE, and DTC_OVERLAY_FILE is analogous to OVERLAY_CONFIG. There is exactly one board-level devicetree file (BOARD.dts in the board directory), and you extend it with overlays (via DTC_OVERLAY_FILE, e.g.). The application has a main configuration file (CONF_FILE), which you extend with fragments (OVERLAY_CONFIG). It's not a perfect analogy, but I think it's close enough.

```
$ git checkout add/bluetooth_samples
$ git rebase -i HEAD~3

$ git add samples/bluetooth/advertiser/

$ git commit -m scanner

$ git rebase --continue
$ git commit --amend --squash HEAD~1
$ git rebase --continue

# Git already re-ordered and marked the correct commits for squashing, so just save and close.

# Git will now open your editor for commit message adjustment, just use the good commit messages you already have.
# Remember to adjust the line length (72 char limit), see ref below.
# Save and close editor

# Push your cleaned up commit.

body:
@de-nordic thanks for the feedback and sorry for the long delay.
I have now rebased and have made several smaller modifications, most notably: 
- add w1_resume_command
- add w1_write_read
- remove Devicetree ROM ID configuration
- add helpers to be able to set the ROM ID of Sensors via the attribute interface.

Regarding the structure. Your suggestions regarding the layered API seem reasonable to me, I believe I have roughly implemented it already according to those layers, but I definitely have not separated the layers clearly enough.
The layer 1) would mostly correspond to the "link layer" of the specification and 2) would correspond to the "network layer".

For me it is not yet completely clear how you have envisioned the split into 1) and 1a).
Would 1a) simply call 1) functions, or would you allow different implementations for 1a) for devices that support multi-byte 1-Wire r/w operations like DS2485 I2c to1-Wire master. I once already considered replacing the multi-byte read and write functions from the hardware dependent API with generic ones that simply call the layer 1) single-byte rw operations multiple times, but then I realized that there exist several SPI/I2c to 1-Wire bridges(like DS2485) that support multi byte writes. I have never used such external 1-Wire Interfaces and don't know how commonly they are used, but, as you have pointed out above, we should consider those in the design of the API.
Looking into some datasheets, a so called "triplet command" is often available on those devices. The triplet command is used for search operations in the device discovery process. Should we extend the layer 1)  for such a command, or should we leave this out for now. Some external masters can even offload the complete search and crc calculation, but I think those are not so important.
Inspired by your suggestion of a combined rx/tx command I have now added a w1_write_read command. I have added it to layer 2) because it additionally executes a reset_select.

link layer (1) - network layer(2) split: Does the current status approximately match your expectations, or would you split those completely in different header files, ... ?

overdrive mode: The overdrive mode is currently not supported, should we already discuss how the API should be extended to support the overdrive mode or could this be left as a possible future addition.

Strong pullup: Some 1-wire devices have power requirements that exceed the maximal power which can be drawn over the pull-up resistor. Therefore they require the master to activate a strong pull-up after a specified set of commands. The currently proposed API does not provide any means for such actions. Strong pull ups are required by several EEPROMs and devices with an integrated crypto accelerator like the DS28E40 Authenticator.

Line level: I have not yet extended the 1) layer. Would you use this to check if a hw or sw fault may keep the line low?
I suppose the read bit command is not sufficient for your use case? In that case the serial driver should likely also avoid sending any start and stop bit during the process of this measurement and instead use the gpio driver to read the level?

Locking: Currently all network functions lock the bus to make sure the operations are not interrupted. Other zephyr drivers usually don't do this. Could you also weight in if we should transfer this responsibility to the user?

Search: The current implementation searches the bus for devices and executes a callback for each found device. Alternatives I have considered would be to 1) execute the callback only once returning all found devices and 2) instead provide two methods "start search" and "search next". The second one is used in several libraries because it's very similar to what some external 1-wire masters provide commands for.

Terminology: As far as I have understood Zephyr tries to avoid oppressive language, but generally keeps using well known identifiers until new terms are officially approved by the respective standards organization. The 1-Wire specification refers to the bus participants using the widely distributed master/slave terminology, and I don't expect Maxim to release any new documentations where they change this soon. Therefore I am curious if I should try to avoid using the master slave terminology or if doing so would only needlessly complicate the 1-Wire drivers.

body:
Great work, I like the idea that this can be run in parallel with the other tracing cores. 

I'm thinking that we could achieve a slightly neater design which allows separate tracing/tracking configurations (and object tracking without CONFIG_TRACING) if the tracing/tracking enable/disable is managed in the SYS_PORT_TRACING_X macros themselves. That is, instead of "disabling" the SYS_PORT_TRACING_X macro as a whole if CONFIG_TRACING isn't set, we could do something similar to this:

      #define SYS_PORT_TRACING_OBJ_INIT(obj_type, obj, ...) \
         do { \
            #if defined(CONFIG_TRACING)
            SYS_PORT_TRACING_TYPE_MASK(obj_type, \
               _SYS_PORT_TRACING_OBJ_INIT(obj_type)(obj, ##__VA_ARGS__)); \
            #endif

            #if defined(TRACING_OBJECT_TRACKING)
            SYS_PORT_TRACKING_TYPE_MASK(obj_type, \
               _SYS_PORT_TRACKING_OBJ_INIT(obj_type)(obj, ##__VA_ARGS__)); \
            #endif
      } while (false)

This might not be strictly necessary but let me know what you think, with both tracing and tracking disabled this would become the same as

      #define SYS_PORT_TRACING_OBJ_INIT(obj_type, obj, ...) do { } while (false)

Re: `samples/modules/tflite-micro/hello_world/sample.tensorflow` failure on `qemu_x86`

Twister reports a failure for the `samples/modules/tflite-micro/hello_world/sample.tensorflow` sample on `qemu_x86`, in spite of its output being correct, because QEMU eventually crashes and returns a non-zero exit code.

After enabling logging:
```
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: Page fault at address 0x2 (error code 0x10)
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: Linear address not present in page tables
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: Access violation: supervisor thread not allowed to execute
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: PTE: not present
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: EAX: 0x00150eb2, EBX: 0x00119441, ECX: 0x00000000, EDX: 0x0015acc0
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: ESI: 0x00150eb2, EDI: 0x00000002, EBP: 0x0015d658, ESP: 0x0015d64c
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: EFLAGS: 0x00000002 CS: 0x0008 CR3: 0x00164000
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: call trace:
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: EIP: 0x00000002
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os:      0x0010e58c (0x15df80)
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os:      0x00000247 (0x14a722)
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: unaligned frame ptr
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: >>> ZEPHYR FATAL ERROR 0: CPU exception on CPU 0
[00:00:00.030,000] <err> os: Current thread: 0x15ae60 (unknown)
[00:00:00.040,000] <err> os: Halting system
```

After enabling stack sentinel:
```
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: EAX: 0x0015d660, EBX: 0x00000247, ECX: 0x00000000, EDX: 0x0015af3c
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: ESI: 0x00000246, EDI: 0x00000020, EBP: 0x0015d60c, ESP: 0x0015d600
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: EFLAGS: 0x00000007 CS: 0x0008 CR3: 0x00164000
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: call trace:
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: EIP: 0x0014a2b7
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os:      corrupted? (bp=0x15d60c)
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: >>> ZEPHYR FATAL ERROR 2: Stack overflow on CPU 0
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: Current thread: 0x15aec0 (unknown)
[00:00:00.010,000] <err> os: Halting system
```

It looks like we have a main stack overflow that causes the main thread entry function stack to be corrupted, and eventually leads to a page fault after the main function exits.

Note that QEMU exits here with a non-zero exit code because `arch_system_halt` is called from the page fault handler, which writes to a special port that QEMU monitors and exits when set.

After increasing the main stack size for this sample, the page fault no longer occurs.

This stack usage increase is likely due to the newlib full variant, which is used by this sample, enabling the C99 format specifier support (see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/sdk-ng/commit/01fb90531b931a77b359e8c358a388056e53e795).

> I know that `cool_stuff` works with the regular board configuration, but how will a user know whether `awesome` snippet is working or has been tested with `cool_stuff` ? And how is it intended to be ensured that `awesome` snippet works thoughout the build system. (Testing all samples for this board with this snippet 😮 )

Because at least initially I see the scope for snippets to be functionality that is not specific to any particular application. If the `mcuboot` snippet is tested for a board once anywhere, you can be quite confident that it will work on any sample/application. I don't consider it much different from the current setup, how do I know that `samples/basic/servo_motor` will work on anything other than a `bbc_microbit`? We can't guarantee everything. Test all board level snippets against `samples/basic/minimal` to at least ensure they compile, and test board specific snippets in sample folders (not that I see much use for that in-tree).

> And is usb really our only good use-case on this.

No. As I've said many times in many places, there are problems that can only be solved cleanly if `zephyr.dts` is minimal and correct. This is a mechanism to provide that, which is why I believe `mcuboot` should be a snippet for every board that supports it. If that and USB are the only two in-tree uses, I still think it is worthwhile.

> This is just a non-starter for our customers, they need an easy way of getting zephyr and being able to test things as they do with any other board, not have to jump through hoops trying to get the most basic sample applications working. For our BL654 USB dongle it's basically a given that almost everyone will be using the CDC port either for Bluetooth or as a general UART and this should cater for those majority of users.

I cannot take this seriously.
1. BL654_USB, https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/arm/bl654_usb/doc/bl654_usb.html, looks like an end product, it is not a development board, even if it would (like nrf52840dongle) it is still very limited in terms of capabilities.
2. Zephyr's main tree is not a BSP for BL654_USB, you have to compromise and understand that not everything here is about your board.
3. It is obvious that we cannot enable USB device support by default at boot time. And there will always be a conflict between configuration at board level and configuration in the samples. So we need **additional option** for the boards like BL645_USB if it should have **best possible coverage** of the samples. There is no way around something like: ```
west build -b nrf52840dongle_nrf52840 samplel -- -DADDITIONAL_OPTION=y```, or a board variant like bl654_usb_usb_on, which is not better.

Taking (1) and (2) into account, what are most basic applications for BL654_USB dongle? Probably none. But useful applications, such as hci_usb or ot-coprocessor, work fine even with minimal board configuration, https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/guides/porting/board_porting.html#general-recommendations.
Finally, [considering the steps](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/arm/bl654_usb/doc/bl654_usb.html#programming-and-debugging) required to get the firmware onto the board, is the additional option (3), like `-DSHIELD=cdc_acm_shell`, to build the firmware is the least evil of all.

> This is not intending to perform a multi-image build, or even multi-image support. It is aimed at the one outcome from the "Common application configuration for boards" talk that I thought was broadly agreed on. Namely that zephyr.dts should only contain information that is valid for that particular build. There is nothing stopping #40555 from setting the "mcuboot" snippet to pull in the correct flash partitions and Kconfig settings.

I know, but in #40555 I try to avoid create two different workflows for the user when using `west build`.
What I mean with that, is that if you do `west build ... -- -DCONFIG_SOMETHING=y` today, you still do the same `west build` after that PR.
And you can opt-in to include `mcuboot` in that `west build` with `west build ... --  -DCONFIG_SOMETHING=y -DCONFIG_WB_BOOTLOADER_MCUBOOT=y`.
And as you see, you are still allowed to use the same flags as always.

If introducing a new `snippet` workflow including the `mcuboot` snippet, then I see some risks in using that `-DSNIPPETS=mcuboot` snippet workflow colliding with the `west build` mcuboot inclusion.
Let's say #40555 starts applying the same snippet, for example: `west build ... --  -DSNIPPETS=mcuboot -DCONFIG_WB_BOOTLOADER_MCUBOOT=y` then how should that be treated ?

Therefore I would prefer not to try addressing / creating a new workflow for the MCUboot use-case just now.


>  I don't consider it much different from the current setup, how do I know that samples/basic/servo_motor will work on anything other than a bbc_microbit? We can't guarantee everything. 

No, but the difference here is that for a sample like `servo_motor`, we do guarantee that it works for that board:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/102ac1ae36048c448d9756c34ccaf7fc53dabf3c/samples/basic/servo_motor/sample.yaml#L8
and similar in the docs: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/samples/basic/servo_motor/README.rst

Whereas as soon as we start placing configs in a common location we must be much clearer on what users may expect.

I do notice that your snippets follows the board, which helps a lot on the concern regarding just a single common location, but it also means a user may not know if `-s mcuboot` will work (but should find out pretty fast).

`mcuboot` and `usb` are good cases.

Hi @gmarull, @nandojve 

> I think that the `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege/nuclei/` location should be `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege/gigadevice`, since you are adding support for a GigaDevice SoC, which turns out to embed a Nuclei RISC-V core (core != SoC). If a lot more SoCs that use this core are added in the future and there is soc/ code that can be re-used, we can likely find the way, maybe `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege/common/nuclei` can be used for shared code.

I tried some possibilities, and I think the directory move to `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege/gd32vf103` is a good way.
gd32vf103 should be under the `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege` because it is implementing RISCV privilege ISA 

SoC configurations placed under `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege` force to have SOC_FAMILY as `riscv-privilege` by the conventions under the directory.
So we can't use SOC_FAMILY as the same role in the ARM directory here.
Directory name must be `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege/[SOC_SERIES]` if under the `riscv-privilege` directory.

By the way, `modules/hal_gigadevice/CMakeLists.txt` determines what driver files uses in gigadevice external modules by **SOC_SERIES** value.

Therefore, I think **SOC_SEREIS** should be gd32vf103 and as a result, the file should place in `soc/riscv/riscv-privilege/gd32vf103`. 

( I think the "SOC_FAMILY=riscv-privilege" rule makes the situation complexity.
I think it is good to add a hierarchy to determine ISA spec, or handle riscv-privilege as an attribute (such as HAS_PRIVILEGE_ISA), and make able to use SOC_FAMILY for SoC family name.)

body:
PR has been update to fix CI failures. One of the CI failures was due to a kernel test making an incorrect assertion, and I've added a change to this PR to fix it. 

`tests/kernel/threads/thread_apis` checks `k_busy_wait` by delaying for 100us, then verifying the thread usage time has increased by at least 100us worth of hardware cycles. 

However, the assertion used the macro `zassert_true(dt >= k_cyc_to_us_floor64(100), NULL);`, which is incorrect: this is comparing the elapsed cycles to the number of microseconds that pass in 100 cycles. For most fast hardware clocks, this assertion will pass, since very few microseconds pass in 100 cycles. However, for the 32KHz GPT clock this assertion will fail. The correct assertion is the following: `zassert_true(dt >= k_us_to_cyc_floor64(100), NULL);`

body:
> @lmajewski, how is it avoided that 2 little_fs systems are mounted on the same disk ?

Please correct me if I overlooked something bus as fair as I remember the `littlefs` is supposed to be used as a separate instances with respect to having `static struct fs_mount_p` and `struct fs_littlefs` structures for each instance. 

In this structure you fill `storage_dev` and `mnt_point` members, which describe the file system which you
are using. In the case of `fs/littlefs_blk/src/main.c` it is `SDMMC`.

Afterwards, the `disk_*` API uses the `storage_dev` (e.g. `SDMMC`) to identify the device to which you are referring.

> > Please correct me if I overlooked something bus as fair as I remember the `littlefs` is supposed to be used as a separate instances with respect to having `static struct fs_mount_p` and `struct fs_littlefs` structures for each instance.
> > In this structure you fill `storage_dev` and `mnt_point` members, which describe the file system which you are using. In the case of `fs/littlefs_blk/src/main.c` it is `SDMMC`.

>

I would propose to extend `struct fs_littlefs` to have this union:

```
	union {
		const struct flash_area *area;
		bool blk_mounted;
	}
```

And then check the `fs->blk_mounted` flag before the `disk_access_init()` is called in the `littlefs_mount()`
(Usage similar to fs->area usage for flash memory).

By using a suggestion from @andyross to dummy WINDOWBASE to 0 and WINDOWSTART to 1, I was able to get ESP32 SOC GDB client to calculate the An registers from corresponding ARn registers. Dummying the window control registers also seemed to fix problems I was having with the sample_controller SOC. 

Although both SOCs can now backtrace and print registers, ARns are unavailable on the sample_controller. It seemed reasonable to me to not send them since I can't get the actual WINDOWBASE / WINDOWSTART to identify the actual ARs. On ESP32, the "fake" ARns (same n as An) are only set because there's no other way for me to send the Ans due to the restricted packet size. Still, if y'all think it best that I send both An and ARn on sample_controller, I can make that change - although it might make me get rid of the SOC abstraction that lets me have one xtensa.py file.

> I basically have these concerns here:
> 
> * I think the modifications to `pm_device_action_run` will in the end perpetuate its usage for manual or custom PM solutions.
>   
>   * `pm_device_action_run` is used by system PM, however, nothing special is required there (domain is a regular device that will come before its children when resuming and after when suspending). TLDR; `pm_device_action_run` can be left as is and system PM will just work.

Not necessarily, the order will be respected but the notification that the domain is on/off not. Devices under a power domain may have handling code for these actions that are different from the simply `RESUME` / `SUSPEND`.

>   * `pm_device_action_run` is introduced in the runtime PM API, however, it does extra work not needed by the runtime API. Why not add the domain changes there?

Because this duplicates a lot of logic. I have no problem in doing it later in case of we identify it as bottle neck. But right now, I think we should keep the code cleaner / simpler.

> * Documentation should be improved to describe usages of power domains, provide an implementation example, usage guidelines, etc.
> * There is now a single implementation (TI) and a really basic test, so I'm not 100% sure this solution will fit other use cases. It would be nice to try to solve another problem with this API (IMO it's a good practice when adding new APIs like this one). This of course can also be covered with more testing/docs when not possible.

I tend to agree, but this pr is introducing a test that exercises the common workflow, checking for the notifications and devices action call order. Also, it has a documentation about the workflow, not to mention that was implemented for one board.
Require multiple targets supporting it (a new feature) for an initial implementation is raise the acceptance bar considerably. This is not breaking or change current behavior.

A implementation guideline I can come up now though.

which concerns exactly are you referring to? I looked at the list of items, most of them are about content and not structure if I am not mistaken.

Lots of details in #33725, but, the main issue we have right now is very suboptimal structure making it very difficult navigating through the docs. For example the separation between API reference and the actual documentation of a subsystem, `guides` becoming a dumping ground for new component without any structure, so you end up having 'Coccinelle' documentation at the same level we have 'Bluetooth' and 'Networking', etc.

For SoCs and hardware support in general this could end up in a new section encapsulating all hardware related information if that what is needed. Goal is to move majority of those items to top level sections that are easier to find and easier to navigate. body:
> I would not deprecate it. It is foreseen to make it work with userspace.

The main reason for removing it is that it is a redundant API. The exact same functionality - with added flexibility - can be achieved by using the existing CAN message queue API along with our triggered work APIs, which has the benefit of fitting in with the rest of the standard Zephyr APIs.

In addition, the triggered work approach does not suffer from the limitations of the CAN work queue API.

I firmly believe that driver subsystems should not wrap functionality provided by other APIs (here, the k_work_q APIs) unless absolutely needed, as this breaks the modularity and interoperability of our APIs. Here, wrapping is not needed and does not provide any gain (rather the opposite considering the limitations of the can_attach_workq() API).

@gmarull I've addressed most comments and replied another ones. Regarding error handling a pm state notification, I had replied in a previous version but basically my concerns are:

```
The problem is what do with another error.

If the domain is resuming the action happens before notify devices, in this case, if a device returns an error we would need to suspend the domain again ? And notify all devices that were already notified ?

If the domain is suspending, what to do, cancel the operation and notify devices that received the notification that the domain will continue active ?

Also, this will require all devices properly return -ENOTSUP or 0 when not handling these notifications. I don't know if initially we should be doing it, but I can change it though.
```

This inconsistency is something that can happen right now AFAIK since dependency between devices is not automatically handled, nothing prevents a device that supports be suspended when its dependents are still active.

The purpose of this new API specific to an RTC driver, is to dissociate the use of an RTC features of the Counter API driver.

Indeed, a use case can require the use of the following 2 functionnalities:
- counting external pulses (via the Counter driver)
- having an RTC time base, and wake up periodically or on programmed alarms (via the RTC driver)

Hence, the interest to separate funcionnalities in 2 drivers

body:
> * `can_attach_isr()` becomes `can_add_rx_filter()` since a filter callback function is not an interrupt service routine (although it is called in isr context). The word "attach" is replaced with "add" since filters are added, not attached. This matches the terminology used is other Zephyr APIs better.

I agree that callback is a better term than ISR. However, I think that the main purpose of the functions `can_attach_*` is to be able to receive data from the CAN bus, i.e. they are the counterparts of `can_send`. Of course it's necessary to set a filter register to do that, but still the purpose is receiving data.

We have two different ways to react on incoming data: Direct callback from ISR context or indirectly via message queue. Both functions set a filter, but the names `can_add_rx_filter` vs. `can_add_rx_msgq` suggest that `_msgq` does not. Also the `msgq` has to be detached by calling `can_remove_rx_filter`, which could be a bit confusing.

Suggestion for different names to make the relationship to `can_send` more clear than `attach`:

- `can_attach_isr(...)` -> `can_receive_cb(...)`
- `can_attach_msgq(...)` -> `can_receive_msgq(...)`
- `can_detach(...)` -> `can_receive_clear(...)`

Properly naming the function to clear the filter for both `_cb` and `_msgq` is a bit tricky. Maybe `attach` and `detach` was not too bad after all, as it somewhat combines setting a filter and receiving data in a single term.
author: martinjaeger

body:
@martinjaeger Thank you for the feedback on this! :-)

> I agree that callback is a better term than ISR. However, I think that the main purpose of the functions `can_attach_*` is to be able to receive data from the CAN bus, i.e. they are the counterparts of `can_send`. Of course it's necessary to set a filter register to do that, but still the purpose is receiving data.

I see what you mean. One could argue that a CAN controller receives all frames it sees on the CAN bus, though (it even sends an ACK for frames for which it has no matching filter). But in order to transfer a received frame to the driver/application, a matching filter needs to be installed. That's my reasoning behind the naming.

In order to solve #26541 (and as part of that, #19502) I am currently working on a similar API for sending CAN frames in sequential manner (e.g. for segmented messages spanning multiple frames). This API will be named accordingly (e.g. `can_add_tx_msgq()` and will thus match `can_add_rx_msgq()`.

I am also implementing an optional, software-based priority queue for applications where the number of available slotted TX mailboxes in the hardware is insufficient (e.g. for the MCP2515). This can be enabled via a Kconfig and will insert the software queue between the `can_send()` API call and the low-level CAN controller driver in a manner transparent to the application. I am not too fond of the `can_send()` API function name either (since it doesn't send, it merely adds the frame to an outgoing queue). I would, however, like to postpone any changes to the transmitting side of the API until that PR is ready.

> We have two different ways to react on incoming data: Direct callback from ISR context or indirectly via message queue. Both functions set a filter, but the names `can_add_rx_filter` vs. `can_add_rx_msgq` suggest that `_msgq` does not. Also the `msgq` has to be detached by calling `can_remove_rx_filter`, which could be a bit confusing.

This is why I added the documentation for `can_add_rx_msgq()` that mentions it is simply a wrapper around `can_add_rx_filter()`. With the current proposal in this PR, the symmetry lies in the driver API, which now exposes `can_add_rx_filter_t` and `can_remove_rx_filter_t`. The rest of the RX side of the API is just wrappers on top of that. We could even add a simple `can_remove_rx_msgq()` wrapper if desired.

> Suggestion for different names to make the relationship to `can_send` more clear than `attach`:
> 
> * `can_attach_isr(...)` -> `can_receive_cb(...)`
> * `can_attach_msgq(...)` -> `can_receive_msgq(...)`
> * `can_detach(...)` -> `can_receive_clear(...)`

Neither of these functions actually receive anything (they merely add a filter for receiving something at a later point), so I find their naming is just as confusing as what we have today. Function names should convey what they actually do as this makes reading the intentions of a piece of source code much easier.

body:
Ok, now it makes more sense to me. It would be quite inconsistent if we kept the `can_send` API as is.

> > I agree that callback is a better term than ISR. However, I think that the main purpose of the functions `can_attach_*` is to be able to receive data from the CAN bus, i.e. they are the counterparts of `can_send`. Of course it's necessary to set a filter register to do that, but still the purpose is receiving data.
> 
> I see what you mean. One could argue that a CAN controller receives all frames it sees on the CAN bus, though (it even sends an ACK for frames for which it has no matching filter). But in order to transfer a received frame to the driver/application, a matching filter needs to be installed. That's my reasoning behind the naming.

So it's a matter of perspective, whether we are talking about the application receiving it (i.e. only frames that match a configured filter) or the controller hardware (receives and ACKs every valid frame on the bus independent of configured filters). As the functions are part of an *Application* Programming Interface I would tend towards the higher-level perspective of the application and not the lower-level hardware implementation.

> > We have two different ways to react on incoming data: Direct callback from ISR context or indirectly via message queue. Both functions set a filter, but the names `can_add_rx_filter` vs. `can_add_rx_msgq` suggest that `_msgq` does not. Also the `msgq` has to be detached by calling `can_remove_rx_filter`, which could be a bit confusing.
> 
> This is why I added the documentation for `can_add_rx_msgq()` that mentions it is simply a wrapper around `can_add_rx_filter()`. With the current proposal in this PR, the symmetry lies in the driver API, which now exposes `can_add_rx_filter_t` and `can_remove_rx_filter_t`. The rest of the RX side of the API is just wrappers on top of that. We could even add a simple `can_remove_rx_msgq()` wrapper if desired.

I would rather not add a `can_remove_rx_msgq()` wrapper that does exactly the same as `can_remove_rx_filter()`. It sounds like it would remove the message queue itself.

> While I see value in being able to quickly configure clock tree using graphical configuration tool (e.g. when testing different configurations, taking power consumption measurements, verifying peripherals functionalities), I am not in favor of enforcing it. First of all, this moves us one step farther from device-tree, instead of one step closer. The reason is that after enabling/disabling a peripheral in device-tree (or configuring a specific clock), we will need to regenerate clock configuration anyway. Next thing is that this PR assumes that clock configuration will be platform (board) specific, while clock configuration will be both platform and application specific in lots of cases (e.g. when just a subset of clocks need to be enabled due to specific power consumption optimizations, dependent on board AND application). Lastly, this generated static clock configuration might be harder to combine with runtime clock configuration needed to be handled manually (written by hand, not generated) anyway.

I agree.

body:
A few comments:

- Communicating the list of blocks in an uintptr_t array is confusing.
  One could think they are offsets into the storage area (I had to look at the
  code to be sure). You should use an array of void pointers instead to make it
  obvious.

- You should avoid `POINTER_TO_UINT()` and its reverse twin. An int typically
  can't hold a pointer on 64-byts systems. I know the implementation casts to
  uintptr_t and it is OK here. But it makes the code clearer (and shorter)
  to perform the cast directly.

- You get uintptr_t in `sys_mem_blocks_free()`, convert them into pointers for
  `free_one()`, and then it is reconverted to uintptr_t. Addressing both points
  above would remove much of that back and forth. It is also fine to do
  arithmetic on an uint8_t pointer and assign it to a void* variable without
  any casts.

- You should consider storing the block size as a shift value. That would
  avoid relying on a divide operation which is quite slow on some MCUs.
  Linux has an `ilog2()` that resolves to a constant at compile time when the
  argument is constant. Having the same for Zephyr would be quite useful here
  and elsewhere too.

body:
I think people are not quite understanding what we are doing here. 

No one is required to use the configuration tools that ship with the NXP sdk. 

What we are including is an input file our SDK ships so that folks creating solutions with our chips can, if they want to, use the configuration tools to generate the correct clock tree values for their particular board and usage. In Zephyr, for NXP based solutions, the previous way of configuring the clock information was with manual code in the soc.c file. Someone plugged in the values in one of the boards into the NXP tool and realized the values were incorrect. So we wanted to provide a method for folks using NXP parts to leverage the configuration tools to generate correct clock values. As you can see, we also include the reference generated clock tree for the target board just as before. 

> Device tree should be the primary configuration point (cf Device Tree design goals), and this change excludes it .I reckon it is mentioned as a long term target, but yet it is excluded today (and long term target is too vague)

We also agree that ultimately the device tree is the way to go for this. We are internally investigating how we can leverage the collateral we have to automatically generate device tree and to do all the error checking of the parameters being selected.

> It is a deviation from [board porting general recommendations]:(docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/guides/porting/board_porting.html#general-recommendations).

I'm not sure which bullet item(s) we are deviating from?

> Question about .mex file upstream in tree per board (is that scalable if applied to all boards? is there any license issue ?)

The .mex file has no license issues. If there is a concern we can apply one to it to clarify. If we are worried about scaling we can consider other options for directing folks to the relevant .mex file up to and including just asking them to download the specific SDK and extracting it out of there (we don't really want to do that). The file is not directly needed to build Zephyr applications and is only being provided as reference.

body:
@Laczen The requirement to run the second core from RAM means that the second image must be linked with the first. This is because the primary core image must know the size of the second core image in order to copy it from flash to ram.

To be clear, it is possible to boot the secondary core directly from flash, but this is not preferred because when both the M7 and M4 cores share access to the flash it will result in delayed instruction fetches and slower execution. Moreover, if both cores share access to the flash, there would need to be additional application code to handle flash writes, since one core writing to the flash while the other reads would create a RWW hazard

body:
> > If this is just one possible way out of potentially multiple ways, then should this be an optional feature ?

Grant tables - is one of the base Xen-related functionalities and I think it should not be turned off separately. All of the memory sharing methods (mapping via adding to physmap etc.) are supported by hypervisor and can be used together in different situation, but grant tables require separate driver.

All Xen-related features are already can be configured by CONFIG_BOARD_XENVM (removes drivers/xen directory) and this approach looks pretty similar to Xen part in for example Linux kernel (such base functionality is configured by single CONFIG_XEN parameter). So, in my opinion, this driver should not have separate config.

I noticed after flashing TF-M that you are unable to go back to a normal non TF-M application doing some variation of:

```bash
$ west build -p auto -b b_u585i_iot02a zephyr/samples/hello_world
$ west flash
```

The standard ST debug tool is unable to erase the flash memory from the secure region, and the previous TF-M image will continue to execute when you reset.

In order to 'recover' the TF-M device, you need to run 'build/tfm/regression.sh' once, and then you can rebuild the non-TFM image and flash it.

This should probably be added as a note to the board.rst file, or the correct command to erase the entire chip should be added if there is an alternative to running 'regression.sh', which is only available as a build artifact of a 'ns' application, and may not be obvious to new users testing out TF-M and going back to a non TF-M app.

body:
> I'm not strictly against this change, but I am curious as to what the usecase is.
> 
> The application will already have been notified about the current name, and in case that the application wants to compare the changes, it could just store the name locally, so this doesn't add anything functionality that isn't already there.

Let's start with the assumption that the application needs to know the previous name of an object. I will demonstrate why this is beneficial in the next section. In the current implementation the application provides the storage for the name as mutable memory and the OTS layer changes the name prior to notifying the application. If the application needs to know the previous name then the application would have to hold a shadow copy of every object's name as we do not know which object will be updated. The name storage is potentially a large part of the memory footprint and I think this would be undesirable. An alternative would be to take a snapshot of the object name on every select as a selected object has the potential to have its name changed. This seems a bit awkward.

Now let's demonstrate why the previous name is needed. Object IDs are allocated by the OTS layer so the application has no control over an object's association with its ID. In a case where an application has the need to persist the object to nonvolatile memory and further more cannot guarantee the order upon which they are read back from this nonvolatile memory, what should be used as the "key" of the object. If we choose the ID, then upon addition of the object during every initialization we would need to rename this "key" which may be an expensive operation. However, if we choose the object name, then the key is only changed when the object is renamed (+1 time for the initial creation). So if the name is the "key" then we would need to know the previous and new name to update the "key".

In my specific use case, the objects are stored on a SPI flash which has a minimal filesystem implemented by [SPIFFS](https://github.com/pellepl/spiffs). The files are named according to the OTS object names (with the caveat that an unnamed object is named after its ID as a temporary name but these are discarded upon a disconnect). In such an implementation I could keep a shadow copy of the name which I update upon every object select but the OTS layer already has a shadow copy that it uses to do duplicate name comparison. It seems more streamlined and less awkward to just present that information to the application.

> Let's start with the assumption that the application needs to know the previous name of an object. I will demonstrate why this is beneficial in the next section. In the current implementation the application provides the storage for the name as mutable memory and the OTS layer changes the name prior to notifying the application. If the application needs to know the previous name then the application would have to hold a shadow copy of every object's name as we do not know which object will be updated. The name storage is potentially a large part of the memory footprint and I think this would be undesirable. An alternative would be to take a snapshot of the object name on every select as a selected object has the potential to have its name changed. This seems a bit awkward.
> 
> Now let's demonstrate why the previous name is needed. Object IDs are allocated by the OTS layer so the application has no control over an object's association with its ID. In a case where an application has the need to persist the object to nonvolatile memory and further more cannot guarantee the order upon which they are read back from this nonvolatile memory, what should be used as the "key" of the object. If we choose the ID, then upon addition of the object during every initialization we would need to rename this "key" which may be an expensive operation. However, if we choose the object name, then the key is only changed when the object is renamed (+1 time for the initial creation). So if the name is the "key" then we would need to know the previous and new name to update the "key".

The above seems to be based on an assumption that the object ID may change between the object being stored to persistent storage and being read back, and therefore can not be used as the "key" to the object.  I believe this is a false assumption.
Based upon reading the OTS specification it seems clear that the ID of an object does not (and is not allowed to) change.  The ID is assigned to the object when the object is created, and is tied to that specific object until the object is deleted.  (This understanding has also been confirmed to me by one of the authors of the spec.)  

If the contents or metadata of an object changes during a connection, the server may indicate this via the "Object Changed" characteristic, giving the ID of the changed object(s).  To check for changes happened when not connected, the client may use the "the OACP Calculate Checksum Op Code or by reading the Object Last-Modified characteristic and comparing these values to previously cached values", also using the object ID.

The immutability of the object ID seems to go even further: If the server sends a "Service changed", the client shall re-perform service and characteristic discovery.  The client should also "re-perform the Select by Object ID sub-procedure or Select by Object Discovery sub-procedure, since any previous selection may no longer be valid" - the implication being the the object ID must still be valid, since one can select by it.

It is correct that the application does not _control_ the assignment of object IDs.  But it certainly is informed about them, and needs to keep track of them, as that is what identifies objects in the OTS API.

So, to try sum up: The object ID _is_ the key to the object, and it is not allowed to change.  Therefore, that also seems to be the logical key to use for permanent storage.  I still have to read the PR itself (will do).  But based upon the arguments in this discussion, this change seems to go against the OTS specification, and I do not believe that it should go in.

(Another thing is that, based on the rationale for the change, there may be a need to add to the OTS implementation a way to store and restore state, to ensure that object IDs and the database do not change e.g. between reboots.)

@asbjornsabo 
You write
> The ID is assigned to the object when the object is created, and is tied to that specific object until the object is deleted. (This understanding has also been confirmed to me by one of the authors of the spec.)

Which I believe to be true, but I think what @ekohandel (and please correct me if I am wrong here), is talking about the ID between reboots. 

If we have 3 objects, {id, name}: {1, A}, {2, B}, {3, C} in OTS, we could store those as {1, A}, {2, B}, {3, C} in Flash, do the reboot, and then populate the OTS service again with the same 3 objects by reading flash. However, since the application doesn't control the IDs, then it cannot guarantee that the OTS implementation will give the same IDs for the same objects when it is repopulated. It could come out as {12, B}, {13 C}, {14, A}, and thus only the names A, B and C can be considered static across reboots. 

It is true that during a connection, the objects shall not change, and possibly even across connections, but when the device reboots, the OTS objects are basically **recreated**, and thus the statement you wrote

> The ID is assigned to the object when the object is created, and is tied to that specific object until the object is deleted. 

Doesn't really apply anymore, as the objects are deleted in the context of OTS.

body:
I have contacted several of the authors of the OTS spec with questions on the lifetime of the Object ID and whether it is supposed to persist across reboots.  Hopefully, this will turn up some information.
(So, far,  one of them has answered that he will answer "tomorrow" (which is late today CET).)

@ekohandel If it is as you  say, that this is not urgent (I thought it might be, due to the feature freeze), I would prefer for us to take the time to get info and discuss before we decide the fate of this PR.  If the Bluetooth ecosystem "expects" the same objects to show up with the same IDs, we should encourage that.  If not, the PR should be fine.

@Thalley You wrote that "However, since the application doesn't control the IDs, then it cannot guarantee that the OTS implementation will give the same IDs for the same objects when it is repopulated"
This is what I think is the root issue.  In such cases, the OTS should make it possible to re-populate to the same state.
This PR is basically a workaround for the fact that it currently doesn't.

I see at least a couple of ways to ensure persistence across reboots.
One is to change OTS to accept IDs at (local) object creation or addition.  Could be in the normal API, or could be a separate "restore" API.

Another way would be to add "store_state" and "restore_state" calls to the API.  These could have callbacks that would provide the app with a serialized data stream for storage, that could later be fed back into OTS for for restoring the state of it.  (The app would not have to know anything about the format of the stream.)

I am also wondering whether this is something (storing and restoring state) that would be relevant for other services as well.  I think it might be, in which case we should come up with something general enough to be at least usable as a pattern for other services.

```c
bool w1_reset_bus(const struct device *dev);
```
should return whether a device is present on the bus (true) or not (false). This applies to most of the functions. Is there a reason not to do it like

int w1_reset_bus(const struct device *dev, bool *devices_present);

@asbjornsabo Thanks for looking further into this. 

I am a bit troubled by the statement that even if the service handles change (i.e. the service has changed), then the IDs shall still persist. Given that a server may have multiple OTS instances, there's absolutely no way for a client to know which OTS services have changed, or which contain the object IDs that the client may have cached. The client will thus always need to "start from fresh" in that case, thus rendering the persistency of object IDs irrelevant in my opinion. 

This is still moot in my opinion as, you also write, the server may at any time (even when a client is connected), delete and create objects (and thus also recreate objects), thus essentially giving the server the power to change the objects (and their IDs) at any time. 

It is clear that you strongly expect the server the keep the IDs consistent, even across connections and reboots. What scenario do you have in mind where the IDs need to be consistent? (also keep in mind that given the above, other non-Zephyr servers may, regardless of what we end up doing, change the IDs at will by recreating them).

If we change the `should` to `shall`, as well as assuming that the released Object IDs also persists through reboots and reflashes, etc. (assuming that the device even has persistent storage....), then if a server recreates an object, it will at least have a new ID. 

@asbjornsabo Would the avoidance of reusing object IDs be any better for your scenario, or is it important that the IDs remain persistent?

body:
Outcome of my email exchange with OTS/OTP author - my questions and his answers/comments.  (Edited to summarize and for clarity.)
(I am following up with a question on "starting anew" on e.g. reboots.)

**Question:** : An issue came up, and I would like to verify my understanding of Object IDs. [...]
My understanding is that

- The Object ID is _the_ identifier for an object
- The Object ID is assigned to the object at object creation, and stays with the object, unchanged, until the object is deleted. (At which time the ID may be reused for another object.)
- Implying that the same object will always have the same Object ID

Is this correct?

**Answer:**
Your description of Object ID was quite correct.

**Question:**
What happens at e.g. reboots, or other “large” changes?
Is the server allowed to repopulate with the same objects, but with other IDs [...]?

**Answer:**
Assuming the objects still exist on the server, then all of the object metadata, including Object ID value, must be preserved
along with the objects.

**Comments related to "service changed"**
The use of “service changed” has recently been the subject of several errata corrections in the Bluetooth SIG aiming to clarify its correct usage.
When a device issues “service changed”, it contains parameters that specify a range of affected attribute handles. The significance of receiving “service changed” is that the specified range of affected attribute handles shall be considered invalid in the client’s attribute cache (usually prompting service discovery to be repeated). It does not have any significance for anything else, such as variables used at service level – i.e., “service changed” cannot be used to signify that object metadata such as the Object ID has changed.

For the reasons mentioned above, OTS and some other GATT specifications have fairly recently been clarified by errata
- https://www.bluetooth.org/errata/errata_view.cfm?errata_id=16269
- https://www.bluetooth.org/errata/errata_view.cfm?errata_id=16271)

[Y]ou are still quite correct to say that the Object ID value shall persist across a service changed. 

**Question:**
Given the current understanding, objects seem very permanent.  But I guess it is still possible for a device to shut down the OTS service, and establish a new one instead?  (Where the new service may contain objects that may happen to be the same as in the previous service.)

**Answer:**
Objects can certainly be deleted. They may be deleted by the client by using the OACP Delete procedure, or they may be deleted at the server itself (e.g., because the user uses a file manager UI on the server), or by other means that are “out of band” as far as OTS is concerned.

If the client attempts to select an Object ID that does not exist, the error message 0x08: “Object ID Not Found” would be returned.

If all of the objects have been deleted, any attempted Object List Control Point operations would receive the error message 0x07: “No Object”

**Update 2022-02-01 - Further answers, on deletion and recreation**
I think deleting all objects, and repopulating the service with new objects (which might have the same content as the deleted objects), in one example of what we have already discussed [...].

I’d like to draw attention to the requirement in OTS Section 2.7.1 (Object ID Characteristic Behavior): “…Once an object has been successfully deleted, its Object ID may be returned to the pool for re-use. However, Object IDs that have not been previously used should be allocated prior to re-using released Object IDs…”

So, the new objects (which might have the same content as the deleted objects) should get new Object IDs – which is what I think you want.

body:
> I still think that for the purpose of keeping and serving the same objects, it will still be a better solution to find a way to store and restore the state of the service, rather than re-creating the same objects with new IDs. But this PR does not prevent doing that.

Agreed, and that can in my mind be done in two ways:
1) The application gets to control the object IDs, and is responsible for storing the objects in e.g. flash and restoring them (if using RAM) on reboot. The stack will then just ensure that not object IDs are duplicated. This will require an API change.
2) The stack is responsible for storing objects in e.g. flash, and can restore them automatically on reboot. 

2) seems to be the more user-friendly version, but will require that for each object the stack obtains the object data as well. Since the object data can change at any time in the application, this sounds unfeasible to me. 1) is less user-friendly imo (the application needs to do more), but is more flexible, and easier for us to implement.

> > I still think that for the purpose of keeping and serving the same objects, it will still be a better solution to find a way to store and restore the state of the service, rather than re-creating the same objects with new IDs. [...]
> 
> Agreed, and that can in my mind be done in two ways:
> 
>     1. The application gets to control the object IDs, and is responsible for storing the objects in e.g. flash and restoring them (if using RAM) on reboot. The stack will then just ensure that not object IDs are duplicated. This will require an API change.
> 
>     2. The stack is responsible for storing objects in e.g. flash, and can restore them automatically on reboot.
> 
>     3. seems to be the more user-friendly version, but will require that for each object the stack obtains the object data as well. Since the object data can change at any time in the application, this sounds unfeasible to me. 1) is less user-friendly imo (the application needs to do more), but is more flexible, and easier for us to implement.

 Is 1) sufficient?  Does the service have other state that may also need to be stored?
 The application already knows the IDs of objects, it may also be possible to do an "intermediate" solution, where the app proposes an ID at object creation/addition, or a separate call for "re-adding", while the service still keeps control of the object IDs.
 
 A third solution would be a save/restore API as I outlined above, where the service basically dumps its state to the application, and the application does the storing on flash.

body:
> Is 1) sufficient? Does the service have other state that may also need to be stored? 

If I remember correctly, the ID is the only value that isn't controlled by the remote client or the application, and is a simple incremental solution in the OTS implementation. 


> The application already knows the IDs of objects, it may also be possible to do an "intermediate" solution, where the app proposes an ID at object creation/addition, or a separate call for "re-adding", while the service still keeps control of the object IDs.

If the service doesn't store anything across reboots, then it won't be able to keep control of the object IDs. As far as I can tell, only the one responsible for storing data in e.g. flash can keep the object IDs across reboots, and as such either the service (or rather the object manager) will need to do that, or the application will need to control the IDs if the application is responsible for storing data in flash. 

> A third solution would be a save/restore API as I outlined above, where the service basically dumps its state to the application, and the application does the storing on flash.

That is also a possibility, and the approach I had with the VCS state a while ago, e.g. just dump a state in a `void *` context value with a given size, that the application can use to store in flash and provide to the service again. Although at this point, it might just be better to have the service store it instead.

body:
> > Is 1) sufficient? Does the service have other state that may also need to be stored?
> 
> If I remember correctly, the ID is the only value that isn't controlled by the remote client or the application, and is a simple incremental solution in the OTS implementation.
> 
> > The application already knows the IDs of objects, it may also be possible to do an "intermediate" solution, where the app proposes an ID at object creation/addition, or a separate call for "re-adding", while the service still keeps control of the object IDs.
> 
> If the service doesn't store anything across reboots, then it won't be able to keep control of the object IDs. As far as I can tell, only the one responsible for storing data in e.g. flash can keep the object IDs across reboots, and as such either the service (or rather the object manager) will need to do that, or the application will need to control the IDs if the application is responsible for storing data in flash.
> 

I think I am in favor of the "intermediate" solution. There are really two phases to the application's interactions with object creation:

1. Initial phase of restoring any objects that were previously present in a service. I think in this phase, the application should not have enabled bluetooth advertising as to prevent collision of objects being added by the application and object being added by a remote client. The object manager is not thread safe at the moment anyways so this is the only way to ensure there are no synchronization issues. If there can't be any collisions then the application should be able to dictate the ID to be used. Having a per object restore mechanism makes things more flexible as a single stored object may be corrupt and can be dropped as opposed to dropping all objects if an opaque service context becomes corrupt.

2. Objects being added after the system is up and running, in this phase (which would currently be not thread safe) the application would just let the object manager allocate an ID on the fly.

So I think introducing an object restore API or augmenting the current application API for adding objects to be able to either dictate/propose the ID or let the object manager chose the ID would address these two phases.

> > A third solution would be a save/restore API as I outlined above, where the service basically dumps its state to the application, and the application does the storing on flash.
> 
> That is also a possibility, and the approach I had with the VCS state a while ago, e.g. just dump a state in a `void *` context value with a given size, that the application can use to store in flash and provide to the service again. Although at this point, it might just be better to have the service store it instead.

I think this option is hard to make power loss safe. The service would have to dump its state on every change (i.e. object addition, removal, etc.) and since the state is opaque the application cannot make optimizations to only store parts that are different.

body:
> > > The application already knows the IDs of objects, it may also be possible to do an "intermediate" solution, where the app proposes an ID at object creation/addition, or a separate call for "re-adding", while the service still keeps control of the object 
> 
> I think I am in favor of the "intermediate" solution. There are really two phases to the application's interactions with object creation:

I would be against having 2 different ways of adding individual objects to OTS, that depend on some internal state, as that could cause confusion on when to use which one. 

> So I think introducing an object restore API or augmenting the current application API for adding objects to be able to either dictate/propose the ID or let the object manager chose the ID would address these two phases.

The challenge here is of course when the device manager should use the proposed ID, or when it should use its own. Unless the ID is 100% controllable by the application or the device manager, then it won't fix the ID issue that @asbjornsabo brought up in the first place. To me, it's an either or situation. 

> > > A third solution would be a save/restore API as I outlined above, where the service basically dumps its state to the application, and the application does the storing on flash.
> > 
> > 
> > That is also a possibility, and the approach I had with the VCS state a while ago, e.g. just dump a state in a `void *` context value with a given size, that the application can use to store in flash and provide to the service again. Although at this point, it might just be better to have the service store it instead.
> 
> I think this option is hard to make power loss safe. The service would have to dump its state on every change (i.e. object addition, removal, etc.) and since the state is opaque the application cannot make optimizations to only store parts that are different.

That's a very good point @ekohandel, and I'm willing to call that option dead on arrival :) 

In many ways I'm in favor of being able to configure the OTS to automatically save and restore objects. Given that the object values are stored in the application, that may be too difficult to implement in a decent way (unless OTS simply stores the metadata, and let the application store the object value). 
If the application wants to store everything in flash, then it either A) needs to keep a copy of all the metadata, or B) need to access that when saving. In the B) case that's the same as the `dump state` option, and A) would require a significant amount of memory to pull off. 

With the split responsibility of storing data (metadata in OTS, and data in app), storing everything in flash is going to be tricky I think.

body:
> The "wx" attributes look wrong for flash. It should rather be "rx", no? Same goes for existing memory entryes you didn't modify.

Good point. That attribute is not used in any way but I'll fix it nonetheless.

> The following commit log text is confusing:
> 
> ```
>   When XIP is enabled, the code_relocation feature is used in Zephyr to
>   move the selected code (that is to copy text section, to initialize data
>   and zero bss) from FLASH to SRAM at run time and execute code from SRAM.
> ```
> 
> Isn't the purpose of XIP to leave .textsection in place and execute them from there? There may be legitimate reasons for wanting to execute (part of) the code from SRAM, but that's not what XIP usually means. Clarification would be nice.

Thank you, that means I'm not crazy :D It took a while to me understand this point but as confusing at it seems it is exactly like that.

Think about that this way: the `code_relocation` feature (in its original formulation) is used to relocate code to specified SRAM memory regions. Now, if XIP is enabled the code that you are going to relocate is taken from FLASH (because it resides there because of XIP). So in this context XIP enabled is simply telling you that the code you are relocating is being mem-copied from FLASH to SRAM.

So, I hope that makes that text a bit more clear.

On a related note, even if supported, I don't think that having `code_relocation` without XIP makes any sense (or even working) at all. But that's another story.

> Also a typo: `s/It's is desirable/It is desirable/`.

body:
@JordanYates  @mbolivar-nordic @jfischer-no I have done some thinking on this.

While I believe the `snippets` concept proposed in this PR makes a lot of sense, then I did some thinking related to the usb use-case.

We have board revisions, and a while back we discussed generalizing this into board variants (on slack as I recall it), where revision is just a specialized kind of a variant.

Now, in addition to a board providing custom variants, Zephyr can provide common variants, like a `cdc_acm`.
That may allow users to build the same board for a `cdc_acm` variant, like this:
`nrf52840dk_nrf52840` or `nrf52840dk_nrf52840@cdc_acm`

Just like boards can default to a specific revision, for example `nrf9160dk_nrf9160` --> `nrf9160dk_nrf9160@0.7.0`
Then a board which requires cdc_acm always, for example: `ble654_usb`, then building for `bl654_usb` is identical to building `bl654_usb@cdc_acm`.

And just like with revisions, it can be made visible (and testable by the build system) whether a given variant is supported, similar to what is done for the revision:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/22c0843485b5d03a8bf1de8499fe1d20d2ded3d3/boards/arm/nrf9160dk_nrf9160/revision.cmake#L6-L7

This further allow users to re-use existing infrastructure where Kconfig snippets and DT overlay may be applied automatically depending on board, variant, (and revision).

I don't see variant support in conflict with snippets, they both serve a purpose.
But the variant will allow to formalize and re-use variants between boards and make it more visible to users what variant type a given board supports.

> This neither makes sense nor is it helpful to provide a generic board-wide (or tree-wide) configuration, as it is possible with our shield support, see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/40645.

@jfischer-no Maybe you haven't noticed, but Zephyr already has different kind of board variants, both formal and informal.

Formal variant is revision.

Informal variant are those used my multi-core SoCs and secure / non-secure targets (cryptocell).

For example, the [nRF5340dk_nrf5340](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/nrf5340dk_nrf5340) board comes in following variants:
- nrf5340dk_nrf5340_netcore: variant identifying network core in the SoC
- nrf5340dk_nrf5340_appcore: variant identifying application core in the SoC
- nrf5340dk_nrf5340_appcore_ns: configuration variant identifying anon-secure application in the appcore in the SoC.

Now, especially `ns` is of interest, as it is a configuration variant, but we don't identify it using `shield` principle.
In which way is a cdc_acm configuration variant of a board significantly different from a `ns` configuration variant, or other variants mentioned above ?

This is the reason why we should formalize board variant handling in Zephyr, and have revision a specialized type of variant.
And having common baseline variant names ensures the board itself will be able to present if a given variant is supported (something the shield mechanism can never provide)

Other boards with informal variants (non-exhaustive list): [lpcxpresso54114](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/lpcxpresso54114), [nrf9160dk_nrf9160](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/nrf9160dk_nrf9160), [mps2_an521](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/mps2_an521)

> > This neither makes sense nor is it helpful to provide a generic board-wide (or tree-wide) configuration, as it is possible with our shield support, see #40645.
> 
> @jfischer-no Maybe you haven't noticed, but Zephyr already has different kind of board variants, both formal and informal.
> 
> Formal variant is revision.
> 
> Informal variant are those used my multi-core SoCs and secure / non-secure targets (cryptocell).
> 
> For example, the [nRF5340dk_nrf5340](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/nrf5340dk_nrf5340) board comes in following variants:
> 
>     * nrf5340dk_nrf5340_netcore: variant identifying network core in the SoC
> 
>     * nrf5340dk_nrf5340_appcore: variant identifying application core in the SoC
> 
>     * nrf5340dk_nrf5340_appcore_ns: configuration variant identifying anon-secure application in the appcore in the SoC.

> Now, especially `ns` is of interest, as it is a configuration variant, but we don't identify it using `shield` principle. In which way is a cdc_acm configuration variant of a board significantly different from a `ns` configuration variant, or other variants mentioned above ?

Related to configuration and devicetree, `_ns` is name agreement only, it does not provide common configuration for all boards, it depends on SoC, and in that case boards have same fragments, see nrf5340dk and bl5340_dvk for example. Of course one could add absolutely the same configuration and devicetree description for all boards that have USB device support and want to use CDC ACM as backend, but that would be stupid, and not maintenance friendly, and also not solve all problems, because it is reasonable to have separate backends for logging and shell, and another one maybe for something else. In contrast, the solution based on shield support like #40645 is omnipotent, it is combinable and works for all boards that have USB device support, whether nrf52840donge or nrf52840dk, downsream and upstream.

> 
> This is the reason why we should formalize board variant handling in Zephyr, and have revision a specialized type of variant. And having common baseline variant names ensures the board itself will be able to present if a given variant is supported (something the shield mechanism can never provide)
> 
> Other boards with informal variants (non-exhaustive list): [lpcxpresso54114](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/lpcxpresso54114), [nrf9160dk_nrf9160](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/nrf9160dk_nrf9160), [mps2_an521](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/boards/arm/mps2_an521)

body:
> > Arbitrary dts extension attributions are allowed by our schema layer, aren't they? I swear I've seen this done somewhere.
> 
> Uhm, I'm not sure I have ever seen something like that. @mbolivar-nordic can you shed some light on this?

I don't know what "extension attributions" means in this context. But there are 3 cases where a DTS property's value is available to C code:

1. It's a standard property (e.g. `reg`, `interrupts`, `ranges`) whose meaning is defined by the DT specification itself
2. There is a devicetree binding associated with the node's compatible property which defines the property's type and therefore how it should be represented in C
3. It's a property of the special `/zephyr,user` node that has "inferred" bindings and is reserved for application developer convenience

Gory details in https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/guides/dts/bindings.html#dt-bindings.

But TL;DR is that neither 1. nor 3. apply, so the value of the compatible is so that case 2 applies.
