body:
> I was thinking I'd seen somewhere some handling where it was possible for derived code (app, whatever) to add bindings to compatibles that are defined elsewhere. Maybe that was a proposal or something?

That's not possible, no. You can extend a binding on a bus-specific basis, e.g. add properties when the node appears on a SPI bus that aren't present when the node appears on an I2C bus. But you can have at most one binding file per (compatible, bus) pair in the current tooling, where the bus may be "null" if there's a "global" or bus-independent binding.

> Basically: this use of an "scratch" property for derived code seems clumsy to me. The point of devicetree as a syntax is that the nodes can have arbitrarily complicated configuration in a (sorta) human-readable syntax. It seems like sort of a wart if we can't use that here.

I don't really disagree that this is clumsy. But as a design decision, DT has to be zero overhead from the C programmer's point of view. So we have to know how to generate macros for every single node at build time, and we do that based on compatible properties in order to have some type checking and other validation in the mix. So there isn't a mechanism for general-purpose sprinkling of additional properties throughout the tree in arbitrary nodes in a way that is accessible to C.

We could debate whether it's worthwhile to add something like that, perhaps for a special predefined set of properties prefixed with `zephyr,` or so. But that's not possible today.

(I have just skimmed through the code so my understanding may be off...)

* By default, static packaging is used which only store pointers to RW strings. With deferred mode, content of those strings may have changed between calling LOG_*() and actually being printed. Is this the case, or did I miss something?

* Dictionary logging, currently, simply dumps the whole package and let the offline python script deal with decoding the packages. So these changes may affect that. Though, as long as the RW strings are inside the packages, it should be fine.

* FYI, The MIPI Sys-T backend will need to support catalog messages (which is basically dictionary logging). However, their scheme and output require tagging each arguments. So basically, instead of `printk("%d %s", 1234, "test");`, you do `mipi_printk(<pointer to "%d %s", ARG_TYPE_INT, 1234, ARG_TYPE_C_STRING, "test", ARG_END);`. And they output the tags with each argument. I think this can be done via forcing runtime packaging with tagging similar to https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/42946, with corresponding changes in cbprintf to package those tags (and ignoring them when printing through cbvprintf). The MIPI backend can take the tagged packages and send them to the MIPI library. So there will probably be some invasive changes coming.

body:
Add more suggestions for this PR.

1. No need to disable all thresholds interruptions in adc_npcx_start_scan(). 
The channels used for reading and comparing thresholds can work at the same time. Or you might lose an event detected by threshold detector when the upper layer calls adc_npcx_start_scan(). We can add the bits of channels for reading to ADCCS in adc_npcx_start_scan() and remove them in ISR.
2. No need to disable repetitive mode in adc_npcx_start_scan()
Let adc_npcx_threshold_enable_irq() and adc_npcx_threshold_disable_irq() determines the adc's repetitive mode. If there is no threshold irq enabled, we can disable repetitive mode. Otherwise, set it back to  repetitive mode.

body:
It seems to me the proposed API is not limited to physical layer of RF front ends, but it defines some link layer (or MAC) features:
* CRC
* periodic receiver
* frame filtering

I understand some radios support these features in HW, but other support more features like ACK receiving or sending, retransmissions, crypto, etc. I think we should follow one of two possible approaches:

1. Define generic PHY RF API, without any link layer features (remove CRC, periodic receiver, filtering), but with more complete list of PHY features like preamble length, preamble content, PHY header configuration, detecting energy level, detecting carrier
2. Continue already existing APIs and implement drivers for radios for specific MAC layer protocols like:
* https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/include/net/ieee802154.h
* https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/include/net/wifi.h
* https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/subsys/bluetooth/controller/ll_sw

body:
> why are the files named `.cc` and `.hh` and not just `.cpp` and `.hpp`.

There's no hard reason for it. The C++ libraries I've integrated with Zephyr so far (CHRE and Pigweed) both use `.cc`. The header extension `.hh` was selected to follow the same pattern and was needed to avoid the linter thinking that the header should be formatter for C (this was an issue with templates as clang-format thought there needed to be spaces around the `<`). I don't believe that Zephyr has a specific guideline for this yet do they? I also believe that the Unix standard is to use `.cc` which most of the Zephyr guides model after so that's why I chose it. I'm happy to change if anyone feels strongly one way or another.

@rettichschnidi, @hubertmis 

Thanks for your feedback!
This API does indeed support features that go above/beyond the physical layer. "RF frontend API" would probably
be a more accurate title.

> 2. Continue already existing APIs and implement drivers for radios for specific MAC layer protocols like:

I can see these APIs making perfect sense for hardware that only supports those protocols but the main driver for me
was multi-protocol RF devices.
I understand that having an API for *all* RF capable devices is probably impossible/impractical. On the other hand
having a separate driver for every protocol a multi-protocol device supports is also something that should be avoided IMHO.

> 1. Define generic PHY RF API, without any link layer features (remove CRC, periodic receiver, filtering), but with more complete list of PHY features like preamble length, preamble content, PHY header configuration, detecting energy level, detecting carrier

I like this approach better than `2.` but how/where would you handle the the link-layer/device-specific hardware features?
The choices I can think of are Kconfig, devicetree and public APIs.
Since this addresses hardware features devicetree would probably the most sensible choice.
Then add a public API for settings that one might want to reconfigure at runtime?

body:
> I think if we're going to respecify the API, we might go a little

Hmmm OK. I was under the impression that I had gone too far already.
More on that below.

> The name isn't great

I totally agree.

> It seems like the z_ prefix for internal names is in less favor now,
> and this is clearly an architecture API.

Well, I thought arch_* is used for kernel common to architecture calls
whereas architecture to kernel common calls always uses z_*. Here we have
the later case.

> We really don't want a third scheme in the API.  Let's fix all the
> architectures in one PR.

Not sure I understand. What third scheme?

> So maybe `arch_isr_complete()`, with the existing semantics but no
> switch handle argument, and `arch_isr_context()` which must be called
> at some point after that with a complete/valid switch handle?

Hmmpfff. I'd need an example to understand how this could work.

> Though thinking on it, the operation of `arch_isr_context()` is just
> to set the switch_handle field on the thread.  That's trivially inlined
> in C but the relevant code is almost certainly going to be in assembly
> on most architectures.  So really we'd just be specifying it as a field
> assignment anyway, maybe with a callable symbol just for
> clarity/documentation.

Well, when I said I might have gone too far above... It is about
the fact that we could simply formalize the definition of
`z_get_next_switch_handle()` where the passed handle value could
have 2 values. Either:

- The interrupted thread's handle, in which case this function returns
  the handle for the next thread to execute, which might be the same
  handle as the one passed in. The thread context must be completely parked
  when this is called.

- A NULL indicating that we want to know what the next thread to run is
  without parking the whole thread state just yet. If there is no other
  thread to run then NULL is returned. It is the responsibility of the
  caller to assign the k_thread_t.switch_handle of the interrupted thread
  with its handle value once the thread context is fully parked.

The beauty of it all is that the above already just works without any change to
the code, even with !SMP. Suffice to formalize it.

And with the explicit field assignment we won't need that tripple-pointer
argument.

And yes, the assignment is most likely done in assembly. And I would avoid
a callable symbol as this forces you to preserve active registers across
the call when a straight forward offsetable store (one instruction) can
do the job.

Yes, the problem in this PR. The power domain driver is not respecting timing parameters. This is required as many devices need to be totally depowered for a certain time before they will reset correctly. If the domain comes back up early the device can be in an undefined state.

> I don't thing we should rush a new API that is a workaround.

I agree that this is a workaround, but I don't see the core issue being resolved quickly, and the very existence of this function call makes it very obvious where updates need to be made when alternate options are available.

body:
> * why string from rodata are not cataloged but appended to the log message?

Sys-T does not use catalog for string arguments. There is no way to tag whether a string in the argument list is a string in catalog or a full string. Therefore, each string argument needs to be replaced with the full string.

> * how to parse catalog mipi syst sample? I run the sample and wanted to run `log_parser.py` with xml file as database but got error.

There is a `systprint` utility in `modules/debug/mipi-sys-t/` that needs to be built. For example, after saving the content of a qemu_x86 run in a text file, you can do `systprint -p -c <build_dir>/zephyr/mipi_syst_collateral.xml <qemu output>` to get the messages. Note that the utility looks for lines (strictly) beginning with `SYS-T RAW DATA:` for messages to be parsed. So depending on the QEMU output, the first line may not print.

My concern is slightly different. Let's say that you have only one SRAM area for Zephyr, so Zephyr is allowed to make use of this area as it pleases. If your regions for SHM and the resource table are directly pointing somewhere in the middle of this region, then it is possible that Zephyr will silently corrupt these regions writing on it.

What you usually want to do is to define several regions: one for the SRAM area for zephyr, and then separate memory regions for SHM and resource table that are well far apart.

Now, I'm not familiar with the memory map of this SoC so I was just wondering how did you choose the addresses and whether those are safe enough.

body:
Okay, let's see if I can get closer to your point.
In this example, there is a section in DDR that is reserved for Zephyr. Since the entire DDR is shared between the two processors, this section is explicitly separated into the Linux device tree.
See the definition in Zephyr:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/soc/arm/nxp_imx/mimx8ml8_m7/mpu_regions.c#L62
And the related Linux device tree node:
https://source.codeaurora.org/external/imx/linux-imx/tree/arch/arm64/boot/dts/freescale/imx8mp-evk-rpmsg.dts?h=lf-5.15.y#n22

So Zepyhr uses the DDR area:
0x80000000 (0x1000000)
And for SHM this one:
0x55000000 (0x500000)

In this case, these areas do not overlap.

But since in these multiprocessor scenarios memory usage is quite flexible and many things have to fit together (Zepyhr DT, Linux DT, linker script), it's easy to configure a system where nasty things happen...

body:
@dbaluta wrote:
> Zephyr misses a proper audio stack(?) and I think it is important to get the interfaces right from the beginning.

That's what this RFC is really all about.  The DAI interface here is aligned with SOF and has been used and supported by multiple vendors (in SOF), so it would seem like a reasonable start for this work. This DAI interface should be useful for other users in Zephyr and certainly SOF could use it (and we could move hw drivers over to Zephyr). We could of course shoot for higher level integration, but that may be a much longer road as different users might have more varied reqs.

The existing I2S interface doesn't really cut it for SOF, as SOF needs to support other interfaces (already now). But with this DAI interface, we could share a considerable chunk of code with Zephyr and benefit both projects. That's not to say we shouldn't/couldn't aim higher, but at least that's a concrete way to start.

Unfortunately, it is not possible to change the name of the resource table section. When resource table relocation is not used and a remote processor is started by Linux, Linux searches the elf for a section called ".resource_table".
For example, if '_resource_table' is used as the section name instead, Linux would no longer find the resource table.

body:
Possibly, the lock around winstream is fine (in trace_out.c) but it effectively is locking character at a time given the way printk works and the log output is setup (1 character size). Which means its very possible for two messages to get mixed up.

But beyond that there also seems to be perhaps a race in how the log backend is used itself. It doesn't seem like there's any serialization on the backend, e.g. process may be called from two contexts and corrupt the output. Something to do with log_core's panic mode flag perhaps? Since in panic mode all log calls are then processed in the context of the log call. In a SMP system this won't prevent the background log thread from continuing to happily pump out log data perhaps from the currently in process message.

I don't disagree this isn't a pretty fix, marking DNM for now, but at least something of a solution (and perhaps a cause) is known now. Will sit on it and sort out a better answer perhaps.

> Thank you very much I also get the blinky working !

One last point, at least on default board configuration, you need to add (which is the config provided on the stm32h747i_disco)
`CONFIG_POWER_SUPPLY_DIRECT_SMPS=y`
Otherwise config used will be LDO core will enter deadlock, in that case, situation can be recovered by the following procedure described in board user manual:
```
If a deadlock occurs because of a mismatch between hardware and firmware PWR settings (SMPS/LDO), the
user can recover the STM32H745I-DISCO board by applying the following procedure:
1. Power off the board.
2. Remove the 10 kΩ resistor from R143 and mount it on R144.
This changes the BOOT0 pin to 1 instead of 0, thus changing the device boot address to boot address 1
and making the bootloader start in System memory. This avoids starting firmware in the user Flash with a
wrong SMPS/LDO configuration versus the hardware board configuration.
3. Power on the board and connect using STM32CubeProgrammer (STM32CubeProg).
4. Erase the user Flash.
5. Power off the board and remove the 10 kΩ resistor from R144 and mount it back on R143.
6. The board is recovered and can be used normally with matching firmware PWR.
```

body:
> Is it necessary to implement platform code? Why not add generic code to shared_multi_heap component which would register memory regions based on device tree?

Because different platforms can have different needs. The interface to register the memory regions is now generic, the information  can be retrieved from DT, but this is not mandatory anymore.

For example a platform would want to have one single big region in DT and allocate several heaps in this region according to some peculiar scheme, etc...

I also feel like cramming even more the DT with some software configuration parameters could be a bit too much.

body:
As it turns out, simply copying the table may not be appropriate for all use cases. At least for the IMX platform, which I took a closer look at.
Although this copy is made this way in the MCUXpresso SDK sample to demonstrate its use with Linux, it does not work properly when the firmware is loaded from the user space.
Since in such a case Linux will automatically install the resource table in the new location and immediately start updating the fields of the table after starting the remote processor, this can lead to conflicts with the copy made in the firmware.

See also this [ML thread](http://lists.infradead.org/pipermail/linux-arm-kernel/2022-April/731516.html).

So since it's unclear how and if this will be fixed in Linux, I'm currently using the updated commit from this RFC (which I just pushed).
Now I first check whether the resource table has already been installed by someone else and in such a case I skip the copy process.
Since some fields of the table may have already been modified by the remote host, it is not possible to compare the full table.

Now that there's a bit more logic, I'm not sure if hiding this magic in rsc_table_get() is still a good idea.
Perhaps it would be better to create a more explicit function for this, even if that would mean that it would also require changes in the examples.

What do you think?

**Re: Failure 1**

This failure is not reproducible with the QEMU 6.0.0 (included in the SDK 0.14.0) emulating the image built using the compiler from the SDK 0.14.1, indicating that this is a QEMU 6.2.0 issue.

NOTE: This issue is only seen on the `i386-softmmu` target and not on the `x86_64-softmmu` target.

Offending QEMU commit is: https://github.com/qemu/qemu/commit/8ae5719cd4d315dba688efbfa092dd063be6f81c

Tracked in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/sdk-ng/issues/461

**UPDATE: This issue is a result of the bugs from both QEMU and Zephyr:**

* Zephyr bug: FPU control word is initialised to an incorrect value of 0 (supposed to be 0x37f)
* QEMU bug: The result of the `fldl st(0)` instruction is affected by the precison control bits of the FPU control word

For now, by fixing the Zephyr bug (i.e. properly initialising the FPU control word), the QEMU bug will no longer affect the execution of the sprintf test, and the SDK update can proceed as is.

The Zephyr bug will be fixed in #44903.

The QEMU bug is being tracked in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/sdk-ng/issues/461 and will be fixed in a future release.

> > @mrkhldn - This would be the **perfect** candidate for a pseudo-device driver + DT bindings 👀
> 
> @cfriedt, this is an interesting idea. Can you help me understand the thinking a bit more? What advantage do we get changing this into a pseudo-device driver?
> 
> @dcpleung, any thoughts on the suggested approach?

@mrkhldn, as @dcpleung mentioned, with a pseudo-device driver + DT, addresses are stored in ROM as constants and driver code can be a lot more generic. I still think it's important to support the dynamic use case, of course.

However, a kind of nice part  about it is that you get multi-instance for free. Additional coredump areas can be specified with complete independence and flexibility for dedicated memory areas in heterogenous layouts (or potentially also DMA memory, or shared bus memory, or really any logged or buffered data). This type of information is fairly helpful in post-mortem analysis.

body:
> I don't think we should go with this solution as this is globally the same as #35165 which was already rejected

@erwango The #35165 has been already accepted and pulled - the `#ifndef CONFIG_NOCACHE_MEMORY` is already present in `soc/arm/st_stm32/stm32h7/soc_m7.c`. 

And the current situation (as it is now in Zephyr repo's - `main` branch) is IMHO just wrong and reduces system performance considerably. Customers are **really** concerned about this.

With this patch we are going one small step forward - with having DCache enabled with DMA running with `__nocache` attribute for crucial buffers, which are really small. 

Some STM32 drivers do require defining the  `CONFIG_NOCACHE_MEMORY` and as a result, now the DCache is disabled for the whole system. 

This patch allows developers to use DCache and also check if their `__nocache` defined DMA buffers also are handled correctly. Until Zephyr gains proper handling of cache coherency, this would reduce the possible performance degradation (as it is **now** noticeable by some Zephyr users).

body:
> I'm just wondering if this approach to configure clocks in a generic way for STM32 MCU series is somewhat standard approach for other SoCs from this manufacturer?

The change is based on a new clock_control API which is generic and proposed in standalone [here](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/43790). I guess the feature itself is also generic as alternate clock source is also something common across vendors (with some exceptions).
This being said, the binding proposal is STM32 specific. It also differs from STM32 Linux bindings (which also differs from STM32 uboot bindings). Aim is to make a first step in direction of a more flexible clock framework as the lack of this feature is blocking in some cases (cf https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/41650 but also wake-up pin selection) and has to be implemented today per driver (cf https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/44988), which has limitations.

body:
Re-formatting the PR to introduce the octospi driver for stm32 MCUs. This version is given by the STM32Cube. Refer to the [AN5050 - Octo-SPI interface on STM32 microcontrollers](https://www.st.com/content/ccc/resource/technical/document/application_note/group0/91/dd/af/52/e1/d3/48/8e/DM00407776/files/DM00407776.pdf/jcr:content/translations/en.DM00407776.pdf)

Introducing 2 possible data modes (spi-bus-width) and 2 possible transfer rate (STR/DTR) through DTS.
Currently SPI STR and OctoSPi STR mode are supported.
The driver was tested on the disco stm32l562e_dk on a Micron MX25LM51245 octoSPI  NOR  flash  in **SPI/STR** and **OctoSPI/STR** modes with a sample like ./samples/drivers/spi_flash adapted for the ospi.
The SDFP is not given by the NOR flash : the command is not answered by the NOR of that board. This is still to be improved.
The NOR flash is able to answer to the ReadID command with : Manuf = 0xC2, Mem Type = 0x85, Density = 0x3A  

For memory configuration, only polling mode is used. DMA transfer is still to be added for NOR flash read/write operation.
Next steps to come:
- [x] check the OctoSPI DTR mode
- [x]  check the SDFP jedec operation
- [ ]   add the DMA transfer  (stm32l5x)
- [ ]   add the DMA transfer  (stm32u5x)
- [x]   adapt to other targets.

body:
Some suggestions:

Instead of having the `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` return value be entirely
arch-dependent, I'd suggest that you define it a bit more. For example,
any negative value could be an errno value indicating that suspending
was not possible for some architecture specific reason. Then a value of 0 would indicate that the system state
snapshot was taken successfully, and a non-zero positive value would
indicate that the system did actually resume from the last snapshot.

This way you won't need `arch_pm_s2ram_was_suspended()` at all as
`arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` would give you that information directly.
Some architectures have the boot reason in a hardware register (cold
boot vs wake-up from sleep) and the resume path does know it is resuming
obviously, so there would be no need for any marker/magic values in that
case.

And defining `arch_pm_s2ram_resume()` shouldn't be needed. This should
never be called by Zephyr application code anyway. At that point you
don't need to define an API for the resume side as the architecture has
to resume by returning from the `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` context and we
don't really care how it manages it at that point.

Final note: might be a good idea to mandate that IRQs be turned off when
`arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` is called, and returned from.

body:
> I'm a bit confused about this though. `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` is
> saving the context, including `lr`. That means that on resume we are
> jumping back exactly after the `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` call so IIUC
> we still need a way (outside of that function) to tell whether we need
> to go OFF or we are just resuming. How can we do that without using a
> third function like `arch_pm_s2ram_was_suspended()`?

It is the value returned from `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` that tells you.

* retval = 0: context is saved

* retval > 0: resumed from sleep

* retval < 0: error

Regardless, even the above suggestion and the original code are
fundamentally flawed in the same way. The moment you take a snapshot
of the CPU registers and you save them on the stack, you can't touch
that stack content anymore. This basically means you can no longer
return and shut down the system later as the simple fact of returning
will expose the stack to a different content i.e. your saved context
and even the caller's spilled registers could be overwritten.

So `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` _must_ suspend the system and return only
upon resuming (or in the case of an error).

Therefore you have two choices:

* `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` does perform the actual shutdown implicitly
  somehow, or

* for more flexibility `arch_pm_s2ram_suspend()` is given a pointer to a
  function (can be C code) that will be called to shut down the system
  after the context is saved so that the stack is not unwound and
  overwritten until the system is resumed.

In both cases the resume path is the same: load the saved context and return
using the saved stack pointer and lr.

body:
> I think this approach overlaps too much with CHRE. Please review the distribution of what each subsystem/module was designed to do and take another look.
> 
> Additionally, I'm not sure why we need another sensor API layer. I believe that the v2 sensor API layer should be enough to power this subsystem without a physical/virtual sensor API.

As we discussed offline, the preferred architecture is like below, with:

- CHRE handles high level sensor fusion with nanoapps based on basic sensors defined in PAL
- Sensor subsystem handles all the basic sensors and their relationships with virtual sensor, multi-clients, sensor arbitration, platform level configurations, and power management support
- Sensor device driver handles individual sensor devices

![Zephyr sensor stack](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/94332734/167382447-88f18528-ddf3-4cf7-b462-fad89598ad80.png)

And here are the reasons on why a cross-OS sensor solution must have sensor subsystem, and how it is different from CHRE and v2 API:
- By defining sensors following HID spec, sensor subsystem can easily support HID applications besides CHRE, which makes cross-OSes sensor solution possible, as HID Sensors are natively supported in [Windows](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/whitepapers/hid-sensors-usages) or [Linux](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/tree/master/drivers/iio/common/hid-sensors)
- Support platform level sensor configurations as required from OS sensing, for example, in [Windows Sensor Enumeration Properties](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/sensors/enumeration-properties), there are ConnectionType, PUID, ... properties, which cannot be supported by either CHRE or v2 API
- Support virtual sensors, this is must needed as virtual sensors are defined in [CHRE PAL](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/system/chre/+/refs/heads/master/chre_api/include/chre_api/chre/sensor_types.h?autodive=0%2F%2F%2F), for example, MOTION_DETECT, STEP_DETECT, UNCALIBRATED_XXX are all virtual sensors, and they cannot be supported directly by v2 API
- Support multiple clients and their arbitration, this is needed as one sensor might be registered by CHRE as well as other Zephyr application at the same time (as shown in figure above)
- Provide the option to make CHRE optional, even in Android, CHRE is not 100% enabled, but sensor framework (in sensor hub sits under CHRE) is must have in all Android devices. The sensor subsystem in this PR is equivalent to the sensor framework, which is mandatory for all OS sensing.

> > * Support virtual sensors, this is must needed as virtual sensors are defined in [CHRE PAL](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/system/chre/+/refs/heads/master/chre_api/include/chre_api/chre/sensor_types.h?autodive=0%2F%2F%2F), for example, MOTION_DETECT, STEP_DETECT, UNCALIBRATED_XXX are all virtual sensors, and they cannot be supported directly by v2 API
> 
> Why not? Why can't a virtual sensor be defined using the V2 API? You could make a compatible string to add a virtual sensor into the sensor subsystem that would look like:
> 
> ```
> / {
>   senss {
>     compatible = "zephyr,senss";
>     lid-angle {
>       compatible = "zephyr,senss-angle-sensor";
>       accels = <&accel0 &accel1>;
>       /* Possibly more configs. */
>     };
>   };
> };
> ```
> 
> Then in the `ssens_angle_sensor.c` you'd do something along the lines of:
> 
> ```
> #include <zephyr/subsys/senss.h>
> 
> #define DT_DRV_COMPAT zephyr_senss_angle_sensor
> 
> /* Uses the V2 API */
> static const struct sensor_driver_api_v2 angle_sensor_api = {
>   ...
> };
> 
> int angle_sensor_init(const struct device *dev)
> {
>   // senss API to use the phandles to register event processing for accelerometer events from
>   // accel0 and accel1.
> }
> 
> #define ANGLE_SENSOR_DEFINE(inst)                            \
>     ...                                                      \
>     DEVICE_DT_INST_DEFINE(inst, angle_sensor_init, ...)
> 
> DT_INST_FOREACH_STATUS_OKAY(ANGLE_SENSOR_DEFINE)
> ```
> 

It's possible to implement virtual sensors in V2 API,  but the implementation need handle multiple clients and arbitration,  then V2 API will finally become a sensor framework or sensor subsystem like this PR.  Take angle virtual sensor for example,  it's opened & configured two acc sensors,  then how does other application to access these two acc sensors ? 

Do we really need a sensor framework/sensor subsystem inside the device layer ?  For some virtual sensors, its may need other inputs from other subsystems, or even from other chip,  such as location,  network connections, and may have complex computing algorithms,  such as DSP，NN,  depends on customer requirements. 
 
Seems not suitable to put all of these inside the device driver layer.  Further more,  just with `struct device *dev` in device driver API,  I don't know how to support multiple-clients and arbitration, if my understanding is wrong, please correct me. 

That's why this PR introduced a user space sensor subsystem,  device driver layer just need handle HW related operations.

> Even with this change you'll still can't support HID without a custom transport layer. There's no way to convert `senss_sensor_value_3d_float` to the HID serialization without this layer. So given that, why not do the conversion to HID constants at the same time? Instead this API requires one of the following:
> 
> 1. An application with _NO_ CHRE will have a transport layer that translates the internal data structs to HID serializations.
> 2. An application with CHRE will need the same transport layer as above, but also:
>    a. Custom transport layer from CHRE since those sensor types will use different constants
>    b. A translation layer between the sensor framework and CHRE
>    c. The writers of an application to need to use different conventions when talking to CHRE vs the sensor subsystem.
> 
> Of course, none of these are impossible. I just don't understand why require 4 different API surfaces when you really just need 1 if you use HID only when you go off chip.

You are right, just like the conversion to CHRE (CHRE PAL), one additional HID module will be needed on top of sensor subsystem for the HID package conversion. However, the point here is not about possibility, it is about the ease of conversion.

On multiple layers of APIs, I agree it is not the ideal state for efficiency, if we only consider one type of application, this definitely can be simplified, but if we are considering multiple OSes as well as IOT sensor applications, such flexibility will require more modules to be clearly divided, and hence results in more layers.

> 
> Can you explain? I'm looking at the enumeration properties and I'm not seeing anything in there that can't be derived. Which exact aspect of this change are you referencing that is providing it?
> 

This is not fully added yet. In current proposal, we have sensor type defined following HID spec, and we have HID specific properties like change sensitivity, friendly name, manufacture, model added in API. More will be added later.

> 
> Why not? Why can't a virtual sensor be defined using the V2 API?
>

If you allow a sensor device driver (hinge angle) register another sensor device driver (accel1 and accel2), then accel1 and accel2 sensor device driver will need to support multiple-clients and configuration arbitration. Because accel1 and accel2 might be opened by motion detection driver, step counter driver as well, and different clients may request different threshold, frequency, etc.

body: All general-purpose clients (such as lighting model clients, or generic clients) support publishing. They do not specify a message to publish because it is envisioned that for the clients, the specific message depends on the end-product. For example, a certain light-switch by a certain manufacturer implementing a Generic OnOff client will always send out "Generic OnOff Set Unack" upon physical button press by the user. As long as publish callback is provided, the user application can call whichever client model API it wants as per the end-product needs. That is the idea.

body:
> It's possible to implement virtual sensors in V2 API, but the implementation need handle multiple clients and arbitration, then V2 API will finally become a sensor framework or sensor subsystem like this PR. Take angle virtual sensor for example, it's opened & configured two acc sensors, then how does other application to access these two acc sensors ?

That's not true, the sensor subsystem will still handle all the arbitration. For example:
1.  Application make a call to the sensor subsystem and asks the sensor subsystem for a sample rate of 100Hz of a virtual sensor.  Alternatively makes the direct request to the virtual sensor.
2. That virtual sensor then makes a call to the sensor subsystem requesting `accel0` and `accel1` to be at 100Hz (note that the virtual sensor doesn't call `sensor_set_sample_rate()` directly, it goes through the subsystem.
3. The subsystem gets the request to set `accel0` and `accel1` at 100Hz and will arbitrate between other requests.
 
> Do we really need a sensor framework/sensor subsystem inside the device layer ? For some virtual sensors, its may need other inputs from other subsystems, or even from other chip, such as location, network connections, and may have complex computing algorithms, such as DSP，NN, depends on customer requirements.
> 
> Seems not suitable to put all of these inside the device driver layer. Further more, just with `struct device *dev` in device driver API, I don't know how to support multiple-clients and arbitration, if my understanding is wrong, please correct me.
> 
> That's why this PR introduced a user space sensor subsystem, device driver layer just need handle HW related operations.

The implementation of the virtual sensor will rely on the sensor subsystem (as per my example above). If you want to add an extra layer of security around this you can even avoid setting the API pointer in the device and instead set it as one of the config options. My concern is really that adding another custom API just makes it difficult to write these virtual sensors. Then again we won't be writing a ton of them. On this point I could go either way. As long as the virtual sensor API is convenient. I don't see a need to a custom hardware API though and from what I can tell the convenience here is that they share a lot of the same API surface. This is why I recommend with just sticking to the V2 API. You'll end up having to wrap all the hardware calls and it's just wasteful in terms of image size, latency, etc.

body:
> Got your idea and concerns now, understand one sensor API (V2 etc) to write all sensors including physical and virtual sensor may simple for developers. But I have some concerns regarding to this approach：
> 
> * 1：If keep sensor subsystem still in user space,  but all sensor drivers (physical & virtual) in kernel space. This will frequently trigger user space/kernel space switching due to sensor scheduling,  not efficiency.

Why is this frequent? This should only happen when the subsystem makes a configuration change or needs a one-off sample. Both these cases should be rare.

> * 2:  Some virtual sensor have heavy computing algorithm, and need link some math lib which may not allowed in kernel space,  some computing may need long time, seconds, etc also not suitable in kernel space.  And virtual sensors are always for customization,  customization in kernel space will easy to break the stability of system. Maybe some simple virtual sensors we can put in kernel space,  but not for all,  so as a generic design,  it's better put virtual sensors in user space.

The sensors API doesn't prevent the subsystem from doing the computation in userspace. The two data paths are:
1. Get a one off sample using `sensor_read_data()`. This one will make the userspace/kernel boundary swap like you described, but the result of the call is handled in the context that made the call (userspace in your example). As noted above, these should be rare.
2. Set the sample rate of the sensor and handle the results in `sensor_process_data_callback_t()` which will not be called in kernel space either. In this case, the callback is triggered with the hardware FIFO data. At this point the sensor subsystem can either do processing directly, or more likely queue this data up for processing later on. In either case, these are done in userspace.

> * 3:  For virtual sensors,  there are many differences than physical sensors,  many physical sensors' properties are not suitable for virtual sensors,  such as range,  resolutions,  fifo,  and virtual sensors are focus on data processing (reporters' data) and have special APIs for itself,  if use a single API for both physical sensor and virtual sensor,  will make confusion for developers,  that's why this PR defined a separated sensor API for virtual sensors,  it's more clear,  algorithm developers can focus on virtual sensor APIs,   sensor chip vendors will focus on the kernel space sensor driver development,  maybe need handle the physical sensor wrapper (very thin layer) in sensor subsystem,  and we're thinking about the generic implementation for this wrapper (it's possible since wrapper relies on standard sensor device API),  then,  chip vendors also don't need handle the wrapper by themselves.

Maybe, but the downside here is that there needs to be separate logic to handle the two cases. If they used the same API, you'd be able to make the same calls regardless of the type of sensor. For example the BNO055 does define the range for the rotation angles: pitch, roll, yaw. Resolution is defined as the number of bits per sample when getting raw data. In the same manner, a virtual sensor will be expected to produce data quickly. This often means operating on the underlying sensors' raw data and producing `uint16_t` data with the ability to convert that data to `fp_t` later on. Kconfig values can also increase the accuracy of the virtual sensor so it's possible that the resolution might be different depending on how many bits we want to allocate for the virtual sensor.

FIFO support is a bit more subjective I think . Thought I can see a benefit for having a software FIFO implemented in the virtual sensor to support batching. Alternatively, I can also see arguments for having the software FIFO in the sensor subsystem instead. The up side of having it in the driver is that batching limits can be done per sensor more easily. Since the V2 API already supports the application setting the sensor's FIFO buffer, the memory can still be managed by the sensor subsystem. I believe this is the best option as it allows the virtual sensor to manage it's own watermarks and sending the events, while still allowing the subsystem to manage the memory and thus avoiding unnecessary allocations.

> One concern I have with the deprecation option: if we use the `bt_mesh_health_cli_*` prefix this becomes inconsistent with the configuration client API naming (which doesn't have "cli" in it). We can either ignore this concern, use the stable API process (i.e. break the API backwards compatibility) or to change the configuration client API as well.

From the nRF Connect SDK experience, I would see beneficial of adding `_cli` infix into every client model API. This helps easily distinguish clients API from server one which could have `_srv` infix. This means that `bt_mesh_fault_update` also has to be renamed to `bt_mesh_health_srv_fault_update`. This will also be future-proof for mesh 1.1 models, which may some API for server side.

What we do in nRF Connect SDK is that we memcpy a new message to the publication buffer every time before calling `bt_mesh_model_publish` if we need to publish a new message (https://github.com/nrfconnect/sdk-nrf/blob/535c7a07689044cc54bc242a4a74014068eee886/subsys/bluetooth/mesh/model_utils.c#L116-L119), which looks like a trick. So it would be a good improvement. One downside could be in this is that if someone wants to trigger publication without changing the buffer. Then converting `bt_mesh_model_publish(void)` to something like `bt_mesh_model_publish(struct net_buf_simple *buf)` will create the opposite issue. But I don't see where it can be needed.

> > @nashif You mentioned to me that the #ifdefs for assigning a SOC identifier in coredump.c are kind of ugly. What do you think about adding an int Kconfig like "XTENSA_SOC_ID" in `arch/xtensa/Kconfig` and default it to 1, 2, 3... in the Kconfig.defconfig for each of the major SOC series (ESP32, sample_controller, ADSP 15, ADSP 18, 20, 25)? I don't see anything existing that could easily be used.
> 
> it is not about ugly. This does not seem to be a sustainable approach where we had to add each board to get this support. Why is this needed and what can we use from the build system to make it work with any board without having to do the #ifdefry we have now.

The coredump Python script (i.e. the one that acts the GDB server) needs to know the SOC (along with the toolchain, with this recent update to support XCC and Zephyr SDK for ADSP) in order to know what the indices of all the registers are used by that SOC + toolchain's specific GDB. For example, Zephyr SDK->APL GDB has different register indices than the Zephyr SDK->sample_controller GDB. When the former wants EXCCAUSE, it asks the GDB server for register 158; the latter asks for register 77. (Similarly, Zephyr SDK -> ADSP APL GDB and XCC -> ADSP APL GDB have different indices, though that's not relevant here.)

Alternatives to remove #ifdefs in the coredump for setting SOC:
- Pass in SOC name as an option to the coredump Python script that starts and remove SOC field from the coredump itself

With the update to support XCC and Zephyr SDK toolchain and ADSP, I already require the user to pass in the toolchain as an argument (e.g. "-t zephyr, -t xcc") to the Python script for Xtensa. This is because (after asking Andy) I found no existing way to get the toolchain in C code (it's in a CMake variable) and so couldn't dump it in the coredump / read it back out. I can add the SOC name as another required argument for Xtensa, e.g. --soc intel_adsp_cavs_15, --soc sample_controller, etc., which would mean I don't have to dump it. This seems like the best alternative to me, even if it's inconvenient for the user.

- Sending a fixed-length string in the coredump with the board name (not great)
- The option I mentioned in my first comment (also not great)

> I would like to get this merged before RC1 tomorrow and there are only two small issues remaining that we need to reach consensus on.
> 
>     * The name of the channel selection field/enum.
>       
>       * We need to choose between "option", "preference", "flags", "opts". I am fine with any of these.
> 
>     * What values should the different enumerations have?
>       
>       * We want the value `0x0` to keep the old behaviour, ie. any ATT channel can be used.
>       * We want to be able to require that only enhanced or unenhanced channels are used, so two bits are used for this.
>       * Do we allow the value `0x3` to mean "any", the same as `0x0`? I would say yes, as it would be unintuitive behaviour for the bit field otherwise.
> 
> 
> @jhedberg @Thalley Please comment on these questions.

My 2 cents:
We want to _ensure_ that a GATT request is sent on an EATT channel (requirement from the higher layer profile HAP). To me that indicates that this is not a _preference_, as preference indicates something that my be overwritten by e.g. the stack. 

In `bluetooth.h` we have `BT_LE_SCAN_OPT_*`, `BT_LE_ADV_OPT_*`, `BT_LE_PER_ADV_OPT_*`, `BT_LE_PER_ADV_SYNC_OPT_*` and `BT_LE_PER_ADV_SYNC_TRANSFER_OPT_*` that are also bitfields of options for a specific instance of something. I think it makes sense to continue that naming scheme. 
In these options we also have a few options that are mutually exclusive, so I personally think that having

```c
	BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_NONE = 0x0,
	BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_UNENHANCED_ONLY = BIT(0),
	BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_ENHANCED_ONLY = BIT(1),
```
Would be the right solution as 
1) 0x00 retains the current behavior
2) We can _ensure_ that something is sent over a specific type of channel (EATT vs ATT)
3) It is expandable. 
4) We can easily document (and verify) that `BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_UNENHANCED_ONLY` and `BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_ENHANCED_ONLY` are mutually exclusive

Without a use case for ATT-only, it could also be shortened to 
```c
	BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_NONE = 0x0,
	BT_ATT_CHAN_OPT_ENHANCED_ONLY = BIT(0),
```

body:
@rettichschnidi, thank you for proposing the factory data system. It is a nice addition.

It does seem strange to use fcb for this, because:
a. fcb does not provide any way to describe the data, you are using a method similar to the settings system to describe the data (which is good, but does not reuse any of the code).
b. fcb is limited to flash only,
c. for systems that are using a different backend (nvs, fs) another backend will be added,
d. fcb is a circular buffer exactly to allow not loosing any data when power is interrupted, and as correctly stated this is not needed at all for the factory data application.

IMO it would be better to create some simple backend for the factory data subsystem that relies directly on flash (or flash_map) or another physical storage system (e.g. eeprom). The backend could be decoupled from the factory data system using simple read/write/erase/getsize routines, so that they could be replaced by something else (e.g. for eeprom usage). As the representation on the backend a simple TLV (type+length+value) or even LV (length+value) could be used that is ended by a `/0`. Walking over the data would be as simple as stepping over the length until the `/0` marker is found.

As an example of how to step in such a tlv system: https://github.com/Laczen/zephyrmodules/blob/master/zb8/zb8/src/zb8_tlv.c
(In this example the tlv area is copied to ram before it is being read)

Another (different approach) could be to store the data as CBOR objects, this could allow the factory data to be written ouside zephyr and directly copied to flash.

> If this is supposed to hold non-modifiable data, why not just put binary dump of structure at some specified address of flash or eeprom?

My (not previously expressed) motivation: Flexibility during production. Not necessarily having to release a new firmware when deciding to add a new field. For example, adding a new "manufactured timestamp" would be as easy as extending the Python script interacting with the device during production.

> Using CBOR or any other FS will just add to flash, and if such APIs are not used elsewhere it is just a waste.

I agree to some extend. However, I think the code size needed for reading out factory data can be kept reasonably low for most use cases. And if not, adding support for custom implementations surely would allow to address this point.

The code needed to write the factory data will never end up in a "live" firmware and therefore can be optimization for usability (whatever that is from a manufacturers POV).

> Dump of binary structure may be easily generated (serialized) and independently flashed (or written to external eeprom) independently from an application.

Another (unstated) goal of mine is to be able to store calibration data in the factory data partition. Some of this data can only be gathered when the Zephyr firmware is up and running. Therefore, upfront flashing is not a possibility. Shutting down Zephyr, flashing it, then restart and verify seems like a worse solution than to just spend some code on letting Zephyr write its own factory data.

> > If this is supposed to hold non-modifiable data, why not just put binary dump of structure at some specified address of flash or eeprom?
> 


> The code needed to write the factory data will never end up in a "live" firmware and therefore can be optimization for usability (whatever that is from a manufacturers POV).
> 
> > Dump of binary structure may be easily generated (serialized) and independently flashed (or written to external eeprom) independently from an application.
> 
> Another (unstated) goal of mine is to be able to store calibration data in the factory data partition. Some of this data can only be gathered when the Zephyr firmware is up and running. Therefore, upfront flashing is not a possibility. Shutting down Zephyr, flashing it, then restart and verify seems like a worse solution than to just spend some code on letting Zephyr write its own factory data.

A little bit in reverse order: got your point, I have gone with such process before where the device would be put into hw test/calibration/priming setup that would also upload the target firmware afterwards.
Because both firmware binaries would be based on the same source they would have the same, versioned,  hw description structure; the only difference would be that the application firmware would be able to read and process 2-3 versions back, to make it work with older hardware (when possible).
Nevertheless the advantage of this approach, when the structure was stored within soc flash, was that it was addressed as ordinary structure that has been stored by test/cal/prim firmware at specified flash location and not overwritten by uploading of the application firmware. Of course such structure is aligned to some page address and you have to have some CRC and version field to verify that it is the structure you expect.
Additional feature of such approach is that you could also re-create the hardware description, while servicing the board, from your factory db and generate hex to flash into the board, when calibration was not required, shortening the process - this is specifically useful when you have separate sensor board and computation board and need only to replace the later, while having the former already calibrated within previous set.

> I agree to some extend. However, I think the code size needed for reading out factory data can be kept reasonably low for most use cases. And if not, adding support for custom implementations surely would allow to address this point.
> 

You can not guarantee that. mcuboot is an example of this: however you will try to make mcuboot small and efficient, you are dependent on Zephyr as the base system for it, so any significant increase in codes size in areas touching flash access (API, bus API and so on) within Zephyr, will increase (or decrease) the flash size requirements within mcuboot, with the later having no control over that happening.

> My (not previously expressed) motivation: Flexibility during production. Not necessarily having to release a new firmware when deciding to add a new field. For example, adding a new "manufactured timestamp" would be as easy as extending the Python script interacting with the device during production.

The flexibility, as far as I can tell from my experience, considering the fact that you do not modify the data in-field, works only one way: you have to support older hardware that is in-field, with old calibration structures, with a new firmware, unless you retrieve these devices and put them through the factory process again.
When you release new hardware, or hardware with the new fields in flash, you should already have new structures describing them, even if your firmware may lag behind and not be able to use them. Nevertheless your firmware should be able to recognize, and process, previous versions of structures at lease a few versions back.

body:
When CONDRST is set, RNG is re-initialized, which adds a latency before entropy to be available. On single core MCUs, `configure_rng()` is done only at entropy driver initialization so this is fine. However, on multi-core MCUs such as STM32H747, `configure_rng()` is invoked for every new entropy generation process and it might be worth checking if RNG_HTCR is already set to the desired value to avoid useless RNG re-initialization.
Note that currently no STM32 MCUs supporting CONDRST are multi-core, but that might change in the future, leading to performance issues.

> Also as per #45776 and [the previous discussion on the scope of the minimal libc](https://discord.com/channels/720317445772017664/954308485489786921/954339280363343883), I am not convinced this should be a part of the minimal libc because:
> 
> 1. The original intent of the **minimal** libc was to provide only the **minimal** amount of functions required to make Zephyr run for testing and validation as per @nashif's comments in the linked discussion.

Yes, definitely.

Another aspect about the **minimal** libc, was to minimize the amount of maintenance necessary as well. This implementation of `strerror()` requires only a negligible amount of maintenance. Quite literally just maintaining `errno.h`, which is something we do already.

I can definitely see the frustration about manually maintaining a separate table of error strings that would rely on a human to remember to update. At least this way it's **minimal** in that sense.

> 2. These functions are not required by any of the Zephyr **internal** components.

Note: `perror()` is a PR to `lib/posix` and not to the libc. It's a common function used on posix systems and references `strerror()` in most implementations. If `perror()` exists, then most likely `strerror()` would exist as well. I would suggest using a Kconfig regardless of the libc though to explicitly include the error string table.

> 3. We will be moving on to using the picolibc as the default C library instead of the minimal libc in the near future, in which case the latter will be reserved only for internal testing and validation purposes and will not be used by end users/products.

That works for me too - I would make this PR to picolibc as well, if it does not already have `strerror()`.

I wouldn't necessarily say with absolute certainty that users/products will not use the minimal libc though. If it's in-tree (rather than a module) that might be enough for some organizations to stick with it, as the cost of adding / updating another repo is large in comparison.

> Nevertheless, I am not necessarily opposed to merging this because we have added other "non-essential" features to the minimal libc before, and this feature can be configured such that it does cause any meaningful footprint increase.

Thanks. Yeah, I thought that would be a concern for sure, and so wanted to make the default "no code size increase".

body:
@de-nordic Thanks for the feedback and sorry for the long delay.

> A little bit in reverse order: got your point, I have gone with such process before where the device would be put into hw test/calibration/priming setup that would also upload the target firmware afterwards. Because both firmware binaries would be based on the same source they would have the same, versioned, hw description structure; the only difference would be that the application firmware would be able to read and process 2-3 versions back, to make it work with older hardware (when possible). 

Surely possible, but it seems rather inflexible. I think it is a valuable to a) be able to add arbitrary new data fields at the production site and b) to access the factory data using a well defined/know mechanism. Hence the "string-key" to value interface, which is similar to the the settings system.

Having to create and deploy a new factory firmware for even the slightest change is something I'd really want to avoid. Also, I think having to know and support every past data structure is (at least) as complicated as using the "string-key"-value interface and assigning sensible default values on the caller site when a value does not exist.

> Nevertheless the advantage of this approach, when the structure was stored within soc flash, was that it was addressed as ordinary structure that has been stored by test/cal/prim firmware at specified flash location and not overwritten by uploading of the application firmware.

How is this a unique feature compared to my proposed factory data? The factory data (FCB or any other) would also be stored in a dedicated partition on a well defined address.

> Of course such structure is aligned to some page address and you have to have some CRC and version field to verify that it is the structure you expect.

FCB does exactly this. One CRC per entry and not a single one over all of the data, but I think it is sensible to reuse what is already existing.

> Additional feature of such approach is that you could also re-create the hardware description, while servicing the board, from your factory db and generate hex to flash into the board, when calibration was not required, shortening the process - this is specifically useful when you have separate sensor board and computation board and need only to replace the later, while having the former already calibrated within previous set.

This should work with every kind of storage backend. Be it FCB, TLV or just a structure dump.

> You can not guarantee that. mcuboot is an example of this: however you will try to make mcuboot small and efficient, you are dependent on Zephyr as the base system for it, so any significant increase in codes size in areas touching flash access (API, bus API and so on) within Zephyr, will increase (or decrease) the flash size requirements within mcuboot, with the later having no control over that happening.

I did not think about MCUBoot. However, a bootloader should be as simple as possible. Why would it need to access any factory data?

> The flexibility, as far as I can tell from my experience, considering the fact that you do not modify the data in-field, works only one way: you have to support older hardware that is in-field, with old calibration structures, with a new firmware, unless you retrieve these devices and put them through the factory process again.

This is my intention. And by not having fixed structures, new FW versions on older HW can deal with `factory_data_load_one()` returning -ENOENT by just using a sensible default value.

> When you release new hardware, or hardware with the new fields in flash, you should already have new structures describing them, even if your firmware may lag behind and not be able to use them.

Not needed when having a (more flexible) key-value factory data API.

> Nevertheless your firmware should be able to recognize, and process, previous versions of structures at lease a few versions back.

In my case: Every single version ever produced :)

Having said all of above and worked a bit on a new PR revision:
* Would you agree on having a key-value API, similar to the settings module, is a good way to go?
* I am tempted to implement the current key-value API by actually using a struct as backend. Just to prove that it is flexible enough to allow this too. My hope is that this will result in a small code size. Thoughts?
* Ideally, I can write up a benchmark of the FCB vs TLV vs custom struct implementations. What else other than code size would be important?
* I realized that I'd rather not put a IO abstraction layer behind the API anymore and save the code size overhead. Will instead make the reusable parts accessible for custom factory data implementations.

body:
I've done initial work to remove `notify` use (#46192). There is one driver left which is a bit more difficult.
However, there is one thing I noticed. Maybe it was mentioned at API call. By introducing a callback with signature `cb(void *context, ...)` we kind of implicitly assume what context will be. For example, if we have a call like
```
foo_tx(const struct device *dev, uint8_t *data, size_t len, async_callback_t *cb, void *user_data);
```
we can only assume (or verbally inform in doxygen) that `context` will be the `dev` device. There is no C API way to commit to this agreement. `Notify` was doing it by having generic callback `cb()` and a module specific function which converted to a module specific callback. It was much more complex but cleaner.

body:
This new client-server approach implemented in #44188 makes a lot of sense when using  `twister`, in fact this is exactly what I felt was missing when I tried to use twister to run ADSP tests a long time ago (and then gave up and went back to testing SOF only...) No one wants to have a Zephyr workspace duplicated on each test system; great job @enjiamai .

However this client-server, "embedded" development model does not make sense for a SOF and https://github.com/thesofproject/sof-test  because:
- SOF is loaded from `/lib/firmware/` by the Linux kernel
- SOF testing requires deploying other files to the test system (dictionary, various binaries,...)
- sof-test does not run remotely, it's installed directly on the test system and run entirely on it.

For the reasons above, SOF already has some various SOF-specific tools to deploy more than just the firmware to test systems.

While SOF test systems are usually not a good place to write and compile code, most of them are running a full-blown Linux Operating System and it would be inconvenient and a waste to treat that OS on SOF test systems as a limited, "embedded" OS and not to take advantage of it to run tests. Even ChromeOS has enough code to run sof-test! https://github.com/thesofproject/sof-test/issues/576

body:
Thank you @aescolar for your comments and suggestions :)

> What are the main motivations for going this direction?

In short:
**My main motivation is to make it easier to use BabbleSim in test purpose in Zephyr project.**

In long:
BabbleSim simulator is a great tool which can be used in automated tests. But to make it possible it needs to be handled in specific way. Due to the fact, that it simulates several devices and wireless physical medium it cannot be handled by typical Twister way, which is designed to work with single device. As you mentioned there was already an attempt to customize Twister to BabbleSim tests, but this idea was finished with conclusion that at this moment it is too complicated: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/33388 

So, in BabbleSim tests, bash scripts are still used as test runner. Using Pytest plugin proposed in this PR can provide achieve following benefits:

-	Introduction standard way of test definition in yaml file. At this moment there are several approaches to this issue, for example:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/tests/bluetooth/bsim_bt/bsim_test_gatt/test_scripts/gatt.sh (most popular way)
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/tests/bluetooth/bsim_bt/bsim_test_audio/test_scripts/mics.sh (in fact there are two test, but in report there are marked as one)
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/tests/bluetooth/bsim_bt/bsim_test_mesh/tests_scripts/friendship/establish.sh (in mesh tests there are used more generic approach)
-	Possibility to group several tests in one yaml file, instead of maintain them in separate files, what is hard for analyzing, like for example there:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/tests/bluetooth/bsim_bt/bsim_test_mesh/tests_scripts/friendship 
-	Possibility to test building and execution in one command.
-	Possibility to quick test filtering from command line.
-	Verification of test ID and simulation ID uniqueness among whole tests.
-	Full log saving (also from test execution).
-	Saving history of performed test sessions (in “historical” directories like `bsim_tests_out_1`, `bsim_tests_out_2` etc.)
-	More “accurate” JUnit xml report – with information about skips and test execution time of each performed test.
-	Possibility to use ready Pytest plugins (for test parallelization or for generate other types of report like json or html).
-	Using yaml files for test definition can give opportunity to merge this test runner with Twister in the future (only when Twister will be “ready” to handle multiple devices in one test).

---

> It would seem it is only supported to run one type of device/one app in a given test(?) (This is how most if not all tests upstream are today, but I'm really surprised there is none mixing apps upstream)
This system would benefit a lot from supporting building different apps and running them together in the same test.

Yes, at this moment there is support to run only one type of app. I used this approach, because as you observed at this moment there are no tests with mixed applications. And I agree that it could be valuable to have such possibility for the future. I am wondering if this should be introduced in this big PR, or maybe it should be done in next PR as a new functionality. 

---

> Supporting the Phy check mode would be really nice

What do you mean by supporting check mode? At this moment you can pass to simulated phy `-c` arguent in yaml definition, like there:

```yaml
tests:
  bluetooth.bsim.gatt:
    extra_args:
      - "-DCMAKE_C_FLAGS='-Werror'"
      - "-DCONFIG_COVERAGE=y"
      - "-DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON"
    bsim_config:
      devices:
        - testid: gatt_client
        - testid: gatt_server
      physical_layer:
        name: bs_2G4_phy_v1
        sim_length: 60e6
        extra_run_args:
          - "-c"
          - "-v=4"
```

And then you can observe in `bsim_tests_out/bluetooth_bsim_gatt/bs_2G4_phy_v1_out.log` file, the result of this check:
```
p_2G4:  Check: Device  0, Tx: found 0/1199 differences (0.0%)
p_2G4:  Check: Device  0, Rx: found 0/1206 differences (0.0%)
p_2G4:  Check: Device  0, ModemRx: found 0/1200 differences (0.0%)
p_2G4:  Check: Device  1, Tx: found 0/1212 differences (0.0%)
p_2G4:  Check: Device  1, Rx: found 0/1239 differences (0.0%)
p_2G4:  Check: Device  1, ModemRx: found 0/1199 differences (0.0%)
```
I guess that you would like to pass this option in command line, to avoid modification of each yaml file. Should I add this in this PR or should it be done in next one?

---

> It would be very nice to be able to get the run commands out to be able to run them by hand (say one device in gdb or valgrind so)

These commands can be found in plugin log file (`bsim_tests_out/bsim_test_plugin.log`). Moreover, if you call pytest with this additional flag: `-o log_cli=true` you can observe all used commands in your terminal (you can copy it and use in your purpose):

```
$ pytest tests/bluetooth/bsim_bt/ -k "gatt" -o log_cli=true
...
INFO     bsim_plugin.BabbleSimRun:BabbleSimRun.py:73 Run BabbleSim simulation with commands:
/home/redbeard/bsim/bin/bs_nrf52_bsim_bluetooth_bsim_gatt -s=bluetooth_bsim_gatt -d=0 -testid=gatt_client &
/home/redbeard/bsim/bin/bs_nrf52_bsim_bluetooth_bsim_gatt -s=bluetooth_bsim_gatt -d=1 -testid=gatt_server &
/home/redbeard/bsim/bin/bs_2G4_phy_v1 -s=bluetooth_bsim_gatt -D=2 -sim_length=60e6 -c -v=4
...
```

---

> About platform_allow, would that being defined as a whitelist for CI purposes prevent out of tree boards from being run with?

> Supporting selecting the board and boards roots from the command line would be nice. Also to be able to pass arbitrary cmake options to all builds like for example to add an extra ZEPHYR_MODULE

> It would be nice being able to run other arbitrary "devices" in the simulation, not just the ones built with Zephyr. That would be useful for example to have interferers (again, I'm surprised nobody seems to be using this in upstream tests)

I agree that it would be valuable. As I mentioned before, I was focused to deliver “minimal” version of this plugin to be able to run current tests. In my opinion handling of CLI arguments or run arbitrary “devices” could be introduced in next PRs. But if in your opinion this is necessary, I can try to introduce it in this one.

---

> The maximum test timeout would probably need to be configurable per test 

I agree, good point.

---

> You could try to detect same sim_ids/same test scenario names in different files as that would cause mysterious failures

It is already implemented here:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/076f65b13e6a16405f3c40c8b3b3fd254abb19be/tests/bluetooth/bsim_bt/conftest.py#L115-L128
`sim_id` is based on test scenario name. So, if test scenario names are uniqueness, then `sim_id` too.

---

> A sidetrack:
> Why do you say
> > Moreover, this system does not allow to introduce tests, which can base on already existed samples (like samples/bluetooth/central_hr and samples/bluetooth/peripheral_hr) or tests written in Ztest test framework.
>
> I would expect that to work fine today, so if this is something that it is preventing you from doing what you want it would be nice to address it.

I analyzed this bash scripts system once again and I have to say that you are right. I was convinced that, it is impossible, but now I see, that it is doable. Sorry for this – I just removed this sentence from PR description. Thank you for paying attention :)

body:
> Dear @povergoing, let me explain. Grant tables are essential base Xen functionality, previously Zephyr worked without this only because it was not implemented and it now looks incomplete. Without such basic functionality it can not be called Xen PV guest.

``Xen PV guest`` refers to OS that was modifying to run on top of Xen without HW virtualisation support. This mode doesn't exist on Arm.

> Usually, operating systems (Linux, Mini-OS, Unikraft etc.) initialize this when found Xen support without any options (Xenbus too). Also, this driver will be used in both domU and dom0 modes because it is used by frontend and backend PV drivers. So I don't think that it should be turned off.

The grant-table is only necessary if you want to use Xen para-virtualized driver. There are some setup where a user may not need it if they decide to assign all the devices and/or use virtio.

If Zephyr wants to target such setup, then I think it would be good to provide an option to disable the grant-table driver. This would allow to remove any unused "drivers". The same could be said for the event channel driver and the xenbus one.

body:
> It generally made things more, not less, readable. I didn't run checkpatch after, that might be an interesting bout to see if they agree.

`checkpatch.pl` is both a formatting tool and linter. The clang solution uses `clang-tidy` as the linter and `clang-format` as the formatter. As long as `clang-format` and `checkpatch.pl` agree on formatting, we should be good.

It should be noted that the clang tooling actually uses LLVM as the C / C++ parser, so it's quite accurate as it's derived from the AST. IIRC, `checkpatch.pl` might only be suitable for C, so we may eventually want to replace it with `clang-format` and also introduce `clang-tidy` into CI.

Of course, there is also [scan-build](https://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/) for static analysis, which uses LLVM and leverages the AST as well.

> `checkpatch.pl` is both a formatting tool and linter. The clang solution uses `clang-tidy` as the linter and `clang-format` as the formatter. As long as `clang-format` and `checkpatch.pl` agree on formatting, we should be good.

It would be nice to introduce `clang-tidy` as well. The only issue I have observed with `clang-format`/`checkpatch.pl` is within macros:

```c
	static const struct jm101_config jm101_config_##i = {                  \
		...							       \
	};                                                                     \
                                                                               \ /* <- clang-format starts line with spaces here, not tab, checkpatch complains about leading spaces */
	DEVICE_DT_INST_DEFINE(i, jm101_init, NULL, &jm101_data_##i,            \
```

However, I guess we could _patch_ checkpatch to ignore those edge cases. Our _abuse_ of nested macros can confuse `clang-format` as well, for example,

```c
	static const struct jm101_config jm101_config_##i = {                  \
		.uart = DEVICE_DT_GET(DT_INST_PHANDLE(i, uart)),               \
		.addr = DT_INST_PROP(i, address),                              \
		IF_ENABLED(CONFIG_JM101_TRIGGER,                               \
			   (.touch = GPIO_DT_SPEC_INST_GET_OR(i, touch_gpios,  \
							      {}), )) /* */    \ /* comment added to force line break here, otherwise clang-format doesn't work well */
	};                                                                     \
                                                                               \
	DEVICE_DT_INST_DEFINE(i, jm101_init, NULL, &jm101_data_##i,            \
```

But overall, I had a good experience with it, specially when refactoring code.

body:
Based on my past experience with product line platform code, here are a couple things to keep in mind:

a. Not all end users will have the freedom to use a modified Zephyr repository.  Some are only allowed to reuse what is provided.
b. When defining APIs, assume some users will need to have multiple instances of any arbitrary component.
c. When defining APIs, assume that downstream users will need to extend "enumerations" (e.g., result code defined values) as well as structures (e.g., via CONTAINER_OF())

The above points lead to needing both context and user data parameters. Lets consider when two identical instances exist of communication hardware (e.g., I2C controllers, ethernet controllers, USB OTG controllers, etc).  We will create a separate driver instance for each and may create a separate protocol stack instance for each.  The protocol component instance data is accessible via `userdata`, the driver component instance is provided through `context`.  If the protocol instance is only talking to one driver instance, then `context` may not be needed, but if it is talking to multiple instances of the same component (e.g., timers, GPIOs, etc.), then `context` is used to determine the source of the callback instead of providing a separate callback function for each source.

body:
Driving by again.  I know I promised to avoid the bikeshed, but if it's happening anyway...  No vote from me, trying not to engage too much, just giving opinions:

I gotta be honest: solving the "callback context pointer" vs. "intrusive data structure / CONTAINER_OF" conflict by adding both of them strikes me as the undeniably **worst** resolution possible.  We've all heard of design-by-committee, right?  This is it.

Personally I like intrusive pointers for efficiency reasons (so do the Linux people, FWIW).  But I can live with an opaque context pointer too.  It's just one word of storage for every registerable object.  That's a real and measurable memory cost but not an outrageous one.  And it means the API is clearer and no one needs to explain intrusive data structures on discord, which is a plus.

But putting them back in in addition to the opaque pointer: (1) does nothing to address the efficiency cost, in fact it adds **even more** overhead to pass the needed arguments (in contexts where they can't be inlined out, anyway), and (2) requires that every client of this API then document their own convention about how that context pointer works, which means that we'll be explaining this stuff forever anyway.  I think the only real advantage is just legacy porting overhead given all the pre-existing intrusive code.

Strongly, strongly recommend that if we have people who simply refuse the intrusive scheme, that we go with context pointers only.

Said my bit.  Going to go hide now.

> void the bikeshed, but if it's happening anyway...

I'm trying to avoid that and back us up to what the requirements are on this interface.  Remember, the domain of Zephyr Project includes safety-critical systems, where every line of code must ultimately trace back to at least one top-level system requirement. To minimize future rework and breaking changes, we ought to attempt that now.

For a composable, extensible, reusable event-based platform we need an extensible general API for asynchronously completing a request. 

I propose general asynchronous completion must support:

  d. passing the completion result back across interrupts/threads
  e. the completion result coming from a component other than the one that received the initial request
  f. indicating the request instance being completed
      (which covers multiple outstanding requests from each of multiple instances of a component)
  g. indicating standard alternate completion results due to asynchronous operation (e.g., cancelled)
  h. be extensible to support the propagation of any output data
  i. clearly indicate whether the result is due to a supported condition (e.g., timeout on external data) or an unsupported one (e.g., giving a mutex from a thread that does not own it).  Note: If unsupported conditions are always handled as a catastrophic failure (i.e., k_panic()) then this requirement does not apply.

If we are evaluating this API as an extensible general API for asynchronous completions, then what additional requirements must be met?

If we are **not** evaluating this API as an extensible general API for asynchronous completion, then what are the requirements we are trying to meet with this API?
