body:
I don't think there will ever be more than one wakeup timer in an RTC, just more alarms, since any counter capable of causing an interrupt, can be used as a "wakeup timer" during runtime, the only thing it does different is running when the device is powered down... I don't think there needs to be an id for the wakeup timer for this reason, so we could simplify the code by removing the timer id enum.

Using enums to specify alarm id is a too rigid approach i would say, as it will require updating the API every time a "better" RTC device (with more alarms) is supported, and it can easily lead to issues where two parts of an application are setting the same alarm by accident, which is a bug that can be hard to track down.

Instead, an id (or handle), could be returned when using the **alarm_set** function, this will alert the application if it tries to set more timers/alarms than the RTC supports, and will prevent two+ parts of the application from using the same alarm/timer. 

This would require a new function like "alarm_give" or similar to make it available again, but remove the need for the enums, making it support "infinite" alarms/triggers from the start in a safer manner.

A compromise would be to add a similar function as the one implemented in the counter API, where you have a **uint8_t channel** argument, which can be probed by using the **counter_get_num_of_channels()**, which is not safer, but more flexible.

This branch contains our proposal to what we would like the RTC API to look like, this is useful comparison and discussion:
https://github.com/bjarki-trackunit/zephyr/compare/main...bjarki-trackunit:add_rtc_driver_api

I also think we should move away from using the struct tm structure as it is 36 bytes which can be optimized, the tm_day for example is stored as an int... I created a datetime structure which is more appropriate for low ram devices

Hi @jhedberg
I don't intend to force approach suggested by me in this PR and I am open for discussion. I would be glad to discuss other possible solutions for my original issue. On my end the update is needed for Fast Pair use-case, I make sure to introduce approach that would fix other related use-cases (new API also fixes: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/38336).

I fully understand that in general updating callbacks after connection is established may introduce risk of races. Since Fast Pair specification actually requires changing bonding capabilities reacting on GATT write (that's the moment when we are aware that we should follow the procedure for a given connection), we cannot completely avoid possibility of race here (e.g. we cannot guarantee that connected Central would not behave improperly). I used atomic pointer to avoid unexpected behaviors and clearly indicate problem to the end user (no better solution comes to my mind, but maybe I missed something).

body:
@MrGreensWorkshop Thanks for your feedback. Do I understand correctly that you are proposing a generic PIO driver instead of a per peripheral one? There were a few reasons for implementing it this way:
1. PIO is most useful for implementing uncommon peripherals such as PS/2 or DVI. Therefore, it was assumed that most users would prefer ready to use peripherals, that could be enabled as if they were "regular" peripherals, instead of having a generic PIO driver which would require some extra work to make into a specific peripheral.
2. Implementing PIO peripherals through specific driver APIs allows users to use those peripherals using existing Zephyr API. For example, now you can use the PIO UART as a console, or write a character with `uart_poll_out`, instead of having to use something like `pio_uart_poll_out` or `pio_write`.
3. We preferred not to bother with distributing `pioasm`, since it was only provided as source code as part of `pico-sdk`. With the current implementation, only the driver's author has to bother with installing the assembler.

And finally, the current implementation still gives access to PIO API, so for special cases a user can still write a custom PIO driver, as part of an out of tree Zephyr driver, or simply as part of the application.

body:
> This seems like the wrong layer to be operating at. SYS_INIT is the bottom layer of the initialization stack, and the API is intentionally minimal. Giving it a "name" with complicated semantics[1] seems clumsy.
> 
> Can't we track the mapping of device to SYS_INIT struct in some kind of out-of-band way without polluting the base API?
> 
> [1] Which aren't specified here! That's the clue that you have a layering violation: when you have to add a feature that has no defined behavior for the benefit of something else.

The desire here is not to bypass the device API for some device functionality, it is to provide a way to reference external `SYS_INIT` instances. The name of the `struct init_entry` generated by the device API can already be deterministically reconstructed. The core problem being solved here is that:

1. Hardware devices (struct device) can depend on software "devices" (SYS_INIT)
2. We need some method of registering the software "device" as a dependency of the hardware device, so that we can say "This software needs to be initialised before this hardware", for #22545)
3. It is not possible to do the above, if the names of the structs generated are literally random. There is currently no way to reference anything created by `SYS_INIT`
author: JordanYates

body:
Right, it's a layering violation.  SYS_INIT is being forced to understand what a device is (or rather: grow a "name" for use by the device layer).  But SYS_INIT is the simplest possible way to do initialization code (vs. putting it inline in z_cstart() anyway).  Many of its important users aren't part of the device model at all.

Instead, wouldn't it be nicer to have code in the device layer that enumerated the device, traversed the tree, and emitted an in-order, guaranteed correct set of SYS_INIT structs on its own?  That is, don't have devices use SYS_INIT at all, and instead of a device layer init call that they register?  Seems better still, no?
author: andyross

body:
> Right, it's a layering violation. SYS_INIT is being forced to understand what a device is (or rather: grow a "name" for use by the device layer). But SYS_INIT is the simplest possible way to do initialization code (vs. putting it inline in z_cstart() anyway). Many of its important users aren't part of the device model at all.

This is not just a problem for devices. The ideal goal is to get away from the level/priority scheme and have a nice tree generated at compile/link time that guarantees correct ordering. This also means that there would need to be some method of saying this `SYS_INIT` depends on that other `SYS_INIT`. Maybe `SYS_INIT(hci_driver_init)` depends on `SYS_INIT(bt_rpmsg_init)` for example. You can't communicate that with random names.

>Instead, wouldn't it be nicer to have code in the device layer that enumerated the device, traversed the tree, and emitted an in-order, guaranteed correct set of SYS_INIT structs on its own? That is, don't have devices use SYS_INIT at all, and instead of a device layer init call that they register? Seems better still, no?

How could the device layer know which `SYS_INIT` macros a given device depends on? An init call sounds like a runtime mechanism, which is fundamentally not possible when the point is to work out the initialisation order. Maybe it is better, but I cannot visualise what it is supposed to look like.

body:
> This also means that there would need to be some method of saying this SYS_INIT depends on that other SYS_INIT.

But tha't not the API being submitted, this is just adding a "name" with no dependency tracking.  FWIW: I think that's a great idea, though.  (Though again I don't see why it has to be modifying the extremely simple low-level API instead of being implemented as a layer above it, like the device layer that already has all that info!)

Maybe we should defer this until we have the full scheme to review?

> How could the device layer know which SYS_INIT macros a given device depends on?

Ideally because it generates it:  The app says "Here is my device.  Here are its dependencies.  Here is its initialization function.  Please call it at the appropriate time, kthx"  Then the device layer build integration goes and makes that happen, presumably by emitting a bunch of SYS_INIT() expansions in generated code.

Again, SYS_INIT isn't that design.  It's just a super-simple way to get a C function to run at boot, and apps are currently using it.  Let's not pollute the API for current apps for the benefit of code that is at a higher level and can presumably get even better integration.

(This isn't a -1, btw, just an aesthetic issue).

body:
> > > > On multi-core MCUs such as STM32H747, configure_rng() is invoked for every new entropy generation process and it might be worth checking if RNG_HTCR is already set to the desired value to avoid useless RNG re-initialization.
> > > 
> > > 
> > > In this case, the configure_rng() is done by the acquire_rng(), and could be :
> > > ```
> > > static void acquire_rng(void)
> > > {
> > > #if defined(CONFIG_SOC_SERIES_STM32WBX) || defined(CONFIG_STM32H7_DUAL_CORE)
> > > 	/* Lock the RNG to prevent concurrent access */
> > > 	z_stm32_hsem_lock(CFG_HW_RNG_SEMID, HSEM_LOCK_WAIT_FOREVER);
> > > 	/* RNG configuration could have been changed by the other core */
> > > 	if (LL_RNG_GetHealthConfig(rng) != DT_INST_PROP(0, health_test_config)) {
> > > 		configure_rng();
> > > 	}
> > > #endif /* CONFIG_SOC_SERIES_STM32WBX || CONFIG_STM32H7_DUAL_CORE */
> > > }
> > > ```
> > 
> > 
> > This is not possible because `configure_rng()` does not only write RNG_HTCR and perform NIST-related configuration, it also enables the RNG and RNG IRQ, which could have been disabled by the other core. For example on STM32WB55, the M0 core disables the RNG after use.
> > This also assumes the other core won't change NIST-related configuration (in RNG_CR) without also modifying RNG_HTCR, but I guess in any real world scenario all cores in a MCU will use the exact same "NIST configuration", so that may not be actually an issue
> 
> @taltenbach so is it fine from this perspective ?

It is not in the sense the RNG is reconfigured even if the current configuration was already the proper one. A simple check in `configure_rng()` of the current `RNG_CR` and `RNG_HTCR` values would be sufficient to avoid that. But, as I said, since at present all STM32 MCUs supporting CONDRST are single-core, meaning that `configure_rng()` is only called once at startup, so that is not a real issue at the moment, but might be in the future.

body:
> if we are officially removing support for 3rd party build systems

I do not see how this is "removing support for 3rd party build systems." It has never been required/stated/documented that users **must** include the `zephyr.h` in their application, so it would be incorrect for one to rely on `zephyr.h` to define `__ZEPHYR__` anyway, not to mention that would be unnecessary because it is already defined by the build system.

Moreover, third-party build systems, which does not really make sense at this point but if you ever choose to do it for whatever reason, would be required to define `__ZEPHYR__` globally anyway for the reason stated above. As far as I understand, supporting third-party build systems (as in building the Zephyr itself using something other than the Zephyr's own CMake-based build system) has never been one of our goals and does not really make sense at this point due to the inherent complexity of the Zephyr build process and the heavy reliance on the Zephyr-specific macros in the CMake files.

Also what has been said in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/47268#discussion_r913075244.

body: I think the problem is in the design itself. Let's say picolibc wants to have certain Zephyr-specific code. It will use `__ZEPHYR__` guard for that. Now, picolibc goes and says, “oh, I need to include zephyr.h for that!” It includes it and everything “works fine”. Now, a poor guy using FreeRTOS + picolibc gets a build error: “Could not find <zephyr/zephyr.h>”, and he says “what the hell is that, I'm not using Zephyr! FreeRTOS is better! Please take that out!”. So, the header approach is problematic. It is the job of the build system (Zephyr or external) to tell it's building for Zephyr, same as I'll get `__llvm__` if compiling code on LLVM.

Note that I dropped the changes to LSM6DSO as I can unable to get IBI to work. LSM6DSO reports IBI payload length to be 9 bytes. Another thing is that the controller driver was re-written to not use the NXP HAL. So it would be great if someone from NXP can enhancement the driver down the road.

body:
> Can you give an example of some properties that you'd advise against defining a default due to a dependency?

@MaureenHelm this rule was originally suggested by Peter Bigot. If we have

```
properties:
   foo: ...
   bar: ...
```

And changing `foo` from its power on reset value can only be done safely with an accompanying change in `bar`, then his argument was that making them both `required` forces the user to make a conscious choice, whereas allowing defaults for both `foo` and `bar` would allow the user to change `foo` without also having to change `bar` at build time, resulting in an incorrect configuration.

I find the argument convincing but don't know of any hardware like that off the top of my head.

body:
I am OK with adding the `BT_KEYS_OOB` flag.

I am not happy with the `BT_GATT_PERM_READ_128B`/`BT_GATT_PERM_WRITE_128B` flags because it's not at all clear what it means. I don't think we have selected an objective definition of what it means for a link to have '128 bit entropy key encryption'. LESC JustWorks connection under a MITM attack is completely readable by the attacker. Yet it fulfills the requirement. A link secured with Legacy pairing (even using JustWorks) that was not sniffed during pairing and has a 128b LTK key is as safe as LESC. Once the LTK is established, the encryption mechanism is the same. Yet it fails this requirement.

The closest meaningful promise I can think of is 'Key exchange was safe from passive sniffing, (but not necessarily from MITM)'. That assumes the OOB implementation cannot be sniffed. And that may be a real attack vector if NFC is used.

Since this is an Audio spec definition, I think the implementation should go in that layer. The read and write handlers of the services can return `BT_ATT_ERR_AUTHENTICATION`. I see `BT_GATT_PERM` as a convenience, not a one-size-fits-all.

body:
@hakehuang @congnguyenhuu 

I tested this PR both in `Command Prompt` and in `Powershell` with and without administrative rights and so far everything works correctly to me. 

I used following commands for tests:

```
python scripts\twister -p nrf52840dk_nrf52840 -T samples/hello_world -vv --inline-logs -j 8 --device-testing  --device-serial COM4
```

and

```
python scripts\twister -p nrf52840dk_nrf52840 -T tests\kernel\common -s tests\kernel\common\kernel.common -vv --inline-logs -j 8 --device-testing --hardware-map map.yml
```

In second case I used following map file (generated by hand):
```yaml
- connected: true
  id: 000683593489
  platform: nrf52840dk_nrf52840
  product: J-Link
  runner: nrfjprog
  serial: COM4
```

I'm wondering if it could be valuable to give Twister users possibility to generate hardware map on Windows OS. After analyzing I observed that the problem (in my case with `nrf52840dk_nrf52840` platform) is connected with lack of information about USB product string ID of connected hardware. I observe this missing information only on Windows OS - on Linux everything works okay. Quick workaround for this can be as follow:

```diff
diff --git a/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/hardwaremap.py b/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/hardwaremap.py
index ec980771f6..cf74ce08e9 100644
--- a/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/hardwaremap.py
+++ b/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/hardwaremap.py
@@ -276,6 +276,10 @@ class HardwareMap:
                 # assume endpoint 0 is the serial, skip all others
                 if d.manufacturer == 'Texas Instruments' and not d.location.endswith('0'):
                     continue
+
+                if d.product is None:
+                    d.product = "unknown"
+
                 s_dev = DUT(platform="unknown",
                                         id=d.serial_number,
                                         serial=persistent_map.get(d.device, d.device),
```

And then generated hardware map on Windows can look like this:
```yaml
- connected: true
  id: 000683593489
  platform: unknown
  product: unknown
  runner: unknown
  serial: COM4
```

On the one hand it could be still valuable because it help to generate skeleton of hardware map file, but on the other hand such long list of `unknown` parameters can be misleading for beginner user - this solution requires that user know how to fill correctly all unknowns.

since we missed the dev-review, my comment from above again:

> If we officially at a point where we are saying, you CAN'T build zephyr with anything else but the zephyr build system, then we should document this somewhere and make it clear, explain that __ZEPHYR__ only comes via the build system etc.

This line in zephyr.h was added for a reason (supporting 3rd party build systems), while not directly documented, like many other things in zephyr, it is something that someone might depend on, could have depended on or something else we do not know. The fact is it is a line in a public header.

If we are are going to remove something supporting a "feature", documented or not, we have to review the whole thing and not just drop a flag to reduce the number of line in zephyr.h, clearly this removal is not fixing a direct issue.

I am not saying we should keep it and I am not going into the argument of why this is good or bad, what I am asking here is  clarify through documentation that to build zephyr, you have to use the zephyr build system, third party build systems are not support ("anymore) and that you should not depend on __ZEPHYR__ coming from headers, etc. etc.
While we are at it, do a sweep and see if other thing like the item below (exports) exist to support third part build systems. The exports feature is could still be useful, unrelated to 3rd party build systems.

This could be done in the release notes, in the build system section or wherever you want.

We should manage this type of cleanups with more care and always consider that someone out there might be using this  while we continue on improving public interfaces and documentation for end-users.

The exports feature is could still be useful, unrelated to 3rd party build systems.
> 
> This could be done in the release notes, in the build system section or wherever you want.
> 
> We should manage this type of cleanups with more care and always consider that someone out there might be using this while we continue on improving public interfaces and documentation for end-users.

Hi @sjanc
Implementation provided in the PR already ensures that authentication callbacks used for given connection are not altered during pairing. The only difference is that my proposed API assigns callbacks directly to SMP and returns error code if it's no longer possible (e.g. because SMP procedures have already started). Assigning the callbacks to connection slightly increases memory consumption and it does not improve anything (it may even lead to new race conditions, because authentication callbacks would then be stored in two places and copied between them). body:
Hi @alwa-nordic 

> I would like to note that this API smells a bit of race condition. It can only be used after a connection is established, but before the remote initiates an SMP procedure. This can, for now, be done safely in `bt_conn_cb.connected`. But that's because of hidden/undocumented thread-priority reasons.

The race condition is in theory possible, but the vendor-specific procedure must be triggered before device receives SMP request anyway (otherwise device is unaware that it should use vendor-specific procedure instead of regular pairing and cannot react properly no matter which implementation is used). Also in the worst case (e.g. if peer actually starts SMP before informing that it's going to follow vendor-specific procedure) device would try to follow default pairing procedure which would still be correct behavior.

> Is it correct that the intended use of this new API is to select the pairing method? Would it work to instead extend `struct bt_conn_auth_cb` with a `.select_pairing_method(bt_conn, bt_conn_pairing_feat)` that can downgrade `smp_pairing_req`:`rsp->io_capability`?

If we would like to modify device's behavior during pairing, we would need to modify other authentications callbacks anyway, so I think that the additional callback is not enough here. The whole pairing flow is modified, it's not only about the IO capabilities. Also if we report given set of IO capabilities, we would need to ensure that we provide needed authentication callbacks (currently IO capabilities are reported relying on used set of authentication callbacks which prevents errors here).

body:
Hi @Thalley

> > Is it correct that the intended use of this new API is to select the pairing method?
> 
> That is actually a good question. This PR fixes #38336, but the issue that is being fixed only states that this should be possible, but does not give any use cases or reasons for it (which is also lacking in the PR description).

Since feature introduced by this PR could be used for various use-cases, I added only a short, generic description in the PR and commit message:
`Change introduces authentication callbacks used only for specified BLE connection. The feature can be used by devices that require reporting specific bonding capabilities only when pairing using vendor-specific procedures.`

**Fast Pair use-case**
Since this use-case was discussed in details during review of my previously proposed solution which was a separate PR (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/46637), I provide short description of Fast Pair use-case below:

```
An example of use-case is bonding using Fast Pair. In that case Central triggers vendor-specific BLE bonding procedure using GATT write to predefined characteristic before sending SMP request. Then devices use Numeric Comparison pairing method to achieve MITM protection. The only exception is the fact that encrypted passkeys are exchanged by devices over GATT instead of displaying them and waiting for user input. If Central does not trigger the vendor-specific BLE bonding procedure, regular pairing is used.
```
For additional details, see Fast Pair specification: https://developers.google.com/nearby/fast-pair/specifications/service/gatt

** Solved issue **
For https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/38336, the new API can be used to override the authentication callbacks right after connection is established for a given Bluetooth local identity (on connected callback). That was already discussed with @kapi-no.

The very last statement from zmake tells twister if the whole binary passed/failed. As an example if you compiled some tests into your binary but never ran them, we have a hook to signal that the binary is a failure. body:
> This is technically correct and very reasonable.
> 
> But really this mess with the idle thread is a design bug we should fix at some point. The root issue here is that we allow the system to have zero preemptible priorities, and when that is true the architecture layer can use that hint[1] to eliminate some code from the interrupt return path: if you know the interrupted thread cannot be preempted, then you never need to context switch at interrupt return time.
> 
> There are two big reasons this optimization isn't very valuable though: first, you still need the context switch code for cooperative switching, and almost all architectures end up sharing almost all that code with the interrupt return path anyway[2]. You don't actually save much code, and to the extent you save cycles it's only a tiny handful (just enough to do the "if the threads are different" check) and at the **wrong side of the interrupt**. Generally you want to work top optimize interrupt **entry** latency. Exit latencies are much less critical.
> 
> And the second reasons is that having saved that code from the interrupt exit we then need to put its logical equivalent (a cooperative context switch via thread yield) right back into the idle thread. Because the idle thread always needs to be preemptible, by definition. And because we're doing it there, after interrupt exit, we're actually **hurting** latencies for any thread that was woken up.
> 
> It's just a mistake. We should ensure that there is always at least one preemptible priority for the idle thread and remove all the legacy complexity.
> 
> [1] IIRC ARM32 is the only one that actually does this.
> 
> [2] IIRC including ARM32!

So, It mean idle thread should not be cooperative thread though `CONFIG_MULTITHREADING=y`

body:
> > I know that someone has probably made a good argument for this, but why are we using identical DT compat identifiers for both physical and emulated peripherals. I've always been a bit unsure about that.
> 
> I discuss this in some detail in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/47388#discussion_r916334794.
> 

@alevkoy 

Yeah, to be honest, I still think that they should just have different compat strings (e.g. suffixed with `-emul`) and the regular device machinery should be used. It adds an extra layer of unnecessary complexity.

Even if the node does not refer to a physical device, it's still fine. We already have several pseudo devices that use DT bindings, for example, another RFC proposes using DT for network configuration.

Differentiating between a physical and emulated peripheral is also not really necessary, since arbitrary device tree overlays can be specified at build time via the command line, or even a completely different board can be defined. Differentiating via compat string (or even an `emulator` boolean DT attribute) would probably suffice for the simplest cases.

Thanks for providing an explanation, in any case.

I do very much agree that emulated peripherals, and the ability to control and configure per-instance behaviour with DT-bindings of those emulated peripherals, is incredibly useful. Just am not super convinced that the extra EMUL macro-machinery is needed.

> > > I know that someone has probably made a good argument for this, but why are we using identical DT compat identifiers for both physical and emulated peripherals. I've always been a bit unsure about that.
> > 
> > I discuss this in some detail in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/47388#discussion_r916334794.
> > 
> 
> @alevkoy 
> 
> Yeah, to be honest, I still think that they should just have different compat strings (e.g. suffixed with `-emul`) and the regular device machinery should be used. It adds an extra layer of unnecessary complexity.
> 
> Even if the node does not refer to a physical device, it's still fine. We already have several pseudo devices that use DT bindings, for example, another RFC proposes using DT for network configuration.
> 
> Differentiating between a physical and emulated peripheral is also not really necessary, since arbitrary device tree overlays can be specified at build time via the command line, or even a completely different board can be defined. Differentiating via compat string (or even an `emulator` boolean DT attribute) would probably suffice for the simplest cases.
> 
> Thanks for providing an explanation, in any case.
> 
> I do very much agree that emulated peripherals, and the ability to control and configure per-instance behaviour with DT-bindings of those emulated peripherals, is incredibly useful. Just am not super convinced that the extra EMUL macro-machinery is needed.
> 
> cc @gmarull @galak @yperess 

The reason for the same compat string is to prevent duplication and reduce the chance for errors. As a very simplified example, let's assume we have a device tree like:

```
&i2c0 {
  dev@0x80 {
    reg = <0x80>;
    ...
  };
};
```

In this example, we're able to:
1. Create the device struct/driver
2. Create the emulator
3. Automatically bind the emulator to the bus

If we used a different compat string, I'm assuming you would want a separate node. In that case, you would need to duplicate the properties of the driver node. Also, if you have 2 nodes you can't put them both on the same bus since you can only have 1 node on the same address.

> > > > I know that someone has probably made a good argument for this, but why are we using identical DT compat identifiers for both physical and emulated peripherals. I've always been a bit unsure about that.
> > cc @gmarull @galak @yperess

> The reason for the same compat string is to prevent duplication and reduce the chance for errors. As a very simplified example, let's assume we have a device tree like:

Which errors are we trying to reduce? 

Reducing duplication in terms of code? Maybe auxilliary functions (although those can be made common). Register definitions though can just be done in header. This would be pretty easy to achieve just having the physical vs emulated driver side-by-side. In fact, it would be pretty easy to test an emulated peripheral against its physical counterpart in that situation.

If you mean duplication in terms of device tree, we have a fair bit of that already, but it's manageable, especially with inheritance (e.g. bosch,bmi160-i2c.yml, bosch,bmi160-i2c-emul.yml) and C-style `#include`s.

> ```
> &i2c0 {
>   dev@0x80 {
>     reg = <0x80>;
>     ...
>   };
> };
> ```
> 
> In this example, we're able to:
> 
> 1. Create the device struct/driver
> 2. Create the emulator
> 3. Automatically bind the emulator to the bus

All of those things are just general device tree and driver features already.

> 
> If we used a different compat string, I'm assuming you would want a separate node. In that case, you would need to duplicate the properties of the driver node. Also, if you have 2 nodes you can't put them both on the same bus since you can only have 1 node on the same address.

It can be, or it could be the same node name, or it could just be a chosen node (which is preferred). Duplication is something that we manage with DT already - even just using C-style `#includes` in DT can help to reduce that. 

I'm not sure if I follow w.r.t. having the same 2 nodes on the same bus at the same address, etc, because that shouldn't really be possible physically or logically. What I would do though, if testing a collection of emulated devices, is create a separate, mostly identical board definition, use emulated compat strings, and also use chosen properties.

I'm fairly certain that would achieve all of the same goals while reusing the usual DT machinery.

body:
Hello andyross,
I'm not sure what counts as public API or not for zephyr, but it is documented in zephyr API [1] and is explicitly mentioned as "user-accessible" (as long as it is placed in a proper position)

This macro is supposed to be used when employing the "item-based" ring buffer: in this case, all items must be 32-bits (so, there is a type). Therefore, the rounding-down cannot happen, as long as the user respects the API.

It seems to me that there are three ways to allocate a ring-buffer for item-based:
1. Use a uint32_t buffer with the `SIZE32_OF` macro, and use `SIZE32_OF` for the item-based API (ring buffer size);
2. Use `RING_BUF_ITEM_DECLARE` (but this will not work inside a struct, for instance); and
3. Use a uint8_t buffer and `sizeof`, but you will need to take care with the API (i.e., you cannot pass `sizeof` for item-based API calls)

I would say the `SIZE32_OF` is useful if you plan to use the item-based ring buffer. However, AFAIK, there are only tests on the tree using this API.

[1] https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/kernel/data_structures/ring_buffers.html

I have given it more thoughts and I believe there might be some misunderstandings on the API. On the I2C side, the introduction of the LVR (Legacy Virtual Register, associated with the device which describes the characteristic of the I2C device, e.g. if it can tolerate high SCL rate) requires I2C devices to be registered with the I3C controller so the controller can be initialized accordingly (for example, if a I2C device cannot do more than fast mode and not tolerant of high SCL rate, the whole bus is limited to fast mode speed). The virtual controller is there to facilitate I2C registration with the I3C controller. This is why the I3C controller does not provide the exact I2C API to I2C devices (by declaring the I2C api first in the I3C API struct) to (kind of) force developers to be aware of capabilities of all devices on the bus (and not simply blindly mixing I2C and I3C devices).

Hopefully this clarifies a bit on why the virtual controller is there. Even with using multi-API interface, the device registration step should not be skipped for I2C devices.

> > I have given it more thoughts and I believe there might be some misunderstandings on the API. On the I2C side, the introduction of the LVR (Legacy Virtual Register, associated with the device which describes the characteristic of the I2C device, e.g. if it can tolerate high SCL rate) requires I2C devices to be registered with the I3C controller so the controller can be initialized accordingly (for example, if a I2C device cannot do more than fast mode and not tolerant of high SCL rate, the whole bus is limited to fast mode speed). The virtual controller is there to facilitate I2C registration with the I3C controller. This is why the I3C controller does not provide the exact I2C API to I2C devices (by declaring the I2C api first in the I3C API struct) to (kind of) force developers to be aware of capabilities of all devices on the bus (and not simply blindly mixing I2C and I3C devices).
> > Hopefully this clarifies a bit on why the virtual controller is there. Even with using multi-API interface, the device registration step should not be skipped for I2C devices.
> 
> so who is responsible for defining these limitations? Are they properties of the virtual controller? Are we missing APIs in I2C to convey what devices are capable of on the bus? Not sure I quite understand how your example of a I2C device being limited to 'fast mode' would actually work.

The capability is encoded in the LVR, which is the 3rd element in `reg`. LVR is for I2C devices under I3C bus (and is introduced along with the I3C spec). This needs to be populated by the developers in devicetree.

According to the spec, I3C devices can do 12MHz. However, the spec says that only fast mode and fast mode plus are supported for I2C devices (at least officially). In addition to this, if the I2C device has a 50ns spike filter on SCL, the controller hardware can generate SCL so SCL pulses are short enough for the I2C devices to ignore them. In this case, I3C devices can still go up to 12MHz (as I2C devices do not see pulsing SCL). However, if any I2C devices on bus does not have the spike filter, the bus is then limited to the highest speed this I2C device can support (which is fast or fast+). Whether the I2C device has spike filter, and its highest supported speed are encoded in the LVR (and thus in the devicetree).

We could also deviate from what the Linux kernel on the DTS binding, but we will need to store the LVR (Legacy Virtual Register) separately.
> 
> I think this its reasonable to introduce `I2C_DT_REG_ADDR` that handles give you back a sane value based on being on a I2C or I3C bus.

This will probably depend on controller implementation. The current `i3c_i2c_device_desc` struct has a field for controller to store private information. If we use macro to produce a static struct, the private data is not going to be there. The controller may not be able to function correctly without this data.

I know of a controller where you need to program the registers to specify what devices are on the bus (... think lookup table in hardware). The index to the entries in the table is then used for data transfer operations. In other word, the driver does not tell the hardware which device address to use, but instead an index in the lookup table. So the private data field described above can be used to store the index. Or else every transaction requires looping through the table to find the index.

> > 
> 
> I get that, but seems like you'd than need to have an associate for each I2C device with an LVR value for that device (rather than on general LVR value). So that feels like a mess to encode in devicetree. I think its better to work with @teburd and figure out what minor tweaks we make to the I2C layer to handle this.

If I may say I really like that the implementation enables backwards compatibility with existing I2C devices through the virtual controller without requiring device drivers to be updated. It's a fantastic feature of this PR, and something @XenuIsWatching made a strong point to push for.

That said I get the concerns about applying the term and information for LVR to all I2C devices on the virtual controller as the spec describes it as a per device register.

LVR however is a lowest common denominator description of device capabilities. If even one device doesn't have the 50ns spike filter, its as if none of them have it. If even one device doesn't tolerate high data rates then its as if none of them do. So while the spec says LVR is a per device attribute for the purposes of Zephyr and ease of compatibility I actually agree with @dcpleung's approach here in making it a bus property that applies to all devices under it. It's closer, in that regard, to being akin to the i2c bus speed property.

That said, it might be sensible (as there are reserved bits in LVR) to more explicitly break out the properties of LVR into named bus attributes in device tree for the virtual i2c controller to avoid the confusion with the spec. Something along the lines of "hdr_tolerant" and reusing the existing speed property. Properties that would directly tie into the LVR indexes noted in the spec for describing device compatibility with higher data rates.

As it is, this looks really nice to me already though and I don't think the idea of a common LVR is a blocker.

body:
> @teburd So what happens when someone wants to use a devicetree from linux that supports I3C and has LVR specified per device - for I2C devices?

In this case, the driver will need to be changed so it can instantiate an instance under I3C bus.

I understand that on Linux, you can have both I2C and I3C devices under I3C bus. The driver layer takes care of device registration. However, that depends on dynamic memory allocation (for bus-related device structs) at runtime which we are trying to avoid here. Moreover, we don't have binary devicetree in memory to grab info at runtime, which is also required for automatic device registration.

On Zephyr, all active devices declared under the I3C bus need to register themselves with the controller. And their drivers need to call the corresponding functions, and to declare the bus-related device structs themselves. body:
If we are okay with changing the I2C subsys.

Note that `struct i3c_i2c_device_desc` has an extra element to store controller private data. As I have mentioned above, some controllers do not use target device address for transfers, instead, they use an index to a hardware lookup table. This can be stored in this private data field. If we are to create a static struct every time we call I2C transfer functions, the I3C controller driver will need to go through some lookup table to grab the index for every call to transfer functions (not just once per transaction, since we have no way of passing the index around between function calls). Of course, if everyeone is okay with the I3C API interface embedding the I2C API in addition to all the `i3c_i2c_*()` APIs. So that the driver can decide whether they want to incur the penalty of going through the lookup table. (Though, if we are not using this type of controllers, then we don't need to pay the speed penalty, but simply space penalty for extra code.)

body:
If we want to maintain straight compatibility to I2C, we will need to accommodate the use case where `i2c_transfer()` will be called with `I2C_DT_SPEC_GET()`. And everytime `I2C_DT_SPEC_GET()` is used, a new struct is created (mostly in stack). If we totally throw out this use case, then the only difference is the extra private data field. Every new struct would not have the private data, and would mostly be zero. And now the controller needs logic to distinguish between some private data (which could be zero), and an uninitialized field of zero. Or we can totally skip the private data and use the I2C device address all the time, with index lookup if necessary. However, if we do away with the private data, it will go out of sync with the equivalent I3C device desc struct which (also) has the private data field.

Let me elaborate a bit more on the lookup table. The controller I described has the lookup table in hardware (whether in its SRAM or a larger register file). The index stored in the struct is the entry index to this hardware table. Without this being stored, looking up the index needs to go through the hardware/SoC bus (e.g. MMIO) to the controller hardware.

Updated the PR so that I2C devices can function without modifications on I3C bus without the virtual controller:

body:
What's the use case here?

The problem I have with this PR is that we should try to avoid and discourage the usage of `mmu_regions.c` entirely. That was a quick and dirty way to be able to have a 1:1 (direct) mapping in the MMU when the MMU driver was in its infancy. Now the correct way for a driver to have its MMIO space mapped is by using the Device MMIO API.

In your example the CCM driver should be using the Device MMIO API to map its own space without having to resort to extend the `mmu_regions.c` at all. If an application doesn't need that driver (and its MMU mapping) then it can simply remove it from the DT (and the mapping will be gone with it).

The only reason `mmu_regions.c` is still there is because the GIC driver is not a proper driver and cannot use the Device MMIO APIs (yet).

So, from a technical prospective this PR is fine but I'm worried this will basically enable the bad habit of using `mmu_regions.c` instead of modifying the drivers to properly support the Device MMIO APIs.


See #46477 for an extensive discussion on this topic.

@povergoing @SgrrZhf what do you think about this?

I agree with that driver should take responsibility to do the MMIO mapping.

But Carlo said "the big issue with Zephyr is that 95% of the drivers are not using the device MMIO API",  especially in some cases user maybe use hal driver directly which is not a standard Zephyr driver, and in general some hal driver will be shared with other RTOS, so not possible to modify hal driver to add MMIO mapping.

Another concern is some hal driver is using physical address directly, if we don't do 1:1 mapping, hal driver should has memory access issues.

So my suggestions is we need to ask drivers to support MMIO mapping if it is possible, in the other way, provide user another easier method to do 1:1 mapping.

Thanks.

Also should look to use the binding for silvaco (in addition to `nxp...` https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/devicetree/devicetree-rebasing.git/tree/Bindings/i3c/silvaco,i3c-master.yaml

Could you be certain that there is no customization of this IP in NXP SoC? I am worried that there might be some differences which require vendor-specific code down the line.

> * Wonder what thoughts are on splitting up `include/zephyr/drivers/i3c.h` further.  Maybe pulling the devicetree stuff into `include/zephyr/drivers/i3c/devicetree.h`.  Moving 'target' mode support into its own header (if we should even support it right now).

I simply modeled this after `i2c.h` as everything is cramped into `i2c.h`.

> * The whole device tracking  / device_find bits feel like we need more work.  Is this related to the controllers that need to build a lookup table?

Those functions are needed since the controller driver is now responsible for creating the device descriptors (instead of each target device driver doing this on its own, and registering the struct with the controller). So that each target device driver needs to grab a reference to its own device descriptor from the controller. I3C devices need to match the PID (which should be unique for all devices on a board) as addresses are dynamically assigned (so they can't be used for matching). I2C devices are easy as their addresses are static so these can be used to match 1-to-1. The device descriptors for I3C devices are a must to store runtime information, and for I2C devices, they are indeed there to aid with the hardware lookup table (if needed).

body:
> 
> Why should this function be optional? I think that this is a common operation and there is no need to load it conditionally. 

How often do you format your storage?

I know use cases where the FAT FS or LittleFS partitions are generated at compile time and merged into hex, as they contain GUI or other resources used by applications; this is not a perfect use but there is no write operations used there, nor anyone wants to format anything when mount fails.

> I could make it optional in FATFS where `mkfs` operation is truly optional, but in littlefs that operation is always available (but it is triggered only if the file system is not detected).

And this is actually not good thing, because this means that if something fails you can get your data on LittleFS device destroyed for no reason, and is not entirely true, search for `FS_MOUNT_FLAG_NO_FORMAT`.

I am not a fan of formatting device when you can not access it, by default. I have already experienced data loss when I was unfortunate to plug SD card, with MBR and two partitions, into a device that did not recognize my SD and got it wiped, while I was just trying to move some data onto that device.

body:
> I personally think that these two approaches don't go against each other.
> 

Not necessarily, but I wanted to ensure that especially your use-case was not covered by the library proposal.

> My solution is based on idea that I want to relocate all _files_ on some path. In my usecase it is easier, because I don't bother what libraries are there.
> 

So in this case, let's continue, but adjust your proposal.
Instead of adjusting the python script, then we should improve on the CMake side.

A disadvantage of the Python script is that it's much harder for users to directly debug which files got included.
Also the glob will run on each build, thus slowing incremental builds.

Instead the `zephyr_code_relocate()` should be extended to support a list of files.

This will allow a user to do:
```
file(GLOB_RECURSIVE relocate_sources "*.c")
zephyr_code_relocate(${relocate_sources} <location>)
```
or if only a single level is desired
```
file(GLOB relocate_sources "src/*.c")
zephyr_code_relocate(${relocate_sources} <location>)
```

this will provide much more freedom to users as to how they want to glob files.
Also it has the benefit on being executed at configure time, thus not impacting incremental builds.

Users can easily see which files are included for relocation by using `--trace-expand` or a `message()` / `print()` function in CMake.
They can even look directly in the Makefile or build.ninja.

This proposal will require a small change on how arguments in `zephyr_code_relocate()` is handled.

Combining this with support for generator expression, as commented here:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/50791#discussion_r985779474

This means a single solution should be able to support both ways.

Side note: as part of this, we could consider to deprecate support for the regex in the python script itself, but that would be outside the scope for the above proposal.

> Fixes #36882

It is workaround but mitigates probably 99% of cases. Problem is that when UART is shared, it can be intercepted by logs and this is what happens here. Disabling logging in FS also fixes the problem.
> 
> Note that this only fixes the specific issue mentioned, there might be other potential errors emitted if filesystem errors are encountered

that is true

>  however the `mcumgr` client is actually to blame for this as it should be searching through the received data for the mcumgr start header, 0x06 0x09, which it does not do.

No it is not. The problem is that the client is in the middle of receiving frame that has been marked with start of header tag, but got additional characters inside. Because this is UART and CBOR a client basically sees stream of characters, following the start of header tag, and tries to process it as it is; unfortunately it gets something that is not part of packet in the middle so it fails.

00000040  41 59 32 39 6d 5a 68 6b  48 67 76 39 6d 36 41 3d  |AY29mZhkHgv9m6A=|
00000050  3d                                                |=|
```
The 0x06 0x09 start header can be seen, and the full packet is there, I'm not sure why there isn't a 0x0a end character but other than that, the packet is not split up. The issue where UART data *does* interleave mcumgr commands from what I've seen is due to usage of `printk` - noted in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/38947 the solution to that is to process printk messages in the logging system - PR at https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/50594 however this has had the side effect of causing many tests to fail to output any data, but in my testing, once that is enabled, shell/log/printk output does not interleave mcumgr packets. My test system for this, albeit it is on a single core processor not an SMP system is to have timers that output log and printk data at random times whilst having a mcumgr client continually fire commands and wait for full uninterrupted responses from the device, this normally falls over in less than 5 seconds when normal printk is used, I had it running for multiple minutes with printk output through the logging system before ending the test

> 
> ```
> #if DT_NODE_HAS_STATUS(DT_NODELABEL(mx25r64), okay)

> #elif DT_NODE_HAS_STATUS(DT_NODELABEL(gd25q16), okay)

> #endif
> ```

> but doing so doesn't really seem right.
> 

Is there an option to use chosen `zephyr,flash-disk` for that purpose? For example
```
chosen {
    zephyr,flash-disk = &mx25r64;
};
```
This would allow code like this
```
    flash_dev = DEVICE_DT_GET(DT_CHOSEN(zephyr_flash_disk));
```
This is flexible and easily allows to set default value in DTS or board overlay, while at the same time easily allowing to replace it in app overlay by doing `/delete-property/ zephyr,flash-disk` on the `chosen` node.

There is also an option, less nice and flexible, to use specific label, for example
```
zephyr_flash_disk_0: &mx25r64 : { };
```
and in code:
```
   flash_dev = DEVICE_DT_GET(DT_NODELABEL(zephyr_flash_disk_0));   
```

In both cases Kconfigs are no longer there and there is no need for `if` sequence, as flash disk selection is done in DTS.

IMHO using Kconfig to select flash disk is not best approach, because the Kconfig will require updates every time when new flash devices or boards with such devices are added; when the DTS is designated for selecting flash disk, and you add new board with new flash, all you have to do is to point to it with chosen or label, and you do not have to touch Kconfig, or the flash disk driver code.

body:
> IMHO it is acceptable that you get a corrupt build when you include a third-party definition of ARRAY_SIZE that does not return the array size.

Source code that redefines system/compiler provided macros should do that explicitly by `undef`, and have it documented. I do not think it is good, for the system, to walk out of the way.

`MIN/MAX` are non-standard macros, not defined by C standard, and may or may not be provided by systems.

> 
> There is already prior-art for ifndef with MAX and MIN, so it should be permitted to also do this for ARRAY_SIZE.
> 

`ifndef` thing is not eniterly true:
For example FreeBSD:
 https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/ffbc2a58b13a9239269e661fe23f86c587cc7638/sys/sys/param.h#L329-L331
just defines `MIN`/`MAX`, no checks.

Glib does not even bother to `#ifndef`, it just goes for `#undef`
https://github.com/GNOME/glib/blob/2843eef4a4fdccbef5782b8a5b7cd121c8b91ca0/glib/gmacros.h#L887-L894

~~Linux kernel sources do not have "global" `MAX` definition.~~ Update 2022-10-06: I was wrong here, it does via include/linux/kernel.h, I am sorry for that.

GNU libc, https://codebrowser.dev/glibc/glibc/misc/sys/param.h.html#101, doesn't bother to `#ifndef` either.

> 
> I agree we should not allow ifndef of SUCCESS, because that is obviously ambiguous.
> 
> But MAX, MIN, and ARRAY_SIZE are well defined.

Not by system. Looking at Linux kernel sources, there is no `MAX`, `MIN`, `ARRAY_SIZE` definition provided by kernel headers, system interface headers.
Looking at FreeBSD, the `ARRAY_SIZE` is only defined by subsystems, for local use. Also there is also something named `nitems` where some `ARRAY_SIZE` definitions use like
```
#define ARRAY_SIZE(x) nitems(x)
```

which is generally defined as:
```
#define nitems(x)       (sizeof((x)) / sizeof((x)[0]))
```
basically what ARRAY_SIZE(x) does, right? Except for this one definition: https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/main/tools/build/cross-build/include/common/sys/param.h#L70-L74.
Seems that results will differ, depending on header order.

If you include to your code some library that redefines stuff provided by system headers, or toolchain headers, it is on you to `undef` or change header order; that lib needs fixing.

Including header files should not be art of sudoku, where you are only sure that Zephyr headers could be pushed down below everything else, because they are sorry to have been included and will move out of others way just to avoid arguing. 

I am more willing into doing this Glib way: "I am system header better put me on top because I `undef` your stuff without asking".
And then everything else has do do `undef` explicitly, or `ifndef ` the `sys/util.h` provided macros.

This is system header, it is used in Zephyr code base and whatever identifiers it provides, when included into subsytem code, driver code, and so on, it should provide identifier with definition that is within `sys/util.h'; this should not be dependent on header order.

* multi-instance from the start,
* allow concurrent use of all types at the same time,

The USB mass storage example does not work in Zephyr 3.2.0 when built with `-DCONFIG_APP_MSC_STORAGE_FLASH_FATFS=y`. It worked fine in earlier releases, therefore it is a regression.

The naive fix is to change the `"MX25R64"` to `"mx25r6435f@0"` and `"GD25Q16"` to `"gd25q16@0"` in `samples/subsys/usb/mass/Kconfig`. It would solve the regression, i.e. the USB mass storage example would just work.

[Your comment](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/50856#pullrequestreview-1126795930) about the need to remove Kconfig option essentially discarded the "simply patch the regression" option and led to discussion what would be the correct approach.

The [naive `#ifdef` chain](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/50856#issuecomment-1265373828) is questionable as it would just get rid of the Kconfig option but would still leave the underlying issue intact. The `zephyr,flash-disk` solution seems actually harmful as it adds a chosen node that is already known to be flawed at the time of introduction.

> First: the disk API is a bit "weird" and unlike other device APIs, because it uses a `struct disk_info` to wrap a `struct device`, so what are the "instances" here? Instances of device? Of struct disk_info? The API documentation is not clear on how it fits together. Can 2 `disk_info` structs share the same `device` struct? If so, which one is the "instance" you are speaking of? None of the documentation links I pasted above seem to clarify that. Is this just undocumented, or did I miss something?

From USB point of view, the "instance" refers to LUN (logical unit). The host accesses each LUN as block device. It is not necessary to expose whole flash device as a LUN. The pretty simple use case would be to have part of flash chip containing user data and the other part to hold some assets like firmware graphics, blobs or even actual code. Therefore the partition approach instead of disk approach is pretty appealing.

body:
Just to make it 100% clear:

For `arm_add_q31` declared as follows by CMSIS-DSP:

```
  /**
   * @brief Q31 vector addition.
   * @param[in]  pSrcA      points to the first input vector
   * @param[in]  pSrcB      points to the second input vector
   * @param[out] pDst       points to the output vector
   * @param[in]  blockSize  number of samples in each vector
   */
  void arm_add_q31(
  const q31_t * pSrcA,
  const q31_t * pSrcB,
        q31_t * pDst,
        uint32_t blockSize);
```

We want something like:

```
  /**
   * @brief Q31 vector addition.
   * @param[in]  src_a      points to the first input vector
   * @param[in]  src_b      points to the second input vector
   * @param[out] dst       points to the output vector
   * @param[in]  block_size  number of samples in each vector
   */
DSP_FUNC_SCOPE void zdsp_add_q31(
  const q31_t *src_a,
  const q31_t *src_b,
        q31_t *dst,
        uint32_t block_size);
```

i.e. same type system and names, "identical" argument names adjusted for different naming convention

Not:

```
/**
 * @brief q1_31 vector addition.
 * @param[in]  lhs      points to the first input vector
 * @param[in]  rhs      points to the second input vector
 * @param[out] dst      points to the output vector
 * @param[in]  count    number of samples in each vector
 */
DSP_FUNC_SCOPE void zdsp_add_q1_31(const q1_31_t *lhs, const q1_31_t *rhs, q1_31_t *dst,
				   uint32_t count);
```

i.e. no types like `q1_31_t` and `q16_16_t`, no different argument names (changes due to different naming convention is fine, but it should stay more or less the same -- e.g. no change from `block_size` to `count`),

> @desowin, would it not be better to define a readcopy buffer for each instance and the flash_disk_data to be extended with:
>     * a pointer to the readcopy buffer
>     * the mutex

I don't really see much benefit with doing so. The buffer is only used during writes (and only when writing less than a full page) and USB Mass Storage class cannot multiplex write commands to multiple LUNs (i.e. previous write must be finished before new one can be issued). body:
> This could be renamed `CONFIG_DISK_MAX_SUPPORTED_ERASE_BLOCK_SIZE`, with better description how it affects system. We need this buffer anyway whether disk with run-time provided or compile-time provided erase block size is used. At this point this is property of software, that allows it to work with devices with different characteristics.

It should be maximum value from the set of minimum erase block sizes of all `zephyr,flash-disk` partitions. The minimum erase block size is determined by hardware.

> Note also that erase block size may be stored within file system information on mkfs.

The filesystem is completely transparent to `zephyr,flash-disk`. The flashdisk is essentially a block device wrapper over flash devices. The need for the `read_copy_buf` is due to underlying hardware limitation (can only erase in whole blocks, i.e. there is no way for software to erase less bytes at a time), not a software one (filesystem or whatever).

If `flash_erase()` cannot erase the `page_size` bytes (not less not more) as returned by `flash_get_page_info_by_offs()` then I would consider the problem to be in the flash driver.

> What should then a device with DTS setting `erase-block-size` do when memory device with such file system is connected to system?

Not care at all. The flashdisk layer does not need such information.

> Setting `erase-block-size` with DTS is giving disk certain hardware characteristics, which is not true for devices like SPI connected memories where erase block size can be often configured at run time.

The "configured at run time" is very misleading. The software can use one of supported erase sizes. The minimum possible is what is relevant to flashdisk driver (if the `zephyr,flash-disk` partition spans across non-homogeneous sized sectors, then it is the maximum value of the minimum possible erase size of all sectors used by the partition).

> When you connect flash disk on SPI and the flash-disk node states that the disk has `erase-block-size` 4096B, but file system configuration read from disk states 16B, what does the system should do now?

Filesystem is different layer. Flashdisk does not and should not care what data it holds.

> However before trying to do this the question should be answered if a shared buffer is allowed or not: I think there can be situations were 2 flashdisks need access to the readcopy buffer at the same time (e.g. when copying from/to each other) and this might require two buffers to avoid a lockup. This would mean that each disk really needs its own buffer.

The only situation when you would need two flashdisks to access `read_copy_buf` is when **writing to both at the same time**. The example you provide does not require simultaneous access to `read_copy_buf`. The `read_copy_buf` is not needed nor used when **reading**.

The way `read_copy_buf` is used is:
- acquire `read_copy_buf_lock`
- read flash memory data into `read_copy_buf`. This is necessary because the write will only partially modify the page, but the hardware can only erase no less than `page_size` bytes at a time (e.g. writing only 1 "flaskdisk 512 byte sector" out of 8 "flashdisk sectors" = 1 "page"). The code actually reads more than strictly necessary, but that keeps the code simple (optimization is definitely out of this PR scope).
- Put the new data in `read_copy_buf` at appropriate location, so the `read_copy_buf` contains the desired state on disk
- Write `read_copy_buf` contents to flash memory
- Release `read_copy_buf_lock`

As the data to be written is already held somewhere in RAM by the time `read_copy_buf_lock` is acquired, I see no possibility for a lockup.

I don't really think the code complexity changes at all if there is one or multiple buffers involved. In my opinion the reduced RAM usage justifies having just one buffer.

The only reason for having per instance buffer would be writeback caching (to limit number of erases when subsequent sectors are written) but that is optimization and definitely way out of the scope of this PR (which is to solve the hardware description problem). But even with caching, it would still probably work just fine with just one buffer.

body:
> I can't seem to find any magic environment variables to tell gdb to use my virtualenv python.

The Python-capable GDB from Zephyr SDK assumes that you have installed Python using Homebrew (since that is the package manager recommended by the GSG) and looks for the libpython using an absolute path at `/usr/local/opt/python@3.8/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.8/Python` (thanks to how libpython is named on macOS, we cannot really just look for `Python` here).

If you have Python 3.8 installation under a different path, then you will have to patch the GDB executable:

```
install_name_tool -change /usr/local/opt/python@3.8/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.8/Python ${YOUR_LIBPYTHON_PATH} arch-zephyr-elf-gdb
```

body:
@kristofer-jonsson-arm what you should do is actually to create a Kconfig in the sample folder, like `zephyr/samples/tflm_ethosu/Kconfig`.

And then in that file write:
```
config TFLM_ETHOSU_TAINT_BLOBS
        bool
        default y
        select TAINT_BLOBS

source "Kconfig.zephyr"
```
that will set `TAINT_BLOBS` to `y` without the need to give the setting a prompt.
The reason for using the construct with a `select TAINT_BLOBS` is because it allows for other parts of the build system to actually see why TAINT_BLOBS was selected.

Whereas the option of just defaulting `TAINT_BLOBS` to `y` in the Kconfig doesn't provide the same tracing in other tooling.
Thus it becomes harder to trace back why `TAINT_BLOBS` is enabled.
(a bit philosophical discussion when talking about a sample that needs to select this, but this is the main reason for this way of using `select TAINT_BLOBS` and not having it user configurable).

> Thanks for taking this on. Just interested to know, are there significant shortcomings in the regulator API as it is implemented today (besides the issues this PR fixes). I tried to follow the Linux API whenever possible, but the API was only tested with a PCA9420.

Last time, I didn't saw the RFC, but now I understand it.

My biggest issue with that RFC (and that PR) is the rarity of separate charger IC and fuel gauge IC in the embedded world. Most boards that feature some kind of battery related IC have either fuel gauge IC, charger IC or an IC that combines them both. Example is [MAX77818](https://www.maximintegrated.com/en/products/power/battery-management/MAX77818.html).
This device has to have two separate drivers, because it is both a fuel gauge and a charger. This isn't impossible (Linux's MFD), but I think it is unneeded complication, at least compared to Linux's power_supply.

Yes, I know, SBS is an example of separate charger and fuel gauge (SBS battery), but firstly rarely embedded device uses SBS, and secondly if you want to change charging parameters (at least in the case you can), (most of the time) you need to communicate the change to the SBS battery, and then the SBS battery will communicate the changes to the charger.

As a last example, the very integrated [AXP202](https://dl.linux-sunxi.org/AXP/AXP202%20Datasheet_v1.0_en.pdf) from X-Powers.
Linux gets away with using 3 instances of power_supply driver: battery, ac-power, usb-power. (I am not counting the regulator interface and etc.)
With this RFC, you will need to use 4 instances of 3 drivers: 1 - battery, 1 - charger and 2 of something else for usb and ac power monitoring, for the same functionality. And they all will have some very similar APIs.
And in both cases, you will need to have some userspace driver for more advanced processing.

body:
> My understanding is that `__restrict` will break this behavior.

Correct, when using __restrict the assumption/precondition is that there is no overlap between the inputs and outputs. As the compiler may do SW pipelining and reorder/schedule load and store instructions in an optimal way, as in this example:

```
for(i = 0; i < 20; i++)
   *a++ = *b++;
}
```
Without restricted pointers:
```
ld.ab %r2,[%r1,8]
st.ab %r2,[%r0,8] ; Stall for LD to complete
ld %r2,[%r1,-4]
st %r2,[%r0,-4] ; Stall for LD to complete
```
With restricted pointers
```
ld.ab %r3,[%r1,8]
ld %r2,[%r1,-4]
st.ab %r3,[%r0,8] ; Notice compiler uses R2 and R3; interleaving accesses
st %r2,[%r0,-4]
```

Looking at the definitions of the basicmath functions, they seem to imply that inputs cannot be modified/overwritten as they have the 'const' qualifier (though that's not the C semantics as aliased pointers are not forbidden or prevented by const.).

For a generic Zephyr API, I'd be ok to take the strict definition: when output is overlapping input buffers, the result is not guaranteed. That leaves freedom to implementations, and works both with backends that allow overwriting inputs and that don't.

body:
@ruuddw @SiyuanCheng-CN @teburd @stephanosio 

Upon further review and consulting with some of our compiler guys I've reached the following conclusions:

### RE: `__restrict`

We should not allow `__restrict` as a pointer attribute in this API. By definition it means that the behavior of `a += b` is undefined and can break with different compilers or even versions of the same compiler.

### RE: `__agu`

This seems perfectly reasonable, though I would like it to go in a separate CL so we can have a focused discussion on how are we going to add architecture specific attributes to this API (which I assume we'll be running into quite a lot and this will be a long discussion that I don't want my other work to be blocked on).
author: yperess

body:
I agree with the __restrict 'risk' and the AGU is obviously not relevant for all architectures/implementations. Therefore the proposal is to add these via macro's that user can configure/define: if not applicable for a certain implementation backend, the preprocessor removes them.
The main discussion I think that needs to be resolved (independent of interface implementations) is the semantics that we want. Should a = math_op(a,b) and b = math_op(a,b) both be supported by any implementation backend? Or only reuse of the first (or second)? Should it be supported for any math_op, or only for simpler ones?
My preference would be to have the interface semantics defined more strict (i.e. adhering to our optimized __restrict), but if the majority prefers the semantics to be defined including in-place/argument aliasing support we will find other ways to have optimal DSP performance and compatibility with the ARC dsp library for our users.

Therefore the proposal is to add these via macro's that user can configure/define: if not applicable for a certain implementation backend, the preprocessor removes them. Should a = math_op(a,b) and b = math_op(a,b) both be supported by any implementation backend? Or only reuse of the first (or second)? Should it be supported for any math_op, or only for simpler ones? My preference would be to have the interface semantics defined more strict (i.e. adhering to our optimized __restrict), but if the majority prefers the semantics to be defined including in-place/argument aliasing support we will find other ways to have optimal DSP performance and compatibility with the ARC dsp library for our users.

That seems fair, I guess the tradeoff we're looking at is:

### Option 1

Disallow in-place DSP operations. Which will allow for `__restrict` and generally require more memory in places where in-place arithmetic would have been used.

### Option 2

Disallow `__restrict` optimization thus making in-place operations possible (potentially saving some memory) at the cost of some performance.

body:
> Note that my intention was for this to apply to all past, present and future common macro names, not only the ones that already exist in Zephyr. This would be in line with PRs like https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/52488.

I do not think the language in this PR does address new macros being introduced into Zephyr. When we decide to use a new macro or renaming an existing macro to something that conflicts with modules, we are asking modules to change something they used already and did not conflict with zephyr before. I guess the question is, what is "common" and does the fact that Linux uses the macro makes it common? 
i have an issue with renaming or prefixing a macro we use in zephyr, common or not, so it does not conflict with someone else using the same macro. But I do not understand why we have to use a Linux macro name when we can  continue using the existing name, or if we do not like it, use some other name that does not conflict with anyone. 

We might be able to "negotiate" and have modules, especially HALs, move to what ever zephyr is using or rename, but this is calling for trouble and conflicts in general when we decide to adopt something into the tree that pre-existed elsewhere. 

We need to be cautious with the language of the rule if we decide to adopt this approach.

body:
Architecture WG:

- History of the RTC API in Zephyr:
   - https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/23526#issuecomment-603363339
   - https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/41287#issuecomment-1072240109
   - This PR
- @bjarki-trackunit presents the differences between this PR and #41287
   - Supports:
      - `rtc.h`: Simpler counter API, with promise to work on power down
      - `rtcc.h`: Calendar-based API
      - `wakeup_timer.h`: Simple timer that wakes up the system
   - The reason for the 3 APIs is the huge difference in functionality across RTC models and MCU models
- @stephanosio thinks is a good idea to split up the APIs from the counter one, given the different nature of these devices
- @cfriedt: Part of the reason why the RTC API became relevant again, is because Stephanos, Keith Packard & I discovered a layering violation in the libc. Currently, PicoLibC (and newlib, FWIR) call into posix functions for clocks. However, we can't have the libc relying on POSIX functions. We need an actual hardware API for a clock that includes calendar functionality. So the proper layering would be libc -> Zephyr RTC(c) API, and then the POSIX subsystem should also ideally reference the Zephyr RTC(c) API
- @stephanosio mentions that we might need to unify time handling in a single place in Zephyr
- @nashif agrees with @stephanosio's comments on both splitting up and unifying the time handling in Zephyr

body:
Looks nice. I will withdrawn my PR https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/51212.

I will reflect what I read and understood from the code. The text may server as basis for a documentation.

=== start doc text ===

Static Code Analyzer work differently and depending on the tasks they perform, require more or less build information.
The following, possibly incomplete list of, constellations are known:
1. Stand-alone SCA's execution: during a build an information file (e.g. compile_commands.json) is generated. Those information then are used to launch the SCA. Build and SCA runs execute separately. An integration into the build system is not required and done. Typically the linking step cannot be considered in that constellation.
2. SCA execution during build
  2.1. The compiler / linker call is replaced by a call to the SCA in the build system. The SCA then calls the compiler after executing itself. The path to the compiler executable and all compiler command line parameter need to be known to the SCA. The build system needs to be modified to replace the compiler by the SCA call.
  2.2. The compiler / linker call is intercepted on an OS level (similar to a virus scanner). The SCA executes itself with all the command line parameters that were passed to the compiler call and then returns control back to the compiler executable. The SCA requires to know the path to compiler executable to be intercepted.

In the Zepyhr OS build system the SCA integration has been solved as follows:

- The variable `ZEPHYR_SCA_VARIANT` selects the SCA tool to be used during the build process
  - Pass `ZEPHYR_SCA_VARIANT` when starting a build either directly to cmake or otherwise west using `-DZEPHYR_SCA_VARIANT=\<sca-variant-name\>`
  - \<sca-variant-name\> has to correspond with one of the folder names in /cmake/sca/ e.g. 
   /cmake/sca/**sparse** or 
   /cmake/sca/**cppcheck**
- The variable `SCA_ROOT` sets the root paths for your out-of-tree configuration of a SCA tool.
  - `SCA_ROOT` may be a list of several locations/paths separated by either semi-colons or spaces for your out of tree sca tool configurations
  - Since a SCA configuration is executed from for all paths in `SCA_ROOT`, the last entry in `SCA_ROOT` has the highest priority
  - If there are several configurations for the same `ZEPHYR_SCA_VARIANT` name in different locations all preceding will get overwritten by the last found, also the in-tree configuration
  - Empty (non existing) locations of configurations for `ZEPHYR_SCA_VARIANT` will be ignored.
- A custom out of tree sca configurations need to comply with the following structure:
        \<root-location(s)\>/cmake/sca/\<sca-variant-name\>/sca.make
	optional: \<root-location(s)\>/cmake/sca/\<sca-variant-name\>/\<sca-variant-name\>_\<lang\>_lancher.tmplt
	- sca.make: You have the freedom to implement what ever is required to get your SCA configured and integrated. sca.make will only be called once in a build run and **not** repeatedly when compiling the sources. Therefore sca.make is the right place to do once per build configurations of the SCA such as:
	  - writing SCA configuration files formatted according to your SCA's preference (consider cmake's https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/command/configure_file.html), 
	  - preparing and installing a launcher script which will call the SCA (see below)
	- \<sca-variant-name\>\_\<lang\>\_launcher.tmplt: SCAs which are called as a replacement of the compiler and call the actual compiler after executing themself best use cmake's `CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_LAUNCHER` feature (see https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/prop_tgt/LANG_COMPILER_LAUNCHER.html). For that purpose \<sca-variant-name\>\_\<lang\>\_launcher.tmplt can be implemented, which will be called by cmake as a replacement for the compiler itself. Preferably the \<sca-variant-name\>\_\<lang\>\_launcher.tmplt is a cmake script, but could be any other script / executable that runs in your environment (OS, installed tools)
	    - Once per build configurations are best not be done in the launcher script\(s\), since the script\(s\) will be called repeatedly for each source file.
	  
Please take the "sparce" (tbd: add link) integration as a simple example for case 2.1 and a good starting point for your own SCA integration.

=== end doc text ===
  
If I mirrored the implementation incorrectly somewhere, I would be glad to know.
Feel free to correct the text if you think it can be used as documentation basis but is not understandable enough.

We have not integrated our companies SCA (Axivion Suite) yet, but I am quite positive that it will work for us and for most.

I would also rename \<sca-variant-name\>.template to \<sca-variant-name\>_\<lang\>_launcher.tmplt or similar.
1. There may be several launcher: for C and C++ and the linker
2. If it is a launcher I would name it that way somehow. If there is a common understandable abbreviation for launcher also that could be used to shorten the file name.

body:
## Update

### Wakeup timer API dropped
The wakeup timer API is nearly identical to the counter API, except for setting the timeout in ms instead of ticks. When creating an emulated driver for it, it became clear that I was essentially just wrapping the k_timer in a device driver API. For these reasons, the wakeup timer API has been dropped.

### Added emulated RTC and RTCC devices and drivers
The emulated devices can be added to any board, and behave nearly identically to a real RTC or RTCC (they loose track of time when system resets).

### Added tests for RTC and RTCC device drivers
The tests validate the behavior of RTC and RTCC devices through the RTC and RTCC APIs. The tests look for any board with the alias `rtc` and `rtcc` respectively to designate the device to test. The tests currently automatically run for the native_posix board.

### Added emulated RTC and RTCC devices to the native_posix board
The native_posix board now includes an emulated RTC and RTCC device. Drivers for the devices are included if `CONFIG_RTC` or `CONFIG_RTCC` are enabled in Kconfig. They adhere to the simulated time of the posix boards since they use the sysclock to track time.
