body:
>An RTC and and RTCC emulated device using the emulated RTC and
RTCC device drivers has been added to the native_posix board
providing support for RTC and RTCC for the native_posix board.
>
>In the future, this may completely replace the native_rtc source
files as the RTC and RTCC make this redundant.

I'm not opposed to the PR in itself, but one note: this commit description seems to misunderstand a bit the native_rtc purpose and misrepresent a bit what this particular commit does.
The native_rtc.c/h provided by the native_posix board is a "HW model" equivalent/very low level API which was not used thru any (not yet existing) Zephyr driver.
That aimed at providing a mechanism for a future driver (like the one this PR's API is enabling) to hook to either the simulated time or a pseudo host time, which would both not reset at simulation start (unless explicitly selected), and would be controllable from command line and programmatically from tests ( https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.1.0/boards/posix/native_posix/doc/index.html#peripherals ). > Should some information be runner / flash tool specific defaults and not board based ?
> 
> So that nrfjprog default will only issue --recover once and not each board having to specify this information.

The problem with this is linkage, for the nrf5340 if you recover the application core, it clears the application core, but if you recover the network core, it clears both cores, for another MCU it might only clear a specific core, so it's not really possible to know how to do that. This is a problem because it then matters in what order images are flashed, if an application is created which adds a bluetooth image and is flashed normally, assuming with recover, the application core will be flashed first, then the network core (because of the order of images being added), and thus the MCU would not boot because the application core would have no code. SoC based would make more sense than board based because an nrf5340 is an nrf5340 no matter what board it is on, so this can be migrated to soc-level for boards v2 in the future instead of being board-specific.

body:
> @yperess I want to leverage ZTest in my main application without having to create new test applications so that tests are performed under my application context. I could modify my code to not link my main function when ZTEST is enabled and use `test_main` instead but:
> 
> * I don't want the report to be printed only when returning from test_main(), but right after the tests are run (asap)

`test_main()` should be running the tests, is the issue that you're trying to merge it with your application logic so this function has extra latency (or doesn't return?)

> * I don't want to stop my application after tests are run
> 
> I could certainly find solutions to bypass the current behavior and make it work for my use case but I thought this was probably easier to remove definition of `main()` from ztest and make calling the tests easily accessible.
> 
> Let me know what you think

I have 2 concerns currently that I'm trying to work around:
1. We do have initialization code in ztest's `main()` function, so as that changes you (or any other downstream user) would have to keep up with the changes.
2. ztest tightly binds to twister so similar to issue #1, you might have to keep up with changes to other parts of ztest (not just the `main()` function).

Would you be able to rename your application's main function instead based `CONFIG_ZTEST`? So what I'm suggesting is:

### Rename your main entry point
```
#ifdef CONFIG_ZTEST
void app_main(void *arg0, void *arg1, void *arg2)
#else
void main(void)
#endif
```

### Add a new thread that's only linked in when testing
```
/*
 * Include the following in your CMakeLists.txt:
 *     target_add_sources_ifdef(CONFIG_ZTEST app test_main.c)
 */

extern void app_main(void *, void *, void *);
K_THREAD_DEFINE(app_main_tid, CONFIG_MAIN_STACK_SIZE,
    app_main, NULL, NULL, NULL,
    CONFIG_MAIN_THREAD_PRIORITY, 0, 0);

void test_main()
{
  /*
   * Use a condvar here to wait for the tests to all run,
   * you'll need to trigger that from app_main or where
   * ever in your application you call:
   *     ztest_run_registered_test_suites()
   */
}
```

It's not as pretty as just replacing the `main()` function, but it should give you more flexibility without having to debug strange errors if we ever make changes to ztest. Alternatively (not trying to dissuade you from using ztest) if you don't want to use twister, you could link in gTest instead which would give you the additional flexibility you want, in theory it's possible to modify gTest to work with twister but I haven't had time to look into it.

@nashif  If I understand correctly, your are fine with the proposed refactoring, as long as all the required features will be added? Grzegorz added features you suggested. 

I guess what also we need to discuss is ` IMO we are overloading and misusing the current syntax and scheme` i.e. How the scheme should look like. I went through your PR #52179 and I think I see what you meant. You are proposing some additional level of organization, where platforms/simulation/toolchains etc. will have extra dedicated entries. At first I found it useful (but problematic since it will break our CIs and some simultaneous merges will have to follow to adapt CI). However, after longer consideration I think the solution Grzegorz proposes will serve us better.

In Grzegorz's solution an entry in quarantine yaml is more flexible, and I will argue why it is good for us: All used keys (scenario/platform/simulation/etc) can be mixed together creating a desired combination of what to quarantine.  Also, regexes can be used to all fields, not only scenarios. If in a given entry a certain key (e.g. scenario) is missing it means no specific value chosen, i.e. take all possible.  So having everything skipped on a given platform or simulation is also possible. This was pointed by Grzegorz in his latest comment.

I think the schema you're proposing might quickly end as obsolete and would require yet another modification. E.g. What if you'd like to combine scenarios with other fields, e.g. simulation? I can see a case when we don't want to skip all `simulation: qemu` but e.g. only logging related tests on qemu type platforms. Or (in future) all drivers tests on a given toolchain. In your schema all new keys have their own sections and cannot be used in combination with any other key.

As for organization and not introducing a mess in the quarantine file. I think, if needed, we can use comments to organize the file. They will be skipped by twister, but can help humans to organize entries. E.g. 

```
###### Mixed keys  ##################################
- scenarios:
  - kernel.common.(misra|tls)
  comment: "link to issue"

- scenarios:
  - kernel.common
  platforms:
  - nrf53.*

####### Platforms  ##################################
### Use this section to store platforms to be fully skipped ######

- platforms:
  - nrf99.*
  comment: All nrf99 family boards got their dts corrupted. Issue: xxxx
   

####### Simulators ##################################
### Use this section to store simulators to be fully skipped ######
- simulations:
  - qemu
 
```

Also, by definition quarantine should be used as a temporary solution, so the yaml will be a living document, where after fixing entries are dropped. So it won't keep growing indefinitely.

I am also worried that without a proper recognition it could end up as some yet another feature only few people are ever using. I think making it usable would require a commitment (don't mean by you, rather a testing wg level, etc) to mark more tests with `platform_key`

Anyone needing to run twister --all on on the in tree suite or subsets of tests to ensure builds and tests work on all relevant platforms would benefit. This greatly reduces the amount of work required to validate code in cases where...

* Testing on each arch with a simulator is enough
* Testing once on each platform with a particular soc/soc family/soc series/cpu core is enough given
  a set of hardware platforms.

The first case is really pure code libraries where there's no significant hardware interaction other than architecture specifics. 

The second use case, which this could lend itself to (though would require more metadata in the platform yaml) is if I'm testing an IP block driver, do I need to test this driver on every board and soc that includes this IP block? That's a significant amount of time to do!

Maybe as an extreme example...

twister --all -T tests/subsys/rtio with this patch takes 45s, without it takes 30min. As the author of the subsys I can tell you its sufficient if the test suite runs once per arch and on a simulator.

The twister docs suggest that you can run all tests

twister --all --enable-slow

Good luck! It's close to a million test builds, many of which are effectively duplicated effort rebuilding tests for the same exact code paths... over... and over... and over. This is my attempt and trying to provide a tool to remove the duplicated efforts.

@eivindj-nordic, things that I don't like and need fixing:

a. CONFIG option name, this should be something like `CONFIG_FCB_ALLOW_FIXED_ENDMARKER`,
b. The endmarker should not be `CRC8_CCITT_INITIAL_VALUE`,

@mbolivar-nordic easiest way for testing the second one is to build a first image which enables security features, e.g. readback protection, so you could build an application with sysbuild and MCUboot enabled whereby the MCUboot images enables readback protection - without this patch, MCUboot would be flashed and the second image would not be flashed, with this, both images will be flashed.

The first one is only half of a fix, taking the example of the nrf5340, if you had a sysbuild image that has multiple images for the application core, then flash using `west flash --recover` - without this patch, each image will run with --recover, deleting the previous flash data, leaving the MCU in a broken state, with this patch, --recover will only be ran once and additional images being loaded will not recover the device. The half that this does not fix is the board priority part of the problem, when you have e.g. network and application images all part of a single sysbuild project, because on the nRF5340, using --recover on the application core only affects the application core but doing it on the network core affects both cores, so if you had a project set up which built and flashed the network core image first then application core image - this would be fixed as above, but if you have it the other way around, building and flashing the application core image first, then the network image core's --recover command will erase the application core's image, leaving it empty. The solution for this other half is with a cmake priority system as described in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/53650 but that has not been implemented yet (the prior PR fixed this by doing the ordering at flash time using python)

Then I guess I did a good test, as it jumps to higher minor version.

> but alternatively we could specify a maximum supported version in a separate variable and update that for each release.

That would be `find_package()` implementation itself.
A package must report if it is not compatible with a required version, so that a `0.16.x` can report FALSE if it is incompatible when a `0.15.x` is requested. Not sure this is handled either in this PR 😉 

So if a package is backwards incompatible, then it should set `PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE` to `False`.
Ref: https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-packages.7.html#package-version-file

> I think really this is a bit hackish and would be better for cmake to handle it 

I completely agree. There are several use-cases we must ensure are working if we decide to make a fully working solution.
A trick we are using in `Zephyr` package is to look for version `0.0.0` with `EXACT`, cause that will always fail, and then we use the variable `<package>_CONSIDERED_CONFIGS` to select the Zephyr.

Maybe something similar wrt. Zephyr SDK can be done.
Get all versions by asking for `0.0.0`, and then work our way backwards from highest till lowest until there is a working match.
Ref:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/80f87b94806bef4f893b18f1dc8cea070382dd6b/share/zephyr-package/cmake/zephyr_package_search.cmake#L72

body:
@nashif Changes in the workflow and example of usage:

if "filter:" is NOT USED in testcase/sample.yaml or there are other than "dt_" or "CONFIG" keys in filter: no changes to the workflow

if "filter:" is USED and only has "dt_"/"CONFIG" based entries in testcase/sample.yaml start the workflow from an extra stage: `"filter()"`. This stage calls the existing cmake stage, but expands with extra args used by package helper:
```
        if filter:
            filter_stages = self.get_cmake_filter_stages(instance)
        res = self.run_cmake(args_expanded, filter_stages)
```
and
```
        if filter_stages:
            cmake_filter_args = [
                f'-DMODULES={",".join(filter_stages)}',
                f'-P{canonical_zephyr_base}/cmake/package_helper.cmake',
            ]
``` 

Filter stages can contain "dts" and/or "kconfig" keys. It tells which stages are requried from cmake package helper to perform the filtration. 

Then the package helper script is called to extract dts and/or kconfig without completing the whole cmake (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/41302). 
Next, twister checks if the test should be skipped by matching the entries from "filter:" from yaml with extracted dts and kconfig. Those are the same checks which were already used for the same purpose, however currently those checks are run after the full cmake. The point is that there are many cases, where we couldn't filter based on dts and/or kconfig because the full cmake was failing and had to use methods like platform_allow.

The test for mcuboot with sysbuild is an example of such issue. @danieldegrasse had to use platform_allow to limit the execution. However, there are more platforms that can run the tests. According to @de-nordic the platforms able to run mcuboot can be distinguished by:
```
filter: dt_nodelabel_enabled("boot_partition") and dt_nodelabel_enabled("slot0_partition") 
            and dt_nodelabel_enabled("slot1_partition")
``` 
This shows the issue with the current workflow: Such filter cannot be used since platforms without mcuboot configured would fail the full cmake and we won't be able to do the filtration. One can replace platform_allow in testcase.yaml with the above filter and try executing 
`scripts/twister -v --platform=nrf52840dk_nrf52840 --platform=nucleo_l073rz --platform=nsim_sem -T tests/boot/test_mcuboot`

Without the PR:
- nrf52840dk_nrf52840: the filter finds matching nodes and build continues. Good.
- nucleo_l073rz: twister fails with cmake dt build failure:
``` 
devicetree error: /chosen: undefined node label 'boot_partition'

```
- nsim_sem: fails with cmake kconfig error:
```
warning: FLASH_MAP (defined at subsys/storage/flash_map/Kconfig:10) has direct dependencies FLASH_HAS_DRIVER_ENABLED with value n, but is currently being y-selected by the following symbols:
 - MCUBOOT_IMG_MANAGER (defined at subsys/dfu/Kconfig:25), with value y, direct dependencies <choice> (value: y), and select condition <choice> (value: y)

warning: FLASH_PAGE_LAYOUT (defined at drivers/flash/Kconfig:54) has direct dependencies FLASH_HAS_PAGE_LAYOUT && FLASH with value n, but is currently being y-selected by the following symbols:
 - STREAM_FLASH (defined at subsys/storage/stream/Kconfig:7), with value y, direct dependencies y (value: y)

warning: USE_DT_CODE_PARTITION (defined at Kconfig.zephyr:88) has direct dependencies HAS_FLASH_LOAD_OFFSET with value n, but is currently being y-selected by the following symbols:
 - BOOTLOADER_MCUBOOT (defined at Kconfig.zephyr:762), with value y, direct dependencies !MCUBOOT (value: y), and select condition !MCUBOOT (value: y)

error: Aborting due to Kconfig warnings

```

With this PR (since with it only dt is required for filtering):
```
INFO    - 1/3 nsim_sem                  zephyr/tests/boot/test_mcuboot/boot.mcuboot        SKIPPED (runtime filter)
INFO    - 2/3 nucleo_l073rz             zephyr/tests/boot/test_mcuboot/boot.mcuboot        SKIPPED (runtime filter)
INFO    - 3/3 nrf52840dk_nrf52840       zephyr/tests/boot/test_mcuboot/boot.mcuboot        PASSED (build)
```

I discussed the usage of package helper with @tejlmand and adapted the workflow with his suggestions. Torsten, can you back up on why this change is useful?

@danieldegrasse I had to modify the PR after your acceptance. I had to add stages selection for package helper script, so we can quit just after dt in case kconfigs are not required for filtration. It was needed for mcuboot as the example above shows that some platforms will fail the kconfig cmake stage.

body:
> When using this API, should the init function enable the RTC? I don't see any enable / disable API calls.

Enable/disable (on/off/resume/suspend) is the responsibility of the pm subsystem https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.0.0/reference/pm/index.html#device-pm-apis and https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.0.0/reference/pm/index.html#device-runtime-pm-apis

If PM is enabled for an RTC, I would recommend maintaining the enabled state of the RTC in the init function, since disabling/enabling the RTC even for a moment will lead to the RTC time drifting. I would therefore also recommend not enabling PM device runtime for the RTC.

I will implement PM for the ATMEL SAM driver as I have described here for reference.

**Note: TSC vote is not about code review, it's about allowing the exception for being past feature-freeze**

* Ready again
* This module has been more or less ready to merge since October but was delayed on reviews for fixes to other subsystems
* Also again, just to clarify, some Thrift sources are re-implemented in Zephyr as a workaround for Zephyr's lack of support for `std::thread`, `std::mutex`, etc. Those are on the [C++ Roadmap](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/45785)
* Once Zephyr has support for `std::thread`, `std::mutex`, etc, we can drop the workarounds to use unmodified upstream sources.
* Yes, upstream Thrift header files end in `.h` and not in `.hpp`. Yes, the copies of those files with slight workarounds need to keep the `.h` extension. Yes, that has already been discussed here. No, they will not be renamed, because it is not part of Zephyr's C++ coding style to force external projects to name C++ header files with the extension `.hpp`.
* Mainly, the only sources that will persist in the modules/ directory are related to SSL / TLS and require some finesse due to Zephyr's TLS socket implementation

Prefix is for data to use at the beginning of the area to know that it is valid, likewise verification is a checksum that can be added to the end - both can be used, either can be used or neither can be used. The use cases:

- Prefix: Allows knowing if valid data has been set, if this is not set, it can be ignored, or it can be used by multiple different systems/images with different prefixes for different reasons
- Verification (checksum): Allows knowing if the data is valid and was written completely before the device was rebooted or power cycled, if there is a checksum mismatch, it can be ignored

I will move both of these (and the verification) to the common code instead of implementation specific code.

That area is essentially the same as how I've implemented it, I would prefer a way of it reserving the memory itself without the user having to do it (i.e. decrementing amount of RAM that application can use) but for now it'll just have to work like that.

I prefer the name clear rather than memset. I will need to revisit the read because I will probably remove returning the read byte size, if someone tries to read too much, it can just return an error, and the currently missing function (get details) will return details including the size (available to the user i.e. without prefix or verification bytes) that the end application can use.

Note that this will be brought up in the architecture working group meeting today

body:
I've just discovered this PR.  I have recently written a full featured driver for the Microcrystal RV3032 RTC.  My driver creates a counter device, two eeprom devices for user nvram and eeprom, and sensor device for the temperature sensor.

There were of course limitation in the counter API.  I created a custom interface for RTC functions, similar to the existing RTC as counter drivers.

This API address some of those limitations, but there are still missing abilities.  Also consider the existing ds3231 RTC driver, which has an extended RTC API.  Can that be ported to this API?

1. The method to get supported alarm fields, `alarm_get_supported_fields`, does not take the alarm id as an argument.  The RV3032 has three time based alarms, which have different features.  The mask will not be the same for all of them.

2. The RV3032, and plenty of other RTCs, support sub-second time reporting.  This API only supports `struct tm` for times, which does not get more precise than a second.  My RV3032 RTC extension API had two methods for this:
```
/* Return current time, if hsec is non NULL, returns hundredths of a second. */
int rv3032_rtc_get_time_tm(const struct device *dev, struct tm *tm, uint8_t *hsec);
/* Return time in POSIX epoch as a timespec. */
int rv3032_rtc_get_time_ts(const struct device *dev, struct timespec *ts);
```
I suggest adding a sub-second field (probably in µs or ns, rather than the more device specific hundredths) to the time functions.  Or switch to `timespec`, but this has drawbacks since the RTC itself uses a broken down calendar time representation.  Also POSIX time_t/timespec don't contain the day of week information.

3. There is no way to start and stop the RTC.  The counter API allowed this.

5. The RV3032 has a periodic countdown alarm.  It will repeatedly trigger every time its period elapses.  This is conceptually different than the calendar based alarms this API supports.  The API provides no way to express an alarm that occurs every 10 seconds or every 5 minutes.

7. The RV3032, and many other RTCs, can timestamp events which are not calendar, nor timer, based alarms.  Examples from the RV3032 are: temperature high threshold, temperature low threshold, external event input pin.

9. There also also alarms, which might not have a timestamp, such as temperature threshold events, battery backup switchover events, and power reset events.

11. There is no way to accurately read or calibrate the RTC.

13. There is no way to accurately set the RTC.

For the last point, look at the existing DS3231 API.  It's possible to set the RTC to be accurate to less than 1 second.  What's necessary is have an async method which takes both a `struct tm` with the time to set as well as a Zephyr system timer timestamp that matches the point which that struct tm represents.

Then the driver can schedule a operation at exactly some number of seconds from the Zephyr timer timestamp.  This operation syncs the RTC to the second.  There are several ways this might be done: Program entire RTC time field.  Just program the seconds field.  Have the RTC stopped, then start it to sync.  Use gpio output pin that causes RTC to sync to the second.  The RV3032 can do all these.

W.r.t. to reading the RTC accurately, it would be desirable to timestamp with the Zephyr timer the irq of events.  This allows the comparison of the RTC to the system timer.  While is possible to do this in the irq handler function, this function will be called from a workqueue and after any I2C/SPI transactions to read at least the RTC's irq status register.  It's much better to timestamp as the first operation in the interrupt handler.  This avoids the considerable jitter from the workqueue latency and the I2C transaction.

body:
> 1. The RTC API describes only time and calendar based alarms, not counters, those use the counter API.

But an alarm every 5 minutes, on the minute, _is_ a time based alarm.

> Calibrating the RTC is a "manual" process, the API allows the user to set the calibration offset when the user has determined what that offset should be.

Without being able to timestamp the interrupt handler in the driver, it's not possible to accurately perform the process.

Accurately means less than one hundredth second.  Preferably to the accuracy the RTC supports, e.g. the RV3032 can be synced to 1/4096th second.

The way one should do this is to generate a periodic alarm from the RTC, then timestamp that IRQ with the system timer.  The system timer is needed to establish a common time frame with whatever is calibrating the RTC.  It could be the BLE Current Timer Service.  A GPS PPS input.  A gpio output from the MCU to an external TIC.  Lots of ways.

But all of them need the timestamp.  Getting a callback that an alarm occurred "sometime" in the past isn't enough.  It needs to be that an alarm occurred exactly so much in the past.  Exact is of course relative.  The Zephyr system timer is reasonable.

body:
> @semihalf-duda-patryk, if we could standardize the interface that allows syscall to do its functionality there would be no need for `z_vrfy_flash_ex_op` to call vendor functions.

We are trying to add a syscall which will be used for many purposes. Our interface will be common denominator of all functionalities we are trying to expose with it - some code to describe operation and buffer used by it.

https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/kernel/usermode/syscalls.html#verification-memory-access-policies mentions that:
```
If the kernel makes any logical decisions based on the contents of this memory, this can open
up the kernel to attacks even if checking is done. This is a class of exploits known as TOCTOU
(Time Of Check to Time Of Use).

The proper procedure to mitigate these attacks is to make a copies in the verification function,
and only perform parameter checks on the copies, which user threads will never have access to. 
```

It means that we have to make a copy of provided buffer in verification function. To do that without vendor specific structures definitions, we need to provide size of a buffer while calling syscall.

Another thing is that:
```
Many system calls pass in structures or even linked data structures. All should be copied.
Typically this is done by allocating copies on the stack.
```
If we want to avoid interpreting provided buffer in verification function we can't pass any pointers inside the structure.
I think, in case of additional data (e.g. if we want to implement some extended operation for writing,) we could use flexible array member (zero length array) at the end of structure, but it also requires passing size of the buffer to the syscall.

body:
There are two possible call paths:
```
Call sequence when CONFIG_USERSPACE and z_syscall_trap, example based on flash_read

flash_read->
        syscall_dispatch->
                z_mrsh_flash_read->
                        z_vrfy_flash_read->
                                z_impl_flash_read->
                                                api->read

call sequence when !CONFIG_USERSPACE or CONFIG_USERSPACE && !z_syscall_trap

flash_read------------------------>
                                z_impl_flash_read->
                                                api->read
```
From above you can see that the verification only happens when there is difference between config and user space (CONFIG_USERSPACE=y) and call is done from user space. Only then verification happens. The verification happens on syscall side m just before driver is called anyway, which means that it can be done by driver itself (vendor specific).
Note also that the verification function or the syscall only defines how callback is called, and does not even have to have the same prototype.
For example for flash read we provide `z_impl_flash_read`, which itself is simple inline function that figures out where `struct device` holds API calls for subsystem it is being called, here it is flash, and calls the `read` callback passing it all it got from API call. We do not provide `flash_read` it is auto generated.
The implementation of flash read is provided here:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/2c3863160d619fb7a1ce8f95035b1fecd982b0fa/include/zephyr/drivers/flash.h#L168-L176
but nothing stops us from doing it as
```
static inline int z_impl_flash_read(const struct device *dev, off_t offset,
				    void *data,
				    size_t len)
{
	const struct flash_driver_api *api =
		(const struct flash_driver_api *)dev->api;
        // The definition should be somewhere more global, this is just an example
        const struct read_op_stuff {
              uint32_t off;
              uint32_t size;
        } ros = { offset, len);

	return api->ex_op(dev, FLASH_EX_OP_READ, &ros, data);
}
```
The verification function for both is still the same, because in both cases it is called BEFORE `z_impl_flash_read` which means that it has exactly the same signature. The call sequence will differ, from the original `read` op based one:
```
flash_read->
        syscall_dispatch->
                z_mrsh_flash_read->
                        z_vrfy_flash_read->
                                z_impl_flash_read->
                                                api->read
```
to
```
flash_read->
        syscall_dispatch->
                z_mrsh_flash_read->
                        z_vrfy_flash_read->
                                z_impl_flash_read->
                                                api->ex_op
```

When we provide `z_impl_flash_ex_op` we directly call `ex_op`, and in `z_vrfy_flash_ex_op` we only know to check the `dev`, because we do not know the other parameter types or what are they supposed to address, which means that vendor specific implementation needs to do the verify work of other parameters - but this is only required for non-standard, vendor specific codes. When we standardize a code we can provide `z_impl_flash_` and `z_vrfy_flash_` functions directly supporting the code, as in the read example above, but still call the `ex_op`, and will not have to extend `api` structure with additional callbacks.

Of course there is some inconvenience dropped on `ex_op` implementation, where driver needs to do verification and `Z_OOPS` by itself (in `#ifdef CONFIG_USERSPACE` block), for vendor specific codes, but this is unfortunate cost of the flexibility we are gaining here.
`z_vrfy_`, which is running in the kernel ring, just makes sure that user does not try to do something funny with parameters. It does not stop `z_impl_` , also running in kernel ring as the `api->ex_op or any other `api->` thing,  from doing YOLO read/write anywhere where kernel can.

@semihalf-duda-patryk Does not even have to provide the `z_impl_flash_ex_op` or `z_vrfy_flash_ex_op`, as only extending the `api` structure with the `ex_op` callbacks gives him everything needed to complete his vendor specific calls.

We even have functions that already do "vendor specific" stuff in flash, that do not evevn have `api` callbacks:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/8e18c5ce1d75023e1386c646a0616774d6202d98/include/zephyr/drivers/flash/flash_simulator.h#L31
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/8e18c5ce1d75023e1386c646a0616774d6202d98/drivers/flash/flash_simulator.c#L479-L499

body:
I really do not care what name is used for this, it can be anything, absolutely anything. But looking over things here I think we should have stopped this earlier as going way outside of scope @bjarki-trackunit I think the idea of having an all encompassing "retention" driver for eeprom, RAM, battery backed RAM, general purpose registers, etc. is a derailment. The whole purpose I envisaged for this driver is to have some area (where that is or what type of device it is I do not care) set aside which is shared between applications on the same MCU/core so that e.g. mcuboot can share information with the user application, or possibly multiple applications, mainly for a unified boot mode or for storing how long a particular application spent executing - this information does not need to persist through a power loss, arguably it absolutely should not.

So with these thoughts in mind, I will rename this driver to something else and throw the microchip driver out entirely, it does not fit the purpose or scope of what the intention of this driver is or ever was set out to be, it can be added to the bbram driver at a later date.

And with that, yes laczen, there is no longer a need for an "is valid" function, because a subsystem can take care of that through software functions - there is no longer hardware for it. The clear function I'm not bothered if it stays or not, it's not something done in hardware but it is an essential function - almost every C or assembly-based embedded project will, at startup, "clear" RAM to 0x00, if the driver itself does it or the subsystem does it through writing 0x00 over and over in a loop doesn't matter, though it is far more efficient for the driver to do it e.g. using memset than it is for a subsystem to have a buffer and call a driver function many times in a loop with the overheads of context switching/user mode.

Regarding synchronization:

The RTC API provides access to the IRQ directly, the driver only configures it. For an "integrated" or "onboard" RTC device, like the ATMEL SAM RTC, you would have access to that devices IRQ directly, for an external device, its INT output pin would be connected to a GPIO, which would trigger the GPIO IRQ. Its up to the application to set some timestamp when the IRQ occurs, if it wants to.

One of the design goals I am adhering to when creating driver APIs is to only task the driver with implementing features which are directly tied to the capabilities of the hardware. The hardware only supports setting and getting calibration, and configuring an interrupt. What calibration value to set and what to do when the interrupt occurs, that is up to the application to decide.

> I still do not see how to set an alarm that triggers every second? That means: 00:00:00.00 00:00:01.00 ... 12:59:59.00
> 
> etc.
> 
> What are the exact `struct tm` and flags values to do this?

At this stage, the RTC API does not support periodic events, it may be added in the future when and if we find a scalable way to implement it. The issue at this time is the following:

Many RTCs support periodic events, however, the time at which the events occur varies wildly, and does not follow a particular pattern. An example trying to create an list for the events which will trigger periodically:
```
#define RTC_EVENT_SECOND BIT(0)
#define RTC_EVENT_MINUTE BIT(1)
#define RTC_EVENT_HOUR   BIT(2)
```

So far, seems fine, but when we start adding some less generic ones which I have observed some RTCs support
```
#define RTC_EVENT_SECOND      BIT(0)
#define RTC_EVENT_MINUTE      BIT(1)
#define RTC_EVENT_HOUR        BIT(2)
#define RTC_EVENT_HALF_MINUTE BIT(3)
#define RTC_EVENT_NOON        BIT(4)
#define RTC_EVENT_MIDNIGHT    BIT(5)
```

The problem here is that its not just the period of the events, but the alignment of them, on the hour, on midnight, not simply every 3600 seconds etc, and that this list is potentially infinitely expandable, we could potentially find an RTC that supports every quarter hour, quarter minute, half second, etc. etc.

I would appreciate any suggestions you can provide which could solve the issue.

My solution is to limit the API to support the most generic events only, second, minute, hour, but that might be too restrictive.

For now, it is out of the scope of this PR to add it however :)

body:
@xyzzy42 We may need to take a few steps back :)

A bus attached (I2C, SPI, etc.) RTC can not invoke an IRQ within the MCU the application is running on. For a bus attached RTC, the `_irq_` functions will all return `-ENOTSUP`.

To achieve something similar to the functionality presented by the `_irq_` functions, many bus attached RTCs have one or more digital output pins that can be connected to the MCUs GPIOs. These digital output pins are often controlled by multiple events, like alarm triggered, periodic event occurred, etc.

The GPIO API allows for registering callbacks that are called from the GPIO port's IRQ, depending on a mask of bits.

All functionality required to get a callback when a event occurs in a timely manner, is achievable for both internal and bus attached RTCs, using these two APIs (when we determine the signature of the rtc_set_event_irq_callback API call)

> Have you looked at the existing DS3231 Zephyr driver? How would an application do what that driver does?

The DS3231 stores the system time when the callback occurs, which is used as a foundation to synchronize the RTC with system time. The application can achieve this using either the available GPIO edge triggered callback for bus attached RTCs, and when we determine the signature of the RTC API `_irq_` function for periodic events, and its implemented, that can be used for internal RTCs

The API you have described already does support a PPS event.  The only problem is using an unset mask to clear the alarm.  If that was not done, then the a mask of `0` would indicate an alarm every second.  Since none of the `struct tm` fields are matched against, their value does not matter.

> `#define RTC_EVENT_NOON        BIT(4)`
This is done via `tm_hour = 12, tm_min = 0, tm_sec = 0`, and a mask of `HOUR|MIN|SEC`.

> `#define RTC_EVENT_HALF_MINUTE BIT(3)`
Not sure what this means exactly, but it could be `tm_sec = 30` and mask = `EVENT_SEC`.

As for other periodic alarms, see the Linux RTC API.   It describes those with `RTC_IRQP_READ`, `RTC_IRQP_SET`.

body:
> A bus attached (I2C, SPI, etc.) RTC can not invoke an IRQ within the MCU the application is running on. For a bus attached RTC, the `_irq_` functions will all return `-ENOTSUP`.

I'm aware of how it works, I've written multiple Zephyr drivers and dozens of Linux drivers.  Including Linux and Zephyr drivers for external RTCs.

In Zephyr, an external (I2C/SPI) device's driver usually has an `int-gpios` property that references the GPIO line used for interrupts.  Its Zephyr device driver will initialize this GPIO and install an interrupt handler on it when it initializes.  Look at either of the DS3231 or MCP7940 RTC drivers in the Zephyr tree.  They both install irq handlers.

However, these handler can not perform I2C operations from IRQ context, so they only trigger work functions.  These work functions read the RTC status, then use that to invoke the alarm handler callbacks that have been registered with the counter API.

Since this RTC API here can not handle the types of alarms the existing drivers support, they will, as you have said, also need to support the counter API.  This means the interrupt handler must retain this design.

It seems like you're creating a new type of API for Zephyr, where the device does not handle its own interrupts.  Instead the application would register the GPIO IRQ itself?  I'm not aware of any Zephyr drivers which work in this manner.  Can you provide an example?  Any driver which has in its bindings `int-gpios` or `irq-gpios` should provide an example of those where the driver handles the interrupt itself, of which I count 62.

body:
> I discussed the usage of package helper with @tejlmand and adapted the workflow with his suggestions. Torsten, can you back up on why this change is useful?

I think the comment by @PerMac https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/53499#issuecomment-1400100993 summarizes one of the advantages very well.
Developers don't need to just add a single or two platforms to `platform_allow:` when what they really want is to have a given test case runable on platforms meeting the requirement.
Problem today is that because of Kconfig failure, and thus CMake failure, then it must manually be decided what platform to choose.

Another advantage is performance. When having a lot of boards, then it's faster to only run code until devicetree has been processed and then do filtering, instead of running whole CMake, including Kconfig, compiler setup, CMake code for libraries, etc. for platforms that will anyway be skipped.

I did some measurement long time back where running dts was ~170ms vs full CMake ~890ms, (numbers exclude the CMake startup of ~350ms, don't ask me what CMake is doing in those 350ms).

One may say it's a small gain, but running sufficient number of times, then it adds up.
And on top of that, we can have more test suites capable of running on boards, as they no longer need to be limited by `platform_allow`, as the dt filter will be working properly.

> I would go so far as to say as well, that Zephyr should have an RTC present _by default_ (and we do not normally default things to yes), even if it is simply the `rtc_emul` device. Furthermore, we should use Kconfig to have other parts of code depend on the presence of an RTC.

The rtc_emul driver looks like it is really meant as a test fixture.  It uses *relative* sleeps to keep time.  The flaw in that should be obvious.

But one could write a Zephyr system counter to RTC converter. It would be much smaller and faster than the rtc_emul driver and would also keep time.

Considering get_time() and other POSIX calls.

In Linux these do not refer to RTC hardware.  Despite Linux having a RTC driver for decades, I think before get_time() was implemented in libc.  CLOCK_REALTIME and CLOCK_MONOTONIC both refer to the system clock, which is a software construct.  Like `k_uptime_ticks()`.

Mapping them directly to the RTC presents problems.  Suppose one wanted accurate time keeping, like Linux has with adjtimex()?  You need algorithms on top of the hardware to do that.

What happens when the RTC is not set?

Some software loves to query the current time.  Try running programs that use a GUI toolkit under strace.  They do it constantly.  So much that the various get time syscalls use a VDSO system to accelerate them.  Would use need to go directly to an I2C RTC chip?  Way too slow.

And many RTCs only support second resolution.  We expected microseconds decades ago with timevals and now we expect nanoseconds with timespec.  If you go directly to the RTC device, does this mean POSIX is stuck without even milliseconds?!  Even Windows isn't that bad.

body:
@xyzzy42

The rtc_emul is in indeed meant to be used for testing purposes, with boards like native_posix, which is the only board for which it is implemented in this PR :) The first approach I had was also to simply convert from a timestamp to a struct tm, but checking alarms every second, calling the update every second, handling the year 2038 problem, and synchronizing it, was actually more complex than just emulating the RTC as it is on the hardware level.

All RTCs, real or emulated, return -ENODATA if they have not been set, for the emulated driver, this is simply tracked using a boolean, for real RTCs, like the ATMEL SAM, they have bits which tell you if the time and calendar values are valid. They can't check if the time is correct, but they can at least ensure it could be :)

When it comes to querying time, reading and caching the current time, is a potential solution to the polling issue. Implementing this is above the driver level, and therefore for the application or a subsystem to implement.

Subsecond resolution is commonly supported for RTCs on embedded platforms, see stm32u585ai(internal) and PCA2131(I2C). Since the value is stored as an int, there is no loss in using nsec, it will in fact help us with rounding errors when reading subsecond time, as it is often 1/4096 (0.000244140625) , or 1/32768 (0.000030517578125) not exactly pretty numbers :)

> All RTCs, real or emulated, return -ENODATA if they have not been set,

This is handled well in the API I think.  I copied that bit after I saw here into my rv3032 driver.  Also made sure the driver does not reset the oscillator stopped flag until the clock is actually set, so a reboot doesn't lose the clock not set status.

But if one maps a POSIX function like `clock_gettime()` directly to the RTC, then what to return if the RTC isn't set?  ENODATA isn't one of the allowed error codes for `clock_gettime()`.  POSIX didn't seem consider the concept of unset clocks.

> When it comes to querying time, reading and caching the current time, is a potential solution to the polling issue. Implementing this is above the driver level, and therefore for the application or a subsystem to implement.

I agree, it's above the driver level.  I was replying to @cfriedt's comment about POSIX calling into the RTC API.  I don't think you can go there directly, from POSIX to the RTC, for a number of reasons.  One being every clock_gettime() call reading registers over I2C will be too slow.

Something needs create a software concept of the current time and the application/POSIX should have an API into that. This can handle things like not reading registers over I2C constantly, increases the resolution by combining the rtc with the cpu cycle counter or some other higher resolution counter, and so on.

> Subsecond resolution is commonly supported for RTCs on embedded platforms, see stm32u585ai(internal) and

While common, it's not universal.  External RTCs usually don't support that much resolution in their register interface, maybe just seconds, maybe hundredths or 1/256 second.  So the problem is, if `clock_gettime()` were to call into the RTC driver and return the time it gets, then it might only have second resolution.  We really expect better.  Linux returns sub-microsecond resolution.  Zephyr originally used microseconds for the system clock API, before changing to ticks of configurable length.

But I'm just assuming the way Linux does things is right, but going directly from POSIX to the RTC is not how Linux does it, and it seems like it will have problems.

body:
My thoughts on VERSION file vs Kconfig:

- Applications are more dynamic than things like zephyr which can be thought of more as libraries, and there might be different versions of a application depending upon what e.g. device type is being built, this makes the Kconfig version easier to use
- With a VERSION file, it means that the file needs to be updated to change version, this presents problems if for example you need to generate a test firmware update file, for replication purposes it means you would need to update the VERSION file and do 2 builds for each release, or see next point
- Separate VERSION files can be achieved by using APPLICATION_CONFIG_DIR, this means that e.g. an existing application can have it's default VERSION file changed, however the drawback of this (e.g. mcuboot) is that you then need to copy all the project's configuration and board overlay files to the new directory, which then means you have duplicate files that will no longer be kept in sync if the base project (e.g. mcuboot as part of zephyr update) is changed to a different version
- A VERSION file would need additional cmake and other code adding to use instead of the current Kconfig method which simply needed a new Kconfig added and a 2 line python file change
- A VERSION file does however make it clear/easy to see the version of an application from afar e.g. just by someone browsing the files on a web git browser, however this is no longer easy when using APPLICATION_CONFIG_DIR to change it, but likewise if setting the Kconfig through different ways becomes similarly harder to find
- A Kconfig can far easier be used when you have multiple images from sysbuild vs a VERSION file means you need additional handling if you then want to check or use the version of each image

With the above points, my preference is VERSION for "libraries" e.g. zephyr itself, but Kconfig for applications e.g. mcuboot, user projects, etc.

body:
## Update
### RTC API Improvements
Following the latest architecture meeting, the RTC API has been revised. The update (1-second interval) and alarm callbacks are no longer tied to interrupts. The API now distinguishes between alarms by id, based on the DS3231, which has two alarms with different capabilities.

The ATMEL SAM driver has been removed from this PR due to another blocking PR, while the emulated RTC driver remains.

### RTC Device Driver Compatibility

A review of compatibility between the new RTC API and existing RTC device drivers was conducted:

#### MCP7940 and MCUX-IMX-SNVS

The MCP7940, implemented with the counter API, lacks oscillator calibration, update callback, and configurable alarm fields. The new RTC API can fully reimplement both drivers, adding missing features.

#### DS3231

The new RTC API covers most DS3231 functionalities with some tradeoffs. The sync clock mechanism and direct register access remain exclusive to DS3231's API. The new RTC API adds RTC clock calibration.

#### Summary

The MCP7940 and MCUX-IMX-SNVS can be re-implemented with the new RTC API, improving their functionality. The DS3231 can also use the new API, but will retain sync clock and direct register access in its specific API header.

I aim to have this PR approved in the upcoming architecture meeting. If you could kindly address any remaining concerns at this point, it would be much appreciated :)

Updated, the discussion about size of `off_t` vs size of `size_t` doesn't really make any sense for this, `size_t` is either 32-bit or 64-bit, then from the GCC manual https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/File-Position-Primitive.html:
```

Data Type: off_t

    This is a signed integer type used to represent file sizes. In the GNU C Library, this type is no narrower than int.

    If the source is compiled with _FILE_OFFSET_BITS == 64 this type is transparently replaced by off64_t. 

Data Type: off64_t

    This type is used similar to off_t. The difference is that even on 32 bit machines, where the off_t type would have 32 bits, off64_t has 64 bits and so is able to address files up to 2^63 bytes in length.

    When compiling with _FILE_OFFSET_BITS == 64 this type is available under the name off_t. 
```

body:
> > It seems you don't believe me that setting all alarm bits to zero is a valid alarm. Here is a table from the rv3032 documentation. Maybe this will explain better why setting all the match bits to disabled is a valid configuration: ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35062987/226456423-65f97509-3e40-4e6b-82f6-0ce4cd6095eb.png)
> 
> The RTC API alarm time mask is not a 1-1 mapping with any specific RTC device register, it is a higher level abstraction.

What you should see in this diagram is that ALL bits set AT_D, AT_H, AT_M is a valid alarm.
Also valid is NO bits set.  AT_D, AT_H, and AT_M not set is also a valid alarm.

If all match bits set is valid and no bits set is valid, then this can not work:
> `If the mask parameter is 0, the alarm will be disabled.` 

Maybe the RV3032 RTC only supporting minutes confuses the issue?  It would have been better if it supported seconds masking as well.

So I give you the DS12885 datasheet:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35062987/226552261-c0913119-6080-46e7-87aa-2e748f7de36c.png)

The second paragraph describes three possibilities:

1st: "An alarm is generated each when the don't-care bits are in the hours byte."
```c
struct rtc_time alarm_time = {
    .tm_sec = 30,
    .tm_min = 30,
};
uint16_t alarm_mask = RTC_ALARM_TIME_MASK_MINUTE | RTC_ALARM_TIME_MASK_SECOND;
```
The driver should place places don't-cares into all supported fields that are not set in the `alarm_mask`.  This means hours is don't-care.  This achieves the 1st possibility described above.

2nd: "Similarly, an alarm is generated every minute with the don't-care codes in the hours and minute alarm bytes."
```c
struct rtc_time alarm_time = {
    .tm_sec = 30,
};
uint16_t alarm_mask = RTC_ALARM_TIME_MASK_SECOND;
```
Again, don't-care bytes are placed into the fields that are not masked, which are hours and minutes.  Again we have matched the possibility described above.

3rd: "The don't-care does in all three alarm bytes create an interrupt every second."
```
struct rtc_time alarm_time = { 0 };
uint16_t alarm_mask = 0;
```
If we were allowed to follow the same pattern, this would place don't care bytes into all fields not specified, which are hours, minutes, and days.  This would be a valid alarm!  It is described in the datasheet I have just posted as valid.  It was one of three examples the datasheet's authors chose to provide.  But it can't be done, because alarm_mask == 0 is used as a special case to clear the alarm.

It is simple to fix:  Either add a disable method to the API or make it so alarm_time == NULL disables the alarm, rather than alarm_mask == 0.  It seems reasonable to pass in a pointer to a zeroed out rtc_time along with an alarm_mask of zero.  No fields are used (except tm_nsec, but that always has to be zero).

body:
@xyzzy42 Regarding the alarm mask issue (it is becoming hard to continue the comment chain)

We are probably talking past each other.

The RV3032 has the following possible alarm values that map exactly to the following rtc_alarm_set_time() values:
* Alarm disabled -> mask = 0, timeptr = NULL
* match on minute -> mask = 0b0010 and tm_min set
* match on minute and hour -> mask = 0b0110 and tm_min and tm_hour set
* match on minute and monthday -> mask = 0b0110 and tm_min and tm_mday set
* match on minute and hour and monthday -> mask = 0b1110 and tm_min and tm_hour and tm_mday set
* match on hour  -> mask = 0b0100 and tm_hour set
* match on hour and monthday -> mask = 0b1100 and tm_hour and tm_mday set
* mach on monthday -> mask = 0b1000 and tm_mday set

The DS12885 also supports 7 different alarm configurations:
* Alarm disabled -> mask = 0, timeptr = NULL
* match on second -> mask = 0b0001 and tm_sec set
* match on second and minute -> mask = 0b0011 and tm_sec and tm_min set
* match on second and hour -> mask = 0b0101 and tm_sec and tm_hour set
* match on second and minute and hour -> mask = 0b0111 and tm_sec and tm_min and tm_hour set
* match on minute  -> mask = 0b0010 and tm_min set
* match on minute and hour -> mask = 0b0110 and tm_min and tm_hour set
* mach on hour -> mask = 0b0100 and tm_hour set

As shown here, every possible alarm state is covered by the RTC API. I may have made some typos in the configurations as I am writing them by hand, but hopefully this explains my view point. If you can identify times where the rtc_alarm_set_time() does not appropriately cover the capabilities of an RTC devices alarms, that would be a productive way of moving forward :)

As a note, I favor the approach of using the mask, since we have to signal, when reading the alarm time, which fields of the struct are actually set. This can be achieved either by having reserved values (like -1), or with a mask. Both options are perfectly viable, however, the mask is quite explicit, and does not require initializing the entire rtc_time struct to set the values of a few fields of an alarm.

body:
> > Application A is designed for a board by a user, this has version X, multiple versions are released.
> 
> I don't get this or the rest of this comment :(. I'm not trying to be argumentative, I'm just confused. Wouldn't each of those versions require different git commits? It sounds like you are saying you want to have different versions for the same zephyr application directory with the exact same code. This doesn't correspond to "version" as I usually understand it.

There are 2 ways to think of it:

- Common base code but then different transports on top of it, i.e. there might be one piece of hardware but it might use different services to send data. Taking an nRF9160-based product, an initial implementation might be made using Cat-M1 and MQTT, then later support for a different backend using LwM2M might be added, then after that support for using NB-IoT might be added
- Different (variant) hardware, there might be a base version of a product which works as is needed, then there might be a new version of the hardware (not a board respin but actually different hardware, adding new features and parts to the design), so in this case the original hardware might have had 5 releases before the new hardware is created and extra code added to the application repository for this new hardware (the 2 builds use the same common files, the new hardware would include additional files in the build that the original hardware build does not, so there are 2 independent versions. Marketing wouldn't want to release the other hardware version whereby the software version starts on the same as the current original hardware version e.g. "Shipping firmware version 6.1"

As for injecting build numbers during CI, this is easily done (and in fact, projects do already do this) via Kconfig as it can be provided as an argument directly to cmake - e.g. jenkins can do the version numbering itself then provide it as environment variables which can be passed to cmake or west. There's no reason that a VERSION file cannot be used, but either this VERSION file cannot be part of git or the CI system needs to make git commits and pushes to update it otherwise the git tree will be marked as dirty (which from a security audit and ISO9001 view is not good) - this is probably the key to the points above because if you think of it as jenkins or the CI system providing the version number, that makes it easier to explain how all the builds have different independent version numbers (the builds are different tasks, i.e. one set of builds might not be ran for a long period of time whilst others run much more frequently). In the above examples, a VERSION file becomes problematic because you need multiple VERSIONs - one for each build, the 2 ways of doing that is either have the code for each build in a completely separate repo or put the VERSION file in a different folder, which would require use of APPLICATION_CONFIG_DIR and duplicating all project files in all of these folders (both greatly increase the maintenance burden)

> As for injecting build numbers during CI, this is easily done (and in fact, projects do already do this) via Kconfig as it can be provided as an argument directly to cmake

plus a lot of text regarding CI, where I don't really understand why it is important to have individual versions for each build.
When a release is done, for example for Zephyr, then the version is fixed, for example at `3.3.0`, but between releases a `.99` version is in use.

Note, Zephyr offers both a version and a build version.
For the build version, `git describe` is used, and when it is pointing to a release tag, then the build version is identical to the version, like: `v3.3.0`
When building from HEAD / sha, then build version contains the short sha, like this: `v3.3.0-1078-g93f7a6730d12`
But kernel version in this case is `3.3.99` which is in `version.h` together with build version information.

To me it appears that what @nordicjm wants is a build version, not a version, cause he wants it to change with each build and have it used by CI.

Example output from hello world on a release and during development:
```
*** Booting Zephyr OS build zephyr-v3.3.0 ***
```
```
*** Booting Zephyr OS build zephyr-v3.3.0-1078-g93f7a6730d12 ***
```

also notice, that Zephyr already today offer customization if BUILD_VERSION, for example like this:
```
$ west build -b native_posix samples/hello_world/ -DBUILD_VERSION=tejlmand_custom_v1 samples/hello_world/
$ ./build/zephyr/zephyr.exe
*** Booting Zephyr OS build tejlmand_custom_v1 ***
```

if the intention is an application version, then my request to be consistent with Zephyr version infrastructure stands.
Ref: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/55814#pullrequestreview-1349872019

If downstream users want an application versioning scheme as described in:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/55814#issuecomment-1477469181
and in other comments, then they can do so in their own downstream code.

I prefer to keep a Zephyr application feature scheme simple and clear.
Any complex implementation will anyhow not satisfy and meet all the wishes of users, and Zephyr itself will not be using such complexity.

Therefore I believe it's best to have a simple and clean solution upstream.

body:
> @henrikbrixandersen as someone using application versioning in a real end application - how do you do versioning in your application (and mcuboot, since I remember you saying to specifically versioned mcuboot builds) for builds?

I have a set of local Kconfig settings for setting major.minor.patch-tweak (see https://semver.org/). I initially opened #28348 for being able to utilize the CMake `project()` metadata for setting these values in a standardized way, but ended up using custom Kconfigs.

In the application code, these values can be accessed directly using the Kconfig definitions. The application use these for reporting its own version when queried. I have some custom CMake boilerplate code included in the application CMakeLists.txt files, which sets `CONFIG_MCUBOOT_EXTRA_IMGTOOL_ARGS` to include `--version` followed by resulting version string. This way both the application itself and MCUboot is aware of the version of a given application image.

When building MCUboot, I use the same infrastructure for setting a custom version for our bootloader image. Like in the application code, our custom bootloader code is able to access these Kconfig version definitions directly. In order for the application to read out the version of the bootloader on which it was booted (when queried) I have a custom bootloader linker script snippet for placing the version variables at a specific flash address - along with a small library for the application to retrieve the bootloader image version from flash. I have been meaning to look into the custom TLV feature of MCUboot (which was added after my custom implementation) to see if that could be used for propagating bootloader image version to the application instead.

I will review this PR today and see how it compares to my downstream implementation.

Some changes have been applied based on recent reviews from @xyzzy42 @nordicjm and @cfriedt. The changes are sorted and ordered here by reviewer:

* update callback, enabled by `CONFIG_RTC_UPDATE`
* calibration, enabled by `CONFIG_RTC_CALIBRATION`

body:
Just to be clear.

My preference is to have a simple Kconfig which allows users to specify just the imgtool version field.
For example a Kconfig setting named `IMGTOOL_APP_VERSION` / `IMGTOOL_SIGN_VERSION` which is a setting specifically used by `imgtool`, ref https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/55814#discussion_r1140730723.
And to not generate any `app_version.h` file.

Instead, app version handling is left for users to decide.
Kconfig / Version file / version format / app version header generation, etc.
As the discussion in this PR shows, there can be very different opinions regarding how a feature should look like, and so far during the discussion there has been no indication that Zephyr itself will make use of such a feature.
All Zephyr needs is a very simple imgtool version setting.

However, if it is requested that Zephyr provides an app version infrastructure which includes app version header generation, then in my opinion, such an infrastructure should be aligned with how VERSION is handled for for the Zephyr kernel, so we don't need to maintain two systems (and thus fix deps issues in multiple places, see #56235, #40167, #39503).
Also it should be possible for users to just set the imgtool version without enforcing creation of an app version header.
Reason for that is to allow users with custom application version infrastructure to still specify an imgtool version for signing, but at the same time allow such users to keep their custom app version infrastructure and thus be able to opt-out of the Zephyr app version header generation.

> @de-nordic sorry I was unclear -- why is the change of chosen node needed? Won't this break existing users?

No it should not.
While signing image we expect it to be selected by `zephyr,code-partition`, so we should also figure out flash the `zephyr,code-partition` is placed on, instead of using `zephyr,flash`.
If user has previously set `zephyr,code-partition` to partition placed on something different than `zephyr,flash` than it would probably not work for the user anyway. So user would end up correcting `zephyr,flash` to point to flash where `zephyr,code-partition` is placed, or moving `zephyr,code-partition` to that flash.
Basically in previous code we were a little bit out-of-sync with DTS: we would expect `zephyr,code-partition` to point to binary we start with, but use `zephyr,flash` to sign image (which have to be the same for this to work anyway). Common stuff we check was slot labels.

body:
@Laczen I am making a good faith effort to understand, but I'm failing
to see your point.

> @mbolivar-nordic, to be clear: I don't want this in devicetree at all:
> a. This uses devicetree as a means to communicate a software configuration,

You and I have established already in previous comments that there is
precedent and policy for doing software configuration in devicetree in
Zephyr.

This pull request complies with the written policy in the devicetree
documentation.

Therefore, unless there is a change in policy, I do not consider this
a valid objection to the PR from a devicetree perspective.

> b. It is not needed at all, there is a retention area that can be
> used to share information. The subsystem that uses it needs to agree
> on what the format is.

It seems clear to me that there is a need to share retained memory
between different applications, which implies a need to configure the
areas where the retained data goes. So I assume you're not saying
there is no need for retained data *at all* -- but instead the
objection is about how and where it should be configured.

It seems to me that within Zephyr, devicetree is a natural place to
put this configuration:

- you can create a shared devicetree overlay configuring these
  regions, and share it between multiple application builds that
  rely on it using DTC_OVERLAY_FILE

- it would be even more convenient to do this as a system devicetree
  overlay when we have support for that, since then you would only
  have to write it once and it would propagate to all the images whose
  devicetrees were generated from the system devicetree
  (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/51830 for more
  details on system DT)

- you could put this in BOARD.dts if your PCB was for a product that
  had well defined areas that you wanted to be present in all the
  application builds for that board (bootloader, "main" app, etc.)

If you disagree with this, please provide a technical rationale.

> c. It pollutes the dts files,

"Pollute" in this context is a pejorative and emotional/aesthetic word
choice. This is not introducing a toxic chemical or trash into an
environment.

It is difficult for me to see this final objection as anything other
than personal preference. If I'm mistaken, can you please rephrase
with a more neutral choice of words?

> So it is neither a personal preference or a technical problem, this
> is about how to use the supplied tools.

In my opinion, decisions about "how to use the supplied tools" should
be made based on personal preferences, technical considerations, and
project policies. I'm not sure what additional category you're
suggesting we should be considering here when making the decision
about whether to take this PR.

body:
Interesting read.  Here are a few points I didn't see considered:

1. The Zephyr build system fully supports a case where the OOT application source file contains only a space or comment. `main()` is pulled in from the Zephyr repo and all other functionality is pulled in via subsystems and drivers in other repositories. In this case the "application version" clearly represents the built configuration. 
2. Without using command line options the built configuration may be different per board. As long as the built image reports configuration and board information (via interfaces and metadata), then the "version" can be disambiguated.
3. A build may actually contain multiple independent "applications" (e.g., printer+scanner+fax, USB compound/composite/complex device).
4. Over the lifetime of the updatable product the immutable boot image version is fixed while the application image is not. Only the end user can decide on the relationship between those versions. (In fact, future application images may need to query the boot image version to address shortcomings in earlier boot releases.)
5. An "application" repository may contain a tree of application configurations/projects, where each may need a different top-level versioning scheme and version value assignments.
6. Allow for the same level of versioning independence whether each subsystem and interface is in a separate OOT zephyr module or consolidated into one. It should not matter whether the end user follows a T1, T2, or T3 topology either.

> Architecture WG:
> 
> * @nashif states that this should not be in `include/drivers`, because it's not an actual hardware driver
> * @galak agrees, maybe this should be in `subsys/` or even `modules/acpica`

Though we use external acpica module for realize the acpi bus driver functionality, I believe it is still a bus driver and we should treat same way as other popular OS treat it. For example FreeBSD use acpica for realize acpi bus driver functionality. Also by definition ACPI is an hardware abstraction interface for abstract platform HW complexity with the help of platform FW (eg: BIOS) and provide a unified interface to OS so that OS can be easily ported with minimum modification to different platforms (which are ACPI complaint). We can still consider this model as HAL modules where ACPICA is similar to MCU vendor specific code which abstract HW.

To understand the ACPI bus driver concept better , I can provide following details of some of the ACPI bus driver functionalities:
- Enumerate PCI bus/bridge and acpi device such as WDT, RTC, GPIO, APIC, DMA etc.
- Enumerate device resources such as MMIO or IO address, IRQ details
- Retrieve IO configurations such as clk freq, boud rate, polarity etc. for SOC device like I2C, SPI, UART, SMBus etc.
- Bus and other config details for on board sensors
- Retrieve platform configuration such as PCI legacy interrupt routing, APIC
- Retrieve CPU configurations/Information
- Device/platform power management and configuration

ACPI will significantly reduce Zephyr porting effort on newer platforms since it will identify supported devices and cpu/platform/device resource and automatically configure them dynamically during system boot. Please note that most of current DTS information can be removed since acpi will provide those information on run time. The device and platform configuration for these platforms normally provided via BIOS. Hence user can go and modify them via BIOS menu which help to avoid re-build of Zephyr image.

Following block diagram depict overall Zephyr BSP architecture based on ACPI sub system:

Please note that "zephyr acpi bus interface" will provide a generic interface to other Zephyr sub systems/drivers and also provide some glue logics for abstract under lying acpica instantiate and complexity. The acpica is an OS-independent implementation of ACPI and hence OS Service layer will provide necessary logic to port acpica into Zephyr. The OS Service layer for Zephyr already upstreamed into acpica opensource tree.

> address it is not accepting. So, I have given the "target" address instead of "index" for RTC instance.

In this case, I recommend we reuse the existing devicetree compatible:

1. Move the dts bindings file `motorola,mc146818.yaml` from the bindings/counter to the bindings/rtc folder
2. Update it to be based on the rtc-device binding

```
# Copyright (c) 2022, Intel Corporation
#
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

description: Motorola MC146818 compatible Real Timer Clock

compatible: "motorola,mc146818"

-- include: base.yaml
++ include: rtc-device.yaml
```
3. Update the existing node in the dtsi for all in-tree boards using the Motorola MC146818. Notice that the node `rtc` now has two node labels, counter and rtc, to be backwards compatible with apps that use the device as a counter.
```
--		counter: counter@70 {
--			compatible = "motorola,mc146818";
--			reg = <0x70 0x0D 0x71 0x0D>;
--			status = "okay";
--		};

++		rtc: counter: rtc@70 {
++			compatible = "motorola,mc146818";
++			reg = <0x70 0x0D 0x71 0x0D>;
++			interrupts = <8 IRQ_TYPE_LOWEST_EDGE_RISING 3>;
++			interrupt-parent = <&intc>;
++			alarms-count = <1>;
++
++			status = "okay";
++		};
```
4. Add a rule to Kconfig to ensure only either driver (RTC or Counter) is included in the build. If the RTC subsystem is enabled `CONFIG_RTC=y`, the RTC driver in this PR is included, if counter is enabled `CONFIG_COUNTER=y` and the RTC isn't, the counter_cmos.c driver is included. This is acheived with the following changes
```
config COUNTER_CMOS
	bool "Counter driver for x86 CMOS/RTC clock"
++	default y if !RTC
	depends on DT_HAS_MOTOROLA_MC146818_ENABLED
```

> The Zephyr build system fully supports a case where the OOT application source file contains only a space or comment. main() is pulled in from the Zephyr repo and all other functionality is pulled in via subsystems and drivers in other repositories. In this case the "application version" clearly represents the built configuration.
> Without using command line options the built configuration may be different per board. As long as the built image reports configuration and board information (via interfaces and metadata), then the "version" can be disambiguated.
> A build may actually contain multiple independent "applications" (e.g., printer+scanner+fax, USB compound/composite/complex device).
> An "application" repository may contain a tree of application configurations/projects, where each may need a different top-level versioning scheme and version value assignments.

This has been mentioned in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/55814#issuecomment-1473693477 and https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/55814#discussion_r1143037321 and https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/55814#issuecomment-1477469181 and is fully supported in this (and, actually, the inspiration for how this was designed comes from a code base that did just that, 1 set of code, multiple builds for different boards and configurations of boards, each with different version numbers)

> Over the lifetime of the updatable product the immutable boot image version is fixed while the application image is not. Only the end user can decide on the relationship between those versions. (In fact, future application images may need to query the boot image version to address shortcomings in earlier boot releases.)

There is a draft PR adding support for sharing the bootloader (mcuboot) version with the application but it is outside the scope of this PR, though the idea would be that mcuboot would use this option to set its default version (that users are then able to change as they please). The big benefit over this vs a static version file is someone can make as many mcuboot builds as they want with whatever version information they want, the alternative implementation cannot support that because mcuboot would need to be forked and the static version file would need to be changed for each build

body:
The proposed solution seems flawed: the retention system defines an area in a retention memory that includes a optional header and crc check to enable validating that the "retained data" is valid. However as both these are optional (and they need to be because it also supports only 1 byte of info) the validity check is not OK when header and crc are disabled. In that case the retention system should return `-ENOTSUP` (or something equivalent).
The validity check should thus be performed otherwise. The whole construct of header and crc check can than just as well be integrated in the code that uses the retention memory.

As a counter proposal the mcuboot bootmode system could be built around 1 byte of data (that uses a odd parity bit for validity) and put into a retention memory area as the last byte of this area (if the area is larger than 1 byte).

body:
@gmarull 
This PR currently defines the pins like so:
```
pinctrl-0 = <&pio1_uart_default>;
pinctrl-names = "default";
pinmuxs = <&pio1_uart_rx 0>, <&pio1_uart_tx 0>;
pinmux-names = "rx", "tx";
```

And accesses them with:
```
#define DT_PIO_PIN_BY_NAME(node_id, name) \
	RP2_GET_PIN_NUM(DT_PROP_BY_IDX(DT_PHANDLE_BY_NAME( \
					DT_PARENT(node_id), pinmuxs, name), pinmux, \
					PIN_CELL_BY_NAME(node_id, name, pinmux)))
```
Which in driver code looks like:
```
.tx_pin = DT_PIO_PIN_BY_NAME(DT_DRV_INST(idx), tx)
```
#56678 defines pinctrl in the same way, but accesses the pins with:
```
#define DT_RPI_PICO_PIO_PIN_BY_NAME(node_id, p_name, p_idx, g_name, g_idx)			\
	RP2_GET_PIN_NUM(DT_PROP_BY_IDX(								\
		DT_CHILD(DT_PINCTRL_BY_NAME(node_id, p_name, p_idx), g_name), pinmux, g_idx))
```
Note the extra `p_idx`, `g_name` and `g_idx`.
In driver code this will be used as:
```
tx_gpio =  DT_INST_RPI_PICO_PIO_PIN_BY_NAME(inst, default, 0, tx_gpio, 0)
```
So the way I see it, both implementations define the pinctrl in the same manner, the difference is in how each implementation reaches into the pinmux array. This PR does it with devicetree while the other PR does it with a macro inside the driver code.
I think devicetree is the more correct way to do it, both for readability (having the mapping between index and pin role in the same file) and for flexibility (if the mapping is in the driver then you must comply to the driver's pin ordering in the pinmux array, or have to modify the driver to change the index).

EDIT: I see that #56678 does not need to add `pinmux-cells`. However, in that manner the driver forces the pinctrl to be defined in a certain way. In the example above from the UART driver, it is assumed that the pinctrl is called `pio0_uart0_default`, and that the tx and rx pins are at index 0. For peripherals with more pins (e.g. SPI) that would mean that a specific ordering would be needed in the pinmux array. My point is - IMO both implementations use a custom pinctrl scheme
