body:
@yonsch 

> If any of your other changes would require breaking an API later, please say so now, so that I might fix it before this is merged.

I don't think you can change the current API to be compatible with #56678, as the changes would break the current implementation.

#56678 cannot really coexist with `PICOSDK_USE_PIO` since you would end up with different paths trying to allocate the same resources. Also i see `PICOSDK_USE_CLAIM` creating unnecessary dependencies since any multicore topics should be solved through zephyr specific APIs.

The PIO parent driver in #56678 was designed just as a resource allocator/interrupt router. All child devices need to use the PIO registers directly.
Technically, the PIO part in picosdk is just a wrapper over basic operations and IMO contains a lot of unnecessary overhead for what is does, also some use-cases will result in runtime issues.

For example, when you allocate SMs to different devices you will need to modify some bits in some registers applicable only to those SMs. This requires atomic operations and `picosdk` functions accessing those registers don't support that. In case of UART, if you have the misfortune to end up in a RMW situation on the same register with another device you could end up in an undefined state.

#56678 uses these to solve that:
```
2.1.2. Atomic Register Access
Each peripheral register block is allocated 4kB of address space, with registers accessed using one of 4 methods,
selected by address decode.
• Addr + 0x0000 : normal read write access
• Addr + 0x1000 : atomic XOR on write
• Addr + 0x2000 : atomic bitmask set on write
• Addr + 0x3000 : atomic bitmask clear on write
```

To summarize, my approach would be to break any dependencies on external rpi code (other that the HW structs). This might prove beneficial in the long run as external SW could change and break existing implementations.

body:
> It will break some of the implementation, but the question is if it will break an API, or at least require massive changes. For example, if we merged this PR and then you'll need to move lots of DTS around, that would be counter productive. However if you're just replacing a call to `pio_add_program` with your own implementation, that would be more of an "incremental improvement".

#56678 breaks pretty much everything on the source code side:
[rpi_pico_pio.h](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/4fbf811880ab3c5d674cdc0fd1b408dbd673e110/include/zephyr/drivers/misc/rpi_pico_pio/rpi_pico_pio.h)
[rpi_pico_pio_util.h](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/4fbf811880ab3c5d674cdc0fd1b408dbd673e110/include/zephyr/drivers/misc/rpi_pico_pio/rpi_pico_pio_util.h)
[rpi_pico_pio.c](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/4fbf811880ab3c5d674cdc0fd1b408dbd673e110/drivers/misc/rpi_pico_pio/rpi_pico_pio.c)
[uart_rpi_pico_pio.c](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/4fbf811880ab3c5d674cdc0fd1b408dbd673e110/drivers/serial/uart_rpi_pico_pio.c)

So, technically, it's a redesign. On a diff, the only similar thing remaining is `DT_RPI_PICO_PIO_PIN_BY_NAME`.
`pio_rpi_pico_allocate_sm` though it looks similar, is not compatible since there's a use-case where you need to allocate more than 1 state machine in a single call because you need explicit ordering for the `INLINE_OUT_EN / OUT_STICKY` feature.

Another issue is that going with incremental merges will not really work since the UART in #56678 needs the PIO in the same PR. So, it could be an incremental review, but needs to be within a single PR.

As I said in the previous comment, #56678 is not compatible with `pico-sdk`. You could technically have an out-of-tree custom driver and still use the SDK (by manually adjusting the allocation scheme), but you cannot really have a in-tree driver using the SDK.
This break was intentional. While the SDK looks ok and there are some examples, they are not really zephyr driver ready and there are some things that the PIO could do which are not really possible with the SDK.
IMO, adding a new driver should follow the same process as other zephyr drivers do: Read the datasheet / Design / Implement.

So, to summarize:
I'm not against merging the current PR.
Just keep in mind that if #56678 should enter (will be rebased as much as possible), in essence it will be just a big diff on the source side (see the files linked above).

IIRC the situation in the test was roughly like this: The background networking thread caused a lot of RX resources to be blocked (queued) due to initial MLD, NS, ND, etc. But when the networking thread tried to allocate TX packages to handle the incoming packages it got starved while holding on to the mutex as the test thread managed to block remaining TX resources in the meantime. Deadlock occurred because the test thread was waiting itself for some network event or needed some network resource protected by the mutex (some networking function call, RX or assignment of an IP address or something - don't remember the details any more) which would then never happen.

Just pointing it out as I saw the network stack on real devices initially consume a lot of package resources exactly at the same time that userland processes gain control for the first time and may block TX resources in their own initialization routine while waiting for the network to become available.

Reserving a larger TX/RX thread will solve this but it's maybe not so obvious to users? Detecting the deadlock in the network thread (waiting for TX resources with timeout) and throwing a good error message may be a good enough solution then...

On second thought, I think that this might've happen because of the loopback interface nature - it does not send the packet to the wire, but creates a **copy** of it (so it's an exception in terms of packet allocation) and sends it back to the stack. With `iface` buffer being held in `net_pkt_set_iface()` on the RX path (which please note is no longer the case after recent change), we may hit the RX packet shortage.

I think though that "deadlock" is a too strong description for the problem - yes, it may seems so as the whole boot sequence blocked for the 30 seconds, but this was due to DAD procedure failure. The actual impact of the mutex being held was packet allocation failure (there's a 100 ms timeout in the driver) so the packet did not reach back to the stack.

body:
@hakehuang 

> 1. Would this be better to integrate as a west runner, as if we implement frdm_k64f board in renode, we just need to direct the runner as renode?

I'm not entirely sure. One of our goals is to be able to verify if we should run the test at all. This is controlled by 3 factors:

- should the test work for the given platform (this is the current filtering mechanism)
- is the platform supported in Renode at all
- is the specific feature supported in Renode

We used cmake-level integration because each board supported in Renode requires specific parameters to be defined.

If you add your board support to Renode, you still need to provide these parameters, e.g. the script (see [here](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/boards/riscv/hifive1/board.cmake#L4)).

What would be the benefit of having the runner defined?

> 2. Interactiving with irobot does not depends on renode, so this can be a separated feature. Can we convert automatially testcase.yml to irobot file? As in current irobot file, they are just rephase the same content in testcase.yaml and add the few standard steps. so the flow would be, if there is no addition irobot file provoide, we still can use robot way with the `-t run_irobot_test`, and a irobot file for given testcase existing will override the testcase.yaml for irobot otpion.

This is partially true. Robot has many more features than current testcase.yaml can express. For example we can verify the shape of the signal generated by a PWM, we can analyze network packets, and we can call Renode functionality directly. This will not be usable for HW testing (or will be difficult), but we use this integrations in non-public contexts in this way as well.

It should be possible to use Robot runner for current testcases, but I'm not sure if this should be part of this PR.

body:
> @tejlmand The main reason for this change is that there's no way to extend a board downstream.

I fully understand, and I completely agree that we need a functionality like this.
But as soon as we have such functionality, then we must also be prepared that multiple modules starts using this feature.

Imagine both https://github.com/teslabs/spinner and another project like NCS extending a board.
They both become part of same highlevel project, but their extensions are in conflict, then how to handle ?

One option could be to limit the board extension to only be active inside the module who defines it, but then what about a project which might like this to be active on all projects because it offers the use of another / better RNG.
And what about derived projects where you actual want the extension to also be active.

While at the same time there could be samples where you might actually not want such board extension to kick in.

A lot of open questions, which is also why I take careful steps atm.

@keith-packard For some reason, I cannot add comments to your review comment threads, so I am starting a new one:

> Any reason for sticking the non ISO-C functions in backticks? Or are they links to the relevant specs that I'm just not seeing here?

Yes, they are indeed links. If you scroll down a bit more, you will see the link URLs.

> Are you considering all of arch/ to be part of this list?

Yes, because the Zephyr kernel testing needs to be done for every architecture and also the minimal libc can be useful during the initial bring-up of a new SoC/board.

> That seems almost as unbounded as drivers/

Not necessarily. The `arch/` (aka. architecture port) is as much of the "Zephyr kernel" as the `kernel/` itself, containing the essential architecture support code for the kernel (e.g. CPU initialisation, interrupt handling, context switching, ...). Moreover, such code rarely needs to use any C standard library functions anyway.

> I'm wondering if this is a good place to note that patches adding use of additional ISO/IEC C functions are welcome as long as they are accompanied by implementations of those functions for the minimal C library. I'd like it to be clear that the goal is *not* to restrict the usage of standard functions unnecessarily, just to ensure that the repository can be built without use of external code.

Sure, I will add a comment about introducing a new C standard library function to the Zephyr kernel scope/minimal libc -- that adding a new function to the list is allowed as long as it is justifiable (reviewed case-by-case).

The goal is to regulate, not restrict unnecessarily.

Architecture WG:

- @fabiobaltieri asks how to enforce A.4: We will build the "zephyr kernel" against the minimal libc to ensure those don't use any C standard lib functions outside the list
- @nashif asks why the logging subsystem is included. @stephanosio replies that the kernel uses the logging subsystem
- @evgeniy-paltsev asks why would we allow something like `malloc` in the kernel. @stephanosio replies that this is only about the C standard library, not whether the function makes sense in the kernel
- @nashif states that he agrees with @evgeniy-paltsev that things like `malloc` or `qsort` don't make sense in the kernel.
- @stephanosio presents rule A.5, that lists the functions that are non-standard but allowed in the zephyr codebase
author: carlescufi

body:
> * @evgeniy-paltsev asks why would we allow something like `malloc` in the kernel. @stephanosio replies that this is only about the C standard library, not whether the function makes sense in the kernel
> * @nashif states that he agrees with @evgeniy-paltsev that things like `malloc` or `qsort` don't make sense in the kernel.

@nashif @evgeniy-paltsev As discussed in the Architecture WG meeting today, the purpose of the "Rule A.4: C Standard Library Usage Restrictions in Zephyr Kernel" is to restrict the usage of the libc functions in the "Zephyr kernel" to what is provided by the minimal libc, and not necessarily to give the green light on these functions being used in the "Zephyr kernel" -- that would be subject to a different set of rules (i.e. secure and safe coding practices, and most importantly the common sense).

I will add a comment in the "Rule A.4: C Standard Library Usage Restrictions in Zephyr Kernel" to clarify that the use of the C standard library functions listed in the rule are subject to the secure and safe coding practices, and the functions being listed in it does not imply that their use in the "Zephyr kernel" is unconditionally justified or permitted.

> This type of device with attributes and sensor values sounds like it could fit into the existing sensors API. What is the rationale for introducing a new API, apart from naming?

This has already been answered several times. Additionally, the correct place to have this discussion is in the issue itself #56635.

As for using the sensor subsystem specifically, in my experience one of the largest notebook customers in the industry scoffed at the idea of using the sensor subsystem aimed at EC peripherals for charging. If we do not provide this API, EC customers will continue using out-of-tree code to implement their charging power trees in various ways.

I have also mentioned that this PR is intentionally very slim. I understand that it doesn't look like much at the moment but there are a lot of inter integrated circuit communications and management that are best served by a dedicated API (Please refer to the Linux power supply class for examples of some, but not all, of the potential helper functions needed to manage a charging tree). High power density charging systems are rarely highly integrated given the requirements of their process geometries. 

I also kept this pretty slim expecting the initial review of this API to take a long time. However, nothing in this PR is truly revolutionary from what was proposed in the first mention of the charging API in #44847.

body:
> @cfriedt I'm a bit stuck with using interrupts and semaphores, I was about to switch to them on my display driver, then I stopped and paused because that would pose a problem, a problem for me at least, I want to be able to use the display from a bootloader (i.e. mcuboot) and imposing semaphores then means I would need to build mcuboot with mutlthreading support, just enabling that option without using the functions in code adds 4KB to a bootloader build which isn't a small 

@thedjnK - the issue I have here is that you are "optimizing" the Driver API for your particular use case (operating in single-threaded / bootloader mode) whereas the vast majority of users of the API would likely be using it in threaded mode).

The implication, is that this influences the Driver API design in a negative way and would make the API itself quite fragile and error prone. You yourself (I think you've added a MAINTAINTERS entry) would end up fixing bug after bug after bug until the API was reworked anyway.

I'm just suggesting you pay off the tech debt upfront and make life easier for your future self.

You actually can use semaphores in multithreading mode and directly from ISRs as long as the `timeout` parameter is `K_NO_WAIT`. In that case, return `-EBUSY`, `-EAGAIN`, or `-ETIMEDOUT`, so just bring that `timeout` parameter out to your API or alternatively add a default via Kconfig.

One nice aspect of this kind of design is that you could "advertise" it as fully supporting both threaded and non-threaded mode in your API doc and really, it would be setting a good example for others to follow.

As I said before, I see this becoming one of the most use ways of testing and we will have 100s of tested converted or implemented to use this feature, so it is going a core twister testing harness and has to be compatible and following the same rules we use for twister development.

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/7d898edfc5c2e8dfa4bc158c5f74614f15dd833b/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/config_parser.py#L229-L237

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/7d898edfc5c2e8dfa4bc158c5f74614f15dd833b/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/config_parser.py#L210-L214

So, any explicit specifications of `OVERLAY_CONFIG` in `extra_args` should be updated to use these.

By the way, twister's `extra_conf_files` is actually for `CONF_FILE`, and instead it has `extra_overlay_confs` is for `OVERLAY_CONFIG`; so, after this PR is merged, we will either need to rename `extra_overlay_confs` to `extra_extra_conf_files` or rethink how `extra_conf_files` works.

author: nordicjm

body:
@nordicjm, I don't quite understand why you selected the retention subsystem for this functionality:

1. Does mcuboot have functionality to share info with running software: yes it does, it is called the shared memory interface,
2. Does zephyr have the means to use this functionality: yes it has, memory-regions can be declared and reserved for this,
3. Can this be used by other bootloaders: yes it can, it is just a memory-region that bootloaders can write to in their own format without any limitations imposed (and with their own validation if needed), a zephyr specific interface for whatever bootloader can easily be constructed,
4. Is it code efficient: yes it is, it requires no code except to allow access to it when using userspace.

Does this cover all possible storage requirements: no it does not, but all devices have ram so it could be selected by any device. There is no need to increase complexity in bootloader code, as every complexity added will result in a failure possibility.

> The `GEN_ABSOLUTE_SYM()` macro is creating some defines that could (or could not) be used by downstream code that is relaying on those to be present.

Here's one✋ We were relying on `___thread_stack_info_t_size_OFFSET` to present stack usage during debugging in Nordic's VS Code extensions. 

I'll acknowledge that these aren't technically part of the API, so we were on shaky ground here, but these generated symbols have no alternative solution that is covered by the API. 

I humbly ask you to please not delete any more of these without providing alternative ways of accomplishing the same use cases. They don't affect production binary sizes and the addition in build time and build system complexity is trivial.

There was a similar discussion in #53951, where some deprecated command line options were removed, then restored. There's definitely value in cleaning up stuff that is actively a burden on the maintainers, but I think this project is big enough that [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/) should be taken into consideration at this point.

@carlocaione that wouldn't do it, no. The symbol we were relying on was actually generated by `GEN_OFFSET_SYM()`, and technically it was #54446 that broke our workflow. I commented on this PR since this is where you started the conversation that applies to all these changes.

If anything, I think the offsets should be added to the thread info object here: 
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/9f37ae902bf30580b32b567c8f95d4b54bfac186/subsys/debug/thread_info.c#L42 
The downside is that this can't be read at compile time in the same way. Also, this object isn't part of the API either, and it's not used anywhere else in Zephyr, so I suppose there's nothing stopping anyone from merging a PR that deletes that without deprecation as well. 

I don't expect that everything that ever existed in zephyr is kept around forever, I'm just hoping maintainers can keep in mind that any change to *the observed behavior* (and not API) will disrupt someone's workflow. That doesn't mean that the change shouldn't be made, it just means that it will always come at a cost.

Thanks for your patience! In the future, if you "lose" commits I would recommend using `git reflog`. This would show you the SHA-1 of *all* recent commits in your repo, even the ones that may have ended up becoming "orphans". This way you can then cherry-pick the changes, or reset to the commit, etc.

> It is still not clear to me if the subject of a commit and the first line of description should be both present or not. When editing here on GitHub in a browser it asks to enter them both. In VS code there is just one edit box.

It's all one "message" but typically the first line is the "title", followed by a blank line, and then the rest would be considered the commit message.

> Is this a normal procedure to propose any change (including in code) as single commit? AFAIK commits can be squashed while merging the PR. Although I never did that on GitHub.

It depends on the project's practices. In Zephyr we don't squash commits and they end up being merged (well, rebased) as-is. In your case, all the changes are part of the same "fixing grammar" thingy so it makes sense to group them, but it may have been two commits if you had e..g first fixed some spelling and grammar error and then proposed reformatting of the file, or moved sections around. Your PR would have still been something along the lines of "Improve Intro section" but then two commits 1/ fix grammar 2/ re-order sections. If that makes sense :)

Anyhow, thanks very much again! If you wrap your commit message so that it doesn't exceed the 75 characters max length, you should now be good to go.

body:
There is some opportunity to increase compiler optimization by providing the public pthread methods as inline wrappers that take a `pthread_spinlock_t*` argument and passes it to an internal function, but first convert the argument to a `pthread_spinlock_t` or `bit`.

The check that `lock` is not NULL can likely be resolved by the compiler at compile time.   It's possible to avoid even allocating space for `lock` and have it live in a register (would need a somewhat limited scope for the lock to be defined over to actually be done).  `*lock` needs to be loaded from RAM on each call, since the compiler can not determine nothing changes it.  But if an inline function (or LTO!) is used, the compiler can see that nothing changes the value and avoid the instructions to reload it.

There is always room for optimization but that can be done on an as-needed basis at a later date with evidence / measurements. Additionally, having something that works and meets the spec is more important, and I would avoid inlining anything that isn't specifically mentioned that it could possibly be an inline function or macro.

Technically, that check isn't even required by the standard and it represents undefined behaviour. I was thinking about making it an `__ASSERT_NO_MSG()` since that can easily be disabled.

> allocating space for `lock` and have it live in a register (would need a somewhat limited scope for the lock to be defined over to actually be done). `*lock` needs to be loaded from RAM on each call, since the compiler can not determine nothing changes it. But if an inline function (or LTO!) is used, the compiler can see that nothing changes the value and avoid the instructions to reload it.

Yep - keeping `lock` in a register would have benefits, but it also isn't clear to me how to return multiple values in registers. Additionally, there is no "invalid lock" value as part of the `k_spinlock` API. We can leave that to future optimization (ideally before the next release).

> Technically, that check isn't even required by the standard and it represents undefined behaviour. I was thinking about making it an `__ASSERT_NO_MSG()` since that can easily be disabled.

The same also for both checks for use of an uninitialized spinlock, undefined behavior in POSIX, but certainly a nice debugging aid.  The second check makes all spinlocks contend for access to the single spinlock protecting `posix_spinlock_bitarray`.  I suppose scaling probably isn't much of a concern.  The flash sharing caused by having all spinlocks be adjacent in memory will not help scaling either.

> Anyhow, I think first we need to agree a basic terminology, and be consistent with it, because right now this text seems to be using its own terms with different meanings.

what own terms with what different meanings, can you please elaborate? This text is trying to solve a problem we have right now. Severity of a bug should not be set based on who uses the feature and how popular a feature is, it needs to apply to the  context of where the bug. This is the only way we will have a general view of what systems and platforms need attention and have problems. If we set severity based on usage and poplarity, then we end up with an unbalanced picture where most bugs are marked as minor (the same way we have those marked with low priority right now). 
Setting severity of a bug will also become a function of who sets the label and how much they care about a certain subsystem.
author: nashif

body:
>  what own terms with what different meanings, can you please elaborate?

The difference of meaning would seem to be in statements like:
"Severity shall be used to classify bugs based on impact to users and community in general."
"Severity: The extent to which an issue or defect can affect the software and defines the
impact that a given defect has on the system."  (i.e. overall severity to the project)
"Severity shall be set based on the context of the bug and not in relation to the
overall impact on the codebase." 

> This text is trying to solve a problem we have right now. Severity of a bug should not be set based on who uses the feature and how popular a feature is, it needs to apply to the context of where the bug. This is the only way we will have a general view of what systems and platforms need attention and have problems. 

Should we, then, try to be more explicit with what we mean and call it "impact on the feature" instead of "severity". (or whatever other wording you'd prefer)

> If we set severity based on usage and popularity, then we end up with an unbalanced picture where most bugs are marked as minor 

We should also reflect with some label during triagging what is the overall priority of the bug for the project as it is very relevant. We could keep using "priority" for those.
Say a "minor" bug that affects all platforms and apps even if not critically, may warrant more attention than, say, a crash that only triggers in some not-common platform when an obscure combination of features is used.

I'd state in the documentation something conceptually like:
"Each bug has an _overall project priority_, which we quantize as high,medium or low. This _overall project priority_ should be estimated as the bug _impact on the feature_ weighted by the _importance of the affected feature(s)_ and by the  _importance of the affected platform(s)_."
"This bug _overall project priority_ is estimated during bug triaging, and guides the overall focus and priority the project will have to fix the bug, as well as its impact on the release criteria"

>>> print(readline.__doc__)
```

This should tell us whether the readline module is based on GNU readline or on libedit.

If the docstring does not contain "libedit", we're good.
Otherwise try the stand-alone `gnureadline` module: `pip install -U gnureadline`.

Regarding how and when auto-completion is triggered, the GNU readline configuration is a two-liner:

```
>>> readline.set_completer_delims(f" \t\n")
>>> readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")
```

The `set_completer_delims()` should allow for auto-completion after a *newline* (i.e. for empty command lines). 

I've noticed the `\n` delimiter is incorrect: it's correct for all platforms when reading or writing files, but here `os.linesep` (actually the *line separator*) should be used. 

I've pushed the fix. I don't have much hope that alone will solve this issue, though (crossing fingers).

Now, could you run the REPL session bellow:

```
>>> import os, readline
>>> readline.set_completer_delims(f" \t{os.linesep}")
>>> readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")
>>> input()
```

And confirm pressing `TAB` (may be twice) will:

- auto-complete Python identifiers and keywords (using the [rl_completer module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/rlcompleter.html) as completer)
- NOT auto-complete an empty command line but actually add `TAB` characters
- auto-complete an empty command line with e.g. file paths (or anything provided by some kind of *default completer*, not sure where this one exactly comes from) if issuing `readline.set_completer(None)` before `input()`

Note that this may contradict the Python readline [API documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/readline.html):

> settings made using this module affect the behaviour of both the interpreter’s interactive prompt and the prompts offered by the built-in input() function.

On my system:

- the Python's REPL behaves as described above, so neither the *interpreter’s interactive prompt* nor the *prompts offered by the built-in input()* honors the expected readline configuration
- `input()` in an `ipython` session does work as expected (auto-completes empty lines); recent versions of `ipython` no longer rely on readline but on the pure Python [prompt_toolkit](http://python-prompt-toolkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), and thus do not mess with the readline configuration in any way

Eventually the GNU readline library's behavior may also be configured by:

- some `inputrc` file, e.g. `/etc/inputrc` or `~/.inputrc`: does this file exist on your system ? what does it say ?
- the shell itself (e.g. `bash` or `zsh`) 

> I did a pip install -r zp/zephyr/scripts/dts/dtsh/requirements.txt before running west dtsh.

The run-time requirements do not install anything related to the GNU readline integration.
I may update it when we know what works best for each platform.

But checking the requirements won't hurt, especially since Python won't propagate exceptions (e.g. for missing imported packages) when running within a readline native callback context: faults will instead silently mess with the command line. 

To be sure, could you confirm `ls -l` executes without error (this should import enough for our test).

## Command line parser

> The command parser also doesn't seem to be stripping leading whitespace:

Thanks for spotting this. The parser is actually fine, but the special inputs `q`, `quit` and `exit` were stupidly (typo ;-) matched with the raw command line, not the parsed command string. Fix pushed.

## Documentation

> My preference would be that the markdown pages in the dtsh directory be converted to .rst so they can be incorporated into Zephyr's documentation pages using Sphinx. Would you be amenable to this approach? 

Yes, sure.

> Discoverability is excellent, but a good manual is also excellent, and it is something we can work together to write and maintain

LGTM. Thanks. I'll get back to you about this when I have a first proposal. 

## Access any property's value

> Maybe a cat command to print the properties in a node?

That's exactly how [*goold old dtsh*](https://github.com/dottspina/dtsh) queries arbitrary property values: the `cat` command accepts parameters like `<path-name>$<property-name>`, which woks well (including auto-completion) since `$` is a valid character neither in path names nor in property names.    

As I've pointed out in the detailed RFC:

- this code base still misses the `man` (currently being worked on) and `cat` commands
- but the RFC is already sizeable, and will require quite some work from its reviewers: I'd prefer we first agree on the initial design, implementation and documentation, then I'll push the missing commands with shortest individual PRs   

So for me the auto-completion not working on macOS is a definitely a known merge blocker. Missing the `man` and `cat` commands is not (or at least should not prevent from dropping the *Draft* flag). Do you share this point of view, or would you prefer the initial RFC to implement `man` and `cat` ?

body:
### RFC - notes on RAM allocation for modules
 
My goal is to have (at least one) user space thread that is executing "untrusted" (ie. possibly buggy!) module code separately from the core kernel, so I was working on supporting an `USERSPACE=y` build as a first step. Currently that is prevented by the `ARM_MPU=n` constraint, that allowed this RFC to focus on linking issues only.

Relaxing that constraint introduces memory use restrictions, so it becomes necessary to have properly separate code and data memory partitions.
Currently, on ARM targets, Flash is read/executable and RAM is read/writable. For loadable modules, we must  also define a RAM memory partition for the stack and heap that is RW to the thread running the code, and also probably a separate partition for RAM code that is executable but not writable. On Cortex arches at least, these must be defined at build time and have strong size/alignment constraints.

These requirements also depend on the type of relocation used in the loaded module: 
* The current design uses partially linked ELFs (Linux kernel style `.o` files), which require code sections to be patched. This means code can't be run from Flash (*), must be moved to RAM and placed in a RX (read/execute) mem partition.
  (\* They could be relocated on write, but then there would be issues when a firmware update changes the core OS image... I don't see this as viable.)

* Loading dynamic ELFs (DLL `.so` files) would not require changes to code sections - code can stay in Flash, only the GOT (basically a list of pointers) needs to be calculated and placed in RAM. There is no need for the RX mem partition. However, that is still useful if the code is to be "hot-run" (loaded in RAM and started, without writing in Flash).

| Module type  | XIP          | RW data | RX code |
|--------------------|--------------|--------------|-------------|
| `.o` in Flash  | No           | Yes          | Yes         |
| `.o` in RAM    | Patched  | Yes          | Yes         |
| `.so` in Flash | Yes         | Yes          | No          |
| `.so` in RAM  | Yes         | Yes          | Yes         |

So I'm looking for feedback on these topics:
* Should we go ahead with defining separate, build-defined memory areas for module code, module stack and module heap? Are there ways to get more flexible partitioning? 
* Should we try to support `.so` files and the optimal case of XIP to reduce RAM memory footprint?
* Are there other related constraints on arches we would like to support beside ARM Cortex?

@mbolivar-ampere , thanks a lot for your detailed reply.


> So the readline I had on my system was the wrong one, it seems.

Unfortunately it's actually *the wrong one*.

While I could patch the call to `parse_and_bind()` depending on the underlying library (GNU readline or libedit), the Python reference manual assumes, without further precision, these libraries behave differently regarding the beginning and ending index of the completion scope: supporting both would imply quite some work (and require a platform to debug with).


```
% pip install -U gnureadline
Successfully installed gnureadline-8.1.2
% python                    
>>> import readline
>>> 'libedit' in readline.__doc__
True
```
> So even with gnureadline installed, it seems readline is the readline version when imported.
> I can import gnureadline without error.

You probably means "it seems readline is the **libedit** version": that's expected, the Python module's name is actually `gnureadline`, and fortunately there's no hidden wizardry here that will automatically import it instead of the `readline` module.

You've already tested the correct approach further in your reply:

```
>>> import os
>>> import gnureadline as readline
>>> readline.set_completer_delims(f" \t{os.linesep}")
>>> readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")
>>> input()
```

And it seems to work:

> Now, typing TAB yields no results when pressing tab rather than inserting tab characters.

The important thing above is that readline has consumed the `TAB` key (getting no results is not necessarily an issue here, I've no idea what your *default completer* could be).

That's promising: dtsh should prefer `gnureadline` to the `readline` module bundled with Python whenever the former is installed.

Did you retry to run `west dtsh` after installing the `gnureadline` module ? 

> I am using zsh because that is the default macOS shell these days, so I expect most Mac users to be on zsh.

But with this, is there a way to enable just one of the optional modules, or can you only enable all of them. E.g. if someone wants to get zephyr and just enable nanopb and thrift, can they do that with west commands? And also do that in their own west manifest which imports the zephyr one?

that is the same question asked here: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/54276#issuecomment-1679092780

AFAIK, the short answer is no. This is where we get into 'package management'.  Optional manifest will serve as a list of modules you can enable in your workspace if you are doing something localy, i.e. in your own manifest. 

You can always modify the upstream manifest locally and pull whatever you want, but what would be the usecase here if those are optional and nothing in the zephyr tree depend on them?  

Maybe you want to add a new subsystem that usess one of those, say you add a new subsystem that uses `lz4` compression. So, in this case, you put it in the main manifest, develop your subsystem and submit this to zephyr moving lz4 from optional to something used in tree.

If you are working on something out of the tree, then you add it to your own manifest and will remain optional upstream...

@nashif In RFC you stated
"failed: A test is deemed to fail if its actual result does not match its expected result." I agree with this, but would like to specify if we are on the same page. IMO failed are reserved only to asserts, i.e. a status "fail" can only be obtained when an assert in a test resulted with False. I find such definition to be very straight forward and not leaving a space for interpretation if sth is a fail or error. Is the test "red" due to a failing assert? Yes -> fail, no (any other cause) -> error. In the current implementation it is not followed. E.g. timeouts are reported as fails which is IMO wrong, since one cannot tell what was the logical value of the tested assertion. This PR is converting old statuses to new objects in 1:1 manner. I marked places where I believe "error" should be used instead of "fail", but don't want to post flooding the comments until we are clear about the difference between error and failure.

Great example!
TBH I'm not a fan of "blocked" status. I know it's origin, and see your point, that with "blocked" you can stress that a give testcase was not executed at all. IMO having just "error" would be sufficient, so the test case that cause an error and all following would just get "error". I think in such case anyone who is analyzing the results always has to start fixing from the first error and checking if there are no more issues with following, not executed tests cases. I wonder if it is even possible in practice to get error in a test case and any other status than "blocked" in the following cases. I mean when there is an error the app crashes (or timeouts) and there is no following execution and hence no new statuses for following test cases. IMO in practice "blocked" is interpreted the same as "error" in case of test cases: something went wrong during the execution, hence pass nor fail can be assigned. I also have an impression such differentiation is causing a confusion among reviewers, because such status is only for test cases. Nevertheless, the logic in your example is sound, hence I won't block "blocked" :). 

>What about the testsuite status? right now this will be marked as fail. When do we mark a testsuite as error?

I would define test suite statues like this:
Pass - Test suite was fully executed (all asserts evaluated, there were no errors). All test cases passed unless they were explicitly skipped.
Fail - A test suite was fully executed (all asserts evaluated, there were no errors). There is at least on "fail" among test case statuses.
Error - A test suite was not fully executed. There is at least one "error" among test case statuses.

There will be two libraries added:
* `gnss_parse` which parses decimal values and integers in integers or in milli, micro and nano units. ("31" -> 31), ("0.982343" -> 982), ("0.982343" -> 982343) etc. using fixed point math
* `gnss_nmea0183` which parses standard messages like RMC and GGA, including conversions from formats like ddmm.mmmm to decimal degrees in nano units, and encapsulating strings in the NMEA format ("TEXT" -> "$TEXT*32")

I don't think Ublox (UBX) messages can be described as generic, since they are specific to one vendor.

The plan is to limit it to a publish-subscribe model for navigation data, keeping/caching the data can be handled by the application.

> > If it would be needed to change the prefix or crc-type the application can not support 2 different prefixes or crc-types.
> 
> Why do you say this. It is implemented in code, using a DT format that we define. If we determine that supporting multiple formats is important (and I think it is) we should extend the retention subsystem to support this. The retention subsystem is new, and has not been included in a release, changing its interfaces is fairly easy to do, especially since using it for boot data is one of the two things it was specifically designed for.
> 
> Saying that we shouldn't use the retention subsystem because it is lacking a feature, but instead should entirely implement the functionality itself is, frankly, rather silly, especially given that the retention subsystem was mostly created for this specific use case. If there are needed features, let's make sure we discuss them, but they need to be implemented in the right place.

I explained this on discord, but for anybody else that wants to understand the problem: the retention system defines the prefix and crc type in the dts. This dts is used by mcuboot and the application. Once it is fixed in mcuboot it cannot be changed. The application will always need to respect what is used in mcuboot. If for some reason this needs to be changed in a new version of mcuboot an application cannot support 2 versions (one for the old mcuboot and one for the newer mcuboot).

Even if by some change it would be possible for the application to support multiple versions (e.g. by creating several retention areas at the same location) the problem is replaced by a problem for mcuboot generation: which one of the several possibilities does it need to choose ?

This is a theory vs. practice thing.  Sure, in principle I don't see any reason to separate them; "post kernel" surely means once everything is running, and everything includes extra CPUs.

body: The `ipm_cavs_idc.c` driver needs to enable IRQ for each core for inter-processor communication only after that core has been up. IIRC, any interrupt would wake up the core to go through the power up process. So we need to be very careful on when we enable interrupt, or else the core(s) would be powering up at the time we are not ready. We cannot assume the hardware state as if it has power-cycled itself to reset state because the audio DSP can be restarted by power cycling only the code (e.g. restarting after crash), while the peripherals (in this case the IPC mechanism) may still be powered and have not gone through reset. Because the audio DSP is part of a SoC which means there may not be a total power cycling of all related hardware. Unless we decouple the interrupt enabling to the SoC layer, we will still need an init level which only starts after `z_smp_init()` has completed. Though, this decoupling would make the driver no longer self-contained as it requires SoC code to make it fully working.

The main requirement for arc_shared_intc_update_post_smp is to get called after all local, per cpu interrupt controllers have been initialized and set up to process IDU dispatched interrupts (round robbing sent to one of the SMP cpus). What are your thoughts on this?

@jukkar GSM_MUX is dependent on UART_MUX, even though its not obvious in the Kconfigs, removing it makes the GSM_MUX effectively useless. 

There is only one configuration used in-tree which uses GSM_MUX, and that is MODEM_GSM_PPP (gsm_ppp.c). MODEM_GSM_PPP enables GSM_MUX and NET_PPP (the ppp.c UART driver), which then selects UART_MUX, since this is effectively a dependency of GSM_MUX.

## Patch notes

### GNSS time struct and parsing added
GNSS time now use the following structure
```
struct gnss_time {
	uint8_t hour;		/**< Hour [0, 23] */
	uint8_t minute;		/**< Minute [0, 59] */
	uint16_t millisecond;	/**< Millisecond [0, 59999] */
	uint8_t month_day;	/**< Day of month [1, 31] */
	uint8_t month;		/**< Month [1, 12] */
	uint8_t century_year;	/**< Year [0, 99] */
};
```
Parsers for date and time have been added to the `gnss_nmea0183` library, and included with the `gnss_nmea0183_parse_rmc` function.

### GNSS API nearly fully implemented for Quectel LCX6G driver
The Quectel LCX6G supports all API functions except the periodic configuration. All other functions have been implemented, based on a dynamic chat script which was made available with this PR #62703.

### Cleanup of utilities
The utilities for parsing gnss time have been moved to `gnss_nmea0183` from `gnss_parse`. Unit tests have been added for them, and the unit tests for `gnss_nmea0183_parse_rmc` have been extended to validate parsing of gnss time

### Sample application
An early version of a sample application has been added which simply calls each API and registers a callback for GNSS data.

### Future work
1. The sample application will be extended to print the gnss data received, and dynamically adapt to the features supported by the GNSS modem.
2. Add a callback for satellites in view and parsing for the nmea0183 gsv message.
3. Extend sample application to register a callback to satellites in view and print this as well.
4. Create a "base" struct for NMEA based modems for generic functionality like NMEA handling and publishing as suggested by @fabiobaltieri 

### Reflection
We are getting near a viable experimental GNSS API and subsystem. Once the GNSS subsystem supports reporting satellites in view, we are ready for a "final" review round to round the edges :)

body:
> @gmarull Isn't this going to limit building "virtual" devices on top of real devices ?

Virtual devices should indicate their dependencies as any other device, no? Also, devicetree was never designed for "virtual or software devices". There's been a recent case with LVGL https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/62757, where software dependencies were indirectly inserted via pseudo-device init functions (LVGL allocator had to be initialized first), something devicetree can't capture, of course. If these pseudo-devices continue to pop-up they'll need to be treated specially, that is, to be initialized after all "real" devices, or create a new level explicitly for them that runs last. I have to say that I've always been skeptical about this _abuse_ of dt, but we need to deal with this for now.

edit: LVGL case could also be fixed by having SYS_INIT(POST_KERNEL_EARLY) -> DT_DEVICES(POST_KERNEL) -> SYS_INIT(POST_KERNEL_LATE).

I'll likely be cherry picking and incorporating more work from there as well. For now some basic minimal libc, mutex, thread, and printk functions are exported in a symbol table.

Performing relocations for ARM32_R_CALL turns out to be more involved as it may require a trampoline function to be generated.

The BL instruction documented here https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0406/c/Application-Level-Architecture/Instruction-Details/Alphabetical-list-of-instructions/BL--BLX--immediate-?lang=en is initially given a target of 0 when building hello.c with partial linking.

Only -33554432 to 33554428 relative offset from PC is allowed for BL but...

When building for NXP's RT685 as I have the offset is actually something more like..

0x30198730 - 0x1800dca5 => 404269707

This is too large of an address offset from PC to be directly done by updating the BL opcode as wanted by the relocation.

Instead logic needs to be added for this scenario and a trampoline needs to be generated and appended within the BL range from the function...

This is nicely described here https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20210616-00/?p=105314'

So updated TODO

~~* [ ] Generate trampoline (veneer) code when linking calls that are too far away~~
~~* [ ] Sort out how reallocating the .text section works such that veneers can be appended/prepended easily. Perhaps setting aside veneer space per undefined symbol.~~

Architecture WG:

- @nashif says that whatever goes to the migration guide must be useful to anyone migrating.
- @henrikbrixandersen added only the new drivers/features in the release notes. In the migration guide the required changes
- @fabiobaltieri agrees to add new features only to the release notes
- @nashif suggests an editorial process at the end that cleans up the contents, removes excess contents and move content to the migration guide
- @kartben mentions that information is missing in some cases, which can be attributed to maintainers not completing the release notes in time

The following belongs in the migration guide and in the migration guide (Required Changes) ONLY :
- Changes in the code that require an action (i.e. a modification of the source code or configuration files) on the part of the user in order to keep the existing behavior of their application. This includes:
   - Breaking API changes
   - Deprecations
   - Devicetree or Kconfig changes that affect the user (changes to defaults, renames, etc)
   - Treewide changes that have an effect (eg. changing the include path or defaulting to a different C standard library)

   - Anything else that can affect the compilation or runtime behavior of an existing application

Remove the sections, and the recommended changes altogether.

under which category does this fall exactly?

>[Trivial](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.5.0/project/dev_env_and_tools.html#trivial)
Trivial changes are those that appear obvious enough and do not require maintainer or code-owner involvement. Such changes should not change the logic or the design of a subsystem or component. For example a trivial change can be:
>>Documentation changes
>> Configuration changes
>>Minor Build System tweaks
>>Minor optimization to code logic without changing the logic
>>Test changes and fixes
>>Sample modifications to support additional configuration or boards etc.

Even if any of those apply, a change marked as trivial can be contested  through review where trivial becomes void and the PR need to follow the standard process. Trivial should never be used to fast track PRs, it is just a way for us to deal with low hanging fruits that are obvious enough to be merged quickly without any thorough review or any further discussion. We are past this point already :)

body:
Hi @tgagneret-embedded, thanks for submitting this! It's been a bit since I've looked at the zspdx code and I don't currently have a test bed set up to try this out, but I wanted to share a couple of thoughts on this just as background.

The Packages and Files defined in the zephyr.spdx document are in a sense "imported" via external document references in the subsequent build.spdx document. That's in order to enable the contents of the build.spdx document to reference the Packages and Files defined in zephyr.spdx.

In other words, in the current setup:
* in [zephyr.spdx](https://swinslow.net/zephyr-blinky/zephyr.spdx.txt), we define e.g. a File with SPDXID `SPDXRef-File-cpu-idle.S`
* in [build.spdx](https://swinslow.net/zephyr-blinky/build.spdx.txt), we then "import" the zephyr.spdx document and assign it the local ID `DocumentRef-zephyr`, with the line `ExternalDocumentRef: DocumentRef-zephyr http://spdx.org/spdxdocs/zephyr-a8bcec5e-993f-4233-8059-4f577c4953f0/zephyr SHA1: 45e9a2938d9eb2b1b4a585256fdd783665fb8fcb`
* then, in build.spdx, we can use `DocumentRef-zephyr` to reference its contents in relationships, such as the following line: `Relationship: SPDXRef-File-libarch--arm--core--aarch32.a GENERATED_FROM DocumentRef-zephyr:SPDXRef-File-cpu-idle.S`

The reason I'm mentioning this is just to note that, for any relationships in build.spdx, you'll want to make sure that the SPDX IDs used in those relationships are either defined locally in build.spdx or else have a corresponding definition in zephyr.spdx.

> All modules reported by zephyr_module.py are included in the SPDX, so there are some package with no source file. Should we remove these empty packages (no associated source code) from the SPDX file ?

This is a good question. When I wrote the zspdx code a couple of years ago, I wasn't fully familiar with the Zephyr build process (and I haven't had a chance to dig more into it since then!) You'll see in the existing [build.spdx documents](https://swinslow.net/zephyr-blinky/build.spdx.txt) that there are several "Packages" with the comment "Utility target; no files". IIRC, these are CMake targets with the target type of `UTILITY` under [CMake's file-based API](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-file-api.7.html#id14).

I had captured them in zspdx and the build.spdx documents, because these utility targets are part of the build chain that I wanted to make sure were captured in the `HAS_PREREQUISITE` relationships. It's a bit kludgy to call them "Packages" in the SPDX sense if they don't actually contain or represent a collection of files, so there may be a better way to do this.

I hope this is helpful! Feel free to let me know if you have any questions about the above comments.

body:
> You are right to mention this but since the reference is only based on the file name, I think my code does not break relationship (and it looks that way). If two files have the same name it seems that spdx library automatically add an index at the end of the reference name.

Thanks @tgagneret-embedded! I agree, as long as the SPDXIDs for Files are not changing, then I wouldn't expect anything to break for the existing relationships in build.spdx.

And yes, the index suffix was set up to help ensure that similarly-named files in different directories still end up with different SPDXIDs. My code for that was a little janky, but I believe it should work as intended.

> To check this and validate the entire SBOM, that would be great to have some tooling, do you know one ?

Good question. The online SPDX tools at https://tools.spdx.org/app/validate/ can be used to validate a single SPDX document, but to my knowledge they don't do cross-document validation of IDs in a separate document incorporated through an ExternalDocumentRef. (See recent discussion at https://github.com/spdx/spdx-spec/issues/870) I haven't tested the online tools with the Zephyr SBOM documents so I'm not sure currently how they would react to the multiple documents with cross-referenced IDs.

The primary "official" SPDX document parsing tools are in Java, Python and Golang, available at https://github.com/spdx. I believe the online tools use the Java version behind the scenes, so Python and Golang may behave differently.

I would rather vote for a solution that fixes the original problem in the first place rather than introducing a new rule in the playbook that VS Code extension can hardly keep up with. As these rules are changing without our knowledge the feature we provide are already broken.

We need to guess from the cmake cache what the original parameters of the build were and match that to what the build system default variables would be. Please consider that majority of the users don't use command line tools anymore but rather an IDE, and that IDE must be supported.

The why: because it was an easy setup that worked and required few steps from users. But yes, it is not too nice.
For users who mind having the build output in the same place as the simulator source, they can set BSIM_OUT_PATH to another directory (it just seemed easier to tell people to just point BSIM_OUT_PATH to the same place as the simulator source)

(what this PR track is aiming at replacing)
2. Run all tests in batch/parallel with run_parallel.sh (~1000), where each test expects the executables for the images it uses already built and ready ${BSIM_OUT_PATH}/bin with those names.
3. 
Replacing 1. and 2. together is where we got into the hairiness of {N images} -> {M tests} dependencies and so forth. So I think @gopiotr idea of tackling 1. first, is a good path. And as he said, it should already be nicer for users to be able to run twister to build the images.

body:
Thanks for your feedback, @JPHutchins.

> I have a strong preference for dependencies like this to live as PyPI packages so that they can:

I agree that maintenance should not be overlooked: this concern is part of the RFC, and I indeed expect it to be discussed.

>     1. be maintained in isolation of the Zephyr repository

Dependencies first go the other way: although this RFC/PR does not affect Zephyr aside from the new West command, DTSh is tightly coupled to the Zephyr's [python-devicetree](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/scripts/dts) library, and to the hardware model it's an API for.

Therefore, when distributed independently, DTSh releases have to pin the python-devicetree versions they're developed and tested with:

- either as a Python requirement that will install the appropriate version along with DTSh: making this library available independently is not a priority of the Zephyr project, and the [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/devicetree/) package is no longer maintained, which rules out this option
- or by re-distributing snapshots of the appropriate versions of the library: this is not ideal, but doable, see e.g. [ci: bundle devicetree Python package ](https://github.com/dottspina/dtsh/commit/5e803eb)

One way or another, Zephyr users will end up with two instances of the python-devicetree library:
- the one that comes with Zephyr, on which it will rely at build-time
- the one installed by/with DTSh

Which raises the question of what should happen when running `west dtsh`:

- should DTSh unconditionally use the pinned version of python-devicetree it has installed (it depends on): since `west build` will still use the library that comes with Zephyr, chances are that `west dtsh` will use a different version, which might prove confusing or misleading
- should DTSh first search for some "current working Zephyr" (think `ZEPHYR_BASE`), and prefer the python-devicetree library found there instead: `west build` and `west dtsh` will then consistently use the same version, but now chances are that you won't run DTSh using the API it's been developed and tested with (it depends on)

>     2. allow Zephyr to easily pin versions

If Zephyr in turn pins DTSh, we add mutual dependencies to the picture.

Although these might be handled through a coordinated release (and testing !) process, I'm afraid this will turn out painful for maintainers and sub-optimal for users, especially when releasing and distributing bug fixes.

>     3. allow users to change the version of a dependency without changing the version of Zephyr

To me, users needing to change the version of DTSh they are using with a given version of Zephyr would show that the above coordinated release process is indeed a failure.

>     4. be used by projects other than Zephyr (more easily)

DTSh still makes little sense outside of Zephyr, as does the python-devicetree library: both might eventually be helpful with e.g. the Linux kernel's Devicetree, but AFAICT we're still far from that.

This doesn't mean DTSh can't be installed independently of Zephyr, and tried to experiment with arbitrary DTS and binding files, see bellow.

> How would you feel about publishing to PyPI and only committing the West integration to the Zephyr repo?

Aside from the personal concerns I've already mentioned, I don't think making the DTSh shell an *external dependency* installed as a Zephyr requirement, while the West command would be maintained upstream, can be acceptable to Zephyr maintainers:

- DTSh being developed and released independently won't save them from reviewing and testing the DTSh versions distributed (*pinned*) with Zephyr to ensure appropriate levels of quality and security: it will just make the process more painful compared to managing pull requests and being able to add unit and integration tests to the project's CI
- installing DTSh from PyPI implies guarantees that a code review alone can't provide: even if you trust the project maintainer as a person, you also have to trust the publishing process, e.g. *Do the repository tags match the release numbers on PyPI ?* or *How are managed the SSH keys used for authenticating uploads ?*

To answer your question, my feeling is thus that if DTSh were to be maintained, as much as possible, *in isolation of the Zephyr repository*, we would better off abandoning the `west dtsh` command entirely.

Publishing on PyPI has issues, but *could work*: the DTSh project's default branch now mirrors and packages the code base of this RFC, that you can install and run independently of West or even Zephyr (more details [here](https://github.com/dottspina/dtsh)). Note that this package can't provide the West integration: just run `dtsh` instead of `west dtsh`.

Why I think having this upstream could nonetheless benefit to Zephyr users:

- on hand and beginner-friendly: no additional installation or configuration step, just `west dtsh`
- `west build` and `west dtsh` will consistently depend on the same Zephyr hardware model and API, no need to take care of some compatibility matrix
- source code, tests, CI, documentation and issues all in one place
- the Zephyr toolchain misses a simple mean to *see* the final DTS file generated at build-time *like a device tree*
- IMHO, the ability to redirect (*export*) commands output to HTML, SVG or simple text files is also a rationale for an OOTB availability (notes-taking, educational materials, document hardware configuration)

Thanks.

The new command `west simulate` is using a dedicated `west` runner instead of using make/ninja to run a custom target to start Renode. In general, using dedicated `west` runners was suggested by @tejlmand in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/66193#pullrequestreview-1817795562. This also allows for passing specific parameters to runners more easily, and we avoid picking up environment variables post-build for running commands.

We proposed the command to be generic, so it can be used with other simulators to provide a unified user experience.

body:
There was a terrible performance bug in sphinx c domain, resulting in a horrible linear search. Effectively turning the problem of symbol reference matching into O(n^2)... 

https://github.com/sphinx-doc/sphinx/issues/10966

It's been solved at least for C, though not yet C++

https://github.com/sphinx-doc/sphinx/pull/12162

With this change to sphinx things improve quite a lot. Sphinx still has to parse and generate mappings though for all references in RST files. Removing the c domain markers that breathe generates reduces this a good amount even more.

Using pypy further improves the situation.

With this PR, sphinx master, and pypy 3.10 docs build in 120s on my 18 core 10980xe. Prior to these changes it would take nearly 7 minutes!

7mins to 2mins is a good improvement.

I think if we look at this higher level still though, perhaps using sphinx doc which is clearly not fast (python... when is python ever fast), may be has come to the end of the line in terms of acceptable build times. Docs should be *fast* to build so people want to edit and update them. I got here because I was trying to do just that and was fed up with longer build times than I recall the linux kernel taking, certainly much longer than any zephyr firmware build or doxygen build.

For comparison...

doxygen build of zephyr docs takes ~12s

Would it really be so terrble to write the docs in doxygen? doxygen theme is nice now, and clearly doxygen itself is able to generate a pretty nice manual with it https://www.doxygen.nl/manual/index.html

body:
Here's the worst offenders I've encountered.

In `munmap()` you shouldn't call `arch_page_phys_get()` as this will
return -EFAULT if the first page is paged out. Should call `k_mem_unmap()`
directly.

Side note: I think `k_mem_unmap()` should return an error code instead of
void. May always be 0 for now but the prototype should be ready.

`shm_mmap()` looks interesting. This:

- `arch_page_phys_get(shm->mem, &phys)`

followed by:

- `*virt = k_mem_phys_map(phys + off, ROUND_UP(len, _page_size), K_MEM_PERM_RW)`

is going to produce very surprizing results with demand paging indeed.
First, because you use `k_mem_phys_map()` you are bypassing the very tiny
protection against having a physical page mapped twice. It is kinda OK only
with pinned memory which is another way to say that demand paging doesn't
support it.

In your case, what would happen is that you get a second mapping at a 
different virtual address but one that is not tracked by the physical page 
frame management code. So if memory pressure increases and `shm->mem` is not
accessed _irrespective_ of how often that second virtual mapping is used then
the `shm->mem` virtual address will be a prime candidate to be paged out.
And when that happens, the underlying physical page will be recycled for
some other content accessible through some other virtual address that now
will also be visible through the mapping you created with that
`k_mem_phys_map()`, and such content no longer having anything to do with 
the initial `shm->mem` content. And yet, if `shm->mem` is accessed again,
it is unlikely that its content will be paged back into the same physical
page.

In short, this is no good!  ;-)

Now... why do you need a second mapping? Zephyr uses a flat address space

body:
Another issue is that your change will make the function to bail out in the middle of the for loop, leaving already mapped memory after the failing one possibly forever mapped, and never released. A more appropriate place to bail would be where the guard pages are checked. Moreover, the callers actually have to make sure they are unmapping with the same parameters when the region is mapped.

For you to actually hit that assert, you have to pass the two checks for the guard pages first. That means something is horribly wrong for a page in middle of that region to be unmapped. Another reason might be that you are unmapping across multiple virtual regions at the same time. So the boundary guard pages checks would pass, but when you are looping through the pages, you encounter the guard pages in between. For example, region A and region B with guard pages G: `GAAAGGBBBG`. You trying to unmap the whole thing which means the assert would be raised on the middle `GG` guard pages.

Also, this is a very low level API, not to mention being a kernel internal one, one must exercise extreme caution when using it (and also the corresponding mapping function). If garbage arguments are passed to these functions, it is either a coding error, or that memory has been corrupted (e.g. stack overflow, or incorrect pointer de-reference, or cosmic rays). So bailing would be a wise choice in the later case, as correct operations of the whole system can no longer be guaranteed.

Sorry, but the POSIX layer you're creating (and that's highly appreciated
by the way) is _not_ user code. You are managing many different resources
already on behalf of code calling the POSIX interface. That code is the user
not the interface.

Knowing how many times a particular object has been mapped and unmapped is 
the POSIX layer's responsibility, just like the refcounting you already do
elsewhere between `malloc()` and `free()`. You wouldn't free the same memory
twice, right? And you're not calling into the low-level heap allocator to test
if a particular address is still allocated before calling `free()` either.
The assertion in `k_mem_unmap()` is there to catch the equivalent of a
double-free, which is a bug and why it shouldn't be removed.

So it should be no different with `k_mem_map()` and `k_mem_unmap()`.
The first caller to increment the refcount does the map, subsequent callers 
only increment the refcount and get the same already mapped address, and the
last to decrement the count to 0 does the unmap.

Am I missing something that would prevents such implementation?

  - Ztest: At least two sections of string concatnated by dot (`.`) and test case name

- **test scenario entry**: is `<test scenario identifier>`

  - Standalone: String in the YAML files with at least three sections of string concatnated by dot (`.`)
  - Ztest: String in the YAML files with at least two sections of string concatnated by dot (`.`)

> I think the rename from section to segment is a bit confusing to be honest, as ELF has segments that we aren't actually using. Using the same term, segment, is likely to make people believe we are looking at and using ELF segments. That's not the case today.

I do agree in principle, but I think it's reasonable because:
1. our segments are very similar in role to what ELF segments exist for, and
2. while reading code, it's not possible to confuse LLEXT segments with ELF segments.
   LLEXT code completely ignores ELF segments, there isn't a single reference to them.
   On the other hand, we currently have two completely different things called `sections`, and that makes the code painful to read, understand and review.

I'm all ears for a better name, and I think @pillo79 is also open to suggestions :smiley:

I did think about `region`, but it's used extensively in Memory Managment stuff, [such as here](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/build/dts/api/bindings/base/zephyr%2Cmemory-region.html#std-dtcompatible-zephyr-memory-region). When will LLEXT inevitably(?) start interacting with MM, we're going to end up in the same situation ("MM region or LLEXT region?"). `domain` and `partition` are also [already in use](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/kernel/usermode/memory_domain.html#memory-domains), and best avoided.

`segment` does not seem to collide with anything MM-related in Zephyr, as far as a quick glance tells me. (let's ignore x86, ok? :shushing_face:)

When will LLEXT inevitably(?) start interacting with MM, we're going to end up in the same situation ("MM region or LLEXT region?"). `domain` and `partition` are also [already in use](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/kernel/usermode/memory_domain.html#memory-domains), and best avoided.
>

The mapping we have today in mem[] is sections to addresses. The functions operating on it copy sections/free sections makes good sense as they manipulate this mapping. Renaming this to segments isn't right, mem[] and its vectorized members (mem_on_heap, mem_size) are not a mapping of ELF segments to addresses.

If we wish to move towards a different set of mappings, e.g. mem[] maps to memory partitions (ro/rx/rw), and we have a different mapping for elf sections to addresses, which may or may not reside in the memory partitions, which may or may not reside on the heap... then I think that's a nice way to move but this is post 3.7. I'd also prefer us to use the zephyr memory naming scheme in this case (partitions) as it can better relate to how Zephyr does memory regions with permission bits. It also doesn't overlap with the idea of ELF segments which we aren't using at all today and may want to use in the future.

What we have now describes a bad way of working, which almost nobody wants or can follow. So we end up with different modules doing different things, and some of them badly left behind. Those are the exceptions.
What is proposed here is simple: _**If there is an upstream, submit upstream.** Your change will then be synchronized automatically to the module after being merged upstream, and you can update the pointer in the Zephyr manifest_.
Many upstreams for our modules are incredibly accommodating and willing to take our fixes, and are by far the best to review patches to the code.
Sending a patch to a fork is not a good idea, and is very rarely needed.
It has never been needed for any of the modules I maintain. And I have never needed to submit aiming at getting the change thru the Zephyr downstreams unless the downstreams were *way* behind due to them following the current recommendation (Anyhow, I have always got my changes upstream first/at the same time without any hassle).

The idea of auditing/controlling changes to modules with an upstream is wishful thinking:
We have downstreams of projects developed somewhere else. 
It is that somewhere else where changes are decided. Just because we clone a repo does not suddenly mean we have the bandwidth or ability to take over that project development.
The only thing we could "audit" is to have a check in CI that ensures that when we update the pointer from the Zephyr manifest to a new version of a module, we would check licenses or the like.
But we don't need to check that something silly was done in some commit or branch to which we don't refer. It just does not matter for us.

At some point, to not actually freeze all DTSh development until this is approved or rejected, I somewhat rebased a new project branch onto the source code in this PR minus the West command (DTSh v0.2.0-rc1), and made it the default after a few additional patches to better take into account both installation types, bundled with Zephyr or downloaded from PyPI (DTSh v0.2.0).

The commit history could permit to cherry-pick just a few things, or I could rebase this PR onto the latest DTSh release (v0.2.2) or any tag in between. And that's what bothers me: I don't know what to do ?

What is certain is that reviewing this RFC as it is would make no sense: we're now far from the idea of merging this, then adding short incremental PRs (something like when the rabbit can't ever catch up with the turtle, you know).

I still personally think that developing and maintaining DTSh upstream as a Zephyr extension to West makes sense:
- on hand and beginner-friendly: no additional installation or configuration step, just `west dtsh`
- Zephyr (e.g. `west build`) and DTSh (`west dtsh`) will consistently depend on the same Zephyr hardware model and its Python API; this is otherwise an issue when a Zephyr user installs DTSh from PyPI, which has already been discussed here, but you can also take a look at [ci: possible multiple different versions of python-devicetree](https://github.com/dottspina/dtsh/issues/2) if that doesn't sound obvious

Knowing how the logic works I find this description confusing and possibly wrong.  I think it won't help in understanding the logic and can lead to faulty assumptions. IMO, without proper explanation the scope selection rules in one place the user will continue to ask the same questions.
Reading the description I am getting an understanding that platform_allow is directly related with determining the platform scope, but it is not. The point of platform_allow should by no means be used to tell twister where to run and using it in that way is wrong and dangerous. That's why I am against putting this description in platform_allow section. 
 Platform_allow is a filter. Platforms out of it will be skipped (filtered from the scope) when running twister. A user is suppose to tell twister which tests to run on which platforms. If platforms are not given, twister will try to guess the scope starting by picking a list of "default" platforms. Again, platform_allow will filter this list. If something's left, twister will run on not-filtered platforms. If there is nothing left, twister will pick all platforms from platform_allow as the scope.
