body:
Thank you for making this PR. It's great to get the ball rolling! Let's make Rust in Zephyr great!

But, I think this PR tries to do a bit too much too quickly. I think the most important first step is to ensure building and linking is done correctly. I think would be best to focus on this and de-scope other parts of this PR for later. Please read on below where I try to explain.

## LLVM triplets

This PR is using LLVM for compiling Rust, which I think is a good idea. But it does mean we need to think about ABI compatibility with the Zephyr toolchain.

Linking with LLVM objects is not a Rust-specific problem, and we should solve this first, possibly in a language-agnostic way. We should start with a solid foundation on how to correctly build LLVM objects for linking with the Zephyr ABIs.

I think the as first thing on the roadmap to Rust, Zephyr should have an utility that selects a foolproof LLVM target specification. And we must have tests that can verify that it works at runtime, e.g. by calling various types of functions and checking for data corruption.

The reason this may be a concern is that Zephyr defines its own ABI, which may or may not be equivalent to any of the well-known LLVM triplets. For example, in Zephyr `int` is always 32 bits, even on 64-bit platforms. Without a test suite, it's too easy to mess up here.

The PR uses the well-known `thumbv8m.main-none-eabi` and others. We need tests to confirm that we are not making a mistake here.

For prior art, see [tylerwhall/zephyr-rust target specifications](https://github.com/tylerwhall/zephyr-rust/tree/master/rust/targets), which defines new LLVM triplets for Zephyr OS. This project also Apache-licensed.

## Kconfig in Rust

I feel a framework for exposing Kconfig values in Rust should be done at a later stage, since there are many ways to do this and it has attracted comments on how to map the Kconfig values onto Rust types. I think it's better to defer this work, so that the initial Rust support is not delayed by this.

Rust already has `core::env!` for accessing environment variables at build time. I believe this is a good-enough solution for passing in Kconfig variables for now. It's simple enough to copy from Kconfig variables to environment variables in CMakeLists.txt.

I also worry there are good reasons for why `core::env!` is not like this PR, generating a module with symbols for all environment variables. Of course, it's fine to experiment.

## Safety in samples

The sample declares `printk` as a two-argument function. But `printk` is actually a variadic C function. This not the same type so it is probably unsound.

Safety is integral to Rust culture. I think that all Rust samples code should be `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to reflect that. That means FFI calls in samples must be trough safe wrappers.
author: alwa-nordic

body:
> But, I think this PR tries to do a bit too much too quickly.

So, I think we have different philosophies about what we need to do to get rust support into Zephyr. Yes, there is stuff that we need to do "right", but if we are too careful, we'll never get anything at all. My goal here is just to go through the build stuff, and I have a _lot_ of other stuff in process that needs to builds to be able to happen. I guess I'd rather have it work well in a limited situation than solve everything before anything can go in.

> triplets...

So, getting this right is important, but this is also difficult to come up with tests for. One possibility is to just be more restrictive about it, and pick configurations that we know work.

But, I don't think the calling is as difficult of an issue as you are imagining. Generally, getting the triple wrong is more likely to result in either code that doesn't run at all (using the wrong CPU), or fails at link time (usually from hard float mismatch).

Matching the Zephyr types is important, but I wouldn't think of that as a compiler or toolchain, but a matching the ABI. It is also not addresed at all yet, as we aren't really calling anything.

> Kconfig

I disagree about delaying it. I'm open for other ideas on how to do it, but getting access to them is foundational for most later work. Do you have specific concerns about how I'm doing it?

I'm not quite sure I understand how `core::env()` is useful. It can't be used for conditional compilation, which is one of the primary needs for getting to bool Kconfig values.

> samples

As far as the samples, it isn't intended to stay that way, and in fact, my other PR has already removed it.

Basically, I'm concerned about spinning, while bike shedding things that really aren't that important. One of my goals is to make using Rust inside of Zephyr as nice (well, hopefully nicer) as writing C code. Coming next is making the DT available to Rust code.
author: d3zd3z

body:
A little more on my philosophy here. There are probably 30-40 things that need to be in place for Rust on Zephyr to even be slightly useful. If we sit around and try to come up with the "perfect" solution to all of these problems, I don't think we'll ever get to the point where there is something useful. These pieces can certainly be improved once we get there. Maybe some of this could be worked on in parallel. But, not being able to even build something basic will keep us from ever getting past the first few things.

In other words, I'd like to keep things that are experimental away from affecting the rest of Zephyr. Perhaps as we really figure out what is needed, some things like target selection can be improved on, but I'd really like to get to the point where someone could reasonably write an actual application in Rust that runs on Zephyr. That means it needs kconfig, it needs to see the device tree, and have accessors into the device tree to give it save wrappers to be able to use real Zephyr devices. Threads, syscalls, synchronization, logging, etc all needs to be there before it's really useful. I think we are much better getting the pieces in place, adequately, not perfectly, will give this a much better chance of success. Once it is actually useful, the pieces can be improved and perfected. This is, in fact, how the rest of Zephyr's development has happened.

I do agree that, for example, applications shouldn't need unsafe. That was just a temporary placeholder until there is enough functionality to have something to safely call. It is surprising how much it takes to get there.

body:
> One limitation limitation, however, that wasn't immediately clear to me looking at it and at #75900 , is that all `static inline` function (such as `k_msleep()`) get optimized out, and fail to resolve by the linker.

So solving this is a much deeper part of this work that is presented at this level. There are a couple of possible approaches. One is, as you say, to basically drop down some code that will get the C compiler to emit linked versions of the inline functions. Part of the necessity of this is that _every_ use of `static inline` is actually wrong. According to the gcc docs, it should be `extern inline`, and then there should be one instance where the code is brought in.

This could be done with some simple wrappers of C functions that just call the inline function. Since it is inlined, it will be expanded, and the definition would be basically what the inline function has in it.

The disadvantage here is that the inline doesn't happen when rust makes use of this code. So the code is a bit slower when running in Rust.

The other possibility is to actually implement all of the inline functions in Rust as well. Given the large number of these, it is probably a bit of an overwhelming maintenance nightmare, and automatically converting inline C declarations into Rust is not an easy problem. There are also lots of things that are implemented as macros that really are just code.

I'm open to ideas on how to best handle this. For some of the stuff I'm playing with in #76074, I've written the code in Rust (it doesn't add any C code, such as wrappers). Please take a look at that if you have any comments about the direction I'm taking.

> can this be a subsystem

Why couldn't it?

> (no limitations on id etc)

I don't see what you're talking about? There are no such limitations.

> Shouldn't this be part of modules/mbedtls?

No, for at least the following reasons:
- PSA Secure Storage is not the same thing as PSA Crypto.
- And it's completely separate from Mbed TLS. It's not part of nor depends on Mbed TLS specifically in any way. It just happens to be using PSA Crypto (which could be provided by something else than Mbed TLS) for the AEAD operations in the base implementation, but that's an implementation detail.
- In fact, PSA Secure Storage is separate from Mbed TLS to the point where it could be used without Mbed TLS, because even if using the PSA Crypto API it could be implemented by something else than Mbed TLS (e.g. [wolfSSL](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/75828)).

> > can this be a subsystem
> 
> Why couldn't it?
> 
> > (no limitations on id etc)
> 
> I don't see what you're talking about? There are no such limitations.
> 

Please correct me if I'm wrong: The proposed subsystem is also used directly by PSA-Crypto/MBEDTLS to store keys. If it is zephyr that defines what PSA-Crypto should use as id to store keys it is OK to use it as a subsystem, if OTOH it is PSA-Crypto that defines what is used as id to store it should be part of module/mbedtls (that includes PSA-Crypto)

It is also not a good idea from maintaining point of view to implement an externally defined API as a subsystem.

> > Shouldn't this be part of modules/mbedtls?
> 
> No, for at least the following reasons:
> 
> * PSA Secure Storage is not the same thing as PSA Crypto.
> * And it's completely separate from Mbed TLS. It's not part of nor depends on Mbed TLS specifically in any way. It just happens to be using PSA Crypto (which could be provided by something else than Mbed TLS) for the AEAD operations in the base implementation, but that's an implementation detail.
> * In fact, PSA Secure Storage is separate from Mbed TLS to the point where it could be used without Mbed TLS, because even if using the PSA Crypto API it could be implemented by something else than Mbed TLS (e.g. [wolfSSL](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/75828)).

 I know that there is (will be) a clean separation between mbedtls and PSA-Crypto, but at the moment this is not yet true and module/mbedtls covers both mbedtls and PSA-Crypto.

The problem I'm seeing is not that the subsystem is using PSA-Crypto (and yes this can be changed to wolfSSL, ...), the problem is that the subsystem is **used by** PSA-Crypto for key storage and this might be out of control of zephyr.

Implementing PSA Secure Storage as part of module/mbedtls would still allow secure storage to be used by zephyr applications but it would need to follow the "rules" set by the configuration of PSA-Crypto (e.g. these are the id's that are allowed to be used) and any API changes would be handled by changes to module/mbedtls without influencing a zephyr subsystem.

@carlescufi, what is your opinion on adding an externally defined API as a subsystem ?

Are you talking about PSA when saying "externally defined API"? If so, there was a decision in the security working group to use PSA as the standard crypto API for Zephyr.

author: carlescufi

body:
Hi @Laczen 

> > > can this be a subsystem
> > 
> > 
> > Why couldn't it?
> > > (no limitations on id etc)
> > 
> > 
> > I don't see what you're talking about? There are no such limitations.
> 
> Please correct me if I'm wrong: The proposed subsystem is also used directly by PSA-Crypto/MBEDTLS to store keys. If it is zephyr that defines what PSA-Crypto should use as id to store keys it is OK to use it as a subsystem, if OTOH it is PSA-Crypto that defines what is used as id to store it should be part of module/mbedtls (that includes PSA-Crypto)
> 
> It is also not a good idea from maintaining point of view to implement an externally defined API as a subsystem.
> 
> > > Shouldn't this be part of modules/mbedtls?
> > 
> > 
> > No, for at least the following reasons:
> > 
> > * PSA Secure Storage is not the same thing as PSA Crypto.
> > * And it's completely separate from Mbed TLS. It's not part of nor depends on Mbed TLS specifically in any way. It just happens to be using PSA Crypto (which could be provided by something else than Mbed TLS) for the AEAD operations in the base implementation, but that's an implementation detail.
> > * In fact, PSA Secure Storage is separate from Mbed TLS to the point where it could be used without Mbed TLS, because even if using the PSA Crypto API it could be implemented by something else than Mbed TLS (e.g. [wolfSSL](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/75828)).
> 
> I know that there is (will be) a clean separation between mbedtls and PSA-Crypto, but at the moment this is not yet true and module/mbedtls covers both mbedtls and PSA-Crypto.
> 
> The problem I'm seeing is not that the subsystem is using PSA-Crypto (and yes this can be changed to wolfSSL, ...), the problem is that the subsystem is **used by** PSA-Crypto for key storage and this might be out of control of zephyr.

The usage is out of control ? Zephyr is implementing a well defined interface for that, as long as we do it properly (respecting all requirements) we should be good.
> 
> Implementing PSA Secure Storage as part of module/mbedtls would still allow secure storage to be used by zephyr applications but it would need to follow the "rules" set by the configuration of PSA-Crypto (e.g. these are the id's that are allowed to be used) and any API changes would be handled by changes to module/mbedtls without influencing a zephyr subsystem.

Another PSA Crypto implementation may require PSA Secure Storage. If the PSA Crypto "somehow" brings its own PSA secure storage we can simply disable it. The interface for the application is still the same.

> 
> @carlescufi, what is your opinion on adding an externally defined API as a subsystem ?

We are already doing it for crypto. Using something that is established increase portability. For example, if ones is already using these features with TF-M, changing to a target without TF-M won't require changes.
author: ceolin

body:
Hi @ceolin,

> 
> The usage is out of control ? Zephyr is implementing a well defined interface for that, as long as we do it properly (respecting all requirements) we should be good.
>

The problem is the requirements are unclear and they might change in future. However we can avoid this, see further on.
 
> > @carlescufi, what is your opinion on adding an externally defined API as a subsystem ?
> 
> We are already doing it for crypto. Using something that is established increase portability. For example, if ones is already using these features with TF-M, changing to a target without TF-M won't require changes.

I should have been more carefull in the wording: it should be read as: "What is your opinion on implementing an externally defined API as a subsystem". Are we already doing this for crypto, we are certainly using an externally defined api inside subsystems, but is an implementation done as a subsystem?

When we add an external library to zephyr we are forking this external library and adding some glue logic to the fork to allow use of zephyr drivers/subsystems when required. PSA-Crypto needs some glue logic in order to use zephyr for persistent storage of keys (and mbedtls is also using this for storage of other items). This glue logic would implement `psa_its_get(), ...`. In TF-M this this glue logic is not needed because PSA-Crypto can use the TF-M provided implementations.

Now the next step is we would like to "use" the API for securely storing application items. It is not possible to use all id's because some of them might already be defined by PSA-Crypto glue logic or the TF-M implementation. We can "import" the externally defined ranges, but they might change. An alternative would be to let the module define what range we can use, IMHO this would be the simplest: let TF-M or the glue logic define what id's can be used by a zephyr subsystem for secure storage (e.g. reserve a start id and range for application storage). The zephyr subsystem could then "use" (not implement) the TF-M or PSA-Crypto glue logic to provide the secure storage.

> this basically does what I commented on in [#62649 (comment)](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/62649#issuecomment-1757608037), correct?

Yes, correct. This change modifies the scheduler and queue management. Instead of using `LifoQueue`, it now uses `deque` and `dict` (registered with a `BaseManager` to be shared between multiple processes).
* `dict` is used for `done` instances to quickly check if the processing of required testinstances is finished.
* `deque` is used for `pipeline` instances to allow postponing the processing of a task (re-adding the task to the front of the queue) if the required instances have not been processed yet.

body:
Great and long awaited change.

About the board finder introduction, this raises one point IMO:

The supported features listed in each board reflect the current default configuration of the board (ie current set of enabled nodes in the dts file), but it doesn't reflect the full capabilities of a given board (which includes the available nodes that are not yet enabled), but that user can however need in his application.

So, along with the board finder addition, I'd propose to update `boards/index.rst` with a note along those lines:
"Following boards capabilities reflect current default boards configurations which might not reflect the full set of capabilities (which can be found in SoC dtsi description)"

Aim is to minimize confusion at reader side between:
- the features that are just not enabled as part of the default configuration (but which they'll be able to use as part of their application configuration)
and
- the features that are not yet implemented

body:
Thanks, @erwango!

FWIW the more I think about it the more I lean towards introducing this in two stages:
- Introduce basic board "lister", that does not look at hw capabilities and really just lists boards / their pictures / ram-rom as per yaml files. See https://builds.zephyrproject.io/zephyr/pr/79160/docs/boards/index.html. Same UI except that the hw capabilities are not there yet. 
- Introduce more advanced "finder" leveraging capabilities deduced from DTS. 

> About the board finder introduction, this raises one point IMO:
> 
> The supported features listed in each board reflect the current default configuration of the board  [...]

Yep, I am actually pointing this out in my initial comment :)

> The features enabled out-of-the-box (DT nodes with status="okay") for a Hello World scenario might not reflect all the actually supported features of a board, as some might be disabled by default and only enabled when needed through overlays. We might need to either add a "disclaimer" to the generated list to set expectations, or find a way to generate the list based on the full set of DT nodes that could be enabled (i.e. instead of looking at okay nodes, looking at all nodes granted they have a matching compatible?).

To expand on this, and to you point about wording this as "... which can be found in SoC dtsi description ..." I wonder if the heuristic could be:
- for all "okay" nodes: consider the feature to be supported, period.
- for all disabled nodes *but* with a matching compatible in-tree, show the feature as "supported maybe" granted there is a matching compatible. This would be a good indicator that the feature is likely there for there is a driver for this node, and is only an overlay away from being available to the user.

But in any case, yes, a disclaimer should be there to set the expectations, since the system will never be 100% perfect and we don't want folks to assume something is not there when it is, and the other way around.

body:
> But after a discussion on discord, the question was posed if `Kconfig` symbols for tooling is desired. The argument being that tooling should not modify the binary result, and `Kconfig` symbols are intended for SW feature enablement/configuration. See [CodeChecker SCA configuration](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/sca/codechecker.html#configuring-codechecker) for comparison.
> 
> I'm not opposed to this but wanted to see what others think. CC @henrikbrixandersen @tejlmand

I'm seeing pros / cons on both a CMake cache variable vs Kconfig approach.

A big pro on Kconfig is that we have good tools for browsing and organizing settings, so that it becomes clear what settings are available. Also Kconfig provides support for `depends on` and `select`.
Also all Kconfigs has help text and thereby becomes visible in the docs.

CMake cache variables are often added with no documentation, and we lack a good overview.
This means that a given setting easily becomes hidden / secret knowledge.

This was initially my preference for Kconfig.

An alternative could be to design a principle around CMake's option feature, and adopt this principle to all SCA tools and elsewhere where it make sense. The each SCA tool can provide a `option.cmake` file and allow users to overwrite such file using:
`-D<SCA_NAME>_CONF_FILE=<alternate-conf>` while at the same time allow adjusting just individual settings.

Such approach, if documented properly, will have the benefit of:
- a single `options.cmake` file per SCA tool, which can be adjusted by the user.
- `options.cmake` provides information about valid tool settings.
- `options.cmake` can later be processed by doc-build, and thereby give the benefit we have from Kconfig.
- `option()` supports [CMakeDependentOption](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/CMakeDependentOption.html#module:CMakeDependentOption) which does provide some dependency support and thereby a little of benefit offered by Kconfig. This will most likely be sufficient to cover the needs of SCA tools.

Perhaps this is a better long term approach which keeps tools separated from actual sw configuration.

> A big pro on Kconfig is that we have good tools for browsing and organizing settings, so that it becomes clear what settings are available. Also Kconfig provides support for `depends on` and `select`. Also all Kconfigs has help text and thereby becomes visible in the docs.
> 
> CMake cache variables are often added with no documentation, and we lack a good overview. This means that a given setting easily becomes hidden / secret knowledge.
> 
> This was initially my preference for Kconfig.
> 
> An alternative could be to design a principle around CMake's option feature, and adopt this principle to all SCA tools and elsewhere where it make sense. The each SCA tool can provide a `option.cmake` file and allow users to overwrite such file using: `-D<SCA_NAME>_CONF_FILE=<alternate-conf>` while at the same time allow adjusting just individual settings.
> 
> Such approach, if documented properly, will have the benefit of:
> 
>     * a single `options.cmake` file per SCA tool, which can be adjusted by the user.
> 
>     * `options.cmake` provides information about valid tool settings.
> 
>     * `options.cmake` can later be processed by doc-build, and thereby give the benefit we have from Kconfig.
> 
>     * `option()` supports [CMakeDependentOption](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/CMakeDependentOption.html#module:CMakeDependentOption) which does provide some dependency support and thereby a little of benefit offered by Kconfig. This will most likely be sufficient to cover the needs of SCA tools.
> 
> 
> Perhaps this is a better long term approach which keeps tools separated from actual sw configuration.

I completely agree with your pros for the Kconfig approach instead of the CMake cache variables. The first draft of this PR was implemented
with the CMake chache variables and that was very confusing and felt very hidden and complicated to use for others because the tool has many configuration options with different report, report outputs and analysis. That's why I prefer the Kconfig options because of the documentation aspect. I also understand the argument that kconfig should only be used for sw feature configuration.

Two questions arise for me at this point:
- How do we find a solution to the fundamental problem of how SCA tools should be configured? ( e.g Kconfig, Cmake cache and cmake options) And should this perhaps be discussed in a larger context than this PR?

- How can we bring this PR to a conclusion? Because this PR should be merged before the 4.0 release, because the Safety WG / Committees has work planned which is based on this integration. Of course when the point is solved with the additional configuration and the cmake call instead of the west call.

I also have the feeling that we have gone round in circles because the Cmake Cache variable variant is preferred again, which was already implemented at the beginning.

author: pdgendt

body:
> Not really, I now allow to pass positional arguments as the unknown arguments to pip install, which I don't think would work to also pass the projects. For example:
> ```
> $ west packages -p zephyr pip --install --upgrade
> ```

Fair point, I haven't noticed that you were passing positional arguments to the native tool.
Have you considered aligning arguments to the native tool (pip) to follow same semantics as `west build` ?

For `west build` then the positional argument is the source dir, and arguments after a `--` are passed as-is to the underlying tool.
In the `west build` that is CMake.

From `west help build`:
> ```
> usage: west build [-h] [-b BOARD[@REV]]] [-d BUILD_DIR]
>           ...
>           [source_dir] -- [cmake_opt [cmake_opt ...]]
>
> Convenience wrapper for building Zephyr applications.
> 
> ...
> positional arguments:
>       source_dir            application source directory
>       cmake_opt             extra options to pass to cmake; implies -c
>                             (these must come after "--" as shown above)
> ```

One benefit of that is that it makes it clearer what is passed to underlying tool (pip) and what is processed by the extension command.

Like:
```
$ west packages pip [project ...] -- [pip_opt [pip_opt ...]]
```

Note, your proposal with using `-p <project> pip [pip_opt]` is also acceptable.

body:
> 
> how are such combos possible?
> 
> suite: fail case: not run suite: pass case: not run suite: not run: case: skip suite: error case: not run

Current implementation of Twister does not allow for such combinations. Mainly because the runnability is decided on a per-Suite level and runnability is the deciding factor for the NOTRUN status. It is not, however, theoretically impossible - if we ever check runnability for a singular Case, those could be proper combinations.

It would require significant Twister changes which are not planned, however, so I'll mark them as not proper.

body:
thanks for your comments @marc-hb .
They always provides good feedback.

Let me give my response on how I see then naming and how this feature could be developing / where I see its boundaries.

> > I'm not convinced that "requirements" or "dependencies" would be better. The intention is to make it easier for users and module owners to list or install packages from different package managers.
>
> I think the more important "design" question behind the name is: is this new command intended only for requirements/dependencies? Or will it expand to other, non-required packages in the future? 

I think packages is a broad enough term to avoid tying it to pip itself but allow for other managers in future if we consider it a need.
A little more on this boundary below.

As for the name `requirement-files` in the `pip` section, then I think the change from tag name `requirements` to `requirement-files` makes the relation to the pip feature `requirements file` https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/reference/requirements-file-format/ clearer.
Thus aligning the name in the `pip` section of the yaml makes it more self explanatory what this is about in the `pip` world.

Se `requirement-files` in this context is not Zephyr requirements but the pip feature and the file type passed to pip.

> I mean it all looks like this is ready to turn into a full-featured "meta" package manager but without actually saying it. A small, convenience, innocent PR just getting... the foot in the door ;-)

True, this could be a risk.
I would put the boundary for the tools Zephyr requires, which is stated in the getting started:
https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/getting_started/index.html#getting-started-guide

There we refer to `pip` https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/getting_started/index.html#get-zephyr-and-install-python-dependencies.
If using this logic, then other package managers we could consider to support would be: `apt` (Ubuntu), `brew` (MacOS), `chocolatey` (Windows) as those are mentioned in [Install dependencies](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/getting_started/index.html#install-dependencies).
But it requires someone with a desire to add / implement support for those.

Personally I don't think the gain is large enough as those other tools are not as dynamically added / updated / removed as the pip packages. Also the OS'es themselves are having good native tools to handle updates. 

I believe this is aligned with what I wrote earlier: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/78610#pullrequestreview-2312682185
I'm not against a west extension command for handling this, but I was against placing this in the manifest.

Furthermore I believe this PR to be a good step in a direction which would allow us to easier cleanup the Zephyr `requirements-extra.txt` and move packages like `protobuf` to the Zephyr module  which actually has this requirement.

- it enforces Python 3.10+ recommended practices for type hinting (I mean `ruff check` reports Python 3.9 type hinting as compliance errors): e.g. *before* you could not subscript `dict`, and have to use `typing.Dict`, but starting with Python 3.10, IIRC, you shall subscript `dict` and `typing.Dict` is deprecated, `Optional[T]` is deprecated in favor of `T | None` (which I honestly find less intuitive depending on the context), etc 
- it enforces a  rigid imports organization
- it enforces a rigid formatting (incompatible with the `black` configuration I used)

My concern is not that `ruff` may be a little opinionated (quoting Jens Gustedt in modern C, "Coding style is not a question of taste but of culture."), but that passing the CI will now require a considerable (and unexpected) amount of work: the whole DTSh codebase must be reviewed.

This kind of awkward situation happens when rules need to be applied retrospectively to a large code base. I'm not sure what to do at this point, or how to approach this issue.

Any idea is more than welcome.

Thanks.

You can create an exludes file, as was done with the zephyr codebase itself.

```shell
cd scripts/dts/dtsh
echo 'extend = "../../../.ruff.toml"' > .ruff.toml
ruff check --output-format=json | ../../../scripts/ruff/gen_lint_exclude.py >> .ruff.toml
ruff format --check | ../../../scripts/ruff/gen_format_exclude.py >> .ruff.toml
```

The problem is not that existing code doesn't follow our coding guidelines, it's that the guidelines give quite a lot of freedom for how compliant code may look like, i.e. you could have two quite different looking pieces of code, yet both be compliant with the guidelines. There are many aspects of coding style that the guidelines don't take any stance to - take for example variable naming: we have many places using `int err;` for int-type error variables and many others using `int ret;`. body:
This is great—it really is—and I will provide feedback on the suggested additions that I don't see any reason not to include.
What this doesn't address (not that I have an obvious solution to this) is the double standard that can be, and I'm pretty sure will still be, observed where "experienced" maintainers/contributors can get away just fine with sometimes really large PRs that touch multiple areas (sometimes for good reason, as maybe said PRs are already as small as can be, but certainly not always), making it less than obvious to newcomers why they would be doing anything wrong after all given what they see on other PRs. You took two PRs touching boards/SoCs and this is certainly an area where large PRs from vendor themselves tend to not necessarily be frown upon. In fact—and not saying this is done intentionally—they sometimes pack so much that the somewhat opposite problem arises: PR gets merged easy-peasy, but contains changes that *should* have actually been submitted separately and would have had a different assignee, except they didn't see the PR in time...

To put it differently, I find it unfair to tell contributors something along the lines of "RTFM wrt how to 'properly' contribute" when their natural tendency will always be to use common sense and what they observe as being some kind of norm. "Do as we say, not as you see...".

Am I making sense? Thoughts?
author: kartben

body:
I totally get what you mean and I think what you call "double standards" and "unfair", others would call it... "trust"?

Contributors with a good track record tend to get less scrutiny whereas brand new people rarely get any slack. I don't think this is intrinsically wrong because the risk level is actually different and trusting old timers reduces the total review workload which is always, always a problem[*]. But there is a very fine balance and it can definitely go too far sometimes.


[*] code reviews are like everything else in QA: everyone wants quality but no one wants to pay for it.

> What this doesn't address (not that I have an obvious solution to this)

Me neither - I don't think there is any easy way to solve this besides maintainers trying to keep an eye on their own biases and helping each other. This is not an exact science.

If anything at all, I hope this PR only helps mitigate such "unfairness" by clarifying a guideline that should apply to all?


BTW there is a common misconception that newcomers cannot review code. It is true that new reviewers cannot be as thorough but they can still be very useful:
- new eyes can help spot tribal knowledge
- they can still find issues and lower the total review workload
- great way to learn and progress
- last but not least: only way to notice and draw attention to such "double standards"!


> where large PRs from vendor themselves tend to not necessarily be frown upon.

This is a bit of a special case because... who cares if vendors break ONLY their own products? Small exaggeration to get the point across, it's getting late. You see what I mean.

> but contains changes that should have actually been submitted separately and would have had a different assignee, except they didn't see the PR in time...

Now _that_ is 100% wrong and should be flagged - and probably reverted temporarily!


> making it less than obvious to newcomers why they would be doing anything wrong after all given what they see on other PRs. 

What I'm trying to reinforce in this PR is: smaller PRs are also in the interest of _the submitter_ themselves. Even experienced people who managed to fly quickly "under the radar" don't want to end up wasting time post merge dealing with regressions, drama and reverts. Do they?

Hi @kartben,

Yes, great, that might be helpful.
 
> One piece of feedback from my side is that this might need to be split across several PRs.

I agree that the size of this PR is a concern (@pdgendt also seemed a little discouraged).

I tried to soften the effort required by organizing the changes into successive commits, each dedicated to a single task, and depending only on the previous ones. But, in the end, 36 commits proved no less overwhelming than 115 files ;-)

What kind of division into multiple PRs were you thinking of ?
One idea that comes to me would be to dedicate a PR to what I call the model layer: this could help to review all DTSh uses (and interpretations) of the `edtlib` API without being confused by the whole thing.

I'm willing to dig deeper, but it seems to me that we should first agree on the type of integration (Zephyr main tree or external module/project), as it means different PRs anyway (and may be a different review process).


> Wouldn't it also be opportune to have this as a module? It can evolve/be maintained separate from zephyr itself that way.

Hi @pdgendt,

@decsny suggested a somewhat similar approach a few months ago, adding DTSh to Zephyr as an *optional module* [1].

I welcomed the idea, my only real concern was not figuring out how to install the missing Python requirements (`rich`, plus `gnureadline` on macOS) from there. This discussion ended here. 

Before answering you, I reconsidered this type of approach, and I am still undecided.

An optional module integrates with the Zephyr build system, which could give us some *hook* to install the missing Python requirements: it seems a ugly hack to me, and I'm not even sure DTSh would qualify (make sense) as a module. Besides, users having to go through the `west config manifest.project-filter` dance is not really an out-of-the-box experience.

*External tooling*, "software that assists the compilation, testing or simulation processes but in no case ends up being part of the code compiled and linked into the final image" [2] sounds interesting.

IIUC, we then have three options:

1. the `scripts/` folder in Zephyr main tree, e.g. `scripts/dts/dtsh` as in the current PR
2. a West project hosted within the zephyrproject-rtos GitHub organization
3. an optional West project hosted outside the zephyrproject-rtos GitHub organization  

The second option seems to me a good compromise to have DTSh both available OOTB, and *maintained separate from zephyr itself*.

If we choose this approach, my only remaining concerns will be:
- I still can't see how to install the `rich` and `gnureadline` Python dependencies from an external West project; I may be missing something obvious, any ideas are welcome
- less worrying, but still an issue for which I don't know a *clean* solution: adding the `edtlib` library to the Python system path with some (convoluted) `sys.path.append()` is okish when running the West command itself, but hardly scale to an external project that e.g. should be able to run its unit tests (what CI path would go from e.g. `zephyrproject-rtos/dtsh/tests/` to `zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/scripts/dts/python-devicetree/src/` ?)

To summarize my thoughts:

- I understand the size of the PR may be inappropriate for an integration into Zephyr main tree
- I'm fine with the idea of developing and maintaining DTSh as an external West project, preferably within the zephyrproject-rtos GitHub organization to make the tool available out-of-the-box (not optional) 

If we choose this option, we must make it clear as soon as possible: this will lead to different PRs and may imply some infrastructure/organizational setup. I will also really appreciate any help in working through the above concerns.

As I understand it, feature freeze for zephyr 4.1 is planned for mid-February: I'll do my best to respond to any feedback promptly.

Thanks.

[1] https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/contribute/external.html#integration-as-optional-modules
[2] https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/contribute/external.html#contributing-external-tooling

I'd prefer this as an optional module over in-tree functionally.

Rationale: it's self-contained, quite large, deals with another "tooling space" than the rest of the project - visualization of a standardized format (while also handling Zephyr-specific bindings, I know) - and doesn't have any in-tree dependents. 

Personally, a visualization tool like this does not fit into my workflow, and I would thus not use it (I've tried it, it's nice, just not for me). While I am (of course) biased after working with devicetree for so many years, I can't help thinking newcomers would be better off actually reading (generated) DTS source files to understand the underlying mechanisms instead of putting a whole different view on top of it, somewhat mystifying the format even further.
author: henrikbrixandersen

body:
@henrikbrixandersen , thank you for these interesting comments. 

> I'd prefer this as an optional module over in-tree functionally.

Indeed, this appears to be the most acceptable approach now.

> Rationale: it's self-contained, quite large, deals with another "tooling space" than the rest of the project - visualization of a standardized format (while also handling Zephyr-specific bindings, I know) - and doesn't have any in-tree dependents.

DTSh does have dependencies in Zephyr main tree, though: the Python devicetree library (aka edtlib).
This is an issue I don't really know how to address properly.

> Personally, a visualization tool like this does not fit into my workflow, and I would thus not use it (I've tried it, it's nice, just not for me). While I am (of course) biased after working with devicetree for so many years, I can't help thinking newcomers would be better off actually reading (generated) DTS source files to understand the underlying mechanisms 

This was indeed my approach as a newcomer: accompany the reading of the documentation with that of actual DTS files, starting from `build/zephyr/zephyr.dts`.

I then felt that a few conveniences might speed up my understanding:
- not having to manually lookup (and open) the binding files where things are actually *described*      
- being able to see a devicetree as a tree
- being able to query a devicetree with a slightly more semantic interface than a text search 

Now, looking back, I think the main interest for beginners is how DTSh integrates the DTS with its bindings, e.g.:

```
/
> tree /soc/flash-controller@4001e000 -l
                             Description                                                          
                             ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
flash-controller@4001e000    Nordic NVMC (Non-Volatile Memory Controller) [↗]                     
└── flash@0                  Flash node [↗]                                                       
    └── partitions           This binding is used to describe fixed partitions of a flash (or… [↗]
        ├── partition@0      Each child node of the fixed-partitions node represents… [↗]         
        ├── partition@c000   Each child node of the fixed-partitions node represents… [↗]         
        ├── partition@83000  Each child node of the fixed-partitions node represents… [↗]         
        └── partition@f8000  Each child node of the fixed-partitions node represents… [↗]         
```

Opening `nordic,nrf52-flash-controller.yaml`, `soc-nv-flash.yaml`, or `fixed-partitions.yaml` in your favorite text editor is then as simple as *clicking* the corresponding `[↗]`.

This is just an example, you get the idea: the available human-readable information is merged with the DTS and, perhaps more importantly, all related files are one *click* away (YAML binding files, but also the board's DTS and SVD files, etc). I think having these resources at hand can be really helpful for newcomers, and support their curiosity. Besides, I still often find more convenient to follow these links than to browse the file system when I'm looking for the specification of a compatible string or property.

The ability to export command output to different formats can also save time when illustrating teaching materials or taking notes.

> instead of putting a whole different view on top of it, somewhat mystifying the format even further.

This is a concern I first thought about when wondering if DTSh might be useful to others, and then again when I wrote its documentation.

I think that, for Zephyr/Devicetree newcomers who are comfortable with Unix-like system shells, `ls`, `tree` and `find` should sound obvious, without actually adding an abstraction layer on top of the devicetree: the hierarchical file-system metaphor seamlessly applies to DT paths, and these commands should behave *as expected* and be sufficiently self-described (`-h` and detailed auto-completion). IMO, these newcomers will have no difficulty using DTSh for simple things like the above example, without feeling too much the kind of mystification that you fear.

But I agree it should not be recommended for Zephyr/Devicetree beginners who are also not familiar with Unix-like shells: reading Zephyr documentation and the Devicetree Specification will be much more beneficial than spending the same time reading DTSh's user guide or memorizing its keybindings.
I would happily insert this warning at the top of the DTSh module installation instructions ;-)

Architecture WG:

- This effort began when @dottspina was trying to learn Devicetree and found that browsing the files without the actual bindings to complete the info, there was just not enough there to give a real view of it
- A full demo of the shell is performed by @dottspina, including showing devices, buses, with a lot of powerful command-line formulas
- @henrikbrixandersen suggests to have this as a separate package, especially because changing anything in the bindings or Devicetree handling in general would require fixing DTsh as well, which is an unreasonable amount of burden on developers that want to change things in how Zephyr uses Devicetree
- @bjarki-andreasen agrees with the comment just above
- @dottspina describes how this was originally planned to be part of the main zephyr tree, but after it was decided against due to the maintenance and size concerns
- The integration options could be as follows:
   - Place all the dtsh python code in a repo that is then pulled by `west` as an optional module. The `python-devicetree` package in that case could be imported directly from `zephyr/scripts/dts/python-devicetree` because a Zephyr module always has the zephyr tree on disk. Additionally, then the west command would be contained in the dtsh module repo. This doesn't really solve the maintenance concern if we consider optional modules to have to be always in sync with the rest of the forest and with zephyr in particular
   - Publish a new PyPi package, `dtsh`, which relies on a published `python-devicetree`. Then we could have a west command in the the main tree, `zephyr/scripts/west_commands` which requires `dtsh` as a Python package. We could even add `dtsh` to our `requirements.txt`. This approach however requires the `python-devicetree` maintainer (ping @mbolivar) to commit to publishing new versions to PyPi regularly. It also requires deciding whether zephyr itself should transition from using the in-tree copy or move to the Python package

body:
@carlescufi, thank you for posting the minutes of the meeting here.

Yes, we are now considering only two approaches:
- integrate DTSh as an optional module that defines and implements the new West extension
- an in-tree new West extension, DTSh itself being added to Zephyr's extra Python requirements

For both options, the bulk of DTSh is maintained (developed, tested, documented, merged) within a dedicated repo.

Below are the main differences I see, and what might be my personal choice.

I'll update the RFC and initiate the corresponding new PRs as soon as we have decided on this.

**Optional module**

In-tree changes are minimal:

- `submanifests/optional.yaml`: module definition, maintenance is mostly upgrading the module's `revision:` for each new Zephyr release
- `doc/develop/west/zephyr-cmds.rst`: West command documentation and installation instructions, should only rarely need updates (e.g. when `west dtsh` options change)

But not fully OOTB (like any optional Zephyr module): 
- the new West extension is not discoverable: won't appear in `west -h` before the user installs the module
- additional manual steps are needed to enable the module and install its dependencies (and optionally integrate with West commands auto-completion)

**In-tree West command**

In-tree changes include:

- `scripts/west-commands.yml` (and `scripts/west_commands/completion/*`): definition of the new West extension, needs little maintenance
- `scripts/west_commands/dtshell.py`: implementation of the West extension, simple wrapper (65 LOC) that inserts the in-tree `devicetree` package into the Python system path and starts DTSh; low maintenance for which I can volunteer
- `scripts/requirements-extra.txt`: the `dtsh` PyPI package is a new extra Python requirement, maintenance is upgrading the required version of DTSh for each new Zephyr release 
- `doc/develop/west/zephyr-cmds.rst`: West command documentation 

User experience:

- OOTB for those wishing to discover DTSh: no additional manual installation steps, integrated with West help and auto-completion
- a typical Zephyr installation (as of the Getting started Guide) will pull DTSh and its dependencies ([rich](https://github.com/Textualize/rich), plus [gnureadline](https://pypi.org/project/gnureadline/) on macOS) from PyPI: adding such requirements may need some special kind of approval

**Pros and Cons**

An optional module is a more conservative (less intrusive) approach, while an in-tree West extension provides a simpler user experience.

| Approach               | *Pros*                                  | *Cons*                             |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Optional module        | minimal in-tree changes and endorsement | less OOTB than we first thought    |
| In-tree West extension | OOTB user experience                    | adds DTSh to Zephyr's requirements |

I personally don't have a strong preference: if adding DTSh to `zephyr/scripts/requirements-extra.txt` is acceptable, which I'm not convinced of, let's go for an OOTB user experience, otherwise an optional module will be just fine.

Thanks.

body:
> I hope there is some way we can get this into CI, just to reduce the possibility of regressions for IAR users.
> 

There is nothing practical stopping us. It has been a goal of IAR all along. However we have identified the following issues:
* CI resources/pipeline runtime has been a worry of the community.
* Tuning warning levels and tests to avoid making PRs overly difficult. IAR toolchain is stricter in many ways, but hopefully this will be seen as increasing code quality and standards compliance.
* Some way for PR makers to be able to get a hold of our tools/licenses IF something goes wrong in CI, so they can test locally. I could imagine this being very frustrating.
* In practice including the toolchain zip in CI and adding a github secret with a license key. I don't know exactly how to make this happen, but I wouldn't imagine it being particularly difficult.

Currently we run in-house pipelines that will point to main as soon as we get merged, but these will by nature be reactive.
We are experimenting with running in-house jobs on PRs, but that is not being run consistently right now.

body:
> Some quick notes after a quick and incomplete read. The big worry here is performance: this is adding two function calls and a bunch of tests to the context switch path for one somewhat obscure feature, and that's sort of a non-starter. At the very least, this should emit code that does an absolute minimum of work (e.g. just check a boolean on the thread struct) before returning into the main switch path. Calling out into a separate stack frame is spending a ton of cycles we can't spare.

Thank you  for your brief review, I have corrected most of the requests. FWIW, the functions called in the context switch are there to just start/stop the CBS timer if the thread belongs to a CBS.  There is nothing else.

By the way, the absolute worst measured overheads in the XIAO ESP32C3 (RISC-V, single-core, 160MHz) were of 128 clock cycles for switching in and 139 clock cycles for switching out. These translate to a period in the magnitude of _nanoseconds_. The averages were (obviously) lower: 110.92 and 90.94 clock cycles, respectively. Does that looks inadmissible?

> Does the problem really require tracking budget across cooperative switches anyway? Can't you do this with a timer a-la timeslicing? Seems like this is taking a ton of overhead for what would normally seem like a fairly coarse decision. Thread deadlines are usually on the order of a tick, not a cycle.

Yes it does. If thread X preempts CBS Y, the CBS needs a way of re-starting its budget timer when thread X finishes and it is allowed to resume execution. I couldn't make that work without including these functions in k_swap.

body:
> @kartben how would this feature support board revisions were the features may be different between revisions?

The metadata is already correctly captured for each board target, and when using the Sphinx directive in a board's doc page you get as many tables as board targets, basically. Probably not ideal when there are lots of combinations of variants/revisions so I'm thinking a future iteration will perhaps use a tabulated view.

In the board search form however, it's the union of all the supported types of hardware features across all the variants/revisions of a board that's used to determine if a board matches a given query. I.e. if board X as variants v1 and v2 and only v2 has, say, a display, searching for a board that supports "display" will include board X in the results.

> does the general audience find it useful to have the dts binding information in the table? I'm asking because that information seems so specific. It always seemed to me that the board pages table of features was useful from a generic sense; ADC, UART, GPIO, etc...

I tend to agree - define "general audience" though :) While it might be noise for some people, it can also be a useful "shortcut" for folks doing the initial quality assessment of a given board/port, since having a link to the binding's doc page allows them to then be just one click away from looking at the source code of the driver. But yeah, not all audience types, probably. 

In the same vein, something that might be useful to some and noise to others would be to add a column listing the main Kconfig option(s) guarding the feature (see e.g. https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/raspberrypi/rpi_pico/doc/index.html#supported-features). We don't quite have the metadata at hand to infer that information just yet but I guess my point is, and probably related to the beginning of my reply re: tabulated view, the UI/UX of the Supported Features table shall be improved overtime, and will likely end up being somewhat configurable by the user so that they can hide/unhide things they typically care/don't care about.

Or maybe some similar custom status that indicates that as far as Devicetree is concerned the peripheral is properly configured, but there is some action needed from the user (ideally indicated as a comment on the node, I guess!) before they actually okay it for it e.g. requires a competing peripheral to be disabled first.
> 
> @kartben what is wrong with just using the presence of the node as indicative of support regardless of "Okay" or "disabled"?

@dleach02 
There are many boards in-tree built on a reasonably capable MCU but that just happen to have a form factor such that some peripherals are simply *not* usable, no matter how hard you try, for they're not physically exposed. Think e.g. this guy https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/ezurio/bl654_usb/doc/bl654_usb.html - it wouldn't make sense to say the "board" has QDEC support since it's not using it internally, let alone exposing pins enabling users to use it. 

> Optionally, but it would make things event more complex, we can instantiate 2 kind of searches [...]

I actually like that idea. I think we would still want the table of supported features to limit itself to only what's actually "okay", but for search, yeah, the users could check a "Show SoC peripherals" checkbox (*un*checked by default) or something. Checking the box would remove the filtering on okay nodes to instead take into account *all* nodes.

Users would then have a rough idea of things that they *may* be able to enable on a given board and what the underlying SoC has to offer (but doesn't necessarily *support* btw: the presence of a matching "compatible" is no guarantee that the driver doesn't throw some kind of `#error SoC family not yet supported`)

Copyright The Zephyr Project Contributors

> Although this might place some burden on developers, I think it's acceptable [...]

Integration into the Zephyr main tree was the initial intent of this RFC:
- the idea was an out-of-the-box user experience (no additional installation or configuration steps), possible only with this approach
- as you pointed out, this allows `dtsh` to consistently (both at run-time and for CI) depend on and import the `devicetree` package provided by the Zephyr version *it comes with*, like do the West commands and other scripts that depend on `edtlib`
- having the devicetree shell in `zephyr/scripts/dts/dtsh`, next to `python-devicetree` with which it's so closely coupled, felt natural; it seemed to me that this *proximity* could also prove beneficial to the evolution of the `edtlib` API (of which dtsh is an extensive client)

But the size of the resulting PR (source code, unit tests, West command, documentation) somewhat discouraged reviewers, and worried maintainers: AFAICT, there was then some kind of consensus for an *out-of-tree* approach, e.g. an optional module, and we triaged the acceptable options in an Architecture WG meeting (@carlescufi posted the relevant minutes [here](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/59863#issuecomment-2634546360)).

Lastly, it was suggested "to publish a pypi package of dtsh so users could simply install it from there":
- this is how dtsh is distributed for around two years ;-)
- but ugly integration with `edtlib`, to the point where Zephyr users unknowingly rely on different versions, possibly incompatible at the DTS/bindings level, when they build applications and then run `dtsh`
- no integration at all with Zephyr, which is what this RFC is about

So, I'm glad to read now that integration into the Zephyr main tree might be acceptable, though a little confused ;-)  

I am more than willing to continue working on this RFC (e.g. restructure/split the PR, curate unit tests and add the CI bits, narrow the initial functional scope, etc), but what to actually do, and with what priority, highly depends on the approach we choose. If any (we can also decide to leave things as they are today, and simply close this RFC).

My *personal* preference would remain integrating dtsh into Zephyr main tree (most consistent and straight forward development process, OOTB user experience), if it ultimately turns out to be acceptable.
I'm also fine with *out-of-tree* options, IMO they're a bit more convoluted (I mean regarding the dependency of `dtsh` on `edtlib`), but arguably easier on reviewers and maintainers. 

However, I can't decide any of this for myself ;-)

Thanks.

body:
Hi Vdragon,

Thank you for your valuable feedback regarding the use of the auxdisplay
API. I understand the merits of leveraging a more generalized display
framework like auxdisplay, especially for managing simple displays like
7-segment displays.

However, in this particular case, I opted to use the tm1637 driver because
it is specifically designed for the TM1637 7-segment display module, which
is the hardware I am working with. The tm1637 driver provides low-level
control tailored to this hardware, ensuring a more direct and optimized
implementation. This choice allows me to manage the display more
efficiently without the need for the additional abstraction layers that
auxdisplay would introduce.

While auxdisplay could be a viable alternative for general display
handling, it is more suited for displays that require a higher level of
abstraction and flexibility, like character LCDs or more complex display
modules. For this simple use case involving a 7-segment display, I believe
that the tm1637 driver simplifies the implementation and avoids
overengineering.

That said, I completely understand the desire for consistency within the
Zephyr ecosystem, and I’m open to exploring how we might integrate tm1637
functionality into the auxdisplay API to better align with Zephyr's broader
display handling framework. If this integration helps maintain consistency
without compromising on performance, I'd be happy to discuss it further.

I believe both approaches have their merits, and I appreciate your insight
on this matter. I’m looking forward to your thoughts and any further
suggestions you might have!

Best regards,
Tinu K Cheriya

> the main question now is whether we really need a new ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT (atfe)

It's not an easy question...

On one hand this new toolchain is just a variant of LLVM and thus it make sense to use it through the `llvm` way. 
But on the other hand, ARM is communicating officially on it as their _next generation toolchain_ and release it as a standalone product (like their GNU ARM version). 

I don't know if we have some knowledge on how many Zephyr users use a custom toolchain, or at least know that they could use another toolchain.
My guess is that most of the users won't take the time to understand the whole mechanism behind Zephyr's llvm toolchain and will just look for the support of "ATfE" on Zephyr's website.

So I would tend to say that Zephyr should show up that it supports ATfE.

body:
@AlexFabre @tejlmand should this topic be brought up at the [Toolchain WG meeting](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/wiki/Toolchain-Working-Group)? One of the reasons I mention it is that we still do have a `gnuarmemb` toolchain variant, which is pretty much the GCC equivalent of a potential `atfe` variant. Should we try to align and then perhaps remove `gnuarmemb`, or allow both?
Note however that `gnuarmemb` was added a long time ago, well before the current SDK architecture and before many of the changes to the build system that allow ATfE to work almost out of the box now. That's also why I wonder if we could replace `gunarmemb` with `cross-compile` instead.
author: carlescufi

body:
> One of the reasons I mention it is that we still do have a gnuarmemb toolchain variant, which is pretty much the GCC equivalent of a potential atfe variant. 

It is, and you can achieve the same by setting `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=cross-compile` and then set `CROSS_COMPILE=<path>/arm-none-eabi-` in environment, ref: https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/toolchains/other_x_compilers.html.

I actually considered back in time if this should be deprecated, but for the GNU ARM Embedded, then it means going from one setting, `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=gnuarmemb` to both `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT` and `CROSS_COMPILE`, not to mention the noise it will introduce.
Also for GNU, the C compiler and linker are invoked with the cross-compile prefix, for example `arm-none-eabi-gcc` /  `arm-none-eabi-ld` , unlike clang, which natively is a cross-compiler and is always named `clang` and just invoked with different target flags.

The same mess is found in `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=host`, which just uses `gcc` but for the system you're using, ref: https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/toolchains/host.html.
Again, LLVM/clang is much cleaner, as you just use `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=llvm`, also when compiling for the host.

So let's avoid the mess and mistakes from GNU when integrating LLVM.
As side-note, `xtools` was removed here: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/51332,  https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/51332.
One reason was that users can achieve exactly the same using `cross-compile`.

> Should we try to align and then perhaps remove gnuarmemb, or allow both?

I would prefer to cleanup the GNU handling, including `host`, question becomes how to handle the cross compile prefix without annoying users unnecessarily (as they are used to current `gnuarmemb` and `host`).

> IMHO this would be more logically readable as:
> 
> ```
>     return !__builtin_add_overflow(a->tv_sec, b->tv_sec, &a->tv_sec) &&
>            !__builtin_add_overflow(a->tv_nsec, b->tv_nsec, &a->tv_nsec) &&
>            timespec_normalize(a);

From my perspective, that is worse - there are 5 logical operations instead of 3.

> Yes, `__builtin_add_overflow()` returns true on error but that's in the name. 

I'm sort of thinking I would prefer to just append `_overflow`. To me, it's less useful to add multiple extra logical operations.

> Here we have `timespec_add()`.

Yeah, I could definitely rename that to `timespec_add_overflow()`. That would be in-line with all of the `math-extras.h` functions.

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/include/zephyr/sys/math_extras.h

> Next, I'm a little concerned by the optimization. This:
> 
> ```
>     int64_t sec = (ts->tv_nsec >= NSEC_PER_SEC) * (ts->tv_nsec / NSEC_PER_SEC) +
> +                 (ts->tv_nsec < 0) * DIV_ROUND_UP(-ts->tv_nsec, NSEC_PER_SEC);
> ```
> 
> That's potentially two divisions just for the purpose of avoiding a branch. On many architectures (if not most) a branch is still cheaper than a division, even more so if the division ends up in a library call given a 64-bit dividend.

Agreed.

What I initially had is only cheap on processors that have e.g. icache, dcache, HW divide, and only cheap compared to potential cache misses.

I would be happy to use `#ifdef CONFIG_SPEED_OPTIMIZATIONS` here, because you are right in pointing out that the usual optimization for Zephyr should be for size.

> And finally, you should add more values to your test case. In particular, tests with tv_nsec being `-NSEC_PER_SEC - 1`, `-2*NSEC_PER_SEC + 1`, `-2*NSEC_PER_SEC - 1`, etc. would provide more coverage.

body:
TL;DR; Option 3 for short term :+1: 

----------------

The long answer:

> @tejlmand So I didn't realize that shields were _always_ being processed, even when no -DSHIELD argument is passed, and the performance penalty is actually quite noticeable

Yes, the general rule is to always load the Zephyr CMake modules, the way it originated from the old boilerplate time.
At this time I would like not to depend module loading on CMake vars, but internally in the code execution of course depends on CMake settings, for example in a `foreach(s ${SHIELD})` loop, which will not execute when list is empty.

> From the documentation of the module it's not 100% clear to me whether it should or should not exit early if no SHIELD argument is given. Can you please provide your insights here? The options I see at this point:
> 
>     1. exit early when no SHIELD argument provided (but this might break the current contract, I dunno)

See above.
Although this will not solve the real problem but will move it from impacting all users to only impact shield users.
Sub-optimal solution imo.

> 
>     2. use list_shields.py to get the list of shields in CMake ; just like, I think, boards.cmake is doing
> 

Yes, and this I think is preferred solution.
Perhaps the `list_hardware.py` is the best place, because `list_boards.py` was kept mainly because of its HWMv1 and west integration. With HWMv1 support removed we can probably clean this up.
However such re-write / list_hardware extension will probably require a bit more work, especially if we want to avoid more python invocations.

>     3. revert this PR if 2., which I personally think might be the best fix, is not an acceptable solution.
> 

I think short term this solution is most viable.

>     4. optimize yaml.cmake performance? I'm sure it's kind of expected that it is slowish, but there might still be some low hanging fruits w.r.t making it faster.

The main reason for `yaml_load()` to be slow is because python is invoked on each yaml file as CMake natively doesn't support yaml.
So it's actually the Python invocation which slows us down.
This is also the reason why a `list_hardware` / `list_shields` will greatly improve spped as there will only be a single python invocation regardless of number of yaml files.
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/369f15d8c914d69d799ff7f8f3c091208f523926/cmake/modules/yaml.cmake#L236-L237

lets put things in prespective, I would not call this breakage, if we do, then we are stuck forever with what we have now, because someone will always be trailing behind using some old version of something. So, if we say we support 20.04 now  which comes with python 3.8, then the breakage was done long time ago when we moved to 3.10 as minimum required python... :-)

Yeah, probably we need to establish some guidelines and announce things a bug more clearly. Alsofigure out a plan for moving tooling to maintained and supported releases, this is not limited to python. 

We need to look at the chain of dependencies (distro/os -> python ) and figure out the timing and align this as much as possible with our SDK, CI and tooling and make sure we do not rely on some old version along the way that does not get security fixes and such, ie.. 

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4598fded-c860-4a1e-8523-adac2f904e15)


ubuntu 20.04 just stopped getting security fixes, why is this the recommended version in our docs until now is beyond me (thank you @kartben  for fixing this). And on top of that, it has python 3.8 which is EOLed.

Then there is python itself:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/33451354-878d-40a1-b1eb-8e54f50c8c96)

We can wait until next year and scrumble to get move to so some new version while 3.10 is being phased out or we can be proactive and get (force) developers ready.

body:
From the [Linux kernel coding style](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v4.10/process/coding-style.html#indentation):

"Tabs are 8 characters, and thus indentations are also 8 characters. There are heretic movements that try to make indentations 4 (or even 2!) characters deep, and that is akin to trying to define the value of PI to be 3."

> I'm not sure we really want to add node.js to the dependencies of that 

Why not? We already have the .NET runtime in the CI Docker image for Renode -- might as well include Node.js too while we are at it.

On a serious note, it would be nice if we could stick to only Python when possible; not because it is better than Node.js, but because it has been the main scripting language of choice by Zephyr. However, in this case, it would be unreasonable to ask `dts-linter` to be rewritten in Python, and the gains from having it in our toolbox would, as we have already seen in this PR, outweigh the losses from installing yet another runtime, which would be, at most, annoyance ...

> Having to pull in node.js is a bit of a concern for me as well, but I think it makes sense to bite the bullet and go for it ; this might actually unlock some interesting stuff for documentation as well, by allowing to start using mermaid.js which I've wanted to do for a long time.

TBH, I think modern TypeScript is a much better choice for complex scripting than Python (or rather, Python with dynamic typing and weird OOP syntax is a truly horrible language to work with in general); not to mention, it is a much more natural choice for Zephyr developers given that most of us are already familiar with C/C++.

Maybe, this could be a starting point for more TypeScript stuff in Zephyr ...

> Cool but we should probably decide now if this can stay on its own workflow or be part of check_compliance.py I'd prefer it to be part of check compliance and be skipped if node is not installed (just because installing it is one more step than the usual "apt-get install ..." and "pip install ..." that we already have in the getting started guide. No strong opinion though, but since this is going to block PR for users together with other linters I'd like to still be able to tell the users that they can use ONE script to check them all before uploading if they want to.

I agree that it would be good to have it be part of `check_compliance.py` and be skipped when Node.js is not installed with a warning.

Also, in general, we should try to minimise the number of CI workflows we have, for maintainability reasons.

GitHub has some known format for workflow outputs so that the annotations show up on the UI together with stuff like code review comments, this is documented [here](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-commands-for-github-actions#about-workflow-commands) apparently. body:
> In general the build system should deal with building software, not flashing, debugging, etc.
And why is it problematic to have the build command doing this kind of work ?

> Because it's too limited. As an example then west flash allows for passing extra arguments to the actual flash tool underneath.

I think the more "conceptual" reason is: the primary design goal of build systems is to manage _dependency graphs_ using a _declarative_ language. In other words, build systems are designed to optimize and figure out what _not to do_. For a build system, a huge success is doing nothing at all when the user asks "make all"!

But flashing and debugging is definitely not that: when users say "flash this" or "debug this", involving some dependency graph is probably the last thing they want.  "Flash this" should just flash this and nothing else: keep it simple. BTW #33425 looks like a great example and demonstration of not wanting any dependency graph involved there.

Theoretically, you could read back the image already flashed, compare it and realize you do not need to flash it again. But: 1. This would likely not save that much time. 2. It would never optimize anything in products where the image modifies itself 3. Users would not trust it anyway. Many developers already tend not to trust build systems and use "make clean" all the time.

Many developers are not familiar with declarative languages and logic and they [hate build systems](https://mesonbuild.com/Design-rationale.html) because they never "do as told" - by design.

Even worse: CMake (among other flaws) can be abused as some portable, imperative, "do as you are told" programming language. Until it can't. Super confusing. Whether you like plain Python or not, it's very hard to confuse readers with it.

Thanks @fabiobaltieri for the #93985 clean up.

> 
> Thanks!

Yes but you are talking only about the "user" type of developer, there is also the "contributor" developer and also the "maintainer" type of developer.  And if the latter two are having to do things like this all the time then it does not make it easier for them, if in general they hypothetically were to have to bend over backwards all the time to handhold unskilled users with tons of UX guardrail utilities.  It would get in the way of them doing their actual work on the actual features they are trying to work on. 

But like I said, it's fine if you want to put this under scripts/dts. But if I/other DT maintainer now have ownership of it and it breaks somehow unexpected in a non-trivial way, or turns out to have a ton of unexpected bugs that get reported about it, or it's not working as intended/expected by users, then my "maintenance strategy" will be to ping you to fix it. And if you don't/can't, then I will not have a problem to remove it if we don't want/can't deal with it and it just confuses people, since it is non-essential as only a visual dev helper utility.

With that said however, it is a good looking tool, I will approve it. But I think it's very important that people start taking maintenance definitions/responsibilities seriously in this project.  Because having overloaded/unrespected maintainers/areas will lead to a bad UX for both contributors and users for a variety of reasons. Every single PR that gets submitted people should be asking the question either out loud or to themself , who is going to maintain this, and if the answer isn't obvious to someone, it needs to be figured out.  Maintenance strategy design is a core aspect of software engineering.
