body:
During development, we often switch between different targets. When working with multiple boards or configurations, it’s helpful to keep builds separate and do not remove them in order to save build time by not having to rebuild projects again from scratch with `--pristine` (even if it is only few seconds). Users especially save time, if also some code generation is done in the cmake configure step.

I think this practice is also common in the Embedded Linux world as well, where developers have build directories for different setups, especially when working with cmake.

To achieve unique build directories, **`build.dir-fmt`** config is already available what we use to ensure uniqueness per board and per project.

## Example `.west.config`

```ini
[build]
# Make builds unique per board per source directory
# Note: {app} alone is not sufficient since it’s only the basename of the project
# and there may be multiple directories with the same name
dir-fmt = build-output/{board}/{source_dir_common}

# Create some symlinks to simplify access
symlinks = build:symlinks/latest:symlinks/latest-{board}
```

## Why fixed paths are useful

Some IDEs (e.g., VS Code) require predictable paths, such as to locate  
`compile_commands.json` for code completion.  

Additionally, subsequent **west commands** cannot always guess the correct build directory:

```sh
west build zephyr/samples/hello_world/ -b nrf52dk/nrf52805
west build zephyr/samples/hello_world/ -b frdm_mcxa346
west build zephyr/samples/basic/blinky -b nrf52dk/nrf52805
west build zephyr/samples/basic/blinky -b frdm_mcxa346
west flash   # This command cannot guess what build folder I want to use
```
Remember, if `{board}`, `{app}` or `{source_dir}` are used in `dir-fmt`, it becomes impossible to guess the correct directory reliably.

## Possible solutions

There are 2 solutions I have in mind:
1. **Store the latest build directory** in west’s config. But this is not nice if this file is touched on each build. Is there some other storage available where this information could be put and read back later? Shall a new config file be introduced for this?
2. **Smarter approach**: let west guess the latest build directory correctly based on specified symlinks.


## Why symlinks help

A practical solution is allowing users to specify one or more symlinks.  
These symlinks are created during the build process and point to the actual build directories.  

This is especially powerful when `dir-fmt` includes `{app}` or `{source_dir}`, making direct path guessing unreliable. Users can build within a unique folder and create a (fix) symlink (without using `{board}`, `{app}` or `{source_dir}`) The symlink can easily be updated without removing the actual builds. 
**Note:** The guessed build directory is simply the first symlink that resolves successfully.


### Example usage

In the configuration above, symlinks let you easily switch between different builds / boards:

```sh
west flash                       # Flash the latest build
west flash -d symlinks/latest    # Same as above: flash the latest build
west flash -d symlinks/latest-frdm_mcxa346   # Flash the latest build for frdm_mcxa346
west flash -d symlinks/latest-nrf52dk/nrf52805 # Flash the latest build for nrf52dk/nrf52805
```

> I'm not sure I get this sorry: is it not simpler for users to just create these symlinks once and forget about them? Why do they need to go through a west config detour instead?

This is not possible since the "latest" build is always a different build directory. If it would always be the same path, then there would be no need for a symlink.

> That sounds like some (design) bug... is it not possible to fix that instead? This must have been already discussed somewhere?

As explained above `{board}`, `{app}` and `{source_dir}` can never be guessed (only if there is some storage where this information is put). Would you prefer to add support for a config store in yml format, e.g. `.west/storage`, to store this information? Is there already something like this available?

I guess that depends on the user.
You can't imagine the things that people don't notice in the CMake output, even though we try to only print the most important :disappointed: 

Regarding the rebuild / no rebuild, then I would say it's just as simple to spot:
```
$ west flash
-- west flash: rebuilding    <--- it tries to rebuild
ninja: no work to do.
-- west flash: using runner nrfutil
...
```
vs:
```
$ west flash --skip-rebuild
-- west flash: using runner nrfutil   <---- Goes straight to flash
....
```

Though if approving the config setting, `flash.skip-rebuild`, then it probably should be highlighted, for example like this:
```
$ west flash --skip-rebuild
-- west flash: skip rebuild   <-- user is informed
-- west flash: using runner nrfutil
....
```

But there is one thing we should have if supporting `west config flash.skip-rebuild true`, and that is to overrule that setting on command line.

For example I can enable sysbuild by default, but deselect it on a specific build, like this:
```
$ west config build.sysbuild true                # Use sysbuild in general
$ west build -b plank --no-sysbuild <sample>     # Do not use sysbuild in this case
```

So if we're going to support `west config flash.skip-rebuild true` then it must be possible to overwrite this on command line, for example by using:
```
$ west flash --force-rebuild
```

Side-note: if introducing `--force-rebuild`, then it probably better to name the flags `--build` / `--no-build` or `--rebuild` / `--no-rebuild`.
>  For this particular one, the benefit seems extremely low. 

Like anything else, I would say it depends.
One thing that have hit me is when trying to run samples in debugger where you might have a reference sample in `build_working`.
The if you do `west flash -d build_working` and forget `--skip-rebuild`, then the build from the working SHA is immediately cleared, and you need to checkout that SHA and rebuild, just to jump back to where you were.
But again, that's just an annoyance, nothing where you spend time tracing down why it's not rebuilding.

body:
Let's go few steps back.

My goal is to address the following four use cases, which commonly arise when working with multiple projects and boards, and frequently switching between them:

1. **Preserve build folders**  
   I want to keep all build folders intact instead of deleting them, in order to reduce build times when switching between projects or boards. This is especially important because reconfiguring with CMake — particularly when time-consuming code generation is involved — can be costly.  

2. **Simplify repeated builds**  
   I want subsequent `west build` commands to work without requiring me to re-specify the project each time. This makes it easier to reuse previous commands and keeps shell history (bash/zsh/fish) cleaner.  

3. **Automatic build directory detection**  
   I want the `west flash` command to automatically determine the appropriate build directory (currently referred to internally as *guess-dir*), so that I don’t need to pass `--build-dir` manually every time.  

4. **Stable paths for tooling**  
   IDEs, plugins, and other tools should have a fixed, predictable location where they can reliably find necessary files (e.g., `compile_commands.json`).

> Right, so build each build in different folders, it doesn't magically delete the folder or do a recompilation unless e.g. source files or repos have changed, you don't need anything new for this.  

True — at least if we use `dir-fmt`. For example, we configure `build.dir-fmt = build-output/{board}/{source_dir_common}`.
By default (without `dir-fmt`), `west build` always outputs to a folder named `build`. Previous builds are removed/overwritten if using `west build -p`.  

> I think you are not understanding how to use the tools, if you go into a build directory and run west flash it will just work  

That’s exactly my point: I want to avoid going into build directories. Ideally, I’d like to run all commands from the west workspace root — which works perfectly fine *without* `dir-fmt`.  

Example without `dir-fmt`:  
```
west config unset build.dir-fmt # disable dir-fmt
west build zephyr/samples/hello_world/ -b frdm_mcxa346 # builds into 'build'
west build   # rebuilds 'build'
west flash   # flashes 'build'
```  
This is convenient: once a build is configured (line 2), it can be rebuilt or flashed with a simple command. No extra steps (like `cd` into another directory) are needed. And the best: The command is always the same, no matter which board was built.

Now, with `dir-fmt`:  
```
rm -rf build # remove old build
west config build.dir-fmt 'build-output/{board}/{source_dir_common}'
west build zephyr/samples/hello_world/ -b frdm_mcxa346 # 'build-output/frdm_mcxa346/zephyr-rtos/samples/hello_world'
west build   # DOES NOT WORK ANYMORE
west flash   # DOES NOT WORK ANYMORE
```  
As soon as `dir-fmt` is enabled, I’m forced to either always pass `--build-dir` or `cd` into the correct build directory.  

> The paths are stable.  

Yes, but with `dir-fmt` the build directory depends on the board. For example:  
- `build-output/frdm_mcxa346/zephyr-rtos/samples/hello_world`  
- `build-output/nrf52dk/nrf52805/zephyr-rtos/samples/hello_world`

That’s why I’d like an option to create a symlink (e.g. `build-latest`) that always points to the most recent build directory. 
With the changes in this PR:  
- My IDE could always read `build-latest/compile_commands.json` which is always automatically my most recent build.
- I could run `west flash` (e.g. in my terminal or within a task in my IDE) without worrying about the actual build path.

_Which_ particular "build location"? Do you mean: the location of the _latest_ build only? Or do you also have other use case(s) in mind? I still haven't seen a loud and clear answer to that basic question, sorry if I missed it.

> Another use case which came into my mind now: .clangd.

How do you know `clangd` does not mind its configuration file and build configuration being swapped at random points in time without notice? I had a quick look and clangd seems to be aggressively indexing and caching stuff to keep response times low:
https://clangd.llvm.org/design/indexing
https://clangd.llvm.org/design/threads

This clangd design really does not seem compatible with the sort of build directory "hotplug" you're after. I bet clangd "mostly" works in many hotplug cases, depending on differences between build configurations, timings and phases of the moon but this really does not look like something "supported" by clangd. I would personally feel safer keeping clangd focused on a single build directory even while building other configurations. EDIT: I mean I would rather accept a known divergence between clangd and the current build rather than the risk of clangd behaving erratically or inconsistently.

This is not specific to `clangd`: you present this "build directory hotplug" idea like something so natural it does not even need an introduction, but in reality I've never seen any build or development tool ever claiming to support this sort of hotplug. Like most concurrency issues, it might work for some time until it fails catastrophically. In fact, I even had to add a delay hack in `west` because merely renaming a directory randomly failed when VS code and others are running: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/west/pull/703. body:
> Additional Nice-to-have feature: easily access the latest build of each board.

Fair.

> From the view of the tooling you always hotplug different builds.

This is a wish.

1. _Incremental_ builds have limited `build/` effects when little has changed in the source and configuration.
1. When too much has changed on the input side, build systems delete all outputs to restart and _build from scratch_. Cleaning all outputs makes it easy for all tooling to notice, invalidate all caches etc.

But entire build directory "hotplug" is nothing like the two normal use cases above, it's a completely new thing![*] Hotplug can very easily confuse tooling into thinking this was just an incremental build. Then it can end up using a _mix_ of  different build configurations.

Of course, when configurations don't differ too much then that mix can be harmless and things likely work most of the time. But nothing and especially no build system should ever provide features that work "most of the time" because 1) those take literally months or even years to debug, 2) build systems have [extremely few maintainers](https://mesonbuild.com/Design-rationale.html).

- https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/west/issues/558 took literally 3 years to understand and mitigate.
- 4cba9e6d425e32 gives another example of a non-deterministic failure that took several years to root-cause.

These are just examples from the top of my head. Everyone knows concurrency issues and intermittent failures are the most time-consuming by far.

tl;dr:
- Remembering the last build(s) does not seem like a very useful feature to me because of all the alternatives that have been listed above - but I don't have a strong objection to it.
- Build directory "hotplug" looks like a really, really bad idea.


[*] I'm _not_ saying there is no concurrency in 1) and 2) and that tooling is bug-free now. I'm saying "hotplug" is a whole new level of concurrency and that most tooling is not prepared for it at all.

body:
> Reminder: when using symbolic links, make sure you test on Windows too.

On Windows, `os.symlink` requires additional privileges (admin rights or developer mode).  
This makes it unsuitable for a cross-platform tool like `west`, so I totally agree with you that my solution is not suitable. 
I will discard my `build.symlinks` feature proposal and close this PR soon.

---

Instead, I’d like to suggest another more flexible approach for solving my use case from above.
(If you agree in principle, I’ll open a new discussion/issue/PR.)

**1. Add support for `build.pre-cmake-cmd` hooks**  
- A user-defined command (format string like `dir-fmt`).  
- Runs right before CMake (Hook)
- Maybe also further hooks make sense: `build.post-cmake-cmd`, `build.pre-build-cmd`,  `build.post-build-cmd`

**2. Add support for `build.default-build-dirs`**  
- A list of one or more candidate build directories (format string like `dir-fmt` with format args `west_topdir|board`)
- Used when west cannot determine the build directory (e.g. `west flash` without `-d`, or when `dir-fmt` contains unset format args like `{board}`)
- If no valid directory is found in those directories, west fails with the same error as today.

**Examples for `build.pre-cmake-cmd`:**  
- Simple command:  
  `pre-cmake-cmd = ln build-output/{board}/{source_dir_common} build`  
- More complex:  
  `pre-cmake-cmd = sh -c "echo pre-built-hook; ln build-output/{board}/{source_dir_common} build"`  
- External script:  
  `pre-cmake-cmd = my-pre-cmake-hook.py {board} {source_dir} {west_topdir}`  

This approach works across all OSes and gives users flexible hook points in the build process.

**Potential use cases:**  
- `build.pre-cmake-cmd`: create symlinks to the latest started build (see this issue)  
- `build.post-cmake-cmd`: ??  
- `build.pre-build-cmd`: ??  
- `build.post-build-cmd`: create symlinks to the latest _successful_ build (but maybe this should be done via cmake instead)

**Full config example:**  
```
# call script which creates symlink "symlinks/latest"
pre-cmake-cmd = my-pre-cmake-hook.py {board} {source_dir} {west_topdir}

# call script which creates symlink "symlinks/successful"
post-build-cmd = my-post-build-hook.py {board} {source_dir} {west_topdir}

# specify latest build directory which is used as fallback if no other was specified
build.default-build-dirs = symlinks/latest
```

**Resulting commands:**  
```
west build -b frdm_mcxa346 zephyr/samples/hello_world/
west build
west build -t flash
west flash
```

body:
> 👉 Which directory should be used within our .clangd file or in our IDE configs?

This is not really a question for `west` or Zephyr but for `clangd` itself. Different external tools will have different levels of support for different levels of concurrent and unpredictable changes in build configuration and build outputs. It must be hard enough for these tools to support "correctly" Make / CMake / meson / Bazel / Soong and what not, so I really think `west` should not go and add some "hotplug" feature(s) that generate even more surprise, combinatorial explosion, concurrency and unpredictability.

As mentioned before, If I had to solve this problem, I would probably try something like this:
- Group all build variations into "families" of configurations that differ "little" from each other. 
- Pick one "representative" in each family: one that compiles the most features and the most code.
- Manually (sorry...) point clangd at representatives, switch when the need arises.

This avoids the risk of confusing clangd (or some other tool) with hotplug while reducing the number of switches. Possibly no manual switch at all if all the configurations are close to each other.

Of course all the complexity is in defining what is a "little" configuration change, i.e. where do you draw this line. On a per-tool basis!

> another question, does the linter tell you what is wrong with your formatting beside generating diffs?

No the linter does generates changes (that may in some cases lead to the same text) and applies them to the current document. Then a diff is generated.

Explanation: 

I had given a try with annotating each edit (by annotating the diff changes). But given the limitation I faced with GIT showing only a limited number of annotations (as can be seen  in the comments above) and technical limitations we will run into as we enforce more rules, I opted to give just provide a diff. 

This is also very common e.g. [black](https://github.com/psf/black)  a python formatter, also only provides diff, prettier - another linter - also cannot annotate each change and this doesn't even give a diff but rather just changes the files. 

The reason why this becomes unmanageable is that text edits must be applied in reverse order. i.e from last line to the top. Also you cannot have overlapping text edit regions.

Therefore to solve certain problems and formatting rules you have to do the formatting in layers.

example I have reached this limitation already. Currently I am working on adding sorting of properties and nodes as per the spec (properties on top and nodes underneath); in most cases this will lead to overlapping text edits when changing tabs and spaces within the node and property it self. 

This can be solved by first sorting and applying the edits internally to get the new code and then run the second layer to fix tabs, spaces etc...

Similarly to wrap lines so as to not exceed 100 characters, another layer will be needed. This is still WIP on my end that will be added later.

Given all the above technical limitations, the only feasible solution I reached is to provide a diff.

Having a tool which annotates each specific error would require to keep track of the position of each text component in the original text source, the more layers the harder and more costly this gets.

Note that syntax issues that stop the linter from formatting are annotated as can be see here

body:
Some point to address from today's TSC:

I know this is long but I am trying to get as much details as possible.

### Do user **Have** to install it on their machines?

Short answer is **no**.

Longs answer:
- The linter will provide a diff of changes needed to make it compliant.
- The linter will generate a patch file to apply, This will fix all the issues reported in the CI Action. This patch file is available as part of the CI and can be downloaded.

Q: But if a user does not want to install this tool, won't this CI check make it more difficult to comply as PR is blocked and user has to manually fix the issues?

A: No, actually this will make things faster. This linter is respecting the rules as described in the coding guidelines so In theory all the changes this linter suggests should be done and flagged non the less. With this in mind the PR should still be blocked! The only difference is that now these infractions will be reported constantly every time. In addition the reporting will be consistent and not up to a humans to explain "add new line", "remove line", "Add space here"

Also the `check_compliance.py` can run locally without node and this and dts-linter, in such case it will skip the dts-linting step locally.

### Concerns with adding Node (yet another _scripting_ language):
- This tool only needs node for runtime. No typescript files will be added to the zephyr repo. 
- Zephyr can keep its policy to not allow Typescript and Javascript as a scripting language and this tool can still be used.
- The only reason package.json and package-lock.json where added was to allow locking the version of the tool to reduce the attack vectors when tool is installed, as recommended by @pdgendt.

### Why Node:
- The dts-lsp is intended to give complete development experience to IDEs like vscode and even VIM or neo vim! 
     - Part of the lsp spec is formatting, which this dts-lsp implements, Hence, it is more scalable reuse this same code. See https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_formatting 
- IDEs like VSCode already are used on Node and hence the LSP will not need any additional dependencies.
- This makes the tool OS type, and OS version agnostic and can run on all platforms with zero to minimal effort.

### Why reusing tools between IDEs and CI make logical sense to me:
- One code base to maintain.
- Changes to one tool will benefit both CI and IDEs, 
- Keeping requirements in sync
- Users that opt to use the lsp in the editor will have a seamless experience as the linting rules for CI and the development environment are the same. 

To date if one looks at the adoption rate for the dts-lsp more than 4.1K users are already using this in VSCode like IDEs and form npm downloads (https://npm-stat.com/charts.html?package=devicetree-language-server&from=2024-12-01&to=2025-10-08) At least 1K+ more are using it in VIM/neoVIM once you subtract server caching downloads and some CIs downloads from when testing this PRs. From the feedback I have, most are zephyr users.

Also if one looks at the dts-linter around 1K+ users are using this CLI tool see https://npm-stat.com/charts.html?package=dts-linter&from=2024-12-01&to=2025-10-08. This number considers server caching downloads and some CIs when testing these PRs

### Concerns with dependencies:

#### There are two types of dependencies:
- Required at runtime,
- Required during development such as types, tool to build and lint typescript project etc...

 #### There are two ways to ship a project
- Bundle i.e generate one .js file 
- Import dependencies at runtime 

First important point is that any dependency needed for development are never needed at runtime and hence these dependencies will never be bundled nor imported at runtime. E.g. in c++ gcc would be a dev dependency

#### Dependencies of dts-linter

Let focus on the Runtime dependencies.

Case 1: Getting runtime dependencies at runtime with no bundling 

- The runtime dependencies must be defined as dependencies in the package.json of the dts-linter and dts-lsp
- When `npm i dts-linter@version` is called, node_modules folder is created and each and every dependency from the dependency list will be also installed
- when the `npx dts-linter...` is called the .js file for the dts-linter will dynamically load modules from the `node_module` folder 
 
**Note** One can see this as the equivalent of a DLL concept where the DLL is loaded at runtime 

**Important notes** 
- The version of dependencies download will depend the version specified in the packeg-lock.json 
- Running `npm audit fix` will update the dependencies and next run will use the new dependencies.

Currently the build process of both these tools ( dts-linter and dts-lsp )  is to bundle, hence if this above options is preferred changes to the build process will be needed.

Case 2: Bundled (current case)
- The runtime dependencies should now be defined as devDependencies in the package.json of the dts-linter and dts-lsp, as in this case we only need them until we bundle into the final .js file.
    - This is also done this way in these repos:
           - https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/package.json
           - https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-languageserver-node/blob/main/package.json
           - https://github.com/kpdecker/jsdiff/blob/master/package.json
    -  if  the dependencies are not move into devDependencies `npm i` will install dependencies that the dts-linter will never use and 'npm audit fix' will give the false impression that something was fixed when the bundled code will not change.
- The dts-linter only depend on the dts-lsp as this cannot be bundled, everything else can be bundled
    - **Note** if needed I can split the dts-lsp and take the parser and formatter out into a separate repo and npm module to allow for this to also be bundled. However this will limit us from using the diagnostic capabilities in the future.  See https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/92334#issuecomment-3310127354 for examples of what the diagnostic tool can find if we ever opt to use it in addition to linting.

**Note** One can see bundling as the equivalent of a static linking in c/c++ context

> @stephanosio @nashif @keith-packard should we also enforce C++17 at the same time, for consistency?

That is probably not a good idea since C++ versions are not necessarily in sync with the C versions, and C++17 is not a mere bug fix over the previous C++11 standard; in fact, [C++17 even removes some existing features](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%2B%2B17#Removed_features).

As for dropping support for the archaic C++ standards prior to C++11 (i.e. C++98 and C++03), that would be reasonable since C++11 introduces many C99 features required by Zephyr.

> > `--rebuild` and `--no-rebuild` are not mutual exclusive.
> 
> I think I disagree here, the last argument should just apply, no?

I think we should stay consistent between `--<flag>` and `--no-<flag>` arguments.

With `--sysbuild` and `--no-sysbuild` we already have:
```
$ west build -b native_sim --sysbuild --no-sysbuild
usage: west build [-h] [-b BOARD[@REV]]] [-d BUILD_DIR]
           [-S SNIPPET] [--shield SHIELD]
           [-t TARGET] [-p {auto, always, never}] [-c] [--cmake-only]
           [-n] [-o BUILD_OPT] [-f]
           [--sysbuild | --no-sysbuild] [--domain DOMAIN]
           [--extra-conf FILE.conf]
           [--extra-dtc-overlay FILE.overlay]
           [source_dir] -- [cmake_opt [cmake_opt ...]]
west build: error: argument --no-sysbuild: not allowed with argument --sysbuild
```

So if we want to allow this PR to use `--no-rebuild` together `--rebuild` then this PR should include a change to `--sysbuild / --no-sysbuild` (and other similar flags, if we have such), so that all such arguments behave the same.

Consistency is important here.

@mbolivar , thanks for taking the time for this. 

> But I got:
>

> dtsh: error: DTS error: legacy 'title:' in /home/mbolivar/zp/zephyr/dts/bindings/pinctrl/nordic,nrf-pinctrl.yaml, use 'description' instead
> ```
> 
> I don't see anything in https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/build/dts/bindings-syntax.html#title that indicates that `title:` is "legacy" -- am I doing something wrong? I'm confused about how to try the latest version. Any advice appreciated. Thanks!

Yes, I also came across this not long ago.
The version of the Python `devicetree` package bundled with DTSh 0.2.4 is incompatible with the bindings defined in Zephyr 4.2, especially the `title` property which was actually considered legacy up to Zephyr 4.1 (see ee17657 and a58e659 for details).

I was hesitant to release the update, not being sure about untested backward compatibility for users of say Zephyr 4.0 that would `pip install -U dtsh` ?
But, as you remind me, DTSh 0.2.4 is incompatible with Zephyr main branch, which is perhaps much worse.

Anyway, I've just pushed DTSh 0.2.5 to PyPI, which includes the Python `devicetree` package as of Zephyr 4.2.1. This should fix your error. Sorry for the mess.

But the root cause remains: although DTSh main branch could (should) track Zephyr main branch more closely, we still lack a mean to *pin* this version of DTSh to that version of Zephyr.
With the **optional** project approach, we could at least have fixed this for `west dtsh`: Zephyr pins the appropriate version of DTSh in `zephyr/submanifests/optional.yaml`, and `west dtsh` imports the in-tree `devicetree` package from `zephyr/scripts/dts/python-devicetree/src`, everything's fine.
But with the move to an **external** project (see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/59863#discussion_r2448634441), I'm afraid we won't be able to reliably prevent these kinds of errors.

 Thanks.

It's a Canadian holiday, so I'll keep it short.

This change adds technical debt, by claiming something (again) belongs to C, when it does not.

There is no C specification that defines `fnmatch()`.

We should avoid fragmenting standards like POSIX and injecting shards of it into places where it doesn't belong. That has historically been a problem in Zephyr.

If there is something wrong with the `fnmatch()` testsuite, that's something to discuss. We should not be dismantling software that is intentionally conformant to standards in order to further individual agendas.

Even if it were not a holiday, I would still NAK this PR, because it is really going in the wrong direction.

body:
history of fnmatch in zephyr, a long one...

- initially added in ext/lib
- moved to lib/fnmatch when we eliminated ext/
- Moved to lib/util/
- Moved from lib/util to lib/posix

Now we are moving it to lib/libc.

Does it really matter where this lives and what Kconfig options enable it? We are getting into endless debates about where it should be and whether god forbid the kconfig enabling it has POSIX in its name and what that all means in termns for compliance and standards and so on. 

At the end f the day, we just need this to work to support some subsystems and functionality we need, it was NEVER about the support for fnmatch itself as POSIX extension, we just need the functionality and we could also implement this with a different name and make it zephyr specific and skip all of this.

Dont really care how this get resolved at the end, but things are starting to get rediculous :(
author: nashif

body:
The other existing exceptions in [Rule A.5](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/contribute/coding_guidelines/index.html#rule-a-5-c-standard-library-usage-restrictions-in-zephyr-codebase) are POSIX extensions to the C library.
Given that fnmatch is used in a few components, it makes sense to me to add it to this rule exception and, just like for the others in this exception (and as the rule requires), place Zephyr's optional implementation in lib/libc/common.

But, I would not mind it being in lib/posix/c_lib_ext as long as we can select it independently of other posix subsystems components.

What we have today, which we should not have is the C library provided fnmatch (from picolibc or others) be always overridden by the Zephyr version; and we should not have a [test in Zephyr for this function that is defective](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/98827/commits/4e1e77c34e7f779948cc07e4c243edee61ea43e3).
This PR fixes both of these.

author: carlescufi

body:
@carles - `fnmatch()` is a POSIX extension to ISO C. It's not part of any C standard and thus not required to be implemented by any C library. Obviously many C libraries do bundle POSIX functions as well, but it's definitely not required. Many libc projects also historically provided POSIX support in separate libraries (pthread, rt, etc).

If you're asking in order to justify moving POSIX code out of `lib/posix` and into `lib/c_lib/common`, it's still not really correct. Nor is it necessary, given that there is a simple way to make those functions available either from the C library or from `lib/posix/c_lib_ext` all without the need to configure any POSIX system interfaces.

Doing so would just be adding more technical debt to the project, which should be avoided.

Indeed, we have spent many years at this point, untangling the assumed POSIX availability in a lot of areas in Zephyr, and making those dependencies explicit (via Kconfig) rather than assumed.

body:
> > If any embedded C libraries do not provide `getentropy()` (which is a relatively new addition to POSIX) or `strfmon()` (which I have in staging), then those can just pull in the Zephyr implementation via CMake to complete the option group.
> 
> There's no real way to provide `getentropy` with just a C library -- this function requires OS support to get real entropy from the hardware. Picolibc would do this by declaring the function in the appropriate header and leaving the function to be provided externally, much as it does with the low-level I/O functions (`read`, `write`, etc).

I agree on this.

Technically, it's possible to indirectly access a PRNG via ANSI C `FILE` I/O and a special file called `/dev/prandom`, but that doesn't really make sense in the context of an RTOS like Zephyr because doing so would be expensive, and in the end, it would still require OS support.

In Zephyr, `getentropy()` should (and does) leverage _direct_ OS support to avoid the code size and runtime costs that would be associated with a purely ANSI C approach.

Personally, I think lumping `getentropy()` as part of `POSIX_C_LIB_EXT` was perhaps a bit short-sighted on behalf of the standards committee for those reasons, but it's there now.

body:
> Why should we embed the lz4 compression path into LLEXT? I know I said I'd be ok with this, but the more I look at this code I keep having this thought.
> 
> I guess my high level thought is this is really useful, but could probably be made into a sample without modifying any LLEXT subsys code?
> 
> Or would this make buffer lifetimes complicated and you feel its nicer to make it a loader? What if the source of lz4 came from littlefs/fatfs? I don't see where this would work today but I imagine it'd be something that people want.
> 
> To me I wonder if this should instead be a sample that combines some of these things together nicely that people can riff on in their application rather than trying to do it for them.
> 
> I can imagine a sample that looks similar to the following... (not correct C code).
> 
> ```c
> int rc = lz4_decompress(comp_data, comp_sz, uncomp_data, uncomp_sz);
> 
> /* LLEXT now in uncomp_data, load as a buffer */
> llext_load(..)
> ```

I integrated decompression with llext to make it *independent* from the loader.
To this end, compressed extensions are loaded in *chunks* with configurable size (new `CONFIG_LLEXT_COMPRESSION_LOAD_INCREMENT`).
Thereby, it should work well with both buffer- and filesystem-backed loaders.

A new type of "virtual" decompression loader could achieve the same thing - e.g., it could be constructed using a new macro `LLEXT_DECOMPRESSION_LOADER`  from an *existing loader*.

*Advantage*: fewer (possibly no) changes to the llext core.
*Advantage*: can be *chained* (e.g., with encryption and authentication) in other loaders.
*Disadvantage*: Current API does not lend itself to resource handling. Loaders can provide a `finalize` callback that is called on error or when loading the extension is complete. It can be used to deallocate the LZ4 decompression context and (on error) the buffer where the extension lives. However, there is currently no callback when the extension is *unloaded*: Thus, the decompression loader would require either a custom cleanup function, or the loader API would have to be extended with a callback that is called during *llext_unload*.
*Disadvantage*: Certain combinations of chained loaders can be insecure, e.g., compression *before* encryption. Integrating the functionalities into llext allows *enforcing* an order.

Correct, this uses the REST API defined by the LFS protocol directly, no dependencies needed. hal_silabs currently deep-links into LFS blob storage, but this is brittle since the only guarantee of the LFS server is that the API endpoint is stable, the blob URLs themselves may in theory change over time. body:
> I think we should accept 3 types of driver APIs: > > 1. Common, vendor-agnostic driver classes: `.h` in `include/zephyr/driver/` and `.c` in `drivers//`. These are public APIs I believe this is what we are doing now so LGTM. > 2. Extensions to existing driver classes: `.h.` in `include/zephyr/driver//` and `.c` in `drivers//`. **These are public APIs** Seems fair to me. This shouldn't be a deterrent either as our `API Lifecycle` allows an API to remain `Unstable` indefinitely, so vendors which don't want to provide stability guarantees can do just that. (to quote: `An API *can* be declared stable after [...]` - not `shall be declared`). However, I will point out that the [`API Lifecycle` policy](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/api/api_lifecycle.html) wording is not currently appropriate for hardware-specific APIs (which these `Extensions to existing driver classes` would all be, I believe?). For example: `[An experimental API for peripherals] shall be promoted to unstable when it has at least two implementations on different hardware platforms` doesn't make sense for APIs which target one specific HW platform. This is a problem since `Public APIs cannot be modified without following the provisions described in the API lifecycle section`. Either the `API Lifecycle` documentation needs to be updated, or a specific API lifecycle needs to be documented and applied for these `Extensions to existing driver classes`. Also, we would need to define a schedule for when this policy becomes effective: there are most likely things currently in `include/zephyr/driver//` that are **not** intended to be `public API`s - so we can't just say "*everything there is public*" - but we also don't want to have headers rotting forever there. > 3. Vendor-specific driver classes: `.h` in `soc//include` and `.c` in `soc//common` or `soc//`. These do not fit the current definition of public, private or internal, we would need to add a new category ("vendor-specific API") in the glossary.
I don't think this is necessary... To quote the glossary, an `internal API` is `any internal function, structure or macro defined anywhere in the Zephyr source tree [...] intended to “extend” Zephyr [...] to be used only between certain software components`, where a `software component` is `a self-contained, modular, and replaceable part of the Zephyr source code` - for example `a driver, a subsystem or an applications[sic]`. Under this definition, I think vendor-specific driver classes (/APIs) would fit as `internal API`s: they are intended to "extend" Zephyr and to only be used between certain software components: the application (*or vendor-specific drivers*) and the SoC-specific code.
...but having a dedicated category may still be better (e.g., allows having specific policies for that particular category). One thing needs clarification for me: *what exactly would go in this class?* From a look at `soc/st/stm32/common/*.h`, we have *mostly* `internal API`s(?) - helper functions for SoC-specific code and STM32-specific drivers - but some of them *might* be useful to applications as well? For example, `stm32_backup_domain_{dis/en}able_access()` *might* make sense to call from the application if it accesses some BKP domain resources without going through a driver. (This is probably a very common situation: SoC-specific code in Zephyr manages a shared resource, and the application may want to access that resource directly but doing so without cooperating with Zephyr could result in the system entering an inconsistent state). So would this class contain only `internal`-ish APIs intended for use only by SoC-specific/vendor-specific code? Or only `public`-ish APIs intended for use by application code? Or both, and if so, how would one distinguish them? Finally, there is one point I disagree with: I don't think we should standardize *where the headers are located in tree* (except that it must be `soc//...`) but *how they are exposed*, i.e. what their include path is. (c.f. my previous comment: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/99750#discussion_r2560734964)
Minor remarks on this topic This gives more freedom to SoC vendors on how they want to structure their SoC-specific code and APIs. For example, building for `STM32H7` could add `soc/st/stm32/common/include` ***and*** `soc/st/stm32/stm32h7x/include` to include path, whereas building for `STM32F4` would add `soc/st/stm32/common/include` and `soc/st/stm32/stm32f4x/include` instead. Another vendor could make a `soc//include/` directory with SoC-specific subdirectories instead... but maybe we **don't** want freedom here, and instead we should enforce a specific format? :man_shrugging:
> The alternative, if we don't want to add a new category in the glossary (i.e. "Vendor-specific API") that can be placed outside `include/` but at the same time can be used by all components in and out of tree, would be to place vendor-specific driver classes like so: `.h` in `include/zephyr//` and `.c` in `drivers//` or `soc//` or similar. I think this would break the "encapsulation" of SoC-specific headers/code. @henrikbrixandersen IIRC had a point about HW-specific-but-not-tied-to-SoC things though, maybe we do need `drivers/` for that, but it is orthogonal to the SoC-specific question IMO.

> So would this class contain only `internal`-ish APIs intended for use only by SoC-specific/vendor-specific code? Or only `public`-ish APIs intended for use by application code? Or both, and if so, how would one distinguish them?

Well, here you are hitting my issue with calling them "internal APIs". I think some of those vendor-specific APIs need to be able to be called by applications, just like you mention in your example. In my view we should not overcomplicate things and use a single category for both types.

> Finally, there is one point I disagree with: I don't think we should standardize _where the headers are located in tree_ (except that it must be `soc/<vendor>/...`) but _how they are exposed_, i.e. what their include path is. (c.f. my previous comment: [#99750 (comment)](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/99750#discussion_r2560734964))
> 
> Minor remarks on this topic
> This gives more freedom to SoC vendors on how they want to structure their SoC-specific code and APIs.
> 
> For example, building for `STM32H7` could add `soc/st/stm32/common/include` _**and**_ `soc/st/stm32/stm32h7x/include` to include path, whereas building for `STM32F4` would add `soc/st/stm32/common/include` and `soc/st/stm32/stm32f4x/include` instead. Another vendor could make a `soc/<vendor>/include/` directory with SoC-specific subdirectories instead...
> 
> but maybe we **don't** want freedom here, and instead we should enforce a specific format? 🤷‍♂️

I think we should at least enforce a location for the header files to be honest, so that users see a consistent view of the `soc/` folder regardless of the vendor.

> 
> > The alternative, if we don't want to add a new category in the glossary (i.e. "Vendor-specific API") that can be placed outside `include/` but at the same time can be used by all components in and out of tree, would be to place vendor-specific driver classes like so: `.h` in `include/zephyr/<vendor>/<class.h>` and `.c` in `drivers/<vendor>/<class.c>` or `soc/<vendor>/<class.c>` or similar.
> 
> I think this would break the "encapsulation" of SoC-specific headers/code. @henrikbrixandersen IIRC had a point about HW-specific-but-not-tied-to-SoC things though, maybe we do need `drivers/<vendor>` for that, but it is orthogonal to the SoC-specific question IMO.

Agreed, I much rather have those outside `include/zephyr`.

So, summarizing, I think we agree on types 1. and 2. but we need to figure out two things about 3.:
a. What kind of APIs will those be? Public? Internal?
b. Where should the headers be located exactly?

No, because there are many use cases that are simply not practical without vendor-specific APIs, and in some cases those cannot be OS-agnostic ones (that could fit in the HAL repo), because they require interaction with the OS (for example, power management). looks like the motivation of this PR and policy is not clear enough, it is exactly that, we do NOT want vendor specific functionality used at a low level to bring up hardware to be exposed as zephyr APIs. Application should NOT be using such interfaces directly.

If we allow this and start doing that, we will have vendors creating SILOs of application facing inerfaces applicable only to those vendors and covered under the zephyr project and exposed as Zephyr project interfaces.

> Yes, if we don't officially support 3.10 and 3.11, but allow them to be used, we'll be in this limbo where issues are the end-user's problem?

I find such a "limbo" useful because it does not block some users (who do not have control on their operating system) for no technical reason.

There can be two different minima:
- A "hard", absolute minimum required which should "fail fast" with a very clear error message (e.g. #104746)
- A "soft", supported minimum tested in CI and validation.

Users between these two can support themselves and send Python patches if needed. If these patches degrade the Python code too much, then reject them and bump the hard limit. This automatically provides a technical rationale that answers the "WHY" question in #92377: because new Python feature "X" is too useful to pass and we want to use it.

body:
@henrikbrixandersen @mathieuchopstm @erwango @nashif @teburd 

My review summary:

First, a reminder of how we define today the types of APIs in Zephyr:

- Public API: https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/glossary.html#term-public-API
- Private API: https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/glossary.html#term-private-API
- Internal API: https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/glossary.html#term-internal-API

I think we should accept 3 types of driver APIs:

1. Common, vendor-agnostic driver classes: `.h` in `include/zephyr/driver/<class.h>` and `.c` in `drivers/<class>/`<vendor_class.c>`. These are public APIs
2. Extensions to existing driver classes: `.h.` in `include/zephyr/driver/<class>/<vendor_class.h>` and `.c` in `drivers/<class>/<vendor_class.c>`. These are public APIs
3. Vendor-specific hardware enablement code: `.h` in `soc/<vendor>/include` and `.c` in `soc/<vendor>/common` or `soc/<vendor>/<series>`. These do not fit the current definition of public, private or internal, we would need to add a new category ("vendor-specific API") in the glossary.

I believe this is enough and it is simple enough to follow and understand, and keeps all vendor-specific driver classes as Zephyr non-public APIs.

The alternative, if we don't want to add a new category in the glossary (i.e. "Vendor-specific API") that can be placed outside `include/` but at the same time can be used by all components in and out of tree, would be to place vendor-specific driver classes like so: `.h` in `include/zephyr/<vendor>/<class.h>` and `.c` in `drivers/<vendor>/<class.c>` or `soc/<vendor>/<class.c>` or similar.
author: carlescufi

body:
Architecture WG meeting:

@carlescufi proposes a new set of categories:

Options with a new peripheral:

1. Extend existing driver class with new, cross-vendor, hw-agnostic public APIs
2. Create a new driver class
3. Extend existing driver class with vendor-specific APIs
4. Add internal APIs that are vendor-specific but not tied to an existing driver class (soc/)

API types:

- Common, vendor-agnostic driver classes: .h in `include/zephyr/driver/<class.h>` and .c in `drivers/<class>/<vendor_class.c>`. These are public APIs
- Vendor-specific extensions to existing driver classes: .h. in `include/zephyr/driver/<class>/<vendor_class.h>` and .c in `drivers/<class>/<vendor_class.c>`. These are public APIs
- Vendor-specific hardware enablement code: .h in `soc/<vendor>/include` and .c in `soc/<vendor>/common` or `soc/<vendor>/<series>`. These would be private and/or internal APIs, and they will be scrutinized in order to avoid creating silos of every silicon vendor doing their own thing. Applications using these APIs, given that they are internal and/or private, can expect no guarantees as to the lifecycle of the same or backwards compatibility (or even disappearing altogether).

For example, in [the section](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/test/twister.html#executing-tests-on-multiple-devices) where hardware map is introduced, there is an example of a hardware map with a `serial` field and, a bit later on, an example with a `serial_pty` field. In both cases the expected command line invocation is:

```bash
./scripts/twister --device-testing --hardware-map map.yml -T samples/hello_world/
```

Or in other words:

```bash
./scripts/twister --device-testing --hardware-map map_with_serial.yml -T samples/hello_world/

./scripts/twister --device-testing --hardware-map map_with_serial_pty.yml -T samples/hello_world/
```

different hardware maps, same command line flags.

My current implementation extends this pattern of use.

```bash
./scripts/twister --device-testing --hardware-map map_with_rtt.yml -T samples/hello_world/
```

But what are you proposing would then look like this (I am ignoring fixtures here for simplicity):


```bash

# Communicate with devices over UART or serial PTY, hw map decides
./scripts/twister --device-testing --hardware-map map.yml -T samples/hello_world/

# Communicate with all devices over RTT, command line arg decides
./scripts/twister --device-testing --device_rtt --hardware-map map.yml -T samples/hello_world/
```

This feels like it goes against what documentation showcases. 

Naturally, I can implement this like that, but I want to make sure that we want that :)


---

> I found also one problem, when you add new test, that should run only with RTT, it must be somehow filtered out, when all testsuite is run (on the CI, where rtt is not used)

I agree, this is something that needs to be implemented.

My proposal on this would be:

* If test configuration is only testable via RTT, then `use_rtt` field must be set. Alternative, more verbose, name could be `depends_on_rtt`, I am open to suggestions.

```yaml
  sample.pytest.rtt:
    harness: pytest
    use_rtt: True
```

* Twister must be provided `--device-rtt` flag, otherwise above test configuration is filtered out or
* the device has `use_rtt` field in the hw map, otherwise above test configuration is filtered out (this line is subject to what we decide above).

Do you think that something like this would be sufficient?
author: MarkoSagadin

body:
> In regards to keeping or removing the use_rtt field from the hardware map

The documentation examples are simple: a hardware map containing devices with `serial` or `serial_pty` fields can include multiple entries, and Twister will run tests on all of them in parallel without any additional command-line flags.
If `use_rtt` is embedded in the hardware map, then you would need a separate hardware map file for every device.

When RTT is forced via `--device-rtt` from the command line, Twister will limit concurrency to one job (due to the port conflict problem). No additional restriction needs to be encoded in the hardware map itself. The same map with multiple entries can still be used on CI - the `--device-rtt` flag controls the transport, while the map handles device discovery.

This is the key difference from `serial`/`serial_pty`: those transports are parallel-safe and need no extra command-line flag, so the transport configuration naturally belongs in the map.
Keeping `use_rtt` out of the map avoids duplicating that limitation in two places and lets teams reuse a single hardware map across transport modes.

> If test configuration is only testable via RTT, then use_rtt field must be set
>  sample.pytest.rtt:
>    use_rtt: True

Sounds good

He have been running such tests for quite some time now (since last September) and there was always some flakiness present. For the most part the stuff worked, but from time to time, a HIL test would fail, due to failing `shell.exec_command()`. Specifically it wouldn't detect that the sent shell command was echoed back by device. Hi @nashif, please have another look when you find time.

I have removed the `use_rtt` field from the `testcase.yaml` and replaced it with a runtime filter modification logic in `scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/testplan.py`. If ``--device-rtt`` option is now given, Twister only runs those test cases that set ``CONFIG_SHELL_PROMPT_RTT`` or ``CONFIG_RTT_CONSOLE`` symbols, others are filtered at runtime. This means that Twister prevents running RTT-configured tests on devices that expect serial connection and prevent running Uart-configured tests on devices that expect RTT connection

I have thought how could this be done some other way, but the only other solution that I could come up with would be injecting RRT symbols into build, based on whether the ``--device-rtt` option is given, similar to the proposal in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/81837.
